# The software development life cycle – every phase

This document describes the software development life cycle (SDLC) as a discipline. For each phase it tells the purpose, the inputs, the activities, the outputs, the roles, the practices with consensus, the contested points, the metrics, the failure modes, the tailoring to the size of the project, and the sources. The text is a neutral description of the discipline and not yet a set of instructions for an engineer or an agent. It is the first research deliverable for a future Claude Code skill named "software-engineering", which must let an engineer or an AI agent work well on any repository. Later research rounds will go deeper on each phase.

Date of this version: 2026-08-21.

Parallel research agents produced the document. Each agent studied one topic and read at least eight authoritative sources, and each section lists its own sources. A critic checked the coverage against ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017, ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 and SWEBOK v4. An assembler joined the parts and collected all sources in section 17.

How to read the document: section 1 defines the terms and maps the stages, the processes and the knowledge areas. Section 2 describes the life cycle models. Sections 3 to 14 describe the phases from concept to retirement, and each of them has the same 13 subsections: purpose, other names, position in the life cycle, inputs, activities, outputs, roles, practices with consensus, contested points, metrics, failure modes, tailoring by project size, and sources. Section 15 covers the supporting and management processes that run across all phases. Section 16 covers security, privacy and compliance across the life cycle. Section 17 lists all sources.

## 1. What a life cycle is

### Definitions

The definitions follow ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, which share one vocabulary; SWEBOK v4 uses the same terms.

- Life cycle: the evolution of a system, product, service or project from conception to retirement. A life cycle model is a framework of processes and activities for that life cycle; it can group the work into stages, and it serves as a common reference for the people who take part.
- Stage: a period in the life cycle of an entity that relates to the state of its description or realization. 15288 names six stages; stages can overlap and can repeat.
- Phase: a time box in a project with a start, an end and a milestone at the end; RUP uses the word for its four time boxes. This document also uses "phase" for one kind of work, for example "the requirements phase".
- Process: a set of related activities that transforms inputs into outputs. In 12207 and 15288 each process has a purpose, outcomes, and the activities and tasks that achieve the outcomes.
- Activity: a set of cohesive tasks of a process.
- Task: a required, recommended or permissible action that contributes to one or more outcomes of a process.
- Artifact or work product: a result of a process that people or tools use, for example a specification, a model, source code, a test report or a release package. 12207 calls a separately identifiable body of information for human use an "information item" and lists examples in Annex B.
- Baseline: a formally approved version of a configuration item, fixed at a specific time and changed only through change control. A tagged release on a protected branch is the everyday form.

### Life cycle stages

ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 covers the whole life of a system and names six stages. SWEBOK v4 uses the same six and adds: "The stages are not supposed to be sequential, by any means." A stage can start before the previous stage ends, and a stage can repeat.

- Concept: identify the needs of the stakeholders, explore ideas and propose feasible solutions; the output is a concept and a decision to continue or to stop (see section 3).
- Development: refine the requirements, describe the solution, build the system, and verify and validate it (see sections 4 to 10).
- Production: produce, inspect and test the system. For software this is the build of the release packages and the supply of copies or of a hosted service; in embedded products it is a real manufacturing stage (see sections 10 and 11).
- Utilization: operate the system to satisfy the needs of the users (see section 12).
- Support: keep the system able to deliver its service through maintenance, logistics and user support (see section 13).
- Retirement: store, archive or dispose of the system (see section 14).

### Life cycle processes

ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 describes 30 processes in four groups. It does not prescribe a life cycle model: the user selects a model and maps the processes, activities and tasks into it (clause 1.4). The processes "can be applied concurrently, iteratively and recursively", and incrementally (clause 1.3). The standard shares its process structure with 15288:2023, so a system and its software can use one set of processes. This document uses the 2017 edition; the IEEE SEVOCAB database cites a 2026 edition, which the research could not read. Each line gives the purpose of one process in short form.

Agreement processes:

- Acquisition: obtain a product or service that satisfies the requirements of the acquirer.
- Supply: provide the acquirer with a product or service that satisfies the agreement.

Organizational project-enabling processes:

- Life cycle model management: define, maintain and make available the policies, life cycle processes, models and procedures that projects use.
- Infrastructure management: provide the infrastructure and services that projects need.
- Portfolio management: start and sustain the projects that the strategy needs, and stop the others.
- Human resource management: provide the people and the competencies that the business needs.
- Quality management: make sure that products, services and the quality process satisfy the quality objectives of the organization and the project.
- Knowledge management: create the capability and the assets that let the organization apply its existing knowledge again.

Technical management processes:

- Project planning: produce and coordinate plans that are effective and workable.
- Project assessment and control: check that the plans are aligned and feasible, measure the status of the project, and direct the work so that it follows the plans.
- Decision management: give a structured frame to identify, evaluate and select between alternatives for a decision.
- Risk management: identify, analyze, treat and monitor risks continually.
- Configuration management: manage and control the system elements and configurations across the life cycle, and keep the product consistent with its configuration definition.
- Information management: generate, obtain, confirm, transform, retain, retrieve, disseminate and dispose of information for the stakeholders.
- Measurement: collect, analyze and report objective data to support management and to show the quality of products, services and processes.
- Quality assurance: make sure that the project applies the quality management process of the organization effectively.

Technical processes:

- Business or mission analysis: define the business or mission problem or opportunity, characterize the solution space, and find the classes of possible solutions.
- Stakeholder needs and requirements definition: define the stakeholder requirements for a system that gives the users and other stakeholders the capabilities they need.
- System/Software requirements definition: transform the stakeholder view of the desired capabilities into a technical view of a solution.
- Architecture definition: generate architecture alternatives, select one or more that frame the stakeholder concerns and satisfy the requirements, and express them in consistent views.
- Design definition: give sufficient detailed data about the system and its elements for an implementation that is consistent with the architecture.
- System analysis: give a rigorous base of data and information to aid decisions across the life cycle.
- Implementation: realize a specified system element.
- Integration: combine a set of system elements into a realized system that satisfies the requirements, the architecture and the design.
- Verification: give objective evidence that a system or system element fulfils its specified requirements and characteristics.
- Transition: establish the capability of the system to provide the specified services in the operational environment.
- Validation: give objective evidence that the system, when in use, fulfils its business or mission objectives and the stakeholder requirements.
- Operation: use the system to deliver its services.
- Maintenance: sustain the capability of the system to provide a service.
- Disposal: end the existence of a system or system element for its intended use, and handle the replaced or retired elements correctly.

### Knowledge areas

SWEBOK v4 (IEEE Computer Society, 2024) divides the discipline into 18 knowledge areas (KAs). A knowledge area is a body of knowledge that the phases draw on, not a phase. Software Architecture, Software Engineering Operations and Software Security are new in v4. Appendix B of SWEBOK relates the supporting IEEE and ISO/IEC standards to the 12207 process model.

1. Software Requirements: elicitation, analysis, specification, validation and management of requirements.
2. Software Architecture: the significant decisions and structures of a system, architecture views and styles, and evaluation.
3. Software Design: the detailed design of components, interfaces, data and user interfaces, with notations, strategies and evaluation.
4. Software Construction: the creation of working software through coding, unit testing, integration and debugging.
5. Software Testing: the dynamic verification that a program behaves as expected on a finite set of test cases, from unit to acceptance level.
6. Software Engineering Operations: deployment, operation, monitoring and support of software in its operational environment, including DevOps.
7. Software Maintenance: the modification of software after delivery, with its categories, process and techniques.
8. Software Configuration Management: identification, change control, status accounting, audits, build and release.
9. Software Engineering Management: scope, planning, enactment, review, closure, measurement, risk, and the management of acquisition and suppliers.
10. Software Engineering Process: process definition, life cycle models and adaptation, process assessment and improvement, process measurement.
11. Software Engineering Models and Methods: modeling, types and analysis of models, and heuristic, formal, prototyping and agile methods.
12. Software Quality: quality fundamentals, quality management, quality assurance, reviews and audits, quality measurement.
13. Software Security: security across requirements, design, construction, testing and operations.
14. Software Engineering Professional Practice: professionalism, ethics, law, group dynamics and communication.
15. Software Engineering Economics: cost, value, risk and the economic analysis of decisions.
16. Computing Foundations: the computer science that software engineering uses, for example algorithms, data structures, operating systems and networks.
17. Mathematical Foundations: sets, logic, proof, graphs, probability and finite state machines.
18. Engineering Foundations: empirical methods, statistics, measurement, engineering design, modeling and simulation, root cause analysis.

The last three knowledge areas are background knowledge, not phases. SWEBOK presents them as the relevant elements of computer science, mathematics and engineering that support the other knowledge areas. Degree curricula teach them before practice (SE2014; CS2023). This document does not teach them, in the same way that SWEBOK names its related disciplines but does not characterize them. The map table below therefore gives the foundations knowledge areas no row of their own. The phases touch them where the work needs them:

- computing foundations in design, construction and operations: distributed styles, data modeling, concurrency, algorithms, debugging, operating systems and networks (sections 6 to 8 and 12)
- mathematical foundations in specifications, tests and risk models: state models, contracts, property-based tests, flow graphs, probability (sections 5, 7 and 9)
- engineering foundations in estimation, experiments, incident analysis and measurement (sections 4, 11, 12 and 15; section 15 gives them a short subsection)

### Process versus phase

A process is a set of activities with a purpose and outcomes. A phase or stage is a period of time with a start and an end. Because the 12207 processes "can be applied concurrently, iteratively and recursively", each process can run in any stage, and most run in many. The team verifies in development, in production and in maintenance, and it manages risks from concept to retirement. RUP makes this explicit with two dimensions: four phases as time boxes with milestones, and disciplines that run in every phase with a different emphasis. Sommerville shows the same four fundamental activities – specification, development, validation and evolution – organized in a different way in each model.

Agile models do not remove the processes. Fowler describes the difference: a waterfall does one activity at a time for all the features, and an iterative process does all the activities for one feature at a time. Scrum still plans, builds, reviews and delivers a done Increment every Sprint; DSDM and the GOV.UK Service Manual keep named phases around iterative work. SWEBOK v4 lists "faster because you need not produce any document" among the misconceptions about agile.

12207 has an annex on agile development (Annex H), and IEEE 2675-2021 aligns DevOps with 12207 and 15288. This document calls sections 3 to 14 phases for convenience; each describes one kind of work and the processes that do most of it. The processes that run across all phases are in section 15, and security, privacy and compliance are in section 16.

### Tailoring

Tailoring is the adaptation of the processes of a standard to a project, and both 12207 and 15288 require it. The normative Annex A of 12207 gives the steps: identify and record the circumstances that drive the tailoring, take the risks into account, get the agreement of the stakeholders, then add, delete or modify processes, activities and tasks. The standard allows full conformance, where all processes are performed as described, and tailored conformance, where the tailoring record shows which processes apply and why. Conformance is about outcomes, not about the volume of documents.

SWEBOK v4 says that no ideal process exists and that processes "must be selected, adapted, and applied as appropriate for each project". The adaptation does not need to keep the names of the standard or to include all of them. The team documents the decisions and the rationale. ISO/IEC 29110 gives profiles for very small entities.

In practice tailoring means four things. The team names the model it uses, even in one paragraph of the README. It scales the depth of each process to risk: a two-person internal tool needs no formal document set, and a safety-related product cannot drop verification and configuration management. Boehm and Turner advise the team to treat every factor outside the home ground of its method as a risk, and to add practices from the other side for that risk. It writes down what it left out and why. And it reviews the tailoring at set intervals, because life cycle model management is a continuous process in 12207. The tailoring subsection of each later section gives the detail for three sizes: a solo developer on a small repository, a small product team, and a large or regulated organization.

## 2. Life cycle models

A life cycle model answers two questions, in the words of Boehm: what do we do next, and how long do we continue to do it? It fixes the order of the stages, the transition criteria between them and the feedback loops. SWEBOK v4 groups the models into predictive, iterative, incremental, evolutionary and continuous life cycles. In 2001 seventeen authors of iterative methods signed the Manifesto for Agile Software Development. Its four values prefer individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and response to change, "while there is value in the items on the right". Its twelve principles ask for delivery "from a couple of weeks to a couple of months", for daily work of business people and developers together, and for regular reflection. The Agile Alliance calls agile an umbrella term and says that a framework should not be the whole methodology of a team.

Most organizations combine models. The HELENA study (Tell et al., 2021; 1,467 data points) found that hybrids are the norm, independent of company size and sector. The respondents used Scrum (674 mentions), iterative development (620) and Kanban (523) most, and 380 of 845 reported "Water-Scrum-Fall". For each model this section tells what it is, where it comes from, when it fits and which known problems it has.

### Code-and-fix

Boehm describes the oldest model as two steps: write some code, then fix the problems in the code. There is no requirements or design step before the first code. It comes from the earliest days of software, when one person wrote and operated a program. It still fits throwaway scripts, spikes and very small tools that the author operates; Royce noted that a sufficiently small effort needs only analysis and coding. Boehm lists three problems. After a number of fixes, the code structure becomes so poor that the next fix is very expensive. The software matches the needs of the users poorly. The code is expensive to test and to modify. The model hides under other names: evolutionary development without architecture work, or "agile" without any requirements or design work, is code-and-fix.

### Waterfall

Waterfall is a sequence of activity phases – system requirements, software requirements, analysis, program design, coding, testing, operations – where each phase ends with an approved document. Boehm describes it as a refinement of the stagewise model, with feedback loops between adjacent stages and prototyping in parallel. The figure comes from Royce (1970), and the word "waterfall" is absent from his paper. Royce called the concept "fundamentally sound" but wrote that its plain implementation "is risky and invites failure". Testing is the first point where timing, storage and usability are "experienced as distinguished from analyzed", and he expected "up to a 100-percent overrun in schedule and/or costs".

He proposed five steps: program design first; document the design; "do it twice", so that the delivered version is the second version in the critical areas; plan, control and monitor the tests; involve the customer formally. Wheeler, Larman and Basili, and Fowler agree that the paper is misread; Fowler adds that Royce kept activity phases, so the paper is not agile either. DoD-STD-2167 (1985) fixed the simple figure as a U.S. defense standard, and Mil-Std-498 (1994) opened it to iterative work.

The model fits when the requirements are well understood and change will be limited, which Sommerville sees mostly in large multi-site systems engineering projects; Boehm names compilers and secure operating systems, but not interactive end-user applications. Fowler has "not come across such a circumstance", and Brooks, cited by Larman and Basili, wrote "The waterfall model is wrong!". The known problems are the late discovery of timing, storage and usability problems, the cost of a late change, and documents that look complete but hide the high-risk parts.

### V-model

The V-model arranges the waterfall activities in a V: the left leg goes down from user requirements through system requirements, architecture and detailed design, and the right leg goes up through unit, integration, system and acceptance test. Each definition level is paired with the verification level that checks it, and the test plan for a level is written when that level is defined. Forsberg and Mooz described it in 1991 for systems engineering; regulated industries – automotive, medical, rail, defense – and public administrations adopted variants. It fits products where a regulator or an acquirer expects verification evidence per level of definition. Its problems are those of the waterfall: one pass, and an expensive change during test. Regulated teams therefore often keep the V as the shape of the evidence – traceability from each requirement to its tests – while they work in iterations.

### Incremental

The team divides the product into increments, and each increment adds a usable part of the functionality. Sommerville describes incremental development as a process that interleaves specification, development and validation, with early increments delivered for feedback. Larman and Basili trace the idea to Mills at IBM in the 1970s and to Gilb's evolutionary delivery in small steps. SWEBOK v4 notes that an incremental life cycle can still be predictive when the requirements are closed before development. The model fits products where early value and feedback matter and where the architecture can carry later increments. Sommerville lists two problems: the process is less visible to managers, because there are fewer documents, and the structure of the system degrades as increments are added, unless the team refactors.

### Iterative and evolutionary (prototyping)

An iterative model repeats the development activities in cycles, and each cycle uses feedback from the previous one. Boehm's evolutionary development model goes further: the stages are expanding increments of an operational product, and operational experience sets the direction. Prototyping is the tool of this family: Royce's "do it twice" is a pilot version, and Sommerville separates throwaway prototypes, which explore requirements, from evolutionary prototypes, which grow into the product. Larman and Basili trace iterative and incremental development back to the 1950s and Project Mercury.

DSDM, created in 1994 by a consortium of rapid application development practitioners, is a full project framework in this family. It keeps named phases – pre-project, feasibility, foundations, evolutionary development, deployment, post-project – and works inside them in timeboxes of two to four weeks. It fixes time, cost and quality at the end of Foundations and varies the features with MoSCoW priorities. Its eight principles include "build incrementally from firm foundations" and "develop iteratively". Business roles such as the Business Ambassador keep the customer inside the team. The GOV.UK Service Manual uses discovery (four to eight weeks, with a decision to go to alpha or to stop), alpha, beta, live and retirement, with a service assessment before a service moves phase.

Evolutionary models fit when the risk of a wrong user interface or of unclear requirements is high and the users can give feedback often. Boehm names three problems: without architecture work the model is hard to distinguish from code-and-fix; early decisions harden into "information sclerosis"; and parts that evolved independently fail to integrate or to bridge to legacy systems.

### Spiral

Boehm's spiral model (1988) is risk-driven. The radial dimension shows the cumulative cost and the angular dimension the progress in each cycle. Each cycle has four parts. Determine the objectives, alternatives and constraints. Evaluate the alternatives, then identify and resolve the risks. Develop and verify the product of the next level. Plan the next phases. Each cycle ends with a review and a commitment of all the people concerned. The question in each cycle is "How much is enough?" of every activity. The answer depends on the risks: "Great amounts of detail are not necessary unless the absence of such detail jeopardizes the project." The model came out of TRW's software productivity system. It contains the other models as special cases: a low user-interface risk with a high schedule risk gives a waterfall, and a high user-interface risk gives evolutionary development. After installation a new maintenance spiral starts, so development and enhancement use one approach.

The spiral fits large, internal, novel projects where an experienced team can judge risks. Boehm names three difficulties. The model is hard to match to contract software, because it "lacks clear criteria for budgeting and scheduling". It relies on risk-assessment expertise: an inexperienced team elaborates the well-understood parts and glosses over the risky parts, which gives "an illusion of progress". And its steps need further elaboration. His risk management plan keeps a top-ten risk list and reviews it monthly.

### RUP and the Unified Process

The Rational Unified Process (RUP), described by Kruchten, is the best known instance of the Unified Process. It came from Rational Software in the late 1990s, with Jacobson, Booch and Rumbaugh, in step with the UML. It has two dimensions. In time, four phases each end with a milestone: inception with Lifecycle Objectives, elaboration with Lifecycle Architecture, construction with Initial Operational Capability, and transition with Product Release; each phase holds one or more iterations. Across all phases run the disciplines – business modeling, requirements, analysis and design, implementation, test, deployment, plus configuration and change management, project management and environment – with an emphasis that changes per phase. RUP is use-case driven, architecture-centric, and iterative and incremental; a project records its tailoring in a development case. It fits larger projects with a novel architecture, where an elaboration phase that settles the architecture and the top risks pays off. The known problems are weight and the temptation to produce every artifact in the catalog; Fowler notes that RUP can be used in an agile or in a heavy way.

### Extreme Programming

Beck created Extreme Programming (XP), with Jeffries and Cunningham, on the Chrysler C3 project from 1996. Jeffries describes it as values and practices for a whole team. The values are communication, simplicity, feedback, courage and respect. The practices are the whole team with an on-site customer, the planning game, small releases, customer tests, simple design, pair programming, test-driven development, refactoring, continuous integration, collective code ownership, a coding standard, a system metaphor and a sustainable pace. Iterations are one to two weeks. Two agile methods of the same period are Crystal and Feature-Driven Development (FDD). Crystal is Cockburn's family of methods for small teams; its seven properties include frequent delivery, reflective improvement and a technical environment with automated tests, configuration management and frequent integration. FDD, from Coad and De Luca, has five processes, chief programmers and class ownership.

XP fits small, co-located teams with a customer who can sit with the team and decide. The known problems are the dependence on that customer, the discipline that the practices require, and misuse: Boehm and Turner cite a team that "claimed to follow XP, but on further investigation had simply stopped documenting".

### Scrum

Scrum is a lightweight framework for complex products, presented by Schwaber and Sutherland in 1995 and named after a 1986 article by Takeuchi and Nonaka. The Scrum Guide (2020) defines it. A Scrum Team has ten or fewer people and three accountabilities. The Product Owner orders the work and owns the Product Goal. The Scrum Master makes sure that everybody understands Scrum and that the team works effectively. The Developers create the Increment. All work happens in Sprints of one month or less, and every Sprint must produce a usable Increment. The events are the Sprint, Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. The artifacts are the Product Backlog with the Product Goal, the Sprint Backlog with the Sprint Goal, and the Increment with the Definition of Done. Scrum rests on transparency, inspection and adaptation and on the values commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. The guide says that Scrum "exists only in its entirety".

Scrum fits product work with a stable small team and a Product Owner with authority, and it was the most used method in HELENA. The known problems are partial adoption and "Water-Scrum-Fall". Partial adoption shows as a Product Owner without authority, no usable Increment, or a Sprint Review without stakeholders. In "Water-Scrum-Fall" a Scrum team sits between a waterfall requirements phase and a release process that cannot release. Velocity is a planning aid, not a measure of performance.

### Kanban

Kanban is a strategy that optimizes the flow of value through a process with a visual, pull-based system. The Kanban Guide defines three practices: define and visualize a workflow, actively manage the items in it, and improve it. It requires a Definition of Workflow, a limit on work in progress (WIP), a Service Level Expectation and four flow measures: WIP, throughput, work item age and cycle time. Kanban University describes the Kanban Method of David J. Anderson. The method adds six general practices: visualize, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally. It also adds change management principles that begin with "start with what you do now". It comes from lean manufacturing. Kanban fits flow-based work with changing demand – support, maintenance, operations – and any team that wants to improve its current process in place. It needs no timeboxes and combines well with Scrum. There are three known problems. The method has no built-in cadence for planning and review. Its measures are comparable only with a stable Definition of Workflow. And teams can set WIP limits that nobody respects.

### Lean software development

Lean software development is a set of principles, not a process. Mary and Tom Poppendieck (2003) translated the lean principles of the Toyota Production System into seven principles for software. The principles are: eliminate waste, amplify learning, decide as late as possible, deliver as fast as possible, empower the team, build integrity in, and see the whole. They add 22 thinking tools and seven wastes, such as partially done work, extra features, task switching, waiting and defects. Fowler lists lean among the agile methods. Lean fits as a lens over any model: it explains why small batches, short queues and fast feedback work, and it underlies Kanban, the continuous delivery principles and the DORA research. The known problem is misuse: a manager who cuts documentation, tests or time to learn as "waste" removes what the principles protect.

### DevOps and continuous delivery

Continuous delivery, in Fowler's definition, means that the software "can be released to production at any time". Fowler gives four tests:

- The software is deployable throughout its life cycle.
- The team prioritizes keeping it deployable over new features.
- Anyone gets fast, automated feedback on production readiness after any change.
- The team can deploy any version to any environment at the push of a button.

Continuous deployment releases every good change. The principles site of Humble and Farley lists five principles: build quality in; work in small batches; computers perform repetitive tasks and people solve problems; pursue continuous improvement relentlessly; everyone is responsible. They rest on three foundations: configuration management, continuous integration and continuous testing.

DevOps, as Microsoft describes it, joins development and operations in one loop of plan, develop, deliver and operate, and the phases are not specific to a role. IEEE 2675-2021 aligns DevOps with 12207 and 15288. DORA measures the result per application with deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time and deployment rework rate; top performers do well on all five, so speed and stability are not a trade-off.

The model fits hosted services and any product that the team can deploy itself; the phases still exist, but each change passes through all of them in hours or days. The known problems are the technical environment it presupposes – without automated tests, integration and repeatable deployment the loop breaks – and the misuse of the measures to rank teams, which DORA advises against.

### Shape Up

Shape Up is the product development method of Basecamp, written by Ryan Singer and published in 2019, in three parts: shaping, betting and building. Before a cycle, senior people shape the work: they set the appetite – the time the company wants to spend – rough out the solution, remove rabbit holes and write a pitch. A betting table decides which pitches get a six-week cycle; there is no backlog, and a pitch that loses can come back later. A small team – one designer and one or two programmers – builds the work and reports progress on a hill chart, which separates the uphill part with unknowns from the downhill part. A two-week cool-down follows each cycle, and the circuit breaker rule ends a project when the cycle ends. The rule is "fixed time, variable scope". Shape Up fits a product company with senior engineers and designers who can shape and who can be trusted with whole problems. The known problems are the dependence on experienced shapers, the absence of a backlog for support work, and the poor fit with regulated or contract work that needs a fixed scope.

### Scaled frameworks

Scaled frameworks coordinate several teams on one product. Nexus (Scrum.org, 2021) joins three to nine Scrum Teams on one Product Backlog; a Nexus Integration Team is accountable for the integration, each Sprint produces one Integrated Increment, and a partial implementation "is not Nexus". Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS) keeps one Product Owner, one Product Backlog and one Sprint for up to eight feature teams; LeSS Huge adds requirement areas and area product owners. LeSS calls itself "deliberately simple", says that "Large-Scale Scrum is Scrum", and puts emphasis on descaling. The Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) is an enterprise operating model with four levels: team, Agile Release Train (ART), large solution and portfolio. Its roles include the Release Train Engineer, Product Management, the System Architect and Business Owners. An ART plans in Planning Intervals with PI Planning, an Innovation and Planning iteration and an Inspect and Adapt event. Essential SAFe is the smallest configuration.

These frameworks fit when many teams share one product and one release. The known problems are overhead and the temptation to add people and layers instead of reducing dependencies; Nexus and LeSS both state that fewer people can deliver more value. Boehm and Turner note that plan-driven methods "scale better to large projects", and SWEBOK v4 says that "scaling up Agile for large projects and portfolios is still challenging".

### Common misconceptions

- "Royce proposed the waterfall." He drew the figure, called its plain implementation risky, and added iteration, a pilot version and customer involvement. The paper is neither a single pass nor agile.
- "The standards prescribe a life cycle model." 12207 and 15288 describe processes and outcomes and leave the model to the user.
- "Agile means no documents and no plans." SWEBOK v4 lists this as a misconception. Agile changes when and how much the team writes; the Scrum artifacts, the DSDM phases and the GOV.UK assessments all produce records.
- "Iteration makes a process agile." Fowler: iteration without adaptive planning is not agile. SWEBOK: an incremental life cycle can still be predictive.
- "High maturity guarantees success." Boehm and Turner list this among the misconceptions. A maturity level measures the presence of a process, not the outcome of a product.
- "A framework can be used in parts and still be that framework." The Scrum Guide and the Nexus Guide say that the result is not Scrum and not Nexus. Kanban, by contrast, asks the team to start with what it does now.
- "DevOps removes the phases." Each change still passes through plan, build, test, release and operate; the phases are short, not absent.
- "Delivery metrics rank teams." DORA and the Kanban Guide ask for measurement per application or per workflow, for improvement, not for a comparison of teams or people.
- "Agile needs no architecture." Boehm warns that evolutionary development without architecture decays into code-and-fix; RUP, DSDM and SAFe keep an early architecture step.
- "The model is chosen once." 12207 makes life cycle model management a continuous process, and DSDM lets a project return to Foundations after deployment.

### How the phases appear in each model

The table shows where each phase of this document appears in the three main families. "Waterfall / V-model" covers the single-pass models. "Iterative / agile" covers incremental, iterative, spiral, RUP, XP, Scrum, Kanban, DSDM and Shape Up. "DevOps / continuous delivery" covers the continuous models.

| Phase | Waterfall / V-model | Iterative / agile | DevOps / continuous delivery |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3. Concept and inception | A feasibility study and a system requirements document before the project starts; a contract or charter gates the start | A vision and a first backlog; RUP inception, GOV.UK discovery, DSDM pre-project and feasibility; Shape Up shaping before each cycle | A business idea enters the plan phase of the loop; hypotheses and experiments replace a one-time study |
| 4. Planning and estimation | One plan for the whole project with a fixed scope, a schedule and a budget; milestones per phase | Release planning plus planning per iteration; estimates are repeated each cycle; fixed time and variable scope in DSDM and Shape Up | Continuous planning; capacity and flow measures (DORA, Kanban) replace detailed long-range plans |
| 5. Requirements engineering | One requirements phase with a baselined specification; changes go through change control | Product backlog refined every iteration; user stories, acceptance criteria, prototypes; DSDM foundations give the high-level requirements | Requirements arrive as small items; feature flags and experiments validate them in production |
| 6. Architecture | An architecture phase before design, with a review | RUP elaboration and DSDM foundations settle the architecture early; agile teams evolve it and guard it with refactoring; SAFe keeps an architectural runway | Architecture aims at independent deployability; the pipeline and the platform are part of it |
| 7. Detailed design | A detailed design phase with a design document per component, paired with unit tests on the V | Design per feature inside the iteration; simple design and design spikes | Design per change, reviewed in the pull request; design for observability and rollback |
| 8. Implementation | A coding phase after the design is approved | Construction inside each iteration, with pairing, test-driven development and collective ownership | Small changes integrated several times a day on the trunk |
| 9. Testing, verification and validation | A test phase after coding, with test levels paired to definition levels on the V | Tests written with the code; customer tests and the Sprint Review validate each increment | Continuous testing in the pipeline; validation with monitoring and experiments in production |
| 10. Integration, build and continuous integration | One integration phase late in the project | Continuous integration inside the iteration; one Integrated Increment per Sprint in Nexus | Every commit builds and tests; the build is the heartbeat of the loop |
| 11. Release and deployment | One release at the end, with a formal acceptance | A releasable increment per iteration; the release decision is separate from the Sprint | Push-button deployment of any version; continuous deployment releases every good change |
| 12. Operations, observability and incident management | Operations start after hand-over to a separate operations group | Operations are often a separate group, with the team on call for its increments; the GOV.UK live phase | The operate phase is part of the same loop and the same team; observability drives the next change |
| 13. Maintenance and evolution | A separate maintenance project or a new waterfall per major release | Further iterations on the same backlog; DSDM can return to Foundations | The same pipeline serves every change; maintenance is not a separate phase |
| 14. Retirement and disposal | Planned at the end, often without a model | GOV.UK names retirement as a phase; a final iteration removes the product | Decommission through the same pipeline; data and traffic migration are changes like any other |

### How to choose and tailor a model

Boehm's rule is the base: let the risks drive the choice. A low risk of a wrong user interface and a high risk of a schedule slip push towards a waterfall; a high user-interface risk pushes towards evolutionary development. Boehm and Turner give five factors to rate a project: size, criticality, dynamism (the rate of change of the requirements), personnel (the skill mix) and culture. A profile on their polar chart shows where the project sits. The home ground of agile methods has small teams, low criticality, high dynamism, skilled people and a culture that thrives on freedom. The opposite profile is the home ground of plan-driven methods. Their risk-based method has five steps. Rate the environmental, agile and plan-driven risks. If one side dominates, use that side. If not, architect the system so that the agile parts stay encapsulated. Set an overall strategy, then monitor and adjust. Every factor outside the home ground is a risk, and the team adds practices from the other side for it.

Four more inputs decide the choice. The contract: a fixed-scope contract favors a plan-driven frame or a DSDM-style fixed-time agreement. Boehm notes that risk-driven models lack clear budgeting criteria for contract work. The regulatory frame: IEC 62304 for medical device software, acquisition standards and the GOV.UK Service Standard each expect certain evidence. NIST SP 800-218 states that teams can integrate its secure development practices into each SDLC implementation. The technical environment: short cycles need version control, automated tests, continuous integration and repeatable deployment, so a team without them builds them first. The stakeholders: Fowler warns that agile needs a customer who wants to collaborate. He writes that "imposing agile methods on reluctant people is fundamentally at odds with the whole notion of agile development".

Some choices stay contested. Timeboxed iterations (Scrum, XP) or continuous flow (Kanban, continuous delivery): most teams combine them, and the release constraints and the stability of demand decide. How much design up front: RUP and DSDM front-load the architecture, and XP and Scrum let it emerge. Boehm and Turner note that "you aren't gonna need it" helps with unforeseeable change but is risky when change is foreseeable. Fixed scope or fixed time: plan-driven contracts fix the scope; DSDM and Shape Up fix the time and vary the scope. Scaled structure or overhead: SAFe adds roles and trains, LeSS and Nexus add as little as possible. How to measure success: DORA's five measures, Kanban's flow measures, the Increment per Sprint, or a maturity level, each with its own caveats.

The choice is rarely pure. HELENA shows that hybrids are the norm, and Boehm and Turner advise a deliberate blend. A good hybrid has a name and a list of its practices; an accidental mix, such as a Scrum team that cannot release, is a failure mode. The output of the choice is a documented model. It states the cadence, the milestones and gates with their criteria, and the roles that decide. It maps the 12207 processes onto the model and records the tailoring with its rationale. It adds a documentation plan scaled to risk, a risk list with early resolution steps, the technical environment, a measurement plan and a review date.

The tailoring per size follows the pattern of the whole document. A solo developer on a small repository uses a light continuous-delivery loop. The loop has a short list of intended changes, work on the trunk, automated tests, and a release when the build is green. A throwaway spike comes before anything novel, and a README states how changes flow and what "done" means.

A small product team picks one frame – Scrum, Kanban, XP practices or Shape Up. It states the cadence, the roles that decide scope and the Definition of Done. It keeps a short elaboration period for novel work, measures the DORA five and the Kanban four per product, and holds a retrospective every cycle.

A large or regulated organization defines an organizational model and tailoring rules, and maps the processes to the required evidence. It keeps explicit transition criteria, configuration management, traceability and independent verification, and uses a scaled framework only when several teams share one product. Iteration is still possible in regulated work; the team plans the V-shaped verification evidence inside the iterations. In every case the team reviews the model at set intervals. It measures the model with a few flow and delivery measures, to learn and not to rank.
