## 3. Concept and inception

### Purpose

This phase answers one question: should the organization do this at all, and what exactly is the problem? It turns an idea, a request or a mandate into four things. These are a stated problem, a set of stakeholders and needs, a vision with measurable outcomes, and a judgement on value, usability, feasibility and viability. It produces the evidence for an explicit go/no-go decision before the organization commits significant money and people. It also sets the boundaries: what is in scope, what is out, how large the appetite is, and how the team will measure success.

Standards (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288, SWEBOK v4 and PMBOK-based texts) and product literature (Cagan, Ries, Torres and GOV.UK) agree on the reason for the phase. The most expensive failures start here, when a team builds a good solution to the wrong problem. A decision to stop is a valid and useful result of this phase.

### Other names

- Concept stage, or concept definition (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288, SEBoK).
- Business or mission analysis process, and stakeholder needs and requirements definition process (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 clauses 6.4.1 and 6.4.2; ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017).
- Initiating process group; project initiation; develop project charter and identify stakeholders (PMBOK Guide).
- Initiation and scope definition; feasibility analysis (SWEBOK v4, Software Engineering Management knowledge area).
- Pre-Phase A concept studies, and Phase A concept and technology development (NASA Systems Engineering Handbook).
- Discovery, or the discovery phase (GOV.UK Service Manual, NN/g, US Digital Service Playbook).
- Product discovery; opportunity assessment; continuous discovery (Cagan, Torres).
- Inception phase; iteration zero or sprint zero (Unified Process, Disciplined Agile, agile inception deck).
- Starting up a project; outline business case; project brief (PRINCE2).
- Scoping and build-the-business-case stages with go/kill gates (Stage-Gate).
- Shaping, pitch and betting table (Shape Up).
- Working Backwards; PR/FAQ (Amazon).
- Feasibility study; TELOS analysis (technical, economic, legal, operational and scheduling feasibility).
- Strategic outline case; five case model (HM Treasury Green Book).
- Problem framing; opportunity framing; front end of innovation; fuzzy front end.
- README-first; readme driven development (open-source and solo projects).

### Position in the life cycle

Before this phase come strategy, portfolio or roadmap decisions, a business need, a customer request, a regulation, a research result, or a PRINCE2-style mandate. After it come requirements engineering (see section 5), architecture (see section 6), planning and estimation (see section 4), and the first build increment. Early planning overlaps with this phase.

In waterfall and V-model projects (see section 2) the phase is a discrete front end. It contains a feasibility study, a business case and a charter, and then the requirements follow (Sommerville, SWEBOK). Gate-based frameworks make the phase explicit. NASA Pre-Phase A and Phase A end in key decision points and the Mission Concept Review. Stage-Gate has scoping and business-case stages with go/kill gates. PRINCE2 starts with an outline business case. HM Treasury builds the business case in stages: the strategic outline case, the outline business case and the full business case.

In iterative and agile work the phase appears as an inception phase, an iteration zero, or a discovery phase before alpha. A GOV.UK discovery takes 4 to 8 weeks in a typical case. Shape Up runs a short shaping and betting cycle before each bet. Product teams also run the phase continuously, with weekly customer interviews, opportunity solution trees and assumption tests in parallel with delivery (Torres, Cagan).

In DevOps and continuous delivery the initial concept work still happens once. The team then tests hypotheses in production with experiments and metrics (see section 12). It reviews the business justification at each stage (PRINCE2 continued business justification, Stage-Gate gates, NASA key decision points). So the first concept phase is a one-time event per product or project, but discovery and justification recur for every new opportunity or stage. For open-source and solo projects the phase is the moment when the developer writes the README, the problem statement and the scope before the code.

### Inputs

- A trigger (PRINCE2 mandate; NASA program needs; Cagan opportunity), for example:
  - an idea, a business or mission need, or an opportunity
  - a customer request or a problem report
  - a policy intent or a regulation
  - a strategic objective, an OKR or a research result
  - a formal mandate from a program or portfolio
- Organizational strategy, mission and business model: who the customer is, what the customer values, and how the organization makes money or delivers public value (SWEBOK v4 economics knowledge area; Green Book strategic case).
- Knowledge of the current state: existing systems, services, data, processes and workarounds (GOV.UK discovery; NN/g; Patton opportunity canvas "solutions today").
- Known constraints: legislation, contracts, legacy technology, budget envelopes, deadlines, procurement rules, and security and privacy obligations (see section 16). The team classifies each one as a hard constraint or a soft constraint (GOV.UK).
- Market and competitive information and existing alternatives, which include existing open-source projects that already solve the problem (Cagan assessment question 4; Fogel "always look around").
- Existing evidence: analytics, support and call-centre data, previous research, and lessons from earlier attempts (GOV.UK Service Standard point 1; NN/g stakeholder interviews).
- Access to real users, customers and stakeholders for interviews, observation and prototype tests (USDS play 1; Torres).
- A sponsor or owner who can spend time and money on discovery, and a budget that explicitly covers research, discovery and prototypes (USDS play 5; PMBOK sponsor).
- Entry criteria: enough clarity to state a problem hypothesis and a target user; a named person who can make the go/no-go decision; a time box; and a small multidisciplinary group (NN/g: 3 to 7 people; the product trio).

### Activities

- **Frame the problem or opportunity statement** – Restate the request as a problem to solve from the user's perspective, not as a feature. An example is "how can we make it easier to find the nearest contact centre", not "build a map". Use a short workshop on who has the problem, what it is, why it matters and where it occurs, or a "5 whys" style interrogation of the real problem. The product is a problem statement of one or two sentences, with evidence of scale and importance, posted where the team sees it.
- **Analyze the business or mission context** – Define the problem or opportunity space in the context of strategy, mission and business model: who the customer is, what the customer values, and how the organization delivers value at an acceptable cost. Identify candidate solution classes, the case for change, the spending objectives and the existing arrangements. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 names this the business or mission analysis process, the first technical process; the Green Book calls it the strategic case. It produces a strategic case, preliminary life-cycle concepts, and a list of solution classes for the stakeholder needs work.
- **Identify and analyze stakeholders** – List everyone who affects or is affected by the effort: the sponsor, users, operators, support, test and training staff, neighbouring teams, suppliers, regulators and policy owners. Record them in a stakeholder register with interest, influence and concerns, often on a power/interest grid. Interview them to learn their objectives, constraints and past attempts. PMBOK makes this one of the two initiating processes; NASA and 15288 treat it as the foundation of stakeholder expectations. Identification continues through the life cycle; it does not end at initiation.
- **Research users and interview customers** – Spend time with current and prospective users early, in the field where possible, and study the whole journey rather than one screen. Use story-based interviews ("tell me about the last time you ...") that stay grounded in specific past behavior, because speculative questions trigger cognitive biases. Add diary studies, contextual inquiry and analytics. The outputs are interview snapshots, user needs statements, journey maps or service blueprints, and a list of opportunities (needs, pain points and desires).
- **Define needs, goals, objectives and the concept of operations** – Turn raw expectations into agreed needs ("what problem are we trying to solve"), goals and objectives with target levels, plus constraints on cost, time, support and performance. For systems with operators, write an operational concept or ConOps that describes how the system will be used over time, with off-nominal cases, and define measures of effectiveness. 15288 clause 6.4.2 and NASA's stakeholder expectations definition own this step; detailed requirements belong to requirements engineering (see section 5).
- **Write the vision, product goal and elevator pitch** – State on one page what the team will build, for whom, why they would choose it, and how it differs from the alternatives. Useful templates are Moore's "FOR ... WHO ... THE ... IS A ... THAT ... UNLIKE ... OUR PRODUCT ..." (used by Sommerville), the inception deck elevator pitch and product box, Scrum's product goal, and Amazon's future press release. The vision is the shared target against which the team judges later trade-offs; Cagan calls it the north star that keeps teams on one course.
- **Define outcomes and success metrics** – Decide how the team will know that the work succeeded, before the build. Prefer outcomes (changes in customer behavior or business health) over outputs ("ship the Android app"). Write them as measurable statements with a baseline and a target, for example as OKRs or as HEART goals, signals and metrics. GOV.UK requires teams to plan measurement in discovery and to track cost per transaction, user satisfaction, completion rate and digital take-up; NASA records measures of effectiveness; a charter lists measurable objectives. The output is a short list of metrics plus a plan to collect them.
- **Explore alternatives and the solution space** – Generate more than one solution before the choice: ideation in design thinking, sketches in a design sprint, solutions under each opportunity in an opportunity solution tree, and trade studies and analyzes of alternatives in systems work. Formal business cases require a long list that the team narrows to a short list. The short list always includes "do nothing" and "do minimum" (Green Book), or "do nothing, do minimum, do more" (PRINCE2). SWEBOK's decision-making process insists that the team cannot select the best solution if it was never a candidate.
- **Assess feasibility on several dimensions** – Judge whether the candidate can be done under the constraints: technical (can we build it with current technology and skills), economic (cost versus value), legal and regulatory, operational (does it fit the processes and integrate with existing systems), and schedule. Sommerville's three feasibility questions, the TELOS list, Cagan's four risks (value, usability, feasibility, viability) and IDEO's desirability, feasibility and viability lenses cover the same ground. SWEBOK's feasibility analysis also produces an initial scope statement, deliverables, duration constraints and a resource estimate. Feasibility is rarely binary; the honest answer is usually "possible, but at this cost and risk".
- **Prototype and test the riskiest assumptions** – Before full engineering, build the cheapest thing that produces evidence: a clickable prototype tested with five users in a five-day design sprint, a smoke test, a concierge MVP, or a feasibility prototype by one engineer. Ries defines the MVP as the version that allows maximum validated learning with the least effort; Kniberg suggests "earliest testable, usable, lovable product" to avoid confusion. Each test targets a named assumption about value, usability, feasibility or viability, and ends with a decision to pivot, persevere or stop.
- **Decide build, buy or reuse** – Check whether an existing product, service, open-source project or internal component already solves the problem, and decide what to build in-house. Fowler's rule: buy or adopt packages for utility functions and adapt processes to them; build only what differentiates. Software Engineering at Google adds the long-term cost of every dependency (upgrades, security, maintainers who leave) and a checklist (tests, compatibility promises, project health). USDS prefers open-source and commodity stacks to avoid lock-in; NASA runs make/buy as a formal decision analysis. The output is a sourcing decision with a rationale and an owner.
- **Estimate cost, benefit and value, and build the business case** – Produce rough-order-of-magnitude estimates of effort, cost and benefits. Then compare the options on the same basis (present worth, internal rate of return, payback, benefit-cost ratio, or cost-effectiveness for non-profit work) over the same planning horizon. Document the reasons, the options, the expected benefits and dis-benefits, the timescales, the costs, the investment appraisal and the major risks (PRINCE2 contents). Large public proposals use the five case model (strategic, economic, commercial, financial and management cases). SWEBOK defines the business case as consolidated information that explains a recommended decision from cost, benefit and risk perspectives for an investment decision. Shape Up replaces the estimate with an appetite: a fixed time budget that the team will spend.
- **Identify initial risks and assumptions** – List what could make the effort fail before planning starts: Cagan's four risks, the SEI taxonomy (product engineering, development environment, program constraints), a pre-mortem that imagines the failed project, "what keeps us up at night" in the inception deck, rabbit holes in a pitch, and the internal FAQ of a PR/FAQ. Record them as a first risk register or an assumption map with owners. The point is to surface the doubts that people otherwise keep quiet during planning.
- **Set scope boundaries and appetite** – Write down what is explicitly out: a NOT list, no-gos, excluded use cases and deferred features, plus hard constraints and assumptions. State how much the effort is worth in time and money (the appetite or a pre-approved budget), and which of time, scope, budget and quality may flex. This protects the team from scope creep and unproductive arguments later, and belongs in the charter, the poster or the pitch.
- **Make and record the go/no-go decision** – Present the evidence to the person or group who owns the money. Get a clear decision: go, no-go, hold, or recycle for more discovery. Record the decision, its criteria, its conditions and the date of the next review. The frameworks agree on an explicit decision point:
  - Cagan ends the opportunity assessment with a recommendation and asks senior management for a clear call.
  - Stage-Gate gatekeepers decide against deliverables and criteria.
  - NASA uses key decision points and the Mission Concept Review.
  - GOV.UK ends discovery with a decision to move to alpha or to stop.
  - The PRINCE2 board authorizes initiation.
  - Amazon reviews the PR/FAQ and rejects most.
- **Charter the effort (pitch, poster, charter or PR/FAQ), then kick off** – Write the short document that authorizes and frames the work and gives the lead the authority to use resources: a PMBOK project charter (purpose, measurable objectives, high-level requirements, boundaries, assumptions, risks, milestones, budget, stakeholders, approval and exit criteria, sponsor), an Atlassian project poster, a Shape Up pitch (problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes, no-gos), an inception deck, or a PR/FAQ. Hold a kickoff with the sponsor, the lead, the team and the stakeholders to agree the vision, the mission and the success tests, the roles, the risks and the ways of working. The output is a signed or agreed artefact of one to a few pages, and a team that can state the same goal.
- **Form the initial team, funds and governance** – Name the accountable leader, the sponsor or decision authority, and a small multidisciplinary group (product, design and engineering, plus research, analysis and domain experts as needed). Secure a budget that covers discovery and prototypes, and contracts that allow iteration (USDS plays 5 and 6). For systems programs, start the systems engineering management plan and the control plans for risk and configuration (NASA Phase A; see section 15). Decide how often the justification will be reviewed and who can stop the work.
- **Start the repository with a README, a license and an honest status (open-source and solo projects)** – Before the code, write the README: what the project does, why it is useful, how to get started, where to get help, and who maintains it (GitHub; opensource.guide). Preston-Werner's readme driven development treats this as the design act. Fogel adds: look for an existing project first, write a concrete mission statement, state clearly that the project is free, list features and requirements, report the development status honestly, and do not hype it. Add a license, a contributing guide and a code of conduct if you want contributors, check that the name is free, and decide what kind of contributions you want.
- **Plan the next phase and define its entry conditions** – Close the phase with a list of ideas and hypotheses to test next, the team and skills needed, the life-cycle approach to use at a high level, the measurement plan, and the review points where the business justification will be checked again. GOV.UK's end-of-discovery checklist is a good template: a viable service exists, it is cost effective, the wider context is understood, there are ideas to test, there is a team for alpha, and the team knows how it will measure success. Keep it "just enough" to start; detailed planning belongs to the planning phase (see section 4).

### Outputs

- A problem or opportunity statement with evidence of scale and importance, and the reframed question to answer.
- A stakeholder register and analysis (interest, influence, concerns), with the key stakeholders named in the charter.
- User research findings: interview snapshots, user needs statements, personas, journey maps or service blueprints, and an opportunity solution tree.
- A vision statement or product goal, an elevator pitch, or a future press release; a concept of operations and operational scenarios for systems.
- Outcome and success metrics with baselines and targets, and a measurement plan (for example OKRs, HEART metrics, GOV.UK KPIs, NASA measures of effectiveness).
- A feasibility report or four-risk assessment that covers technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule feasibility, with the constraints classified as hard or soft.
- An options appraisal: a long list narrowed to a short list that includes do nothing and do minimum, trade study results, and a build, buy or reuse decision with a rationale.
- A business case (outline first, refined later), an opportunity assessment, a Lean Canvas or an opportunity canvas; a rough-order-of-magnitude estimate or a fixed appetite.
- An initial scope statement with boundaries, a NOT list or no-gos, assumptions and constraints.
- An initial risk register or assumption map with owners; pre-mortem results.
- Prototypes, an MVP or experiment results, and the decisions taken from them (pivot, persevere or stop).
- A recorded go/no-go decision with criteria, conditions, funds and the date of the next review.
- A project charter, project poster, pitch, inception deck or PR/FAQ; a kickoff held; a named sponsor, an accountable lead and an initial team.
- For open-source and solo projects: a README with purpose, scope, usage and honest status; a LICENSE file; an issue tracker; a contributing guide and a code of conduct when contributors are wanted.
- Exit criteria: the decision authority has decided to proceed, to stop, or to continue discovery. If the decision is to proceed, there is a viable concept, a cost-effective case, a measurable success definition, a bounded scope, a team and budget for the next phase, and a list of hypotheses to test. A stop is a legitimate exit.

### Roles

- **Sponsor, executive or decision authority** (PMBOK sponsor, PRINCE2 executive and project board, NASA decision authority, Stage-Gate gatekeepers, Shape Up betting table, Amazon leaders) – owns the business justification, funds discovery, and makes and records the go/no-go decision.
- **Product manager or product owner** – frames the problem; writes the opportunity assessment, the vision and the outcome; owns value and viability risk (Cagan); leads the product trio (Torres); communicates the product goal (Scrum).
- **Business analyst** – builds the needs analysis, the stakeholder analysis, the options and the business case; works with finance on benefits and costs.
- **Product designer and user researcher** – own usability risk; run interviews, field studies and prototype tests; produce journey maps and needs statements (Cagan, NN/g, GOV.UK).
- **Lead engineer, architect or tech lead** – owns feasibility risk, rough estimates, technology choices, the build, buy or reuse decision, and the dependency assessment; builds feasibility prototypes.
- **Systems engineer** (systems and mission work) – captures stakeholder expectations, writes the ConOps and the measures of effectiveness, and runs trade studies (NASA, 15288).
- **Project or delivery manager** – drafts the charter, runs the kickoff, checks schedule feasibility, starts the risk register, and arranges governance and reviews.
- **Performance or data analyst** – defines metrics and baselines, and plans data collection during discovery (GOV.UK).
- **Specialists consulted for feasibility** – legal and privacy, security, finance, procurement and contracts, operations and support, policy owners, and domain experts (Green Book commercial and financial cases; USDS budget play; PR/FAQ internal FAQ).
- **Users, customers and operators** – the source of evidence through interviews, observation and prototype tests.
- **Neighbouring teams and stakeholders** – other services, data owners and platform teams whose constraints and opportunities the team must know (inception deck "meet your neighbours"; GOV.UK cross-government work).
- **Open-source maintainer or solo developer** – plays all roles at small scale: writes the README and the mission statement, chooses the license, decides the scope, and decides whether to invite contributors.

### Practices with consensus

- **Frame and validate the problem before the commitment to a solution; reframe solution requests as problems** – A good solution to the wrong problem is waste; evidence about the real problem changes what gets built. Evidence: GOV.UK How the discovery phase works; NN/g The Discovery Phase in UX Projects; SWEBOK v4 ("understand the real problem"); Shape Up Write the Pitch; Atlassian Problem Framing; Amazon Working Backwards PR/FAQ; Readme Driven Development.
- **Talk to real users and customers early, and base decisions on observed behavior, not on assumptions or internal opinion** – People overstate their aspirations; stories about specific past behavior give reliable evidence and reveal unexpected needs. Evidence: US Digital Services Playbook play 1; GOV.UK Service Standard point 1; Product Talk Customer Interviews and Story-Based Customer Interviews; NN/g The Discovery Phase in UX Projects; The Lean Startup Principles; NN/g Design Thinking 101.
- **Define measurable outcomes and success criteria before the build, with baselines** – Outcomes let the decision authority judge value later, and keep the team on behavior change instead of output delivery. Evidence: GOV.UK discovery checklist and Using data to improve your service; What Matters OKR meaning, definition, example; Product Talk Defining Product Outcomes; PMBOK-based Project Charter contents; NASA Stakeholder Expectations Definition (measures of effectiveness); Atlassian Project Poster and Project Kickoff.
- **Identify stakeholders at the start, and continue to identify them** – Unknown stakeholders appear later with requirements, vetoes and constraints that are expensive to absorb. Evidence: NASA Stakeholder Expectations Definition; PMBOK-based Identifying Stakeholders and Managing Their Expectations; ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 introduction; NN/g stakeholder interviews (The Discovery Phase in UX Projects); inception deck "meet your neighbours" (The Carpentries).
- **Assess several feasibility dimensions and all four product risks before the commitment of engineering** – Technical feasibility is only one cause of failure; value, usability, viability, legal and operational fit kill as many efforts. Evidence: SVPG The Four Big Risks; SWEBOK v4 feasibility analysis; Sommerville feasibility study; Wikipedia Feasibility study (TELOS map); IDEO Design Thinking (three lenses); HM Treasury five case model.
- **Compare several alternatives, which include do nothing, do minimum, and buy or reuse, not a single option** – The team cannot select the best option if it was never a candidate; the baseline option shows the true cost of change. Evidence: HM Treasury five case model guide; PRINCE2 business options; NASA Decision Analysis; SWEBOK v4 engineering decision-making process; Fogel "look around first"; Fowler Utility vs Strategic Dichotomy.
- **Make an explicit, recorded go/no-go decision by the person who owns the money, and treat a stop as a legitimate outcome** – Without a decision point, work continues by inertia; most ideas should die cheaply at this stage. Evidence: SVPG Assessing Product Opportunities; Stage-Gate overview; GOV.UK How the discovery phase works; Working Backwards PR/FAQ; PRINCE2 business case; NASA key decision points (Program/Project Life Cycle).
- **Keep inception artefacts short and written: one page for the problem, vision, opportunity assessment, charter, pitch or README** – Short written narratives force clear thought and let stakeholders review before the decision; nobody reads long documents. Evidence: Amazon PR/FAQ (one page plus up to five pages of FAQ); Shape Up Write the Pitch; Atlassian Project Poster; Lean Canvas; Readme Driven Development; SVPG Assessing Product Opportunities.
- **A small cross-functional group (product, design and engineering, plus research and domain experts) does discovery together, rather than hand documents across roles** – Different disciplines own the value, usability, feasibility and viability risks, and the group must test them together. Evidence: SVPG The Four Big Risks; Product Talk Opportunity Solution Trees (product trio); NN/g The Discovery Phase in UX Projects (3 to 7 people); GV The Design Sprint; GOV.UK discovery team.
- **Test the riskiest assumptions with cheap prototypes and experiments before the full build** – Prototypes and MVPs produce validated learning for a fraction of the cost of an engineered release. Evidence: Ries Minimum Viable Product guide; SVPG Product Discovery; GV The Design Sprint; SWEBOK v4 (prototypes verify technical feasibility); Sommerville product prototypes (Engineering Software Products); GOV.UK Service Standard point 1.
- **Identify risks and assumptions early, and write them down** – People do not like to voice doubts in planning; structured techniques surface the doubts while they are cheap to handle. Evidence: HBR Performing a Project Premortem; SEI Taxonomy-Based Risk Identification; PMBOK-based Project Charter (overall project risk); Shape Up rabbit holes; Working Backwards internal FAQ; SVPG The Four Big Risks.
- **Review the business justification at each gate or stage; do not write it once** – Estimates and assumptions change; continued investment needs continued justification. Evidence: PRINCE2 continued business justification; HM Treasury staged business case (SOC, OBC, FBC); Stage-Gate gates; NASA key decision points; SWEBOK v4 ("monitor the performance of the selected alternative").
- **State explicit scope boundaries and an appetite or budget** – A NOT list and a fixed appetite prevent scope creep and unproductive debate later. Evidence: Shape Up Write the Pitch (appetite, no-gos); inception deck NOT list (The Carpentries post); PMBOK-based Project Charter (boundaries and pre-approved resources); GOV.UK hard and soft constraints.
- **Time-box discovery, keep it lightweight, and end it with a decision** – Open-ended analysis delays the lessons; a bounded period with a decision at the end keeps discovery cheap. Evidence: GOV.UK discovery (4 to 8 weeks typical); GV The Design Sprint (5 days); Shape Up appetite; SVPG Assessing Product Opportunities ("quick, lightweight").
- **For open-source and solo projects, write the README first with what, why, how to start and where to get help; add a license; report the status honestly** – The README is the design document and the first impression; a missing license blocks use; hype drives away the right users. Evidence: Readme Driven Development; GitHub About READMEs; Open Source Guides Starting an Open Source Project; Producing Open Source Software Getting Started.

### Contested points

- **How much analysis before the build, versus how much the team learns from the build** – PMBOK-based texts, PRINCE2, Stage-Gate and the HM Treasury five case model expect a documented business case, an options appraisal and gate approvals before significant spend. Lean Startup, Cagan and Torres argue that for novel products the cheapest evidence comes from experiments and MVPs, and that business plans built on untested assumptions are fiction. Shape Up replaces estimates with a fixed appetite. The right mix depends on the cost of a wrong decision, reversibility, capital intensity, regulation and novelty. Public money and safety-critical systems push toward formal cases; consumer software pushes toward experiments.
- **What an MVP is, and who builds it** – Ries defines the MVP as the version that yields maximum validated learning with the least effort, and warns that it is contextual and not for obvious needs. Kniberg shows that people misread the term as a crippled first release, and proposes the earliest testable, usable and lovable product. Cagan separates discovery prototypes (built by one prototyper in weeks) from delivered products. Practitioners often use MVP to mean the first shippable release. Choose the term by audience, and by whether paying customers will receive the artefact.
- **Discovery as a phase with an exit gate, versus continuous discovery** – GOV.UK, NASA, PMBOK-based initiation and the Unified Process treat inception as a bounded phase that ends in a decision. Torres and Cagan argue that discovery must be continuous (weekly interviews, parallel discovery and delivery) because teams make decisions every day. Shape Up runs a shaping and betting cycle every six weeks. Most organizations need both: an initial bounded discovery for a new product or service, then continuous discovery inside delivery. The balance depends on product maturity and the funding model.
- **Degree of formality and written documents** – Amazon requires a written PR/FAQ and silent reading; the five case model and PMBOK charters are formal; Atlassian's poster and the inception deck are deliberately lightweight; agile culture distrusts documents. Cagan's opportunity assessment is ten questions on a page. The choice depends on the number of stakeholders, the funding and approval process, and regulatory needs. The consensus is only that something short and written must exist.
- **Build versus buy versus reuse** – Fowler: buy for utility functions, build only what differentiates. Software Engineering at Google: every external dependency carries a long-term upgrade and security cost, so prefer internal control and ask hard questions before an import. USDS: prefer open-source and commodity stacks to avoid vendor lock-in. McKinley: spend few "innovation tokens". Fogel: join an existing project rather than start one. The answer depends on differentiation, the maintenance horizon, team skills, and the health of the candidate dependency.
- **Who decides go/no-go, and who owns outcomes** – Cagan's opportunity assessment goes to senior management for a clear decision; Stage-Gate uses cross-functional gatekeepers; PRINCE2 uses a project board; NASA uses a decision authority; Shape Up uses an executive betting table. Torres and the empowered-team school argue that leaders should assign outcomes and let teams decide what to build. Organizations differ on how much authority sits with the team versus a gate.
- **Which metrics the team should own** – GOV.UK mandates four service KPIs. Torres warns that business outcomes (revenue) are outside a team's span of control and that traction metrics are too narrow; she prefers product outcomes (customer behavior). OKR guidance asks for aggressive but verifiable key results. HEART suggests user-experience metrics through goals, signals and metrics. Teams disagree on the level and the number of metrics; the choice depends on what the team can influence and what the funder needs to see.
- **Estimate versus appetite** – SWEBOK and PMBOK-based charters expect effort, cost and duration estimates at initiation, with pre-approved resources and summary milestones. Shape Up fixes time (the appetite) and lets scope flex; the inception deck uses trade-off sliders to decide what gives. Contract and funding models often force one approach.
- **Is feasibility a yes/no answer?** – Classic feasibility studies report whether a system is feasible. McKinley observes that the answer is almost never "we cannot", only "too hard at this cost"; SWEBOK frames feasibility as the search for the best approach under constraints. Treat feasibility as a judgement of cost and risk, and make the cost explicit.
- **How early and how public an open-source project should be** – Fogel says do not fear an unready look, but never inflate the status; Preston-Werner says write the README before the code; opensource.guide says first decide why you open-source and whether you want contributors. Whether to announce early, invite contributors, or polish in private depends on the maintainer's goals and capacity.

### Metrics

- Outcome metrics defined in this phase: product outcomes (a change in customer behavior) and business outcomes (revenue, cost, market share), written as OKR key results with a baseline and a target. Caveat: outputs disguised as outcomes, and metrics outside the team's control, are common mistakes (Torres).
- Service KPIs used by GOV.UK: cost per transaction, user satisfaction, completion rate and digital take-up. Caveat: set the baseline from the existing service during discovery, and plan data collection with an analyst.
- User-experience metrics through HEART (happiness, engagement, adoption, retention, task success), chosen through goals, signals and metrics. Caveat: pick a few that map to the product goal.
- Measures of effectiveness, and needs, goals and objectives with target levels, in systems and mission work (NASA). Caveat: stakeholders must validate them.
- Economic measures in the business case: return on investment, payback, present worth, internal rate of return, benefit-cost ratio, or cost-effectiveness for non-profit work, and break-even. Caveat: compare all options on the same basis and planning horizon, state the uncertainty, and include intangible assets (SWEBOK v4 economics knowledge area).
- Startup-stage measures: validated learning, the number of assumptions tested and invalidated, pivot or persevere decisions, and "innovation accounting" milestones instead of revenue (Lean Startup). Caveat: vanity metrics mislead.
- Discovery health indicators: customers interviewed per week (Torres suggests at least one), prototypes tested with real users, time spent in discovery versus the time box (GOV.UK: 4 to 8 weeks), and the share of ideas rejected at the gate (Amazon: most PR/FAQs never become products; Stage-Gate kill decisions). Caveat: a high kill rate is a sign of a gate that works, not a sign of waste.
- Decision quality indicators: a go/no-go decision recorded with criteria; a business case reviewed at each stage; success criteria present in the charter. Caveat: these measure the process, not the outcome.
- Risk indicators: the number and exposure of risks in the initial register by taxonomy class; technology maturity, or the number of unfamiliar technologies ("innovation tokens"). Caveat: early lists are incomplete by nature.
- General caveat: every number set in this phase is a hypothesis. Revisit the baselines and targets after alpha or after the first release.

### Failure modes

- A start from a solution ("build a map") instead of a problem. The team builds the wrong thing well; "a perfect implementation of the wrong specification is worthless" (Preston-Werner; GOV.UK; NN/g).
- No contact with real users. Decisions rest on internal opinion, stakeholder wishes, or speculative interview questions that produce unreliable answers (USDS; Torres; NN/g).
- Discovery that always ends in "go". There is no real decision point and no will to stop; the effort continues through sunk cost after the justification lapses (GOV.UK "it is not a failure to stop"; PRINCE2; Amazon).
- Success defined as outputs ("ship feature X"), or not defined at all. There is no baseline, so nobody can later say whether the work succeeded (Torres; OKR guidance; GOV.UK).
- Business case theatre: a single option, no do-nothing baseline, optimistic benefits, "rose-coloured" FAQs, and criteria chosen to fit the answer; too many or too few criteria. The decision looks evidence-based but is not (Green Book; PR/FAQ; SWEBOK).
- Analysis paralysis and unbounded discovery: long documents that nobody reads, months of research without a prototype, and discovery treated as a predictable schedule. The lessons come late and the money is spent before any evidence exists (Cagan; GOV.UK time box; Shape Up).
- A misused MVP: a partial product with no feedback loop ("bastardized agile"), an MVP for an obvious need, or a team that ships an MVP and leaves. The organization gets neither the lessons nor a usable product (Kniberg; Ries).
- Viability, legal, privacy, procurement and operational constraints discovered late, after engineering has started. Rework or cancellation follows (Cagan "tackle value and viability risk early"; GOV.UK hard constraints such as legislation).
- Technology and sourcing mistakes: utility functions built in-house, bought utility systems heavily customized, dependencies imported without ownership of their long-term cost, and innovation tokens spent on novelty. Maintenance cost and risk grow with no differentiation in return (Fowler; Software Engineering at Google; McKinley).
- Missing stakeholders and neighbours. Late requirements, vetoes and integration surprises follow (NASA; PMBOK-based texts; inception deck).
- Risks unspoken because people will not voice doubts in planning, and no initial risk list. Known problems surface when they are expensive (premortem; SEI).
- No scope boundaries, so the concept grows until it is unaffordable; no appetite stated (Shape Up; inception deck NOT list).
- No single accountable owner or decision authority. Decisions come from a committee and are never written down, so nobody can act on them or revisit them (USDS play 6; Stage-Gate gatekeepers).
- Open-source and solo start-up errors: no check for an existing project, no README or a README that does not say what the project does, no license, an inflated development status, and no decision on whether contributors are wanted. Users cannot find, understand or legally use the project (Fogel; opensource.guide; GitHub).
- Vision drift: the vision exists but nobody uses it to judge changes, so the product slowly becomes something else (Sommerville product management notes; Cagan).

### Tailoring by project size

Five things are essential at every scale. Everything else scales with the project.

- A written problem statement with the intended user.
- A quick look at alternatives, which includes the option to do nothing and the option to use something that already exists.
- One sentence on what success looks like.
- An explicit decision to proceed, with boundaries on scope and appetite.
- A short list of the biggest risks, which includes legal and license risks.

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| Solo developer on a small repository | Spend an hour to a day, not weeks. Write the README first: what it does, why it is useful, how to get started, and the status. Spend thirty minutes to search for an existing project or library that solves the problem (Fogel; the Carpentries inception deck adds this step). Add a NOT list and a license. Pick one success signal, for example "I use it every week" or "ten people install it". Prefer boring technology. Decide whether you want contributors, and say so in the README. | Skip the business case, the charter and the formal risk register. A Lean Canvas or the ten inception deck questions are optional, if you hope for users or contributors. |
| Small team | One to six weeks with a product trio, plus a researcher or analyst when possible. Run a problem framing session, five to ten story-based customer interviews (and keep one per week), an opportunity solution tree, and a one-page opportunity assessment, Lean Canvas or project poster. Check the four risks, test the riskiest assumption with a prototype or a design sprint, define one product outcome with a baseline, decide build, buy or reuse, and get a recorded go/no-go from the founder or sponsor. Use a Shape Up style pitch with an appetite and no-gos, and hold a short kickoff. | A formal business case with a net present value is optional, unless an investor or a customer contract requires it. |
| Large or regulated organization | The same essentials, plus the formal apparatus that governance and law require. Run business or mission analysis and stakeholder needs definition as named processes (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 and 12207, tailored). Write a concept of operations for operated systems. Keep a stakeholder register and a risk register that uses a taxonomy. Develop the business case in stages (strategic outline case, outline business case, full business case) with the five cases, an options appraisal that includes do nothing and do minimum, and a value-for-money analysis. Pass explicit gates (key decision point, Mission Concept Review, Stage-Gate, project board) with written criteria and a signed charter. Involve legal, privacy, security, procurement and finance in the feasibility work. Budget and contract for discovery and prototypes explicitly, and name one accountable leader. Still time-box discovery (GOV.UK suggests 4 to 8 weeks), and still talk to real users. | Few items are optional at this scale. The organization chooses which framework supplies the named processes and gates (15288 and 12207 with tailoring, the five case model, Stage-Gate, NASA key decision points, a PRINCE2 board), and how deep each artefact goes. |

The main tailoring risk at large scale is that documents replace evidence, and that the gate loses its power to say no. The main risk at small scale is that the developer skips the written problem statement and the check for alternatives entirely.

### Sources

- [ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 Systems and software engineering – System life cycle processes (iTeh preview PDF: foreword, introduction, contents)](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/81702/5bd543dddf94457488c8cd8871897567/ISO-IEC-IEEE-15288-2023.pdf) – Primary standard excerpt. Used for the names and order of the technical processes (6.4.1 Business or mission analysis, 6.4.2 Stakeholder needs and requirements definition), the introduction on early definition of stakeholder needs, and the 2023 changes (improved business or mission analysis, new concept definition content). The iso.org pages returned 403.
- [IEEE SA – ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207-2017 Systems and software engineering – Software life cycle processes](https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/12207/5673/) – Official abstract: a common framework for software life cycle processes across acquisition, supply, development, operation, maintenance and disposal; stakeholder involvement and customer satisfaction.
- [SWEBOK Guide v4.0 (IEEE Computer Society) – Software Engineering Management KA (initiation and scope definition, feasibility analysis) and Software Engineering Economics KA](https://ieeecs-media.computer.org/media/education/swebok/swebok-v4.pdf) – Primary source, read through local text extraction. Used for the definition of initiation and scope definition, the purpose and outputs of feasibility analysis, the engineering decision-making process, business model questions, care in go/no-go decisions, prototypes for feasibility, for-profit versus non-profit decision methods, intangible assets, estimation methods, and the definition of a business case.
- [NASA Systems Engineering Handbook – 3.0 NASA Program/Project Life Cycle](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/3-0-nasa-program-project-life-cycle/) – Pre-Phase A concept studies and Phase A activities, key decision points, the Mission Concept Review, trade studies, the ConOps and rough-order-of-magnitude estimates.
- [NASA Systems Engineering Handbook – 4.1 Stakeholder Expectations Definition](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/4-1-stakeholder-expectations-definition/) – Stakeholder identification; needs, goals and objectives; concept of operations; measures of effectiveness; validated expectations as outputs.
- [NASA Systems Engineering Handbook – 6.8 Decision Analysis](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/6-8-decision-analysis/) – Formal alternatives analysis: criteria, alternatives, evaluation methods, make/buy decisions, and when informal decisions are enough.
- [GOV.UK Service Manual – How the discovery phase works](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works) – Discovery purpose, reframe solutions as problems, users, constraints (hard versus soft), existing services, 4 to 8 weeks, the end-of-discovery checklist, and that a stop is not a failure.
