## 4. Planning and estimation

### Purpose

Planning and estimation answer four questions. What will we build, and how big is it? When and at what cost can we deliver it? How do we know that we are still on track? SWEBOK v4 defines software engineering management as planning, estimation, measurement, control, coordination, leadership and risk management. The purpose is efficient software delivery that benefits the stakeholders.

Estimation exists to inform decisions such as funding, prioritization and coordination. Fowler notes that an estimate that drives no significant decision is waste. Planning also exposes uncertainty early, so that the organization makes commitments only when the project has converged enough to support them. Assessment and control then compare the actual progress with the plan. When the two differ, they trigger corrective action, re-planning or abandonment of the project.

### Other names

- Software engineering management (SWEBOK v4, knowledge area 9)
- Software project management, or software project planning (Sommerville, chapters 22–23)
- Technical management processes: project planning, project assessment and control, decision management, and risk management (ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 and 15288)
- The Planning, Measurement and Uncertainty performance domains (PMBOK Guide, 7th edition); the Planning focus area and the Monitoring and Controlling focus area (PMBOK Guide, 8th edition)
- Agile planning: release planning, iteration or sprint planning, backlog refinement, and roadmapping
- Software cost, effort and schedule estimation; forecasting
- Delivery management, program management, and scaled planning (PI Planning, Nexus)

### Position in the life cycle

Planning starts after concept, inception and feasibility (see section 3) produce a charter, a business case or a product vision. It runs until closure. It gives requirements engineering (see section 5) and architecture (see section 6) the scope, the constraints and the first risk list. It receives estimates and technical risks back from them. Monitor-and-control continues through implementation (see section 8), testing (see section 9), release (see section 11) and maintenance (see section 13). The supporting and management processes in section 15 supply the measurement and configuration data that control depends on.

In a waterfall or V-model, a front-loaded planning phase produces a project plan, a WBS, a schedule, a budget and a risk register. Milestone reviews, variance analysis and earned value control the execution. Re-planning happens at milestones. SWEBOK v4 describes a continuum from predictive to adaptive life cycles. Predictive projects invest heavily in up-front plans. Adaptive projects spend less on detailed scope, cost and schedule plans, and more on monitor-and-control processes and progressive elaboration.

In iterative and agile work, planning has several layers. A roadmap sits at the top; GOV.UK iterates roadmaps at least quarterly. Below it come a release or milestone forecast, a sprint plan and daily planning. The team refines the product backlog continuously, and each sprint ends with a review and a retrospective. In DevOps and continuous delivery, the team slices the work into small batches. Flow metrics (throughput, cycle time, WIP) replace much of the up-front estimation, and the team updates the forecasts from actual delivery data.

Across all models, the activity is both a one-time setup and a continuous process. The setup produces the baseline plan, the initial estimates and the initial risk list. The continuous part includes re-estimation as the cone of uncertainty narrows, periodic risk reviews, reports, and re-planning after every increment.

### Inputs

- An approved charter, business case or product vision with a stated goal (SWEBOK: a charter or another initiation document captures the requirements)
- An initial scope statement, a feasibility study and a context diagram; the known constraints on date, budget, staff, technology and regulation
- High-level requirements, a product goal, or an ordered product backlog; for sprint planning, a refined backlog, the Definition of Done, and the past performance and capacity of the team (Scrum Guide)
- A stakeholder list, and the decisions that those stakeholders need from a plan (funding, coordination, dates)
- Organizational policies, the chosen or tailored life-cycle model, and any contractual terms (fixed price, time and materials)
- Historical data: velocity or throughput, cycle times, past project sizes and efforts, calibration data for parametric models, and reference classes of similar projects
- An initial risk profile and the risk appetite of the organization
- The team composition, skills, availability and cost rates; the tool environment used to track the work

### Activities

- **Define the scope and decompose the work** – Agree on what is in scope and what is out of scope. Then decompose the deliverables into a work breakdown structure (WBS) or a product backlog. A WBS follows the 100 percent rule: the children sum to the parent, and they do not overlap. It ends in work packages that are small enough to estimate and track (the 80-hour heuristic and the reporting-period heuristic). SWEBOK recommends an initial WBS and a context diagram at initiation; Scrum uses an emergent, ordered backlog instead. The output is a decomposition that everyone can estimate, schedule and track against.
- **Select and tailor the life cycle and the process** – Choose where the project sits on the predictive-to-adaptive continuum. Base the choice on the stability of the requirements, the risk, and the involvement of the stakeholders. Then select the methods, the tools and the cadence. SWEBOK calls this process planning; 12207 makes it part of project planning. The output is a process plan that says how the team will plan, track and review the work.
- **Define deliverables, milestones and completion criteria** – List each work product, the milestone at which it is due, and the criteria that make it done. In Scrum this is the Definition of Done, a formal commitment that creates transparency. In plan-driven work it is the deliverable list plus acceptance criteria per milestone. GitHub milestones give a solo developer the same mechanism, with a due date and a completion percentage.
- **Estimate size, effort, cost and duration** – Estimate with more than one technique and reconcile the differences (SWEBOK). The table of estimation techniques at the end of this subsection compares the main techniques. Express the results as ranges with stated assumptions; a point estimate hides the uncertainty.
- **Build the schedule and assign resources** – Sequence the tasks by dependency, estimate the durations, find the critical path, and produce a bar chart or an activity network. Sommerville notes that bar charts are the most common representation. Allocate people, equipment and facilities. Make responsibility explicit, for example with a RACI matrix (SWEBOK). In adaptive projects the schedule is a number of iterations, derived from the effort estimate or from fixed date and budget constraints.
- **Budget and staff the project** – Translate the resource needs into cost, add contingency for the known risks, and decide the staff profile over time. Parametric models give effort in person-months, separate from calendar time; COCOMO II notes that a 50 person-month project can take 11 months. Respect Brooks's law: people added late need ramp-up time and add communication overhead (n(n-1)/2 channels), so they usually make a late project later. COCOMO II models the same diseconomy of scale.
- **Manage risk: plan, identify, analyze, treat, monitor** – Write a risk management plan that is scaled to the project. Identify risks continuously with checklists such as Boehm's top ten, WBS walk-throughs, brainstorming and assumption analysis. Analyze each risk as probability times loss (risk exposure), prioritize, and choose a treatment: accept, avoid, mitigate or transfer. Monitor each risk until it is closed. Keep a risk register and review the top-ten list at every milestone or sprint. "Buy information" with prototypes, spikes and benchmarks when the probability or the loss is unclear (Boehm, SEBoK).
- **Create and maintain the roadmap** – Describe how the product will evolve over time: the vision, the stages, the priorities, and who maintains the roadmap (GOV.UK). A roadmap is not a backlog and not a commitment to dates. Tailor the detail to the audience. Update the roadmap at least quarterly, or whenever the priorities change (Atlassian, GOV.UK). It links daily work to business goals and feeds release planning.
- **Plan releases and milestones** – Answer one of two questions: "how much can we deliver by this date" (fixed date) or "when can this scope be done" (fixed scope). Use an ordered backlog, an allowance for unknown work, and velocity or throughput as a range (Cohn). Story mapping and MoSCoW help to slice a minimum usable release. DSDM limits the Must Haves to about 60 percent of the effort and keeps about 20 percent Could Haves as contingency. A forecast is not a commitment; the team updates it after every sprint.
- **Manage and refine the product backlog** – Keep one ordered backlog with one owner (Scrum Guide, Nexus). Refine the items continuously: break them down, add detail, estimate, order by value, and close the items that the team will never do (Atlassian). Near-term items are small and clear; an optional Definition of Ready (clear, feasible, testable) describes this state. Far-term items stay coarse, and the team does not estimate them in detail.
- **Prioritize the work** – Order the backlog with an explicit method, so that the trade-offs are visible. The table of prioritization methods at the end of this subsection lists the common methods. Dependencies and the urgency of feedback also drive the order (Atlassian). Scores inform the decision; they do not replace it.
- **Plan each iteration or sprint** – Sprint Planning answers three questions. Why is the sprint valuable (the Sprint Goal)? What can be done (the Developers pull items against their capacity and their past performance)? How will the work be done (decomposition into items of one day or less)? Keep the timebox: a maximum of eight hours for a one-month sprint, or about two hours per sprint week. Keep the plan "just enough", and never treat the forecast as a commitment to every item (Scrum Guide, Atlassian).
- **Manage dependencies between teams** – Make cross-team dependencies transparent. Then reduce them with changes to the product structure, the communication structure or the process (Nexus cross-team refinement, Nexus Sprint Planning). At a larger scale, PI Planning produces a program board with feature dates, dependencies and milestones, ROAMed risks and a confidence vote (SAFe). Structurally, stream-aligned teams that own a whole slice of the domain, platform teams, and limited interaction modes reduce the hand-offs (Team Topologies).
- **Identify stakeholders and plan communication** – Decide who needs which information, how often, and in what form: steering reports, sprint reviews, roadmap walkthroughs, status dashboards. SWEBOK says that reports must address the information needs of the audience, not internal detail. The GOV.UK governance principles ask leaders to "go see for yourself" and to make decisions at the right level without a delay to delivery. Sprint reviews and show-and-tells are the agile form of stakeholder reports.
- **Monitor, control and report progress** – Collect measurement data continuously. Compare the actual effort, schedule, cost and quality with the plan. Analyze variances and outliers, recompute the risk exposure, and act when a threshold is exceeded (SWEBOK 3.4–3.6; SEBoK assessment and control; 12207 project assessment and control). Controls include corrective action, re-planning, scope change control and, in some cases, abandonment. Plan-driven work uses earned value (PV, EV, AC, SPI, CPI, EAC). Agile work uses burn-down charts, cumulative flow diagrams and flow metrics.
- **Forecast and re-estimate as knowledge grows** – Re-estimate at each milestone or sprint with observed data. Use "yesterday's weather" for velocity. Use throughput-based Monte Carlo simulation for "when" and "how many" questions at 50/85/95 percent confidence. Use service level expectations based on historical cycle time (Kanban Guide). The cone of uncertainty narrows only when the project removes variability through a defined vision, requirements, UI and architecture. Otherwise it stays a cloud (McConnell).
- **Make and record decisions** – For significant trade-offs, use a structured decision process: frame the decision, define the objectives and measures, generate alternatives, assess them, analyze uncertainty and sensitivity, recommend, and record (12207 decision management, SEBoK trade studies). Smaller projects keep a decision log or architecture decision records, so that later re-planning knows why the team made each choice.
- **Review, evaluate and close** – At milestones, sprint reviews and project end, evaluate three things: the satisfaction of the requirements, the effectiveness of the process and the tools, and the performance against the plan (SWEBOK review and evaluation). Closure confirms the completion criteria, archives the material, updates the measurement database, and runs a retrospective to capture lessons (SWEBOK closure; Scrum retrospective; Agile Manifesto principle 12).
- **Maintain the plan as a living artifact** – Size the planning effort by the risk of no plan. Keep the plan under change control and revise it at predetermined points (SWEBOK plan management). To abandon the plan when trouble hits, without re-planning, is a classic mistake (McConnell). The plan, the roadmap, the backlog and the risk register must all stay current to be trusted.
- **Set up lightweight planning for a solo repository** – Use the tools of the repository itself: issues for tasks, bugs and ideas; labels and milestones for groups and due dates; sub-issues or task lists for decomposition; a project board or a roadmap view for status; and a TODO or plan file in the repository when tools are too heavy (GitHub docs). Link pull requests to issues with closing keywords, so that progress updates itself. Estimate only when a date or scope decision needs it.

Table of estimation techniques:

| Technique | How it works | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Expert judgment and Wideband Delphi | Experts estimate in anonymous rounds, then discuss the differences and repeat (Boehm 1981) | An inside view; the group discussion surfaces hidden work |
| Analogy and reference class forecasting | Take the outside view: compare the project with a reference class of similar past projects and use their actual outcomes | Counters optimism bias and strategic misrepresentation (Flyvbjerg) |
| Planning poker with story points | The whole team sizes items relative to each other and reveals the cards at the same time to avoid anchoring | Relative size, not hours; velocity converts points into duration |
| Function points | Measure the functional size from the user's view, per ISO/IEC 20926 (IFPUG) | An ISO-certified method for estimation and benchmarks |
| Parametric models such as COCOMO II | Effort = A × Size^B × the product of the effort multipliers, with five scale factors (PREC, FLEX, RESL, TEAM, PMAT) and 17 post-architecture cost drivers | Needs calibration with historical data; gives effort and schedule separately |

Table of prioritization methods:

| Method | Basis | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| WSJF | Cost of delay divided by job size | SAFe, Reinertsen |
| RICE | Reach × impact × confidence / effort | Intercom |
| MoSCoW | Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have this time | DSDM |
| Kano categories | Must-be, one-dimensional, attractive (also indifferent and reverse) | Kano model |
| Cohn's four factors | Value, cost, risk and knowledge | Agile Estimating and Planning |

### Outputs

- A project plan (or a SEMP-style technical plan) that covers scope, process, deliverables, schedule, budget, staff, risk, quality and communication; in adaptive projects, a lighter plan plus a roadmap and a backlog
- A scope statement and a work breakdown structure, or an ordered product backlog with a Product Goal
- Estimates with ranges, assumptions and the basis of estimate (size, effort, cost, duration), and the model calibration used
- A schedule with milestones, dependencies and the critical path, or a release forecast in sprints with a date range or a scope range
- A budget with contingency reserves, and a staff profile
- A risk management plan and a risk register with exposure, owners, treatments and status; a top-ten risk list
- A roadmap (now, next, later, or quarterly) and a release plan; a sprint goal and a sprint backlog per iteration
- A Definition of Done (and, optionally, a Definition of Ready)
- A communication plan and a cadence for reports; status reports, burn charts, earned value indices or flow metrics; a decision log; retrospective actions; lessons learned and closure records
- Exit criteria: the affected stakeholders have reviewed and agreed the plan; commitments are made only when the uncertainty is acceptable; every iteration ends with a usable increment and an updated forecast; the project closes when the completion criteria are confirmed and the knowledge is archived

### Roles

- Project manager or delivery manager – owns the plan, the schedule, the budget, the risk process, the reports and the control; in small teams this is a shared duty
- Product owner or product manager – owns the vision, the roadmap, the single ordered backlog and value-based prioritization; the Scrum Guide makes this one person, not a committee
- Developers or engineering team – size and estimate their own work, plan the sprint, decompose the items, and flag risks and dependencies
- Scrum Master, team lead or release train engineer – facilitates the planning events and the timeboxes, removes impediments, and coordinates cross-team planning
- Technical lead or architect – supplies architecture-level estimates, identifies technical risks and dependencies, and advises on how to slice the work
- Sponsor and stakeholders – supply constraints, accept trade-offs, attend reviews, and make decisions at the right level (GOV.UK governance)
- PMO, estimation specialists or measurement analysts (larger organizations) – maintain historical data, calibrate models, and run earned value and measurement programs
- Nexus Integration Team, SAFe program roles, or platform and enabling teams – manage integration and cross-team dependencies at scale
- Solo developer – plays every role; keeps the planning artifacts minimal but written down

### Practices with consensus

- **Estimate and forecast in ranges, state the assumptions, and delay firm commitments until work has reduced the uncertainty** – Early estimates can be wrong by a factor of 4 in either direction. Only decisions that remove variability narrow the cone, and commitments made at concept time are not supportable. Evidence: Software Development's Cone of Uncertainty (Construx white paper); COCOMO II Model Definition Manual (range estimates tied to the degree of definition); Agile Planning and Forecasting (Mountain Goat Software, velocity as a range); Estimation (Agile Alliance glossary).
- **Use more than one estimation approach, use historical data, and reconcile the results** – Software effort depends heavily on people and context. A single method, or a pure inside view, is biased toward optimism. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 chapter 9, section 2.3; COCOMO II Model Definition Manual (calibration); From Nobel Prize to project management (Flyvbjerg, PMI); Reference class forecasting: promises, problems, and a research agenda (Cranfield); XpVelocity (Fowler, "yesterday's weather").
- **The people who will do the work size it, with group techniques that avoid anchoring** – Group estimation surfaces hidden work and different perspectives. The conversation is often worth more than the number. Evidence: The Scrum Guide (2020) (the Developers are responsible for sizing); Planning Poker (Mountain Goat Software); Wideband delphi (Wikipedia, Boehm 1981); Story points and estimation (Atlassian).
- **Slice the work into small items and deliver in small batches** – Small items are easier to estimate. They give faster feedback, reduce risk and make progress visible. Evidence: The Scrum Guide (work items of one day or less); Working in small batches (DORA); Story points and estimation (Atlassian: break down items above 16 hours or about 20 points); Story Points Revisited (Jeffries); Work breakdown structure (Wikipedia, work package heuristics).
- **Separate estimates, targets and commitments, and never use estimates to blame people** – Punishment for missed estimates inflates future estimates, damages trust and pushes teams to cut quality. Evidence: 17 Theses on Software Estimation (McConnell, thesis 10); Estimation (Agile Alliance glossary); Sprint planning meeting guide (Atlassian, Dave West); Story Points Revisited (Jeffries); PurposeOfEstimation (Fowler).
- **Run risk management as a continuous loop with a risk register: plan, identify, analyze (probability × impact), prioritize, treat, monitor** – Most project disasters trace back to high-risk elements that nobody addressed early. Risk exposure focuses attention on the few items that matter. Evidence: Software Risk Management: Principles and Practices (Boehm 1991); Risk Management (SEBoK); SWEBOK v4 section 2.5; ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 technical management processes (arc42 summary).
- **Plan at several levels (roadmap, release, iteration, day), re-plan after every increment, and treat the plan as a living artifact** – Requirements change and knowledge grows. A plan that nobody updates loses the trust of the stakeholders. Evidence: Mountain Goat Software release planning pages and Agile Estimating and Planning; SWEBOK v4 plan management; The Scrum Guide; Developing a roadmap (GOV.UK); Product Roadmap Guide (Atlassian).
- **Measure progress against the plan, analyze variance, act on thresholds, and report to the information needs of each audience** – Management without measurement lacks discipline. Visibility allows timely corrective action. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 sections 3.4–3.6 and 6; Project Assessment and Control (SEBoK); Governance principles for agile service delivery (GOV.UK: trust and verify, go see for yourself); The Kanban Guide (flow metrics).
- **Keep one ordered backlog with one accountable owner, and an explicit, shared Definition of Done** – A single source of work prevents conflicting priorities. A shared done criterion makes increments and velocity comparable over time. Evidence: The Scrum Guide (2020); The Nexus Guide (2021); Product backlog: tips for creation and prioritization (Atlassian); Definition of Done (Agile Alliance glossary).
- **Do not add people to a late project to make it faster; reduce the coordination overhead instead** – Ramp-up time, communication channels and limited task divisibility make added staff a net drain late in a project. Evidence: Brooks's law (Wikipedia, The Mythical Man-Month); Classic Mistakes Enumerated (McConnell); COCOMO II Model Definition Manual (diseconomies of scale from communication overhead); The Nexus Guide (scaling down can deliver more value).
- **When requirements are uncertain, fix the time and the budget and negotiate the scope with an explicit prioritization scheme** – Fixed scope plus fixed date plus fixed cost demands stable requirements that rarely exist. A flexible scope keeps dates and budgets credible. Evidence: FixedPrice (Fowler); MoSCoW Prioritisation (DSDM); Iron Triangle Project Management (Atlassian); Project management triangle (Wikipedia).
- **Make cross-team dependencies visible early and reduce them structurally** – Dependencies found in the middle of a sprint cause waits and integration failures. The product structure and the team structure determine how many dependencies exist. Evidence: The Nexus Guide (cross-team refinement, Nexus Sprint Backlog); PI Planning (SAFe: program board, ROAM); Team Topologies key concepts.
- **Reduce uncertainty and buy information: prototypes, spikes, benchmarks and early user feedback** – It is cheaper to learn early than to carry a risk through the whole project. Evidence: Software Risk Management: Principles and Practices (Boehm 1991: prototyping, benchmarking); Risk Management (SEBoK); Software Development's Cone of Uncertainty (Construx: a defined vision, requirements and UI narrow the cone); Working in small batches (DORA).
- **Hold retrospectives and project reviews, and feed lessons and measurement data back into the organization** – Estimation and planning skill improves only with calibrated feedback. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 closure and review topics; The Scrum Guide (Sprint Retrospective); Principles behind the Agile Manifesto (principle 12); Story points and estimation (Atlassian: review past estimates).

### Contested points

- **Whether to estimate at all (#NoEstimates)** – Zuill, Duarte and Jeffries argue that many teams can work in small increments, count finished items, and forecast from throughput instead of estimates. They add that estimates are often misused. McConnell holds that estimation is a learnable professional skill, and that velocity-based forecasts are themselves a form of estimation. He adds that businesses need estimates for budgets and coordination. Fowler takes a middle position: estimate when a significant decision depends on it; without such a decision, the estimate is waste. The choice depends on the decision at hand, the contract, and how much the stakeholders trust empirical data.
- **Story points versus counts of items, hours or cycle time** – Cohn and Atlassian defend story points as relative effort that removes the emotional attachment to dates and resists comparison across teams. Jeffries, who helped to invent them, regrets their misuse to compare teams and to pressure people; he prefers to slice stories small and count them. Kanban-oriented practitioners use cycle time and throughput with service level expectations. The choice depends on whether the team can slice items small, and whether management will misuse points.
- **Does the cone of uncertainty really narrow?** – McConnell and Boehm present the cone as the best-case accuracy for skilled estimators on well-controlled projects. The cone runs from 4x to 0.25x at concept, to about 1.6x after requirements, and to about 1.25x after UI design. Poorly controlled projects get a "cloud" instead. Empirical work disagrees. Todd Little's 2006 IEEE Software study of Landmark Graphics projects found a roughly lognormal, nearly constant uncertainty range through the project. It also found estimates that behaved as targets. Wikipedia notes that the decrease "is not guaranteed". In practice, expect the cone to narrow only if the project actively removes variability.
- **Definition of Ready** – Pichler and many teams use a light DoR (clear, feasible, testable, small), so that sprint commitments are realistic. The Scrum Guide does not include it. Cohn and Scrum.org writers warn that a strict DoR becomes a stage gate that recreates sequential hand-offs. The consensus tilts to a guideline, never a gate.
- **How much up-front planning, WBS and earned value** – Plan-driven and regulated settings (SEBoK, 12207, the PMBOK process view, contracts) expect a baselined WBS, schedule and budget, and often earned value. Agile guidance and the adaptive end of the SWEBOK continuum spend less on up-front plans and more on monitor-and-control. PMBOK itself moved from processes (6th edition) to principles and performance domains (7th edition, 2021). The 8th edition (2025) then reintroduced about 40 non-prescriptive processes and five focus areas. This shows that the question is unsettled even in the standard body.
- **Parametric models (COCOMO II, function points) versus empirical team data** – Parametric models are defensible for bids, large programs, and regulated or contract work, and they need calibration with historical data. Product teams with stable membership usually get better short-horizon forecasts from their own velocity or throughput. Sommerville notes that the size of a system is only known accurately when it is finished; both approaches carry that limit.
- **Velocity and delivery metrics as performance measures** – Fowler, Jeffries and Atlassian say that velocity is a planning calibration, not productivity, and that comparison between teams is meaningless. DORA warns that targets for deployment or other metrics invite gaming, and that its metrics apply at the application or service level. Some management cultures still use these numbers for appraisal; the evidence says that this kills agility and honesty.
- **How to coordinate many teams** – SAFe prescribes cadenced PI Planning with a program board and ROAMed risks. Nexus adds the minimum to Scrum and aims to remove dependencies through backlog decomposition. Team Topologies argues for a restructure of teams and interaction modes, so that fewer dependencies exist at all. The choice depends on how much the organization can change the product and team structure, versus coordinate around it.
- **Fixed-price, fixed-scope contracts** – Fowler argues that a fixed price is possible but a fixed scope is a mirage in agile work; fix the budget and the date and collaborate on the scope. Sommerville describes the price as a business decision that may deliberately underprice, or add a premium for fixed-price risk. Procurement rules in some organizations still force a fixed scope; then detailed up-front estimation and change control become necessary.
- **Where to hold contingency** – DSDM keeps about 20 percent Could Have effort as scope contingency. Cohn's book describes schedule buffers for uncertainty. Boehm and classic cost management keep budget contingencies for identified risks. Extra time added to every task estimate is widely criticized, because it hides uncertainty and inflates schedules. The right form of buffer depends on whether the date, the scope or the cost is the flexible variable.

### Metrics

- Estimation accuracy – actual divided by estimated effort or duration, the magnitude of relative error, and the p90/p10 ratio of outcomes. Caveat: track the distribution, not one number, and do not use it to punish.
- Cone of uncertainty position – the width of the estimated range at each milestone. Caveat: a range that widens signals re-opened scope, not a better estimate.
- Earned value indicators for baselined projects – planned value, earned value, actual cost, schedule and cost variance, SPI and CPI, and estimate at completion. Caveat: they need a scope statement, a WBS and a baseline, and they measure cost and schedule, not value.
- Velocity (story points per sprint) – a team-specific planning aid. Caveat: meaningless across teams, and harmful as a productivity target (Fowler, Atlassian, Jeffries).
- Flow metrics – throughput, cycle time, work item age and WIP (Kanban Guide); a service level expectation such as "85 percent of items finish in eight days or less". Caveat: they need a consistent definition of when an item starts and finishes, and they describe flow, not value.
- Probabilistic forecasts – Monte Carlo "when" and "how many" results at 50/70/85/95 percent confidence. Caveat: only as good as the stability and representativeness of the historical throughput.
- Burn-down and burn-up charts, cumulative flow, milestone hit rate and release predictability. Caveat: Scrum notes that they do not replace empiricism.
- Scope change – requirements churn (McConnell cites about 25 percent growth on average), the percentage of Must Haves (DSDM: over 60 percent is a risk), and the number of open dependencies. Caveat: some growth is normal; the signal is in the trend and in the response, not in a zero target.
- Risk exposure (probability × loss), the number of open top-ten risks, risk burndown, and whether treatments actually reduce exposure. Caveat: beware the "sea of green" – a register where every risk shows green.
- DORA delivery metrics (deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time, deployment rework rate) at the application level. Caveat: outcome context, not targets.
- Working software and stakeholder acceptance as the primary progress measure (Agile Manifesto principle 7; GOV.UK "see the thing"); stakeholder satisfaction at reviews. Caveat: it needs a shared Definition of Done, or "working" means different things to different people.
- Caveat for all metrics: SWEBOK warns that measurement without management lacks purpose. Pick measures from information needs (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15939) and review them in retrospectives.

### Failure modes

- Commitments to dates and budgets at concept or product-definition time, when estimates carry 2x–4x error; the team then manages to the commitment instead of to reality (Construx cone). It hurts because the commitment cannot be met, and the project hides the truth to protect it.
- Optimism bias and strategic misrepresentation: inside-view estimates that ignore how similar projects actually went (Flyvbjerg); overly optimistic schedules are a classic mistake (McConnell). It hurts because the plan starts wrong, and every later decision builds on that error.
- Estimates treated as commitments, and people blamed for misses (Agile Alliance, Atlassian, Jeffries). It hurts because future estimates inflate and people hide information.
- People added to a late project (Brooks's law), with no allowance for communication overhead and ramp-up time. It hurts because the project gets later, not earlier.
- The plan abandoned under pressure without re-planning, which drifts into code-and-fix (McConnell). It hurts because nobody then knows what is left, or when it will be done.
- Uncontrolled scope growth and gold plating with no change control; or the opposite, a Definition of Ready used as a stage gate that recreates waterfall hand-offs. It hurts because the first floods the team and the second starves it.
- Everything marked Must Have (DSDM), or a backlog where deep items are estimated in detail and near items are vague (Atlassian). It hurts because there is no room to flex, and effort goes into items that will change.
- Roadmaps that are not updated, so stakeholders stop trusting them and interrupt the team for status (Atlassian, GOV.UK). It hurts because the team loses focus and the roadmap loses its purpose.
- Velocity or story points used to compare teams or as a productivity target; metric quotas that teams then game (Fowler, DORA). It hurts because the numbers are no longer honest, and the planning signal is lost.
- Risk management done only for reviews: long lists with no prioritization, an automatic "mitigate" choice, treatment plans that look green while the risk is unchanged, and no continuous identification (SEBoK pitfalls). It hurts because the risks on Boehm's top-ten list then materialize. That list names personnel shortfalls, unrealistic schedules and budgets, wrong functions, wrong UI and gold plating. It also names requirements churn, external component and task shortfalls, performance shortfalls, and strain on the state of the art.
- Forecasts from known work only, with emergent work ignored (Cohn), or forecasts from unstable throughput with too little data (Monte Carlo caveat). It hurts because the forecast promises more than the team can deliver.
- Dependencies discovered in the middle of a sprint or increment, because the backlogs were not refined across teams (Nexus, SAFe). It hurts because teams wait, and integration fails.
- Upstream activities (requirements, architecture) shortchanged to start coding sooner (McConnell). It hurts because it multiplies the later cost.
- Measurement without management, or management without measurement; reports full of internal detail that do not answer the question of the audience (SWEBOK). It hurts because decisions are then made late or blind.
- Planning effort out of proportion to the risk: heavyweight plans on a small repository, or no written scope, done criteria or risk list on a large one. It hurts because the first wastes effort, and the second leaves the project without a shared reference.

### Tailoring by project size

Some things are essential at every scale:

- A written goal and scope, including what is out of scope
- One ordered list of work
- Small slices with a clear done criterion
- A short risk list with owners
- A visible status, and re-planning after each slice
- A record of significant decisions
- Estimates in ranges, made only when a decision needs them; estimates never turned into blame; forecasts updated from real data

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| Solo developer on a small repository | Use GitHub or GitLab issues for tasks and bugs, labels and milestones for groups and due dates, and sub-issues or a TODO or PLAN file for decomposition. Add a project board or a roadmap view if there are more than a handful of items. Count finished issues per week as throughput. Use milestones as releases. Write a three-line risk note and a decision log in the repository. A plan file plus milestones is enough; the main risk is that nothing is written down. | Story points, a WBS, earned value and formal risk plans; skip them. |
| Small product team | Pick Scrum or Kanban. Hold sprint planning with a sprint goal, or run continuous flow with WIP limits. Estimate with planning poker, or simply slice small and count. Keep a single refined backlog with one owner, a Definition of Done, a now-next-later roadmap reviewed at least quarterly, and a release forecast from velocity or throughput (Monte Carlo when the data allows). Keep a lightweight risk register reviewed in retrospectives. Demo to stakeholders every iteration. Use WSJF, RICE or MoSCoW to make priorities explicit. | Function points, COCOMO, earned value and formal plans. |
| Large or regulated organization | Implement the 12207 technical management processes as outcomes: a baselined project plan, WBS, schedule, budget and staff profile; a risk management plan and register aligned to ISO 31000 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 16085; decision management records; a measurement program per ISO/IEC/IEEE 15939; and defined reviews and reports to governance. Coordinate many teams with cross-team refinement, PI Planning or a Nexus-style integration team, and reduce dependencies through team design. Keep the agile essentials inside that frame: small batches, empirical forecasts, explicit prioritization, and governance that verifies by a look at working software rather than at paperwork. | Calibrated parametric models (COCOMO II, function points) and reference classes, when a bid or a budget needs them; earned value, when a contract requires it. |

### Sources

- [Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge v4.0, Chapter 9 Software Engineering Management (IEEE Computer Society)](https://ieeecs-media.computer.org/media/education/swebok/swebok-v4.pdf) – Primary knowledge area text; topic breakdown (initiation and scope, project planning, enactment, review and evaluation, closure, measurement, tools), estimation guidance, risk, RACI, plan management, predictive–adaptive continuum
- [The Scrum Guide (2020)](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html) – Sprint Planning topics, Product Goal and Sprint Goal, Product Backlog refinement, Definition of Done, sizing by the Developers, empiricism and forecasts
- [Software Development's Cone of Uncertainty (Construx white paper, McConnell)](https://www.construx.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/CxWhitePaper_ConeOfUncertainty.pdf) – Cone ranges (4x to 0.25x), cloud of uncertainty, narrowing only through decisions, commitment timing, iterative projects
- [The Cone of Uncertainty (Construx web page)](https://www.construx.com/books/the-cone-of-uncertainty/) – Same material in web form; used to confirm quotations
- [17 Theses on Software Estimation (Steve McConnell)](https://stevemcconnell.com/blog/17-theses-software-estimation/) – Estimation as a skill, estimates versus targets versus commitments, response to #NoEstimates
- [Classic Mistakes Enumerated (Steve McConnell, Rapid Development)](https://stevemcconnell.com/articles/classic-mistakes/) – Planning, schedule and scope mistakes: abandoned plans, overly optimistic schedules, feature creep, people added late
- [Software Risk Management: Principles and Practices (Boehm, IEEE Software 1991)](https://www.cs.virginia.edu/~sherriff/papers/Boehm%20-%201991.pdf) – Risk exposure = probability × loss; risk assessment and control steps; top-ten risk list; risk management plans; top-ten tracking
- [COCOMO II Model Definition Manual (USC CSSE)](https://athena.ecs.csus.edu/~buckley/CSc231_files/Cocomo_II_Manual.pdf) – Three submodels, nominal effort equation, scale factors PREC/FLEX/RESL/TEAM/PMAT, 7 and 17 effort multipliers, schedule equation, SLOC and function point sizing, range estimates versus phase
- [COCOMO II (Boehm CSSE)](https://boehmcsse.org/tools/cocomo-ii/) – Overview and purpose of COCOMO II
- [PurposeOfEstimation (Martin Fowler)](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/PurposeOfEstimation.html) – Estimate only when a significant decision depends on it; coordination and resource allocation purposes
- [XpVelocity (Martin Fowler)](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/XpVelocity.html) – Velocity, yesterday's weather, not a productivity measure
- [FixedPrice (Martin Fowler)](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/FixedPrice.html) – Fixed price versus fixed scope; fix budget and date, flex scope
- [Planning Poker (Mountain Goat Software)](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/agile/planning-poker) – Procedure, card values, anchoring avoidance, value of the conversation
- [What Are Story Points? (Mountain Goat Software)](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/blog/what-are-story-points) – Relative effort that combines work, complexity and risk; not hours; velocity
- [Agile Planning and Forecasting (Mountain Goat Software)](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/agile/agile-planning-and-forecasting) – Fixed date versus fixed scope, velocity ranges, unknown work, a forecast is not a commitment
- [The Agile Planning Process Explained (Mountain Goat Software)](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/blog/why-do-release-planning) – Planning levels, and why milestone or release planning is needed
- [Agile Estimating and Planning (Mountain Goat Software book page)](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/books/agile-estimating-and-planning) – Book structure: size versus duration, velocity, prioritization, buffers
- [Definition of Ready: What It Is and Why It's Dangerous (Mountain Goat Software)](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/agile/the-dangers-of-a-definition-of-ready) – DoR as a guideline versus a stage gate
- [The Definition of Ready (Roman Pichler)](https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/the-definition-of-ready/) – Clear, feasible, testable criteria; caveat that collaboration matters more than the artifact
- [The NoEstimates Movement (Ron Jeffries)](https://ronjeffries.com/xprog/articles/the-noestimates-movement/) – What #NoEstimates proposes and its open questions
