- [Estimation (Agile Alliance glossary)](https://www.agilealliance.org/glossary/estimation/) – Pitfalls: point estimates, estimates as commitments, estimates as final
- [Principles behind the Agile Manifesto](https://agilemanifesto.org/principles.html) – Working software as the progress measure, welcome change, sustainable pace, retrospectives
- [Working in small batches (DORA capabilities)](https://dora.dev/capabilities/working-in-small-batches/) – Slice work to a week or less, INVEST, faster feedback
- [DORA's software delivery metrics: the four keys](https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics-four-keys/) – Five delivery metrics, application-level use, warning against targets and team comparison
- [User Story Mapping (Jeff Patton & Associates)](https://www.jpattonassociates.com/story-mapping/) – Story maps organized by user journey to slice releases
- [Chapter 23 Project planning (Sommerville, Software Engineering 10th ed. slides)](http://www.slideshare.net/software-engineering-book/ch23-project-planning) – Price decisions, plan-driven planning, plan sections, bar charts and activity networks, estimation uncertainty, COCOMO 2
- [Software Engineering book presentations index (Sommerville)](https://software-engineering-book.com/slides/) – Index of chapter slides, including chapter 22 project management and chapter 23 project planning

## 5. Requirements engineering

### Purpose

Requirements engineering answers three questions: what problem do we solve, for whom do we solve it, and how will we know that the solution is right? ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 defines it as the interdisciplinary function that mediates between the acquirer and the supplier to establish and maintain the requirements for a system, software or service. SWEBOK v4 frames it as two jobs. Requirements development is "reaching an agreement on what software is to be constructed". Requirements management is "maintaining that agreement over time".

The phase exists because the two largest requirements problems, incompleteness and ambiguity, cause cascading rework in design, code and tests (SWEBOK). A requirements defect found late costs 10 to 200 times more to fix than a defect found at the source (McConnell, Sommerville). IREB states the value principle: a requirement is a means to an end, and its value is its benefit minus the cost to elicit, document, validate and manage it. The output of the phase is a shared, validated understanding, recorded at the level of detail that the project risk demands.

### Other names

- Software requirements (the SWEBOK knowledge area)
- Requirements development and requirements management (Wiegers and Beatty)
- Requirements analysis, requirements definition
- Stakeholder needs and requirements definition; system and software requirements definition (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288, 12207 and 29148)
- Requirements capture, requirements discovery, requirements acquisition (SWEBOK names for elicitation)
- Business analysis (BABOK, IIBA)
- Product discovery (Cagan, SVPG)
- User research and user needs (GOV.UK Service Manual)
- Product backlog refinement (Scrum)
- Specification by example, behavior-driven development (the specification side of BDD)
- Specification, SRS writing

### Position in the life cycle

Requirements work starts after concept and feasibility (see section 3). The business case, the vision and scope, and the concept of operations are its inputs. Its results feed architecture (see section 6), detailed design (see section 7), construction (see section 8) and testing (see section 9). SWEBOK stresses that the "whats and hows" of requirements work depend on the nature of the software, not on the life cycle model. The life cycle model only decides when the work happens (see section 2).

In waterfall, all requirements work sits in one early phase, and it must be mostly complete before design starts. In the V-model, the stakeholder, system and software requirements on the left side pair with the acceptance, system and integration tests on the right side. Each requirement therefore needs a verification method; 29148 names test, demonstration, inspection and analysis as the attribute values. In iterative models such as the Unified Process, the high-level requirements come in inception, and the detail comes in elaboration.

In agile, requirements work is incremental and just in time. The Scrum Guide calls the Product Backlog "an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product", and refinement is an ongoing activity. A change request becomes a backlog item (SWEBOK, IREB). In DevOps and continuous delivery, requirements become small slices with acceptance criteria. The criteria turn into automated acceptance tests, and validation moves partly into production through A/B tests, beta releases and MVPs (IREB validation techniques; see sections 10 and 11).

SWEBOK and IREB agree that requirements work is not a one-time front-end activity. It is a process that continues over the whole service life. IREB Principle 7 says that changing requirements are the normal case. The requirements record also serves maintenance (see section 13): it captures the intent, so that a later maintainer can tell a defect from a feature (SWEBOK).

### Inputs

- Business requirements, the vision and scope, or the product goal (from concept and feasibility); the business case with its objectives and success metrics
- The concept of operations or operational concept, and any contract or statement of work (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 information items)
- An initial stakeholder list and a sponsor; the known user classes; access to real users or to user representatives
- Existing and legacy systems with their requirements and defect databases, interfacing systems, and competitor products (SWEBOK and IREB requirement sources)
- Business process documents, organizational policies, business rules, glossaries, market research, analytics and support logs (GOV.UK: examine the existing evidence first)
- Laws, regulations, standards and contractual obligations that impose requirements (GDPR, WCAG, IEC 62304, safety and security standards)
- Project constraints: budget, schedule, staffing, mandated technology, platform and deployment environment
- A quality model to use as a checklist for quality requirements (ISO/IEC 25010:2023), and a security threat model or another source of security requirements (see section 16)
- A chosen requirements approach: which work products, which abstraction levels, which level of detail, which templates and which tools (IREB 3.1.6, SWEBOK audience analysis)
- For a continuing product: the current requirements baseline or backlog, the traceability data and the change log
- Entry criteria: a sponsor and the decision makers are identified; the problem or opportunity is stated; the system boundary is roughly known; stakeholders are available for feedback

### Activities

- **Define the system context, boundary and scope** – Draw the system boundary and the context boundary. List the external actors and interfaces. Keep an in/out list of what is in scope. IREB Principle 4 says that a system cannot be understood in isolation, so the clarification of the boundary is a genuine requirements task. Cockburn starts use case writing with the system scope and a context diagram. The result is a context diagram, a scope statement and the list of external interfaces, which later bounds every requirement.
- **Identify stakeholders, user classes and decision makers** – Find every person, group or organization that is involved, affected or influential. Include regulators, operations, support, and people who are harmed if the project succeeds (SWEBOK). Group users into user classes by task, privilege, frequency and expertise. Mark favored, disfavored and ignored classes. Write personas where real users are unknown (Wiegers and Beatty ch. 6, IREB 4.1). Agree who decides requirement conflicts: Wiegers recommends a product champion per user class, and Scrum uses a product owner. The output is a stakeholder list with role, availability, relevance and interests, plus a decision-rights agreement.
- **Plan the requirements approach** – Decide which work products to create, at which abstraction level and level of detail, and with which templates, tools and process configuration. IREB lists the factors: shared understanding, design freedom, speed of stakeholder feedback, cost versus value, and imposed standards. Its process facets are linear versus iterative, prescriptive versus explorative, and customer-specific versus market-oriented. SWEBOK recommends an audience analysis: who consumes the specification, and what each consumer needs. The output is a short requirements plan or a team agreement.
- **Elicit requirements from people** – Use several techniques, because no single technique finds all requirements: interviews, facilitated workshops (JAD, JRP, requirements workshops), focus groups, brainstorming, questionnaires and surveys, contextual observation and apprenticing, user story mapping, and low- or high-fidelity prototypes (SWEBOK 2.2, IREB 4.2, GOV.UK user research). GOV.UK stresses research with diverse and struggling users, not only typical ones. Contextual observation reveals barriers that users cannot self-report. Elicitation is active work: users leave important things unstated, and many requirements are tacit (SWEBOK). The output is a set of raw findings, notes, recordings and candidate requirements.
- **Elicit requirements from documents and systems** – Analyze previous versions, defect databases, interfacing systems, process documents, business rules, legal and regulatory texts, competitor products and standards (SWEBOK, IREB). Walk a quality model such as ISO/IEC 25010 as a checklist, so that quality requirements and constraints get attention; IREB notes that they are often neglected. This produces candidate quality requirements, constraints and business rules, with their sources recorded.
- **Analyze and model requirements** – Turn raw input into understood needs. Classify each statement as a functional requirement, a quality requirement or a constraint (IREB). SWEBOK splits nonfunctional requirements into technology constraints and quality-of-service constraints, and it uses the Perfect Technology Filter to separate the two. Ask why repeatedly (5 whys) to find the problem behind a stated solution (SWEBOK). Build models where they help: context, use case, class or data, activity or process, and state models (IREB 3.4, SWEBOK model-based specification). Decompose epics into features and stories, define data and business rules, and find derived requirements. The output is an analyzed, organized set of requirements and models.
- **Negotiate and resolve conflicts** – More stakeholders bring more conflicting requirements. The engineer should not decide alone; the engineer should bring the stakeholders to consensus and keep the decision traceable (SWEBOK 3.4). IREB names the conflict types (subject matter, data, interest, value, relationship, structural) and the resolution techniques: agreement, compromise, voting, overruling, and definition of variants, supported by decision matrices. Wiegers gives decision rules, for example favored user classes win between user classes, and business objectives settle conflicts between corporate customers. For quality-of-service levels, SWEBOK recommends an economic view: find the most cost-effective performance level between the fail point and the perfection point. The output is a set of agreed requirements and a decision record.
- **Specify requirements in a fit-for-purpose format** – Record requirements so that they can be remembered and communicated (SWEBOK). Choose among natural language sentences; structured templates such as EARS ("While..., when..., the system shall..."), the user story ("As a..., I want..., so that..."), the job story ("When..., I want to..., so I can...") and the Cockburn use case form (primary actor, goal level, preconditions, guarantees, main success scenario, extensions); acceptance-criteria based specifications (ATDD, BDD with Given-When-Then in Gherkin); and models or formal notations. For comprehensive documents, use the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 information items (StRS, SyRS, SRS) or the Volere template. Give each requirement an ID and attributes such as rationale, source, priority, type, acceptance criteria and status (SWEBOK 4.5, 29148). The output is the specification or the backlog. The table below compares the formats.
- **Specify quality requirements and constraints measurably** – State each quality attribute with a scale and a target, so that it can be verified. Volere calls this the fit criterion; Gilb's Planguage uses scale, meter, minimum and target (SWEBOK). Use the nine ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics (functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility, safety) and their sub-characteristics to find and name them. Record constraints separately: 29148 defines a constraint as an externally imposed limitation on the system, its design, its implementation or its process. The output is a set of verifiable quality requirements and a constraints list.
- **Capture regulatory, legal and compliance requirements** – Identify the laws, standards and policies that impose requirements, and turn them into traceable requirements with their source. Examples: GDPR Article 25 demands data protection by design and by default at the time the means of processing are determined. WCAG levels A, AA and AAA are referenced by accessibility laws and by EN 301 549. IEC 62304 requires a software requirements specification that includes risk control measures; the requirements must be traceable, unambiguous, testable and consistent, scaled by safety class. The FDA 2023 premarket guidance asks for an SRS that is evaluated for accuracy, completeness, consistency, testability, correctness and clarity, and that is traced to hazards and tests. The output is a compliance requirements set with evidence links (see section 16).
- **Verify requirement quality (requirements verification)** – Check that each requirement and the full set are well-formed before the validation with stakeholders; 29148 calls this requirements verification. Use its characteristics: an individual requirement is necessary, appropriate, unambiguous, complete, singular, feasible, verifiable, correct and conforming; a set is complete, consistent, feasible, comprehensible and able to be validated. Apply writing rules (INCOSE Guide to Writing Requirements: active voice, defined terms, no vague terms, no escape clauses, one thought per statement, no "and/or", consistent units). Hunt requirements smells: subjective language, ambiguous adverbs and adjectives, loopholes, open-ended non-verifiable terms, superlatives, comparatives, negative statements, vague pronouns and incomplete references (Femmer et al.). Maintain a glossary (IREB). The output is a set of corrected requirements and a defect list.
- **Validate requirements with stakeholders** – Gain confidence that the requirements represent the true needs (SWEBOK). In 29148, requirements validation confirms the right system as intended by the stakeholders. Techniques: reviews, walkthroughs and inspections from several perspectives (users check the needs, specialists check the form, builders check the sufficiency); simulation or execution of models; prototypes (wireframes, mock-ups, native prototypes); alpha and beta tests; A/B tests and MVPs (SWEBOK 5, IREB 4.4, Sommerville). IREB stresses four points: involve the right stakeholders, separate defect finding from defect fixing, validate from different views, and repeat the validation. The output is a set of validation records, accepted requirements and change requests.
- **Define acceptance criteria and concrete examples** – Before implementation, the three amigos (business, development, testing) agree what to build and how they will know that it is done (Agile Alliance). Example mapping turns a story into rules, examples and open questions in about 25 minutes (Cucumber). The examples become Given-When-Then scenarios that are both documentation and executable tests (Cucumber, Fowler, North). GOV.UK writes criteria as "it's done when..."; Cohn calls them conditions of satisfaction and values the shared understanding over the wording. SWEBOK notes that ATDD and BDD attack ambiguity but not incompleteness, so combine them with coverage techniques. The output is a set of acceptance criteria and scenarios per item, plus a question list.
- **Prioritize and scrub requirements** – Not all requirements are equal (IREB). Set goals and criteria, choose a technique, involve the right stakeholders, then prioritize (IREB 6.8). Techniques: MoSCoW, with Must Haves at no more than about 60 percent of the effort and Could Haves as contingency (DSDM); Kano classes (must-be, performance, attractive, indifferent, reverse) to weigh dissatisfaction as well as satisfaction (SWEBOK); cost of delay and WSJF, which is the cost of delay divided by the job size (Reinertsen, SAFe); RICE, which is reach × impact × confidence / effort (Intercom); and value, cost and risk formulas (SWEBOK). Requirements scrubbing removes out-of-scope, low-return and unimportant requirements and simplifies complex ones. Scope matching keeps the scope within cost, schedule and staffing (SWEBOK). The output is an ordered backlog or a prioritized baseline. The second table below compares the techniques.
- **Baseline, version and track status** – Put requirements under configuration management like any other deliverable (SWEBOK). A baseline is a formally approved, fixed version of a configuration item (29148). IREB adds configurations (consistent sets of work product versions), version control with a version number, a change history and storage, and a status life cycle per requirement (created, reviewed, agreed, implemented). Record attributes, and use views (selective, projective, aggregating) for reports (IREB 6.5). The output is a set of identified, versioned and statused requirements, and a baseline for planning or for a contract.
- **Trace requirements** – Link each requirement backward to its source (a stakeholder, a regulation, a higher-level requirement) and forward to design, code, tests and user documentation (SWEBOK 7.3, IREB 6.6, 29148 traceability matrix). Tracing serves two purposes: consistency checks (every requirement has design and tests, every element has a requirement) and impact analysis of changes. Standards and regulators often demand traceability (IREB, IEC 62304, FDA), and tools usually support it. Implicit traceability through structure is the lightweight alternative. The output is a set of traceability links or a matrix.
- **Control change** – Plan-driven projects need an explicit process: a request, an optional impact analysis, a decision body (the change control board), notification, and tracking to closure. Everyone must accept that a change changes the schedule, the cost or the scope (SWEBOK 6.2, Sommerville). In agile, a change is another backlog item that the product owner orders; it is accepted when it enters a sprint (SWEBOK, IREB 6.7). Identify volatile requirements early, so that the design tolerates change (SWEBOK 7.4). The output is a change log and an updated baseline or backlog.
- **Refine the backlog continuously and keep items ready** – Break large items (epics) into smaller, more precise items with a description, an order and a size (Scrum Guide refinement; Cohn: detailed enough for the next decision). Check stories against INVEST (independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable; Wake) and the three Cs (card, conversation, confirmation). Use a story map to keep the backbone and the walking skeleton visible and to slice releases (Patton). Some teams adopt a Definition of Ready as an explicit entry agreement (Agile Alliance); see the contested points. The output is a refined, ordered backlog.
- **Measure and improve the requirements process** – Size requirements (function points, story points) to support estimation and to measure change. Track volatility, review defect density, and requirements-related defects found downstream (SWEBOK 7.5, 7.6). Use the findings to adjust elicitation coverage, templates, review checklists and tool support. The output is a set of metrics and process changes.
- **Keep requirements as living documentation for maintenance** – Keep the specification, the backlog or the executable specifications current, so that maintainers can recover the intent years later (SWEBOK: requirements capture intent for engineers who did not write the code). Adzic's living documentation keeps executable specifications and prose in sync. SWEBOK notes that startups later need to recover the requirements behind features to assess change impact. The output is an up-to-date requirements record tied to the released product.

The specification formats compare as follows.

| Format | Shape | Typical use | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Natural language sentence | Free prose, often with "shall"; needs language rules, a glossary and reviews | Any domain; the most common form | SWEBOK, IREB, 29148 |
| EARS | "While..., when..., the system shall..."; patterns: ubiquitous, state-driven, event-driven, optional, unwanted behavior, complex | Systems, embedded and regulated work; origin at Rolls-Royce in 2009 | Mavin |
| User story | "As a..., I want..., so that...", plus acceptance criteria and a conversation; three Cs | Agile product teams; the default backlog unit | Cohn, GOV.UK, Scrum Guide |
| Job story | "When..., I want to..., so I can..."; situation, motivation, outcome | Product design where persona-based stories hide causality | Klement, Intercom |
| Use case | Primary actor, goal level, preconditions, guarantees, main success scenario, extensions | Interaction sequences with alternatives; systems with many actors | Cockburn |
| Gherkin scenario | Given-When-Then, executable with Cucumber | Acceptance criteria that become automated tests and living documentation | Cucumber, Fowler, North, Adzic |
| 29148 information items, Volere template | StRS, SyRS and SRS sections; the Volere requirement shell with a fit criterion | Comprehensive documents, contracts, regulated work | ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Volere |
| Models and formal notations | Context, use case, class or data, activity or process, and state models; formal methods | Complex behavior; high-integrity subsystems | IREB 3.4, SWEBOK |

The prioritization techniques compare as follows.

| Technique | Mechanism | Caveat | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MoSCoW | Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have this time; Must Haves at most about 60 percent of the effort, Could Haves about 20 percent as contingency | Bands, not ranks; too many Must Haves remove the contingency | DSDM (Agile Business Consortium) |
| Kano model | Classes must-be, performance, attractive, indifferent and reverse, derived from a paired questionnaire and an evaluation table | Delighters decay into must-be features over time; dissatisfaction from absence must count | Folding Burritos, SWEBOK |
| Cost of delay and WSJF | WSJF = cost of delay / job size; cost of delay combines user and business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement | Estimates have wide error bars; Black Swan Farming prefers money values and CD3 | Reinertsen, SAFe, Black Swan Farming |
| RICE | (reach × impact × confidence) / effort | A decision aid; dependencies or table stakes can override it | Intercom |
| Value, cost and risk formulas | A weighted value against cost and risk per requirement | Overly rigorous scales invite debate over small differences | SWEBOK |
| Requirements scrubbing and scope matching | Remove out-of-scope, low-return and unimportant requirements; simplify complex ones; fit the scope to cost, schedule and staffing | Needs a decision owner and a record of what was removed | SWEBOK |

### Outputs

- A stakeholder list, a user class table and personas, with the decision makers named
- A context diagram, the system boundary, an in/out scope list and an external interface list
- A glossary of domain terms
- A requirements record in the chosen form: a StRS, SyRS and SRS per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 or a Volere document; or a product backlog with epics, user stories or job stories, acceptance criteria and a story map; or use cases; or executable specifications (Gherkin feature files)
- Requirements models where used: use case diagrams, class or data models, activity or process models, state machines; a data dictionary and business rules
- Quality requirements with fit criteria or Planguage targets, organized by the ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics; a constraints list; a compliance requirements set with sources
- Prototypes (wireframes, mock-ups, native prototypes) and the validation feedback that they produced
- Per-requirement attributes: ID, type, priority, rationale, source, owner, status, verification method, acceptance criteria, dependencies, risk, stability
- A prioritized and ordered set: MoSCoW classes, WSJF or RICE scores, or an ordered backlog; release slices
- A baseline (approved, versioned, change-controlled) or sprint-ready backlog items; the configuration and version history
- Traceability links or a matrix: source to requirement to design, code and tests; hazard to risk control to test in regulated products
- Validation and verification records: review and inspection reports, defect lists, sign-offs, decision and conflict resolution records, the change log
- Exit criteria: the stakeholders agree that the set defines the right system (29148 validation); each requirement is verifiable and unambiguous; each backlog item that is ready for a sprint has acceptance criteria and a size; a regulated SRS is evaluated for accuracy, completeness, consistency, testability, correctness and clarity (FDA) and traced to risk controls and tests (IEC 62304); a baseline exists where contracts or regulators demand it

### Roles

- Business analyst or requirements engineer – leads elicitation, analysis, specification, verification and validation; writes the requirements (Wiegers: users should not be expected to write them); maintains the glossary and the traceability. IREB notes that product owners, systems engineers and developers often fill this role.
- Product owner or product manager – owns the product goal; creates, communicates and orders the backlog items; decides the priority and accepts change (Scrum Guide). In Wiegers' view the role spans the business, user and functional levels.
- Stakeholders – clients who pay, customers who accept, users by class, subject matter experts, operations and support staff, marketing, regulators, professional bodies, and people who are negatively affected (SWEBOK). They supply needs, and they review and validate.
- Product champions or user representatives – actual users who speak for one user class, gather input from peers, resolve conflicts within the class, evaluate prototypes and define acceptance criteria (Wiegers and Beatty ch. 6).
- User researcher and UX or service designer – run interviews, contextual observation and usability tests, and synthesize the user needs (GOV.UK Service Manual).
- Developers and architects – review feasibility and cost, estimate, join three-amigos sessions, derive requirements for sub-teams, and build prototypes (SWEBOK review perspectives).
- Testers or QA – ask "what could happen", write and automate acceptance tests from examples, and check verifiability (Agile Alliance three amigos, Cucumber).
- Sponsor, management and the change control board – approve the scope, the business priorities, the budget and the baselines; decide formal change requests (SWEBOK, IREB).
- Legal, compliance, privacy, safety and security specialists – supply regulatory and security requirements, risk control measures and audit evidence (IEC 62304, GDPR, WCAG).
- Technical writer – turns requirements into user documentation, which can itself serve as part of the specification (SWEBOK, McConnell).
- Solo developer – performs all of the above in miniature: writes the README as the specification, uses issue templates, and decides and records the priorities.

### Practices with consensus

- **Involve real users and stakeholders continuously, not once at the start** – A lack of user involvement is a leading cause of failure. Customers often do not know what they need until they see it, and written documents cannot replace an ongoing conversation. Evidence: Wiegers and Beatty (ch. 6); GOV.UK Service Manual (user research, writing user stories); Scrum Guide (Sprint Review); McConnell (early end-user involvement); Cagan (product discovery).
- **Identify all stakeholder classes and all requirement sources, then pick representatives per class** – A missed source yields incomplete requirements and a bias toward the loudest or best-represented group. Favored and disfavored user classes need different treatment. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 (2.1 requirements sources, stakeholder analysis); IREB syllabus (4.1 stakeholders, documents, systems); Wiegers and Beatty (user classes, product champions).
- **Combine several elicitation techniques, including observation in context, not only interviews** – Users leave tacit knowledge unstated. Observation and apprenticing reveal workarounds and barriers that interviews miss, and creativity techniques find delighters. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 (2.2); IREB (gathering versus design and idea-generating techniques, Kano); GOV.UK (contextual research and observation); Sommerville ch. 4 (interviewing, ethnography, scenarios).
- **Separate the problem and the need from the solution; ask why** – Stakeholders often state solutions. A record of the underlying need keeps the design options open and makes the requirement testable against the real problem. Evidence: SWEBOK (5 whys); IREB Principle 5 (problem, requirement, solution); Cockburn (ask why to find the higher goal); Klement and Intercom (job stories decouple motivation from implementation); INCOSE rule R31 (solution-free).
- **Write each requirement so that it is unambiguous, verifiable, necessary, singular, feasible and complete, and keep the set consistent, complete and traceable** – These characteristics let testers verify, developers build and stakeholders agree. They are the shared core of every major standard and textbook. Evidence: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (characteristics); INCOSE Guide to Writing Requirements; Wiegers (Writing Quality Requirements); IREB (3.8 quality criteria); SWEBOK (3.1 desirable properties); IEC 62304 (traceable, unambiguous, testable, consistent).
- **Control the language: defined terms in a glossary, active voice, no vague or subjective words, no escape clauses, one thought per statement** – Natural language is inherently ambiguous. Language rules and smell detection catch a large share of defects cheaply, as a supplement to reviews. Evidence: INCOSE rules; Wiegers (avoid "user-friendly", "fast", "several"); IREB (pitfalls: unspecific nouns, incomplete conditions, passive voice, universal quantifiers); Femmer et al. (requirements smells); 29148 language criteria.
- **Use structured templates to reduce ambiguity and omissions: EARS, the user story phrase, the use case form, Gherkin** – Templates make requirements uniform, and they force the essential information (trigger, actor, response, benefit, acceptance) to be stated. Evidence: IREB (template-based work products); Mavin (EARS); Cohn (user story template); Cockburn (use case template); Cucumber Gherkin reference; SWEBOK (structured natural language, actor-action, BDD).
- **Specify quality requirements with a measurable target, and use a quality model as a checklist** – Unquantified quality requirements cannot be verified or traded off. Quality requirements and constraints are systematically under-elicited. Evidence: ISO/IEC 25010:2023; SWEBOK (quality-of-service constraints, Planguage attributes); Volere (fit criterion); IREB (ISO 25010 as a checklist); Wiegers (verifiable).
- **Agree concrete examples and acceptance criteria before implementation, and make them executable where practical** – Examples are easier for non-engineers to produce and check than abstract rules. Executable specifications double as regression tests and living documentation. Evidence: Fowler (Specification by Example, Given-When-Then); Cucumber (BDD discovery, formulation, automation; example mapping); Agile Alliance (three amigos, acceptance testing); SWEBOK (acceptance-criteria-based specification); GOV.UK (acceptance criteria); Adzic (Specification by Example).
- **Validate requirements early and from several perspectives, with reviews, prototypes and tests** – Requirements defects are cheapest to remove at the source. Reviewers with different perspectives find different defects, and prototypes expose assumptions that text hides. Evidence: SWEBOK (5 validation); IREB (4.4 review and exploratory techniques); Sommerville (reviews, prototyping, test-case generation); McConnell (10 to 100 times cost escalation); Wiegers (review requirements, evaluate prototypes).
- **Prioritize explicitly and in coarse bands rather than exact rankings; revisit priorities as you learn** – Not all requirements are equal. A fine-grained ranking wastes time and invites argument, while bands support timeboxing and scope negotiation. Evidence: SWEBOK (7.2: focus on groups with similar priority); DSDM MoSCoW (avoid debates over one place higher or lower); IREB (6.8); Scrum Guide (ordered backlog); Intercom (RICE scores are aids, not rules).
- **Expect change and handle it through a defined path: a change control board in plan-driven work, the backlog in iterative work** – Requirements evolve because business, law, technology and understanding change. Unmanaged change breaks the agreement, while rigid refusal produces the wrong system. Evidence: SWEBOK (6.2 change control); IREB Principle 7 and 6.7; Sommerville (requirements management); Scrum Guide (emergent backlog).
- **Give every requirement a unique identifier and attributes, keep artefacts under configuration management, and trace in proportion to risk and regulation** – Identifiers and attributes enable views, status tracking, impact analysis and audits. Baselines give a stable basis for contracts and releases. Evidence: SWEBOK (4.5 attributes, 7.3 tracing, configuration management); ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (baseline, traceability, attributes); IREB (6.2 to 6.6); Wiegers (modifiable, traceable); IEC 62304 and FDA guidance (mandatory traceability).
- **Tailor the requirements process and the level of detail to the context rather than copy a standard process** – No single process fits every project. The right amount of documentation depends on risk, domain familiarity, stakeholder availability, turnover, outsourcing and regulation. Evidence: SWEBOK (4 specification factors, tailoring to organization and project); IREB Principle 9 and chapter 5 process facets; 29148 (applicable regardless of project size or methodology); Cockburn ("sufficient is fine").

### Contested points

- **How much to specify up front and in writing (big requirements up front versus emergent requirements)** – SWEBOK calls specification "the most contentious topic" and says that there are no standard answers. The choice depends on domain familiarity, precedent, the risk of incorrect requirements, turnover, distribution, outsourcing, testing expectations and the contract. Sommerville reports the agile argument: direct customer feedback during development beats analysis and negotiation of requirements up front. McConnell defends upstream investment with defect cost data (10 to 200 times). Cohn argues that the cost-of-change curve is now far flatter, so specifications should evolve with the product, and the main cost is feedback delay. IREB gives criteria: choose a linear and prescriptive process when stakeholders know their needs, when a contract or regulator needs a complete specification, or when work is outsourced; choose an iterative and explorative process when needs emerge, when stakeholders give fast feedback, and when easy change matters.
- **Which representation to trust: natural language, models, or executable examples** – IREB and SWEBOK hold that natural language is expressive but ambiguous. Models reduce ambiguity, but they cannot express most quality requirements, and they must be kept consistent. Formal methods pay off in high-integrity systems, but they burden writers and readers. Fowler and SWEBOK hold that examples and acceptance tests are precise but always incomplete, so they must be backed by conversation and other mechanisms. Most sources recommend a combination of forms; the mix depends on the context.
- **User stories versus job stories versus use cases versus "shall" statements** – Cohn and GOV.UK treat user stories as the default unit, with acceptance criteria and conversation. Klement and Intercom argue that personas lack causality and that stories couple implementation with motivation; they prefer job stories (situation, motivation, outcome). Cockburn's use cases give goal levels, success scenarios and extensions, which stories lack. EARS and 29148-style "shall" statements suit systems work and regulated work. SWEBOK lists all of them as structured natural language options. The choice depends on the audience, the contract, and whether behavior over time or a single interaction is specified.
- **Single product owner versus multiple user representatives** – Scrum assigns one accountable Product Owner who orders the backlog. Wiegers and Beatty argue that one person rarely represents all user classes, and they recommend product champions per class, possibly under a lead product owner; both schemes can combine. Organizations choose based on size, the number of user classes and the decision-making culture.
- **Definition of Ready: helpful agreement or stage gate** – The Agile Alliance documents the Definition of Ready as explicit INVEST-based entry criteria that let teams push back on ill-defined items. The Scrum Guide does not define it, and many Scrum practitioners warn that it becomes a phase gate that reduces collaboration and gives false clarity. Teams that adopt it are advised to treat it as a guideline and to keep the conversation.
- **Numeric prioritization formulas versus categorical or judgement-based prioritization** – SAFe's WSJF and Intercom's RICE give scores that make trade-offs explicit; Black Swan Farming argues that teams should quantify the cost of delay in money. SWEBOK warns against overly rigorous scales and against debates over small differences; DSDM MoSCoW prefers bands; Intercom itself says that scores are decision aids that dependencies or table stakes can override. Kano shows that value alone misleads, because dissatisfaction from absence must count. The right tool depends on portfolio size, data availability and governance needs.
- **The functional versus non-functional split and the word "non-functional"** – SWEBOK keeps "nonfunctional" but divides it into technology constraints and quality-of-service constraints, and it uses the Perfect Technology Filter. IREB uses functional requirements, quality requirements and constraints. ISO/IEC 25010:2023 renamed usability to interaction capability and portability to flexibility, and it added safety, which shows that the taxonomy itself moves. Sommerville classifies non-functional requirements as product, organizational and external. Teams should pick one taxonomy and apply it consistently.
- **How much traceability and formal change control are worth outside regulated domains** – 29148, IEC 62304 and the FDA guidance require bidirectional traceability and baselines. SWEBOK says that the extent of tracing is a factor to decide, "if any", and notes that agile handles change implicitly through the backlog. IREB says that traceability is a prerequisite for requirements management but may be implicit through structure. Practice ranges from full matrices in safety-critical work to issue links and commit references in small teams.
- **Who writes the requirements** – Wiegers holds that the business analyst should write them, because users cannot be expected to write good requirements. GOV.UK says that every team member writes user stories, and Cohn says that the product owner need not write every item. The difference reflects the scale and formality of the product, and whether the artefact is a contract or a reminder of a conversation.
- **Whether the cost-of-defect multipliers still hold** – McConnell cites Boehm (50 to 200 times) and later Hughes data (about 10 times) and argues that prevention still pays. Cohn argues that modern tooling, automated tests and modular architecture flattened the curve. Both agree that requirements should be validated early; they disagree on how much to fix before coding versus after feedback.

### Metrics

- Requirements volume and size – the count of requirements, function points or story points, used to size the work and to measure change. Caveat: story points are team-relative and not comparable across teams (SWEBOK 7.5).
- Requirements volatility or churn – the share of baselined requirements added, changed or deleted per period. Caveat: high churn signals weak elicitation, an unstable business or healthy learning, so interpret it with context (SWEBOK 7.4, IREB Principle 7).
- Requirements review yield – defects found per page or per requirement in reviews and inspections, and the share of smells or rule violations. Caveat: automated smell detection has about 59 percent precision and needs human judgement (Femmer et al.).
- Escaped requirements defects – defects found in design, test or production whose root cause is a requirement; use them to estimate the cost escalation and to improve upstream practices (McConnell, Sommerville). Caveat: the root-cause classification needs a consistent rule, or the count is not comparable between periods.
- Coverage measures – the percentage of requirements with acceptance criteria, with a verification method, with at least one test, and traced to a source; the percentage of design elements and tests traced back to a requirement (SWEBOK tracing questions, IEC 62304, FDA). Caveat: coverage counts links; it does not measure the quality of the linked items.
- Ratio of Must Have effort in a timebox – DSDM advises no more than about 60 percent Must Haves and about 20 percent Could Haves as contingency. Caveat: more Must Haves raises the delivery risk, and the ratio only helps when the effort estimates are honest.
- Prioritization scores as decision aids – WSJF (cost of delay / job size), RICE ((reach × impact × confidence) / effort), and the Kano class per feature. Caveat: scores encode estimates with wide error bars and can be gamed, so use them to structure the debate, not to replace it (Intercom, SWEBOK).
- Cost of delay per week for a feature or for the portfolio queue (Reinertsen, Black Swan Farming). Caveat: it is hard to estimate, but it makes urgency and value explicit.
- Readiness and flow – the share of backlog items that meet INVEST or the team's readiness agreement, and the time from idea to validated requirement to release. Caveat: a readiness checklist can become a gate (Agile Alliance, Scrum.org debate).
- Stakeholder agreement and satisfaction – sign-off or acceptance rates, post-release user feedback, and Kano or satisfaction surveys against user classes. Caveat: GOV.UK stresses that outcomes for users are the real measure; a sign-off is not the same as a good outcome.
- Process quality indicators – requirements process coverage by improvement models, benchmarking, and planned improvements (SWEBOK 7.6). Caveat: indicators measure activity, not the rightness of the product.

### Failure modes

- Skipped or delegated user contact – a manager or marketing speaks for the users, or a single power user represents everyone (Wiegers' "voiceless user class"). The delivered system fits the surrogate, not the users.
- First stated wants treated as needs and coded – Wiegers and Cagan note that customers often do not know what they need until they see it. The result is a rebuild.
- Solutions confused with requirements – a stated design locks in a suboptimal solution and hides the real problem (SWEBOK 5 whys, IREB Principle 5, INCOSE R31).
- Ambiguous and unverifiable wording – "user-friendly", "fast", "as far as possible", superlatives and vague pronouns pass the review and fail in the test (Wiegers, Femmer et al., INCOSE). Each reader builds a different system.
- Neglected quality requirements, security and constraints – they stay hidden until architecture or operations exposes them, when a change is expensive (IREB; SWEBOK: safety and security are often overlooked).
- Template worship – every field of a form is filled, or every story is written as "As a user I want", without a conversation. IREB warns that people focus on formal completion rather than on content; Cohn and Cucumber stress the conversation. The artefact looks complete, and the understanding is missing.
- A flat backlog with hundreds of decontextualized items – nobody can explain what the system does or see the gaps (Patton).
- Too many Must Haves – when the Must Have effort exceeds about 60 percent, the timebox loses its contingency and its predictability (DSDM).
- Fine-grained priority rankings and numeric scores treated as truth – teams waste hours in arguments over one place up or down (SWEBOK, DSDM, Intercom), and the false precision hides the estimation error.
- Gold plating and scope creep through uncontrolled change – no impact analysis, no decision owner, "the customer is always right" (Wiegers, SWEBOK change control). The schedule and the cost drift without a decision.
- Frozen specifications that ignore learning – contractual baselines with no change process, or a refusal to revisit priorities after feedback (IREB: linear processes work only with a change process in place). The project delivers the wrong system on time.
- A Definition of Ready or review gates that stop collaboration – they create a mini-waterfall inside an iteration (Agile Alliance and Scrum community debate), and feedback slows down.
- No traceability in regulated or safety-critical work – the team cannot show that risk controls and tests cover the requirements, and the audit fails (IEC 62304, FDA).
- A spreadsheet or a chat as the requirements system of record for large or long-lived products – SWEBOK notes that ad hoc management is common and less satisfactory; IREB warns that office tools suit only stable, aligned requirements. Attributes, versions and links get lost.
- Dead documentation – the specification stops matching the product, so maintainers cannot tell defects from features (SWEBOK, Adzic living documentation).
- Prototype confusion – stakeholders judge the cosmetic details of a prototype instead of the behavior, or they treat a throwaway prototype as the product (SWEBOK). Validation feedback then answers the wrong question.
- Ignored context and assumptions – interfaces, regulations and environmental constraints outside the system boundary change and invalidate the requirements (IREB Principle 4).

### Tailoring by project size

Some elements are essential at every scale: know who the users and the stakeholders are; state the problem and the goal before the solution; write each requirement or story so that a reader can tell when it is done; record the priorities; keep a glossary of the few terms that matter; validate with a real user or a quick prototype before much is built; expect change and record it. IREB Principle 9 and 29148 both say that the process must fit the situation. The form scales; the intent does not.

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solo developer on a small repository | The README is the specification: write it first (Readme Driven Development) with the purpose, usage examples and non-goals; keep a short "scope and non-goals" list; track requirements as issues with an issue template or issue form that asks for the need, the context and the acceptance criteria (GitHub issue templates); write acceptance criteria as a checklist or as a few Given-When-Then cases that become tests; prioritize with a simple label or a MoSCoW-style tag; a traceability link is an issue number in the commit or the pull request; a CHANGELOG and the README act as the baseline | User stories, story maps, formal reviews |
| Small product team | A product owner or product manager with real user access; a product backlog of stories or job stories with acceptance criteria and INVEST checks; a story map for the backbone and for release slicing (Patton); three-amigos or example-mapping sessions per story (Cucumber, Agile Alliance); a one- or two-page requirements or discovery page per feature (objectives, background, assumptions, stories, open questions, not doing); lightweight user research (interviews, contextual observation, usability tests, per GOV.UK); a quality checklist from ISO 25010 for the attributes that matter (performance, security, accessibility); prioritization by MoSCoW, cost of delay or RICE, used as a conversation aid; change flows through the backlog; traceability through issue links and executable scenarios; a Definition of Ready only as a guideline | SRS documents, formal baselines, requirements management tools |
| Large or regulated organization | A requirements engineering process that conforms to ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 with StRS, SyRS and SRS information items or an equivalent. Planned work products and levels of detail (IREB). A stakeholder list and a user class catalogue with product champions per class (Wiegers). Measurable quality requirements per ISO 25010. Structured statements (EARS, INCOSE rules) with requirements verification and smell checks. Multi-perspective inspections. Approved baselines with version control and a status life cycle. A change control board with impact analysis. Bidirectional traceability from hazards and regulations through requirements to tests (IEC 62304, FDA guidance). Compliance requirements for privacy by design (GDPR Article 25) and accessibility (WCAG). Tool support for attributes, views and tracing. Requirements process metrics. Agile delivery inside such an organization keeps the backlog and the executable specifications as the working view. The baseline and the traceability serve contracts and audits (IREB: regulatory constraints may impose a 29148-conformant process) | Formal methods, except in high-integrity subsystems where SWEBOK says that they pay off |
