## 6. Architecture

### Purpose

Architecture decides the fundamental structure of a system before and while the team builds it. It answers one question. Which elements, relations and principles let the system meet its quality attribute requirements, its constraints and its business goals at an acceptable cost? SWEBOK v4 uses the definition of Bass, Clements and Kazman: architecture is "the set of structures needed to reason about the system". ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 defines it as the "fundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment embodied in its elements, relationships, and in the principles of its design and evolution". Fowler adds a practical test. Architecture is "the important stuff" and "the decisions that you wish you could get right early". People perceive these decisions as hard to change.

The phase produces four things: a shared understanding among the expert developers, an architecture description, a decision log, and evidence that the chosen structure can satisfy the most important scenarios. It also limits the cost of later change. A good architect removes irreversibility where possible.

### Other names

- Architectural design (SWEBOK v4 Software Architecture knowledge area, Chapter 2)
- Architecture Definition process (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 and 12207; ISO/IEC/IEEE 42020 architecture processes)
- Architecture description (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010)
- High-level design, preliminary design or system design
- Solution architecture or technical design
- Architecting (continuous architecture, evolutionary architecture)
- Software design – architectural design stage (older SWEBOK editions)
- Well-Architected review (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud)

### Position in the life cycle

Architecture follows concept, feasibility and the first requirements work (see sections 3 and 5). It precedes detailed design, construction and the test plan (see sections 7, 8 and 9). Requirements and architecture interact. SWEBOK v4 says that architecture "often must shape the requirements through negotiation with stakeholders", so the two run in parallel. Practitioners call this the "twin peaks" model.

In a waterfall or V-model project, architectural design is a distinct stage that the requirements drive. The architecture description is the baseline that detailed design refines and that integration and system tests verify (SWEBOK 3.1; Kruchten's architecture document outline).

In iterative and agile work there is usually no separate stage. Teams do architecture in thin slices. The team prototypes a strawman architecture, scripts it against scenarios and refines it in each iteration (Kruchten). The team reviews a design document before major work starts (Google). Spikes reduce technical risk, and the team writes ADRs when decisions happen. SWEBOK warns that a purely "emergent" architecture is risky for systems whose critical properties do not appear in user stories, for example embedded and cyber-physical systems.

In DevOps and continuous delivery, architecture becomes continuous. Fitness functions run in the pipeline. Well-Architected style reviews repeat at milestones and after significant changes. SRE joins during design instead of after launch. Evolutionary architecture treats "guided, incremental change as the first principle".

In short: the initial architecture is a one-time phase per system or major increment. Architecting – analysis, evaluation, implementation oversight, maintenance, portfolio management and knowledge management (SWEBOK 3.4) – is a continuous process across the life cycle. The phase hands over to detailed design (component internals are deferred; see section 7), to security (the threat model; see section 16), to operations (SLOs and production readiness; see section 12) and to maintenance (erosion and technical debt; see section 13).

### Inputs

- Business goals, product vision and business drivers (ATAM step 2 "present business drivers"; arc42 section 1 "Introduction and goals").
- Concept and feasibility outputs: scope, budget, schedule, and the options already ruled out (see section 3).
- Constraints: mandated technology, regulation and compliance, interoperability with existing systems, delivery deadlines, enterprise or reference architecture, platform standards (Cervantes and Kazman; SWEBOK 3.1; arc42 section 2).
- Functional requirements, in particular the primary use cases that drive structure. Cervantes and Kazman estimate that these are about 10 percent of the functionality.
- Quality attribute requirements and candidate architecturally significant requirements (ASRs), ideally as measurable scenarios (see section 5).
- A stakeholder list with the concerns of each stakeholder (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010; SWEBOK 1.2).
- The existing system landscape: legacy systems, interfaces, data, previous architecture decisions (GOV.UK Service Manual; arc42 section 3).
- Organization and team structure, skills and DevOps maturity (Conway's law; Fowler's microservice prerequisites).
- Operational context: SLO targets, capacity and growth estimates, cost envelope (SRE NALSD).
- Security, privacy and compliance obligations that the threat model must cover (see section 16).
- Technology standards, a technology radar or approved platform services, where the organization has them.
- Entry criteria: a named owner for the architecture, a clear design purpose, and enough ASRs to choose between candidate structures. In regulated organizations, also a defined governance and review path.

### Activities

- **Identify stakeholders and frame their concerns** – List the people and systems that have a stake in the system: users, customers, developers, testers, operators, security, compliance and management. Capture what each one cares about – cost, schedule, function, performance, safety, maintainability, energy use and so on (SWEBOK v4 topic 1.2; ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010). The result is a stakeholder and concern list. It decides which views the architecture description needs and which evaluations matter.
- **Collect architectural drivers and architecturally significant requirements (ASRs)** – Gather the design purpose, the primary functionality, the quality attribute requirements, the constraints and the architectural concerns (Cervantes and Kazman; SWEBOK 3.2.1 "architecture analysis"). Mark the requirements that have a measurable effect on the architecture: wide impact, strict limits, assumption breaking, hard to achieve, high risk or high business value. ASRs are often tacit or vague, so elicit them actively. Negotiate when the initial requirements and constraints cannot all be met. Output: a prioritized ASR list and initial system-wide decisions.
- **Write and prioritize quality attribute scenarios** – Turn each important quality attribute into a concrete scenario with source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response and response measure (SEI QAW and ATAM; Continuous Architecture in Practice). Run a Quality Attribute Workshop or a shorter session: brainstorm, consolidate, vote, refine the top scenarios, and organize them in a utility tree. About ten scenarios usually cover the architecturally significant set. These scenarios are the test cases for both design and evaluation.
- **Set architecture principles and apply reference architectures or platform constraints** – Adopt a short list of principles that guide choices, for example proportionate governance, total cost of ownership, open standards, managed dependencies and reuse (Cabinet Office principles; GOV.UK). Where an enterprise architecture, a product line baseline or a reference architecture exists, record it as a constraint and as ASRs on the system (SWEBOK 2.2 and 3.1). Output: principles and constraints that every later decision must respect or explicitly override.
- **Explore options and synthesize candidate architectures** – Create candidate structures that solve the design problems the ASRs pose, and make trade-offs between them (SWEBOK "architecture synthesis"). Choose an architectural style or a combination: layered or n-tier and client-server, hexagonal or clean, modular monolith, microservices, event-driven, pipes and filters, serverless, CQRS. Use the constraints of the style on purpose. Understand why you select a style before you decide how to apply it (Azure Architecture Center; Richards and Ford). Output: one or more candidate architectures with their known trade-offs.
- **Decompose the system and define boundaries** – Decide the major elements, their responsibilities, their interfaces and their interactions, and defer the component internals (SWEBOK 3.2). Form module or service boundaries around business capabilities and make them enforceable – in a modular monolith through compiler visibility rules, in services through independent deployment and private data (Brown; Grzybek; Fowler's microservices article). Align boundaries with the team structure, because Conway's law applies (Fowler; DORA). Output: building block view, interface list and ownership map.
- **Design the data architecture** – Identify the data access patterns and map them to storage models: relational, document, key-value, column-family, graph, time series, object, search, analytics (Azure data store models). Decide data ownership, the consistency model, transaction scope versus eventual consistency, and where CQRS or event sourcing is worth its cost (Fowler). Prefer one store until access patterns clearly diverge, and avoid a shared database between services. Output: storage choices, ownership and consistency decisions, retention and migration notes.
- **Design the integration architecture** – Select an integration style per interface – file transfer, shared database, remote procedure invocation or messaging – with coupling, timeliness, reliability and data format as the criteria (Enterprise Integration Patterns). Decide between synchronous calls and events, and between event notification, event-carried state transfer and event sourcing (Fowler). Keep endpoints smart and pipes dumb. Output: a context diagram with external systems, interface contracts and the messaging topology.
- **Design the deployment, infrastructure and cloud architecture** – Map software elements to runtime environments: processes, containers, nodes, regions and networks (Kruchten's physical view; C4 deployment diagram). Apply cloud principles: stateless processes, backing services as attached resources, configuration in the environment, automation, and capacity decided from data instead of guesses (12factor; AWS general design principles; Google Cloud Architecture Framework). Choose managed services where they remove undifferentiated work, and record the lock-in trade-off. Output: deployment view, infrastructure model, scaling and failure model.
- **Select technologies and run spikes or proofs of concept** – Evaluate languages, frameworks, platforms and products against the ASRs, total cost of ownership, lock-in, open standards, team skills and the existing landscape (GOV.UK Service Manual; Cabinet Office). Use time-boxed spikes to reduce the risk of a technical approach and to improve estimates. Validate high-risk or novel components with working code before you finalize the design (SAFe; Azure architect role; Kruchten's evolutionary prototype). A technology radar helps an organization govern choices. Output: technology decisions with evidence, recorded as ADRs.
- **Threat model the architecture** – Answer four questions: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good enough job (Threat Modeling Manifesto; OWASP). Draw data flows and trust boundaries, apply STRIDE per element, rank the threats, and choose to mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept each one. Do this during design and repeat it as the system changes. Output: a diagram, a threat list and a control list that feed security requirements and tests (see section 16).
- **Design for operability, reliability and cost** – Define SLOs and capacity estimates, then iterate the design until it is possible, feasible and resilient at scale (SRE workbook NALSD). Build in observability, failure handling, safe automated deployment and recovery, and plan frequent small reversible changes (AWS operational excellence principles; SRE production readiness review). Treat cost as a quality attribute: adopt a consumption model, measure cost per unit of business output and attribute spend to owners (AWS cost optimization principles; Google Cloud Architecture Framework). Output: operability and cost sections of the architecture and inputs to production readiness (see section 12).
- **Document the architecture with views** – Write an architecture description organized by stakeholder concerns and viewpoints (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010). Use a lightweight standard structure: C4 context and container diagrams plus component or deployment diagrams where they add value, or an arc42 template or canvas, or the 4+1 views for large systems. Explain the notation with a key, write for the reader, avoid repetition, record rationale, and update at iteration or release boundaries (Views and Beyond seven rules). Output: the architecture description, kept next to the code.
- **Record architecture decisions (ADRs)** – Write one short record per significant decision: title, context, decision, status, consequences, and the options considered with their pros and cons (Nygard; MADR). Keep the records in the repository, numbered and append-only. Supersede instead of edit, and note trade-offs and confidence (Azure Well-Architected; Thoughtworks Radar). Include only decisions that affect the structure or key quality attributes, or that are hard to reverse. Output: a decision log that acts as the memory of the architecture.
- **Evaluate the architecture against scenarios** – Check that the candidate architecture satisfies the prioritized scenarios, and find risks, non-risks, sensitivity points and tradeoff points (SEI ATAM nine steps; ISO/IEC/IEEE 42030). Scale the method: a full ATAM with many stakeholders for critical systems; a design document review, a Well-Architected conversation of a few hours, or an active review for most work (Google; AWS; SWEBOK 4.3). Evaluate early to avoid one-way doors, again before go-live, and after significant changes. Output: a risk list with actions, recorded in the AD or as ADRs.
- **Define fitness functions and conformance checks** – Turn architectural characteristics into automated checks that run in the build pipeline: dependency and layering rules, coupling and cyclicity metrics, performance budgets, security scans, availability monitors (Thoughtworks; Building Evolutionary Architectures; SWEBOK architecture metrics). Enforce module boundaries with the compiler or the build tools where possible (Brown). Output: executable guardrails that detect architectural erosion early (see section 10).
- **Guide implementation and certify conformance** – Communicate the architecture, pair with developers on the hard parts, review code against the architecture and certify that the implementation conforms (SWEBOK "architecture implementation"; Fowler's Architectus Oryzus). Renegotiate requirements with stakeholders and update the ADRs when reality differs from the plan (Azure architect role). Output: shared understanding, conformance feedback and an updated architecture description.
- **Govern, maintain and evolve the architecture** – Maintain and extend the architecture after implementation, manage the portfolio of architectures of the organization, and share reusable architecture knowledge (SWEBOK 3.4). Apply proportionate governance: a review board or design authority for major changes in large organizations, team ownership with periodic reviews elsewhere (GitLab ARB; Cabinet Office; AWS review process). Track architectural technical debt and risks, plan migrations such as the strangler fig, and accept a sacrificial architecture when growth demands a rewrite (Fowler; DORA). Output: governance records, a debt and risk register, and an evolution roadmap.

### Outputs

- Architecture description (AD): views selected for stakeholder concerns – system context, containers or building blocks, runtime scenarios, deployment, crosscutting concepts – with the notation explained (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010; C4; arc42; 4+1).
- Prioritized ASR list and quality attribute scenarios, often organized as a utility tree.
- Architecture principles and constraints that apply to the system.
- Decision log of ADRs with context, options, decision, status and consequences, stored in version control.
- Evaluation record: risks, non-risks, sensitivity points, tradeoff points, risk themes and agreed actions (ATAM), or review findings and actions (design review, Well-Architected review).
- Threat model: a data flow or C4 diagram with trust boundaries, a threat list and a control list, with the accepted risks recorded.
- Technology selections with spike or proof of concept results.
- Data architecture: storage models, data ownership, consistency and retention decisions.
- Integration architecture: interface contracts, integration styles per interface, messaging topology.
- Deployment and infrastructure model with scaling, failure and recovery behavior; capacity and cost estimate.
- Fitness functions and architecture conformance tests in the repository.
- Risks and technical debt register (arc42 section 11).
- Exit criteria: analysis or a prototype shows that the top-priority scenarios are achievable; the team has reviewed and recorded the high-risk and hard-to-reverse decisions; each critical threat has a control or an explicit acceptance; the team shares the understanding; in large or regulated organizations, the review board or the production readiness review has accepted the design.

### Roles

- **Software or solution architect** – owns the architecture, identifies what is significant, negotiates ASRs, records decisions, runs evaluations and mentors the team. Per Fowler, the best architects raise the level of the team and make few decisions alone.
- **Tech lead or senior developers** – share the architecture work in small teams, write ADRs, enforce boundaries and build spikes.
- **Developers** – bring implementation knowledge, review designs, build to the architecture and report where it does not fit.
- **Product owner or business sponsor** – states the business drivers and priorities, and accepts trade-offs and cost consequences.
- **End users or customer representatives** – supply scenarios and priorities in workshops and ATAM sessions.
- **Operations and SRE** – define SLOs; review capacity, failure modes, observability and deployment safety; join during design (early engagement) and run production readiness reviews.
- **Security engineer or champion** – leads or facilitates threat modeling and reviews the controls.
- **Data engineer or DBA** – advises on storage models, consistency, migration and data governance.
- **Test and QA** – confirm that scenarios and fitness functions are testable, and plan architecture-level tests (see section 9).
- **Enterprise architect, architecture review board or technical design authority** – set principles and reference architectures, and review major changes in large or regulated organizations.
- **Evaluation team (one to three people in ATAM phase 1) and domain experts** – run formal evaluations as third parties at milestones.
- **Platform team** – provides the shared infrastructure, landing zones and managed services that the architecture depends on.

### Practices with consensus

- **Drive architecture from quality attributes and ASRs, not from functionality alone** – Many structures can meet the same functions; the quality attributes and the constraints decide which structure works. Architecture "substantially determines" whether a system can show its required qualities. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 Chapter 2 (architecture analysis, ASRs); ATAM: Method for Architecture Evaluation; Cervantes and Kazman, Architectural Drivers; Continuous Architecture in Practice; Azure Architecture Center, Architecture styles.
- **Express quality attribute requirements as concrete, measurable scenarios and prioritize them** – A team cannot design for or test a vague word such as "scalable". Stimulus, environment, response and response measure make the requirement analyzable, and they give the evaluation its test cases. Evidence: Quality Attribute Workshops (QAWs), Third Edition; ATAM: Method for Architecture Evaluation (utility tree); Cervantes and Kazman, Architectural Drivers; Continuous Architecture in Practice, Quality attributes; arc42 section 10.
- **Describe the architecture as a small set of views chosen for stakeholder concerns, with explained notation** – Different stakeholders need different structures, and one diagram cannot carry all concerns. Views with a stated viewpoint and a key reduce ambiguity and let readers find what they need. Evidence: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 (IEEE SA page; INCOSE update); Kruchten, The 4+1 View Model of Architecture; The C4 model; arc42 Overview; Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond, seven rules; SWEBOK v4 topic 2.1.
- **Record significant decisions with context, options and consequences in short ADRs kept in version control** – Teams lose rationale fast. Without it, new team members either blindly accept or blindly change decisions. An append-only log next to the code stays in sync with the code, and it supports audits and later reconsideration. Evidence: Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions; Architectural Decision Records (adr.github.io); Thoughtworks Technology Radar, Lightweight Architecture Decision Records (Adopt); Azure Well-Architected Framework, Maintain an architecture decision record; SWEBOK v4 topic 2.4; Google Cloud Architecture Framework, "document your architecture".
- **Evaluate the architecture early, with stakeholders, against the prioritized scenarios, and again at milestones** – Architecture errors are cheapest to fix before code exists. Review before one-way-door decisions and before go-live. A review is a conversation about risks, not an audit. Evidence: ATAM: Method for Architecture Evaluation; AWS Well-Architected Framework, The review process; Software Engineering at Google, Chapter 10 (design docs); Site Reliability Engineering book, production readiness review; SWEBOK v4 topic 4.
- **Make trade-offs explicit; there is no best architecture, only a least-worst fit for the drivers** – Every style and every decision trades one quality for another, and the tradeoff points are the most critical decisions. Hidden trade-offs become technical debt and surprises. Evidence: ATAM: Method for Architecture Evaluation (sensitivity and tradeoff points); Fundamentals of Software Architecture, laws of software architecture (Richards and Ford); SWEBOK v4 topics 2.4 and 4.1; Azure Architecture Center, Architecture styles; AWS Well-Architected Framework, The pillars of the framework.
- **Match structural complexity to the problem; do not adopt microservices or other distributed styles without a demonstrated need and the operational prerequisites** – Distribution adds a premium: deployment automation, monitoring, failure handling and eventual consistency. A modular monolith with enforced boundaries delivers most of the benefits for most systems, and a team can split it later. Evidence: Fowler, MonolithFirst, MicroservicePremium, MicroservicePrerequisites and SacrificialArchitecture; Azure Architecture Center, Architecture styles; Simon Brown, Modular monolith; Grzybek, Modular Monolith: A Primer.
- **Separate business logic from delivery and infrastructure mechanisms with explicit boundaries and inward-pointing dependencies** – Ports and adapters, clean architecture and modular monoliths all isolate the core. The team can then test the core without a UI or a database, and the technology can change without a rewrite of the rules. Evidence: Cockburn, Hexagonal architecture; Martin, The Clean Architecture; Simon Brown and Grzybek on modular monoliths; The Twelve-Factor App, "backing services".
- **Align architecture boundaries with team boundaries (Conway's law) so that teams can test and deploy independently** – Systems copy communication structures. Loosely coupled architecture and loosely coupled teams predict higher delivery performance. Design the organization and the decomposition together. Evidence: Fowler, ConwaysLaw; DORA, Loosely coupled teams; Lewis and Fowler, Microservices (organized around business capabilities); SWEBOK v4 topic 1.3.
- **Threat model at the architecture level during design, with a system model and a structured method such as STRIDE, and repeat as the system changes** – Design flaws are cheaper to remove before implementation. A diagram, a threat list and a control list focus the security work on the riskiest components. Evidence: OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet; OWASP Threat Modeling Process; Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, Threats (STRIDE); Threat Modeling Manifesto; The C4 model, Introduction (threat modeling as a use).
- **Treat operability, reliability and cost as architecture concerns from the start: SLOs, observability, failure design, automation, cost per business output** – A team that defers reliability and cost to operations raises the total cost. Well-Architected reviews and production readiness checks exist because these qualities are structural. Evidence: AWS Well-Architected Framework, pillars and design principles; Google Cloud Architecture Framework; Site Reliability Workbook, Non-Abstract Large System Design; Site Reliability Engineering book, production readiness review; Lewis and Fowler, Microservices (design for failure).
- **Design for change and reduce irreversibility; distinguish one-way doors from two-way doors and give one-way doors more scrutiny** – Architecture is what is hard to change. Reversible decisions reduce both risk and ceremony. Evolutionary architecture and fitness functions keep change guided. Evidence: Fowler, Who Needs an Architect?; AWS Well-Architected Framework, The review process and General design principles; Google Cloud Architecture Framework, "design for change"; Building Evolutionary Architectures; GOV.UK Service Manual, Choosing technology.
- **Automate architectural conformance with fitness functions and architecture metrics in the pipeline** – Documentation and reviews cannot stop erosion. Executable checks give continuous feedback on coupling, layering, performance and security, and they make "fit" explicit. Evidence: Thoughtworks, Fitness function-driven development and the Radar entry Architectural fitness function; Building Evolutionary Architectures; SWEBOK v4 topic 4.4; Simon Brown, Modular monolith (compiler-enforced boundaries).
- **Use time-boxed spikes and proofs of concept to retire technical risk before you commit** – Experiments beat speculation. They improve estimates, and they show early when a theoretical design does not work in practice. Evidence: Scaled Agile Framework, Spikes; Azure Well-Architected Framework, Solution architect's responsibilities (proof of concept); GOV.UK Service Manual, Choosing technology (prototype in discovery and alpha); Kruchten, The 4+1 View Model of Architecture (evolutionary prototype).

### Contested points

- **Monolith first or microservices first** – Fowler holds that almost all successful microservice systems started as a monolith. He advises to start monolithic (or sacrificial) and to split when complexity demands it and the prerequisites exist. Tilkov (on martinfowler.com) holds the opposite position: do not start with a monolith when you know the domain well, because a later split is extremely hard and microservices enable parallel development. Tilkov adds that a team that can build a well-structured monolith probably does not need microservices. The choice depends on domain knowledge, team count, operational maturity and how much parallel development you need.
- **How much architecture up front** – The traditional process (SWEBOK, Kruchten's document outline) has an explicit architectural design stage. Agile practice lets the architecture emerge from the code. SWEBOK warns that this fails when the critical properties are not in user stories (embedded and cyber-physical systems). Fairbanks' risk-driven approach and Fowler's design stamina hypothesis take the middle: do just enough architecture to cover the identified risks, and invest in design early, because the payoff line arrives in weeks. The right amount depends on risk, irreversibility, system class and expected lifetime.
- **Heavy formal evaluation (ATAM) versus lightweight reviews** – SEI ATAM is a multi-phase method: about three days of meetings plus weeks of preparation, three to fifty stakeholders, and risks, sensitivity points and tradeoff points as outputs. SWEBOK notes third-party evaluation at milestones. AWS asks for conversations of "hours not days", Google uses design document reviews, and SRE uses production readiness reviews. Most sources agree on scenario-based checks. They differ on ceremony, which should scale with criticality, regulation and the cost of a wrong decision.
- **Architect as a role versus architecture as a shared team responsibility** – Fowler contrasts Architectus Reloadus (makes all important decisions) with Architectus Oryzus (a guide who raises the team). Johnson defines architecture as the shared understanding of the expert developers. AWS wants every team member to own quality. Fairbanks says that architecting is for all developers. Large and regulated organizations still rely on named architects, architecture review boards and design authorities (GitLab ARB, Cabinet Office, Azure architect role). The choice depends on organization size, risk and accountability needs.
- **How much documentation, and in what form** – ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 and arc42 support complete, viewpoint-based descriptions. C4 says that context and container diagrams are sufficient for most teams. Thoughtworks and agile practice say that code and tests replace much documentation, but that the team must record its decisions. Views and Beyond says keep documentation current but not too current. The consensus core is small: context, main building blocks, key scenarios and decisions. Everything else depends on audience, regulation and system lifetime.
- **Architectural purity versus pragmatism in layered, clean and hexagonal designs** – Clean architecture and hexagonal architecture promise independence from frameworks, UI and database. Critics point to indirection and ceremony for small systems. The Azure Architecture Center states that it is sometimes better to relax a constraint than to chase architectural purity. Apply the dependency rule where business rules are complex or long-lived; keep thin applications thin.
- **One database or polyglot persistence** – Fowler: most applications are better off with the relational orthodoxy; use other stores only for strategic projects. Azure Architecture Center: most production systems adopt polyglot persistence, but avoid premature fragmentation and do not add a store without operational maturity. The decision depends on divergent access patterns, scale, and the ability of the team to operate several stores.
- **CQRS, event sourcing and event-driven patterns** – Proponents value audit trails, independent read and write scaling, and looser coupling. Fowler warns to be very cautious with CQRS: most cases he met were not good, and event sourcing complicates schema evolution and external dependencies. Use these patterns for specific bounded parts with a clear need, not system-wide.
- **Serverless and managed services versus control and portability** – Serverless reduces operational cost and scales automatically (Roberts' serverless article on martinfowler.com; the AWS and Google frameworks favor managed services). The drawbacks are vendor lock-in, statelessness limits, cold starts, and difficulty in test and debug. GOV.UK and the Cabinet Office stress that teams must avoid lock-in and must account for total cost of ownership. The balance depends on traffic pattern, latency needs, exit strategy and team size.
- **Central governance versus decentralized decisions** – The Lewis and Fowler microservices article and DORA favor decentralized governance and team autonomy. GitLab's ARB requires approval before major architectural changes. The Cabinet Office asks for risk-based proportionate governance. A technology radar is a middle path that guides but does not block. What fits depends on regulatory load, spend control needs and the cost of divergence.
- **Which metrics say anything about architecture** – SWEBOK lists structural metrics (coupling, cyclicity, complexity, pattern compliance) and notes DORA-style delivery metrics as indicative of the architecture state. DORA ties loosely coupled architecture to delivery performance. Critics note that structural metrics are lifted from code metrics and can be gamed, and that delivery metrics mix process and architecture. Use metrics as signals tied to explicit scenarios and fitness functions, not as targets.

### Metrics

- **Coverage of prioritized quality attribute scenarios** – the number of top scenarios with an analyzed or prototyped response that meets the response measure (ATAM utility tree, QAW). Caveat: the metric is only as good as the scenario set.
- **Evaluation outputs** – the number and severity of risks, non-risks, sensitivity points, tradeoff points and risk themes, and how many of them have owners and actions (ATAM). Caveat: qualitative, and dependent on reviewer expertise.
- **Fitness function pass rate and trend in the pipeline** – dependency and layering violations, cyclic dependencies, coupling and cohesion thresholds, performance budgets, security checks (Thoughtworks; Building Evolutionary Architectures). Caveat: it measures only what you chose to encode, so revisit the set as the system evolves.
- **Structural architecture metrics** – component dependency, cyclicity, cyclomatic complexity, module coupling and cohesion, nesting levels, and compliance with patterns, styles and required APIs (SWEBOK v4 4.4). Caveat: many are code metrics lifted to the architecture level; they can be gamed and have no universal thresholds.
- **Delivery metrics as indicators of architecture state** – lead time for changes, deployment frequency, time to restore service, change failure rate (SWEBOK v4 4.4; DORA). Caveat: they mix process, tooling and architecture; read them together with coupling measures.
- **Loose coupling indicators** – the share of services that the team can deploy independently, the cross-team coordination needed per change, handoffs, upstream failure frequency (DORA). Caveat: organizational metrics, not purely technical ones.
- **Reliability and performance targets from design** – SLO attainment, latency and capacity versus the NALSD estimates (SRE workbook). Caveat: available only after the system runs; use the capacity estimates before that.
- **Cost efficiency** – cost per unit of business output and cost attribution by owner (AWS cost optimization principle "measure overall efficiency"). Caveat: requires resource tags and a definition of business output.
- **Review health** – the number of high-risk issues open after a Well-Architected or design review, and the time to close them (AWS review process). Caveat: depends on review depth and honesty.
- **Decision hygiene** – ADR count per period, the share of significant changes with an ADR, the age of decisions not revisited, the number of superseded decisions (Nygard; Azure ADR). Caveat: counts measure habit, not quality.
- **Threat model coverage** – threats identified per STRIDE category, and the share mitigated, partially mitigated or accepted (OWASP). Caveat: a low count can mean a weak model, not a safe system.
- **Technical debt register size and trend, and architecture erosion signals** – for example boundary violations found in code review (SWEBOK 2.4; arc42 section 11). Caveat: subjective unless tied to concrete items.

### Failure modes

- **Ivory tower or "Architectus Reloadus"** – one person makes all decisions without code or collaboration. The architecture does not match reality, and the architect becomes a bottleneck (Fowler).
- **Premature microservices** – the team adopts distribution before the complexity or the prerequisites (provisioning, monitoring, deployment, DevOps culture) exist. The result is a distributed monolith with the microservice premium and none of the benefits (Fowler; Azure).
- **Big ball of mud** – no enforced boundaries, so dependencies spread and the structure breaks down. "If people can't build monoliths properly, microservices won't help" (Brown; Azure).
- **Lost rationale** – nobody records the decisions, so successors blindly accept or blindly change them, debates repeat, and later changes contradict the original intent (Nygard; Azure ADR).
- **Documentation bigger than the code, out of date, or box-and-line diagrams without a key** – nobody reads it, and readers interpret it differently (Nygard; Views and Beyond).
- **Quality attributes left until late** – the system meets its functions but fails on performance, availability or security, which the architecture already decided (Continuous Architecture; SWEBOK).
- **Vague quality requirements** – "must be fast" with no stimulus or response measure; the team cannot design for them or evaluate them (QAW; ATAM).
- **Threat modeling as a one-time checkbox, a "hero threat modeler", admiration for the problem without fixes, or a quest for a perfect diagram** – the threats stay unaddressed while the activity looks complete (Threat Modeling Manifesto).
- **Operability, reliability and cost treated as someone else's concern** – the reliability engagement starts after launch, and the fixes are expensive (SRE PRR; AWS).
- **Architecture that fights Conway's law** – architecture boundaries that cut across team communication paths make simple interactions complicated (Fowler; DORA).
- **Architectural erosion without fitness functions** – layering and dependency rules degrade with every commit until the intended structure is gone (Thoughtworks; Brown).
- **Shared database between services, a search index used as the primary store, or a new data store added without monitoring and backups** – hidden coupling, data loss and operational surprises follow (Azure data store guidance).
- **Pattern misuse** – CQRS, event sourcing or event chains applied system-wide; flows become invisible, schema evolution gets hard and complexity compounds (Fowler).
- **Resume-driven or fashion-driven technology selection** – lock-in accepted without a recorded decision, and total cost of ownership ignored (GOV.UK; Cabinet Office; Fowler).
- **Review run as an audit with blame** – teams hide problems, and reviews become ceremony and find nothing (AWS review process).
- **Over-engineering and speculative generality** – features built for presumed needs violate YAGNI and add the cost of build, delay, carry and repair (Fowler).
- **Too little design for a long-lived system** – design skipped below the payoff line for a product that will live for years, so each later change costs more (design stamina hypothesis).
- **Emergent architecture for systems whose critical properties do not appear in user stories** – embedded or safety-critical systems never get their critical properties designed in (SWEBOK v4).
- **Architecture by committee or a governance gate that blocks flow** – approval required for everything regardless of risk, so teams route around it (Cabinet Office "proportionate governance"; DORA).

### Tailoring by project size

Essential at every scale: know your three to ten most important quality attribute scenarios and constraints; choose the simplest structure that meets them; draw one context diagram and one container or building block diagram with a key; write an ADR for each decision that is hard to reverse; think through what can go wrong for security and for operations; and keep architecture checks in the pipeline where they are cheap.

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| Solo developer on a small repository | Architecture is mostly a few decisions, so document the one or two that matter: the style (for example a modular monolith or a layered web app), the storage choice, the hosting or deployment model, and any external integration. A C4 context diagram plus a container diagram, or a one-page arc42 canvas, in the README or the docs folder is enough; C4 states that these two levels are sufficient for most teams. Keep ADRs as short Markdown files in a docs/adr folder; three to five ADRs is normal. Apply YAGNI and the design stamina hypothesis: do not build for imagined scale, but keep the core separated from the frameworks so that the code stays easy to change. A ten-minute STRIDE pass over the data flow and a note on backups, secrets and cost is the whole threat and operability model. Skip formal evaluation; a self-review against the scenarios before a big change is the review. A sacrificial architecture is acceptable: plan to rewrite if the project grows. | A stakeholder and concern list, a written design document, a Well-Architected style conversation, fitness functions beyond cheap dependency checks, a technology radar, a formal threat model per feature. Add them when the project gains users, contributors or a longer expected lifetime. |
| Small product team | Add a stakeholder and concern list, a written set of about ten quality attribute scenarios, and a lightweight design document for each significant change, which the team reviews before it writes code (Google-style design review). Use C4 or arc42 with context, container, key runtime scenarios and deployment views; keep it in the repository. Write ADRs consistently and treat the log as append-only. Run a short Well-Architected style conversation at milestones and before launch. Cover security with a threat model per major feature, and agree SLOs with whoever operates the system. Add fitness functions for dependency rules and performance budgets. Prefer a modular monolith with enforced boundaries; split services only when a concrete driver exists and the prerequisites are in place. Make technology choices with spikes and a small internal radar; record the lock-in decisions. | A 42010-conformant architecture description with defined viewpoints, Quality Attribute Workshops and a full ATAM, an architecture review board, enterprise reference architectures and conformance suites, formal production readiness reviews with evidence kept for audits. Add them when criticality, regulation or the number of teams demands traceability. |
| Large or regulated organization | The same core plus formality and traceability. Produce a 42010-conformant architecture description with defined viewpoints, correspondences between views and links to requirements; use arc42 or an organizational framework. Hold Quality Attribute Workshops and run ATAM or an equivalent scenario-based evaluation for critical systems, with an independent evaluation team and documented risks, sensitivity points and tradeoff points. Record every significant decision, its options and its confidence. Route major changes through proportionate governance: an architecture review board or design authority for changes that affect scalability, security, compliance or spend, and a lightweight path for two-way doors. Maintain enterprise principles, reference architectures and a technology radar; enforce them with conformance suites and fitness functions. Threat modeling is mandatory and repeated, with evidence kept for audits. Production readiness reviews with SRE or operations gate the launches. Cost and sustainability are tracked pillars. Architecture knowledge management, a technical debt register and periodic re-evaluation are standing activities. | Full 4+1 documentation, formal architecture description languages (ADLs) and model-based architecting, pattern catalogs, and detailed component or code level diagrams. Use them only where a stakeholder concern or a regulation needs them. |

Optional at every scale: full 4+1 documentation, formal ADLs and model-based architecting, pattern catalogs, and detailed component or code level diagrams. Use them only where a stakeholder concern or a regulation needs them.
