## 7. Detailed design (component, API, data and UX design)

### Purpose

Design turns the agreed requirements and the architecture into a description that is detailed enough to build, test and operate the software. It answers one question: which modules, interfaces, data structures, screens and contracts will the team build, and why these and not the alternatives. SWEBOK V4 splits the work into an outward-facing high-level design stage and an inward-facing detailed design stage. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 calls the same work the design definition process. That process supplies the "how" or "implement-to" level of description.

The main enemy of design is complexity. Design decides what each module hides, what each interface promises, how data is shaped and how it evolves, and how people experience the product. A good design makes change cheap, makes errors visible and recoverable, and makes the product usable by all users. This includes people who use assistive technology.

### Other names

- Software design (the SWEBOK knowledge area)
- Design definition process (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288); software detailed design (ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207)
- High-level design and detailed design (the SWEBOK V4 stages); low-level design (LLD)
- Component design, module design, program design
- Interface design, contract design, design by contract
- API design, API-first, contract-first, API governance
- Data modeling, database design, schema design, information design
- Human-centred design (ISO 9241-210), user-centred design (UCD)
- UX design, interaction design, UI design, product design, service design
- Content design, UX writing, information architecture (IA)
- Design docs, RFCs, ADRs, technical design review
- Domain-driven design (strategic and tactical design)

### Position in the life cycle

Two phases come before design. Requirements engineering (see section 5) gives the problems to solve. Architecture (see section 6) gives the fundamental structures, styles and quality attribute decisions that constrain the design. After design come implementation (see section 8), unit and integration tests (see section 9) and operations (see section 12).

Design outputs feed four later activities. Test design uses the contracts and interfaces. Observability uses the SLIs and signals decided at design time. Security uses the threat model (see section 16). Operations uses the health endpoints, the configuration and the capacity plan.

In waterfall and the V-model, design is a distinct phase between architectural design and coding. ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 names a software detailed design process. Unit and integration tests on the right side of the V verify its output.

In iterative and agile delivery, design is continuous and mostly evolutionary. Teams write short design docs or RFCs for risky changes, and build spikes and prototypes. They rely on refactoring, self-testing code and continuous integration to keep the design simple (Fowler). UX design runs as a parallel track through discovery, alpha, beta and live (GOV.UK), with research and usability tests in every iteration. ISO 9241-210 requires an iterative process that evaluation drives.

In DevOps and continuous delivery (see sections 10 and 11), design must support incremental rollout. This means contract-first APIs with compatibility rules, versioned schema migrations with transition phases, and design for observability and operability.

Conclusion: design is both a gated phase for large, novel or regulated changes and a continuous activity inside every feature. SWEBOK notes that in agile teams the design may stay implicit in code. Other stakeholders (testers, certifiers, operators) often still need explicit design information.

### Inputs

- Approved or stable-enough requirements: functional requirements, quality attribute requirements (performance, security, availability, usability, accessibility), constraints and acceptance criteria.
- The architecture description: components, styles and patterns, interfaces and protocols, data and communication standards, and crosscutting decisions. SWEBOK states that the architecture constrains the design.
- Architecture decision records and an agreed list of open architectural questions.
- Domain knowledge: access to domain experts, a glossary or ubiquitous language, and the existing business rules and data.
- User research inputs: the context of use, user groups, personas, journey maps, analytics, support tickets and a research repository (ISO 9241-210 activities a and b).
- Existing systems and data: the current schemas, the APIs consumed and exposed, and legacy interfaces that need an anticorruption layer.
- Organizational standards: an API style guide (for example the Zalando or Microsoft/Azure guidelines), a design system and style guide, coding standards, a security baseline, an accessibility target (for example WCAG 2.2 AA), and data classification rules.
- Platform and operations constraints: runtime, databases, observability stack, SLOs, capacity and cost targets, and the deployment model.
- Entry criteria: the problem and the scope are written down. The team decides to write a design doc when the solution is not obvious or is contentious (Google design docs). The stakeholders and reviewers are identified. Time is reserved for review and for user research.

### Activities

- **Plan the design work and choose the design strategy** – Decide how much design is necessary, which notations and documents to produce, and who reviews them (SEBoK: initialise design definition). Google writes a design doc when the solution is unclear, contentious or cross-cutting, and skips it for obvious or throwaway work. Choose the strategy: top-down decomposition, bottom-up composition, stepwise refinement, prototypes or tracer bullets. Identify technologies at risk of obsolescence and assess the alternatives for each element: reuse, buy or build. Output: a design plan or the first section of the design doc with context, scope, goals and non-goals.
- **Decompose into modules and components and allocate responsibilities** – Split the system into units that each hide one design decision that is likely to change (Parnas). Prefer deep modules: much functionality behind a simple interface (Ousterhout). Keep coupling low and cohesion high, give each module a single reason to change, and separate the interface from the implementation (SWEBOK design principles; SOLID). Output: a component or module structure with responsibilities, dependencies, scope and visibility rules, states and transitions, and the main algorithms and data structures.
- **Define interfaces and contracts between modules** – Write the formal part of each interface (signatures, types, messages) and the informal part (preconditions, postconditions, invariants, error behavior, performance expectations). This is design by contract (Meyer; Pragmatic Programmer tip). Use interface description languages where they exist: OpenAPI, Protocol Buffers, GraphQL SDL, and AsyncAPI for event-driven interfaces. Make readers tolerant of unknown fields, and capture consumer expectations as consumer-driven contracts so providers can evolve safely (Fowler). Output: interface specifications that a client programmer can use without a look at the implementation (SWEBOK high-level design rule of thumb).
- **Design APIs (REST, GraphQL, gRPC)** – Model the API around resources or domain types, not around database tables or internal functions (Google AIP-121; Azure). Apply HTTP semantics correctly: nouns for resources, standard methods, idempotent PUT and DELETE, 202 plus a status monitor for long-running operations, ETags for conditional requests. Define naming, field conventions, the error format, pagination, filters, idempotency keys and rate limits from the style guide of the organization. Decide the compatibility and versioning policy before the first release, and review the specification with consumers (API-first). Output: a reviewed API specification (OpenAPI, .proto or GraphQL schema) plus examples and a changelog policy.
- **Design the data model: conceptual, logical, physical** – Capture entities, attributes and relationships with business stakeholders (conceptual). Refine them to keys, cardinalities and normal forms independent of a product (logical). Then map them to tables, types, constraints, indexes and partitions for the chosen database (physical) (IBM; Microsoft normalisation description). Normalise transactional data to third normal form by default, and denormalise only for a measured reason. Use dimensional models for analytics. Separate storage messages from API messages, so storage can change without a break for clients (protobuf guidance). Output: ER diagrams or an equivalent, DDL or migration scripts, a data dictionary, and data classification and retention notes.
- **Plan schema evolution and data migration** – Treat every schema change as a versioned migration that runs in every environment, including production (Fowler, evolutionary database design). Keep old and new code working at the same time: add before remove, and use transition phases (views, triggers, dual writes). Never reuse protobuf tag numbers, never change field types, and add only optional fields (protobuf; Kleppmann). Define backward and forward compatibility for stored data and messages. Output: migration scripts, compatibility rules, and a rollback or roll-forward plan.
- **Apply domain-driven design where the domain is complex** – Build a ubiquitous language with domain experts and use it in code, tests and documents (Evans; Fowler). Draw bounded contexts and a context map with explicit relationships: partnership, shared kernel, customer/supplier, conformist, anticorruption layer, open-host service, published language. Inside a context, model entities, value objects, domain events, repositories and aggregates. An aggregate is the consistency and transaction boundary, with external references only to its root. Spend the best effort on the core domain. Output: a context map, a glossary, and a domain model that the code mirrors.
- **Apply design principles and patterns deliberately** – Use principles as checks: information hiding, separation of concerns (Dijkstra), SOLID, least astonishment and simplicity. Add DRY (one authoritative representation of each piece of knowledge) and YAGNI (do not build presumptive features). Use catalogued patterns (GoF, PoEAA, cloud patterns) as vocabulary and proven solutions, but only when the problem matches the problem statement of the pattern. Start simple and introduce a pattern when it earns its place (Fowler; Azure pattern guidance). Output: rationale in the design doc for each pattern or principle trade-off.
- **Design error handling, resilience and fault tolerance** – Distinguish bugs (fail fast) from recoverable errors (typed, handled at the correct layer) (Duffy). Define errors out of existence where possible: choose API semantics that have no failure case (Ousterhout). Standardise the error payload: RFC 9457 problem details, google.rpc.Status with ErrorInfo, or the Microsoft error object. Give each error a machine-readable code and a human-readable message that does not leak internals. Plan timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, bulkheads, queue-based load levelling, compensating transactions and graceful degradation. Defer none of this until after launch (SRE NALSD). Output: an error model and a resilience section in the design doc.
- **Design concurrency, consistency and state** – Decide which operations run concurrently, what is shared, and how state stays consistent (SWEBOK key issues: concurrency, control and event handling, data persistence, distribution). Prefer message passing over shared mutable state where possible (Go guidance). Choose optimistic concurrency with version tokens for rare conflicts, and pessimistic locks or higher isolation levels when conflicts are common (EF Core guidance). Use aggregate boundaries as transaction boundaries, and handle cross-boundary updates asynchronously (Evans). Make consumers idempotent, and use idempotency keys for retried writes (Stripe; AIP-155; Azure). Output: a consistency and concurrency section with invariants, transaction scopes and retry semantics.
- **Design for security and privacy** – Run a lightweight threat model during design: draw data flows and trust boundaries, enumerate threats (for example with STRIDE), decide mitigations, and review (OWASP). Apply least privilege, defence in depth, secure defaults and zero-trust assumptions. Check the API against the OWASP API Security Top 10 (object-level and function-level authorisation, resource limits, inventory). Classify data, and design retention, masking and consent. Output: a threat model, the security and privacy section of the design doc, and security stories in the backlog.
- **Design for testability, observability and operability** – Isolate domain logic from UI, database and transport with ports and adapters, so tests can drive the application without real devices (Cockburn; Evans layered architecture). Think about tests before code (Pragmatic Programmer). Instrument for traces, metrics and logs, and decide the SLIs and the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) in the design (OpenTelemetry; Google SRE). Expose health endpoints, keep configuration in the environment, treat logs as event streams, and design fast start-up and graceful shutdown (12-factor; Azure patterns). Output: test strategy inputs, an observability plan, and an operational readiness checklist.
- **Do user research and synthesise the findings** – Understand users, tasks and environments before and during design (ISO 9241-210 principles a–c). Use discovery methods (interviews, field studies, diary studies, support logs) and exploration methods (task analysis, card sorting, prototype tests). Add listening methods (surveys, analytics) (NN/g research cheat sheet; GOV.UK user research). Synthesise the results into personas grounded in data, and into journey maps with phases, actions, emotions and opportunities (NN/g). Output: research findings, personas, journey maps, and a prioritised list of user needs and problems.
- **Define information architecture and content** – Inventory and audit the content. Group and label it from the mental model of the user (open card sorting). Validate findability with tree tests, then design the navigation (NN/g). Design content together with the service: plain language, one idea per sentence, start with less, test words with users, consistent style (GOV.UK writing for user interfaces). Output: a sitemap or taxonomy, a labelling scheme, a content model, UI copy and error messages.
- **Produce wireframes, prototypes and UI designs with the design system** – Sketch flows and layouts. Then build low-fidelity prototypes for fast exploration, and high-fidelity prototypes to test specific interactions and visual hierarchy (NN/g). Reuse styles, components and patterns from the design system, so the product stays consistent and accessible (NN/g design systems; GOV.UK Design System). Apply the usability heuristics: visibility of status, match with the real world, user control, consistency, error prevention, recognition over recall. Design accessibility in: keyboard operability, focus visibility, target size, contrast, accessible authentication, consistent help, no redundant entry (WCAG 2.2 AA). Output: prototypes, UI specifications, component usage notes, accessibility annotations.
- **Evaluate designs with users and experts** – Run qualitative usability tests with about five representative users per round, and iterate rather than run one large study (NN/g). Use quantitative benchmarks (success rate, time on task, error rate, satisfaction such as SUS) when the question is measurement, with about twenty users. Run heuristic evaluations and accessibility checks with automated tools, manual checks and assistive technology. Get an audit before public beta where rules require it (GOV.UK). Output: usability test reports with prioritised issues, accessibility findings, and an updated prototype.
- **Write the design doc, RFC and ADRs** – Record the context and scope, the goals and non-goals, and the design with diagrams and API sketches. Record the alternatives considered with their trade-offs, and the cross-cutting concerns (security, privacy, observability, i18n, storage) (Google). Keep it short: a few pages for small changes, 10–20 pages for large projects. Record each significant decision as an ADR with context, decision, status and consequences, so future maintainers know why (Nygard; SWEBOK design rationale). Output: a reviewed design document and a decision log in the repository.
- **Review the design** – Hold a review before major implementation starts: the design doc is a form of code review before code (Software Engineering at Google). Reviewers check completeness against the requirements, the open issues, and the security and privacy sections. They check API style guide compliance, data model and migration safety, accessibility and operability (SWEBOK design reviews and audits; Azure API stewardship review). Use static analysis, simulation or prototypes for risky parts. Output: review comments, an approval record, and a list of follow-up actions and accepted risks.
- **Maintain the design and its traceability** – Update the design doc when the implementation diverges, so it stays a trustworthy entry point (Google). Keep traceability from requirements to design elements to tests. Maintain the design baseline under configuration management (SEBoK: manage the design). Manage the deprecation of API versions and schema elements with notice periods (AIP-185). Output: current design documentation, traceability links, deprecation notices.

### Outputs

- A software design description or design doc: component and module structure, responsibilities, interfaces, states, algorithms and data structures, with rationale and alternatives.
- Interface and API specifications: OpenAPI documents, .proto files, GraphQL schemas, AsyncAPI documents, contract tests, an API changelog, and a versioning and deprecation policy.
- Data design: conceptual and logical models (ER diagrams), the physical schema (DDL), migration scripts, an indexing plan, a data dictionary, and data classification and retention rules.
- Domain model artefacts: a glossary (ubiquitous language), a context map, aggregate definitions, domain events.
- The error model and resilience design: an error catalogue and format, retry, timeout and circuit-breaker policies, idempotency rules.
- Security and privacy artefacts: a threat model, data flow diagrams with trust boundaries, mitigations, and security backlog items.
- Testability and operability artefacts: test strategy inputs, an observability plan (SLIs, traces, metrics, logs), health checks, configuration design, a capacity estimate.
- UX artefacts: research findings, personas, journey maps, information architecture, content and UI copy, wireframes, prototypes, UI specifications, design system components, usability test reports, an accessibility audit and WCAG conformance evidence.
- Decision records: ADRs, review minutes, the approval record, accepted risks.
- Exit criteria: the agreed reviewers have reviewed and approved the design. The interfaces are agreed with consumers. The design is detailed enough to code and test (the ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 software detailed design purpose). Spikes or prototypes have reduced the risk of the risky parts. Representative users have tested the prototypes. The accessibility target is designed in. The open issues and their owners are listed. The design doc is stored where future maintainers will find it.

### Roles

- Software engineer or tech lead: owns the detailed design, writes the design doc, decomposes modules, defines contracts, implements and updates the design.
- Software architect: supplies the architecture constraints, reviews designs for conformance, arbitrates cross-team trade-offs.
- API designer or API owner, and an API review or stewardship board in larger organizations: applies the API style guide, reviews breaking changes and deprecations.
- Data modeller, DBA or data engineer: reviews schemas, indexes and migrations, owns data standards and performance (Fowler: DBAs collaborate closely with developers).
- Domain expert or product manager: provides the ubiquitous language, business rules and priorities; objects to awkward model terms (Evans).
- UX researcher: plans and runs research and usability tests, synthesises findings, manages participant consent and ethics.
- Interaction, UX or UI designer: designs flows, information architecture, wireframes, prototypes and visual design with the design system.
- Content designer or UX writer: designs UI text, error messages, help content and naming.
- Accessibility specialist: audits designs and prototypes against WCAG 2.2, advises on assistive technology.
- Security engineer or threat modeling facilitator: leads threat modeling and reviews the security and privacy sections.
- SRE or operations engineer: reviews observability, capacity, failure modes and operational readiness.
- QA or test engineer: derives the test strategy and contract tests from the design, reviews testability.
- Design reviewers and approvers (senior engineers, cross-team experts, the design system team): review and approve design docs and RFCs. In regulated organizations, compliance, legal, and safety or clinical reviewers also take part.

### Practices with consensus

- **Decompose by information hiding** – Each module hides a decision that is likely to change behind a simple, stable interface, and modules are deep (much functionality, small interface). Changes stay local, teams can develop and understand modules independently, and a module imposes minimal complexity on the rest of the system. Evidence: Parnas 1972 (On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules); Ousterhout (A Philosophy of Software Design); SWEBOK V4 Software Design principles (encapsulation, separation of interface and implementation); Code Complete ch. 5 heuristics.
- **Keep coupling low and cohesion high, give each module a single responsibility, and separate concerns** – Tightly coupled systems make changes cascade, and they are hard to test and reuse. Cohesive modules are easier to understand and maintain. Evidence: SWEBOK V4 (coupling and cohesion definitions, Parnas single responsibility); Constantine/Yourdon structured design (via the Wikipedia coupling article); Martin SOLID; Dijkstra EWD447 separation of concerns; Code Complete desirable characteristics.
- **Make interface contracts explicit** – State preconditions, postconditions, invariants and error behavior. Capture consumer expectations, and keep readers tolerant of additive change. Explicit contracts document and verify that code does no more and no less than it claims. Consumer-driven contracts and tolerant readers let providers evolve without a break for clients. Evidence: Meyer Design by Contract (Eiffel); Pragmatic Programmer tip 37; Fowler Consumer-Driven Contracts and Tolerant Reader; SWEBOK formal specification notations (pre/postconditions).
- **Write a short design doc or RFC for non-obvious or cross-cutting work, and review it before major implementation** – Include goals and non-goals, the design, the alternatives with trade-offs, and the security, privacy and observability considerations. Reviewers find design issues when change is still cheap, the team reaches consensus, cross-cutting concerns get attention, and the rationale survives as organizational memory. Evidence: Design Docs at Google (industrialempathy); Software Engineering at Google ch. 10; Pragmatic Engineer RFC process; SWEBOK design rationale and design reviews; Nygard ADRs.
- **API-first or contract-first** – Define the API in a machine-readable specification, and review it with consumers before you implement it. Early peer review catches usability and consistency problems, the contract can generate documentation, clients and tests, and the API stays independent of implementation details. Evidence: Zalando RESTful API Guidelines (API first principle); Azure Architecture Center API design (OpenAPI promotes a contract-first approach); OpenAPI Specification; Google API design guide.
- **Resource-oriented HTTP APIs** – Use nouns for resources, plural collections, standard methods with correct HTTP semantics (idempotent GET, PUT and DELETE, 202 plus a status monitor for long-running work, ETags for conditional requests) and consistent naming. Consistency lowers the learning cost for clients, and correct semantics allow safe retries and caching. Evidence: Azure Architecture Center API design; Azure REST API Guidelines; Microsoft REST API Guidelines; Google AIP-121 and AIP-131–135; Fielding REST constraints (uniform interface).
- **Never break existing clients** – Make only additive, backward-compatible changes within a version, define what counts as breaking, and deprecate with notice before removal. Clients cannot all upgrade at once. Breaking changes push the upgrade cost onto every consumer and trap users on old versions. Evidence: Google AIP-180 and AIP-185; Azure REST API Guidelines (customer workloads must never break); Stripe API versioning; Zalando compatibility rules; GraphQL schema design (continuous evolution); Microsoft REST API Guidelines.
- **Return errors in a structured, machine-readable format** – Give a stable code, a human-readable message and optional details; never leak stack traces. Clients can handle errors programmatically, and users get actionable messages. Consistency across services reduces the integration effort. Evidence: RFC 9457 Problem Details; Google AIP-193 (google.rpc.Status, ErrorInfo); Azure/Microsoft error object; Zalando problem JSON.
- **Paginate every collection** – Use opaque cursors or page tokens, a capped page size and stable ordering, and offer filter and sort options as explicit parameters. Unbounded lists are a performance and denial-of-service risk. Opaque tokens keep implementation details out of the contract, and they stay correct when data changes. Evidence: Google AIP-158; GraphQL pagination (connections, opaque cursors); Zalando (cursor-based preferred); Azure REST API Guidelines (nextLink); Microsoft REST API Guidelines (stable ordering).
- **Make non-idempotent operations safely retryable** – Use client-supplied idempotency keys and store the first result, and make message consumers idempotent. Networks fail and clients retry. Without idempotency a retry creates duplicate charges, orders or messages. Evidence: Stripe idempotent requests; Google AIP-155; Azure REST API Guidelines (Repeatability-Request-ID); IETF Idempotency-Key header draft; Azure Idempotent Consumer pattern.
- **Model data in three levels and normalise transactional data by default** – Model the conceptual, logical and physical levels, normalise to third normal form by default, denormalise only with a known reason, and handle the resulting redundancy deliberately. Normalisation removes redundancy and inconsistent dependencies. The three levels keep business meaning separate from product-specific storage decisions. Evidence: IBM data modeling overview; Microsoft database normalization description; SWEBOK (ERDs represent conceptual, logical and physical models).
- **Treat schema change as versioned, automated migrations with compatibility rules** – Add before remove, use transition phases, keep old and new code working together, and never reuse field tags or change field types. Rolling deployments run old and new code at the same time, and stored data outlives code. Compatible changes avoid downtime and data loss. Evidence: Fowler Evolutionary Database Design; Protocol Buffers dos and don'ts; Kleppmann schema evolution article; Google AIP-180.
- **Design indexes from the access paths of the application** – Treat each index as a cost on writes, and remove unused indexes. Developers know the queries. Missing or wrong indexes are a main source of performance problems, while every index slows inserts and updates. Evidence: PostgreSQL documentation (indexes introduction); Use The Index, Luke (preface).
- **Human-centred design** – Base the design on an explicit understanding of users, tasks and environments; involve users throughout; iterate; evaluate with users; use a multidisciplinary team. Teams cannot predict user behavior. Evaluation with real users is the only reliable way to find and fix usability problems before release. Evidence: ISO 9241-210:2019 principles and activities (as quoted in the Schmidt lecture); GOV.UK Service Manual (user research, design principles: start with user needs, iterate); NN/g usability testing 101.
- **Test usability early and often with small qualitative studies** – Use about five users per round and iterate, and reserve quantitative studies for benchmarks. Five users find most frequent problems, repeated small rounds fix problems and verify the fixes, and metrics need larger samples and are expensive. Evidence: NN/g Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users; NN/g Usability Metrics; NN/g UX research cheat sheet; GOV.UK user research in every phase.
- **Design accessibility in from the start and target WCAG 2.2 level AA** – Test with automated tools, manual checks and assistive technology, not with automated tools alone. Accessibility retrofits are costly, automated tools find only a part of the issues, and public sector bodies and many regulations require AA. Evidence: W3C WCAG 2.2 (Recommendation; new criteria such as focus not obscured, target size, accessible authentication); GOV.UK understanding WCAG; GOV.UK design principles (this is for everyone).
- **Use a design system for products that will grow, and contribute patterns back** – A design system is a style guide, a component library and a pattern library. Reusable, accessible components give consistency, speed and a shared language across teams. The cost only pays off for long-lived work. Evidence: NN/g Design Systems 101; GOV.UK Design System; SWEBOK uniformity principle.
- **Threat model during design** – Apply least privilege, defence in depth and secure defaults, and check APIs against the OWASP API Security Top 10. Design-time mitigations are cheaper than production fixes. Most API breaches come from authorisation and resource-limit design gaps. Evidence: OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet; OWASP Secure Product Design Cheat Sheet; OWASP API Security Top 10 2023; Google design doc templates require security and privacy sections.
- **Design for testability, observability and operability** – Isolate domain logic behind ports and adapters, instrument traces, metrics and logs, expose health endpoints, and keep configuration in the environment. Isolated logic can be tested without UI or database, systems that emit signals can be debugged for unknown unknowns, and operability decisions are hard to add later. Evidence: Cockburn Hexagonal Architecture; Evans Layered Architecture; Pragmatic Programmer "design to test"; Google SRE monitoring (four golden signals); OpenTelemetry observability primer; 12-factor app; Azure Health Endpoint Monitoring.
- **Design resilience in from the start** – Use timeouts, retries with backoff paired with circuit breakers, bulkheads, queue-based load levelling and compensating transactions, and do not defer reliability. Distributed systems fail partially. A team that defers reliability accepts fewer features at a higher cost later. Evidence: Azure cloud design patterns (retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, saga); Google SRE workbook NALSD; SWEBOK key issues (errors, exception handling, fault tolerance).
- **Use domain-driven design in complex domains** – Build a ubiquitous language, draw bounded contexts and a context map, and use aggregates as consistency and transaction boundaries. One unified model does not scale across an organization. Explicit boundaries keep models coherent, and aggregates keep invariants enforceable without global locks. Evidence: Evans DDD Reference; Fowler BoundedContext, UbiquitousLanguage, DDD_Aggregate; SWEBOK V4 domain-driven design method.
- **Keep the design simple** – Apply YAGNI, remove duplication, write intent-revealing code, use patterns only when they earn their place, and remove them when they stop adding value. Presumptive features cost build, delay, carry and repair. Unnecessary patterns add complexity and obscure intent. Evidence: Fowler Yagni; Fowler Is Design Dead; Wikipedia Design Patterns criticism (Norvig, Graham); Azure pattern guidance (choose a pattern for the problem, accept its trade-offs); Ousterhout.
- **Record design rationale and significant decisions (ADRs) next to the code** – Keep the design doc updated when the implementation diverges. Future maintainers need the why, stale docs mislead, and decisions with recorded consequences can be revisited when assumptions change. Evidence: SWEBOK design rationale; Nygard Documenting Architecture Decisions; Design Docs at Google lifecycle.

### Contested points

- **How much design before coding: planned versus evolutionary design** – Fowler argues for evolutionary design backed by refactoring, tests and CI, with a few upfront decisions (storage, layering, domain model) that remain changeable. Google and the RFC process ask for an approved design doc before any major project, but skip docs for obvious or prototype work. SWEBOK notes that in agile teams the design may live only in code, but testers, certifiers and operators may still need explicit design. The correct amount depends on novelty, risk, team size, regulation and how cheap change is in the codebase.
- **API versioning strategy** – Fielding says do not version; evolve through hypermedia and create a new system (new host) only for real breaks. Google AIPs and Microsoft put a major version in the URL path. Azure uses a required date-based api-version query parameter. Stripe pins each account to a rolling date version with per-version transformation modules. Zalando avoids versioning and allows media-type versioning only for unavoidable incompatible changes. GraphQL promotes a versionless schema with deprecation. All agree that teams must avoid breaking changes; the mechanism depends on the client population, caching, tooling and the expected number of breaking changes.
- **REST versus GraphQL versus gRPC, and how much REST purity (HATEOAS) matters** – Fielding and the Azure maturity model treat hypermedia as the defining property of REST. Most published guidelines (Azure, Google, Zalando) stop at resources plus HTTP verbs. GraphQL trades a single flexible endpoint and client-chosen fields for more complex caching, authorisation and performance concerns. gRPC with Protocol Buffers suits internal, polyglot, streaming and high-throughput services (the Google guide focuses on gRPC). The choice depends on the consumers (public web, partners, internal services), tooling, caching needs and team experience.
- **Offset pagination versus cursor pagination** – The general Azure API design guidance describes limit/offset with defaults. Google AIP-158, Zalando and GraphQL prefer opaque cursors or tokens, because offsets break when data changes and perform badly at scale. Offset is acceptable for small, stable, user-facing lists with page numbers. Cursors are preferred for large or changing collections.
- **Error handling model: exceptions, error codes, typed results, checked exceptions** – Duffy's error model separates bugs (abandon fast) from recoverable errors (typed, checked, part of the signature) and criticises both unchecked exceptions and ignorable error codes. Ousterhout prefers to define errors out of existence and to reduce the exception surface. GraphQL makes every field nullable by default, so a partial failure returns null instead of a failed request, while non-null types make guarantees. The choice depends on the language, the reliability needs and how callers can recover.
- **Normalisation versus denormalisation, relational versus document or dimensional models** – Normal forms protect integrity for transactional data (Microsoft), but the same guidance accepts denormalisation when many small tables hurt performance. IBM notes that dimensional (star/snowflake) models deliberately add redundancy for analytics, and that agile and DevOps teams often skip the logical model stage. Document models trade schema flexibility and locality for weaker support of many-to-many relationships (Kleppmann). Access patterns, consistency needs and team skills decide.
- **Clean code and SOLID versus deep modules and longer methods; are design patterns language deficiencies?** – Robert Martin argues that SOLID stays relevant and that "just write simple code" without principles produces tangles. Ousterhout's book explicitly disagrees with Clean Code on method length and comments, and argues for deep modules and fewer, larger abstractions ("classitis" is a red flag). Norvig and Graham (via the Design Patterns criticism) argue that many GoF patterns disappear in more expressive languages. The GoF authors themselves would recategorise some patterns. Most practitioners treat both principle sets as heuristics, not rules.
- **Optimistic versus pessimistic concurrency; shared memory versus message passing** – The EF Core documentation recommends optimistic concurrency tokens when conflicts are rare, and higher isolation levels or locks when operations are short and conflicts are common. It warns against long transactions that wait on users. Go's guidance prefers channels over shared memory with locks. PoEAA offers optimistic and pessimistic offline locks as patterns. The conflict rate, the transaction length and the language runtime decide.
- **Tolerant readers and Postel's law versus strict validation** – Fowler and Zalando promote a liberal attitude to what you accept, so providers can evolve, and Microsoft requires clients to ignore unknown fields. Security guidance (OWASP API Top 10: unsafe consumption of APIs, broken object property level authorisation) pushes strict validation of inputs and of data from third-party APIs. Teams usually ignore unknown output fields, but strictly validate inputs and authorisation.
- **Form and size of design documentation: Google-style design docs, RFCs, ADRs, or code only** – Google uses 10–20 page docs for large projects and mini docs for increments. The Pragmatic Engineer RFC process emphasises organization-wide distribution and selective approvers. Nygard's ADRs record one decision per short file in the repository. Agile teams often keep the design implicit in code and tests. Even advocates warn that docs go stale and that the overhead must not exceed the benefit.
- **When domain-driven design pays off** – Evans himself says that not all parts of a design will be equally refined. He advises teams to invest tactical DDD in the core domain and to factor out generic subdomains. PoEAA offers transaction script and table module as valid alternatives to a domain model for simple logic. DDD jargon applied to CRUD applications adds ceremony without benefit. The complexity of the business rules and the expected life of the system decide.
- **Quantitative versus qualitative usability evaluation, and what satisfaction scores mean** – NN/g says that qualitative tests with five users per round give the best return, and that metrics are expensive (about twenty users per design). MeasuringU shows that SUS is reliable for perceived usability, but it does not diagnose problems and explains only a small part of task performance. Use qualitative tests to find and fix problems, and metrics only to benchmark or to satisfy a measurement requirement.
- **Strong consistency in APIs versus eventual consistency across aggregates** – Google AIP-121 requires management-plane operations to reach a steady state where a subsequent Get reflects the change. Evans recommends synchronous consistency inside an aggregate and asynchronous updates across aggregates. Cloud patterns (saga, compensating transaction, event sourcing) accept eventual consistency for scale. Whether a client can tolerate stale reads decides the design.

### Metrics

- Structural design measures: coupling (afferent/efferent, fan-in/fan-out), cohesion, depth of inheritance, class size, and cyclomatic complexity per method. SWEBOK lists function-based and object-oriented design measures. Caveat: they are gameable proxies; read them together with code review, not as targets.
- Interface depth: the ratio of interface size to functionality, the number of pass-through methods, and the number of public members per class (Ousterhout red flags). Caveat: these are qualitative signals for reviews, not numbers to optimise.
- Design documentation health: the share of significant changes with a design doc or ADR, the review turnaround time, the number of review comments resolved, and the docs updated after the implementation diverged. Caveat: counts say nothing about quality.
- API quality: style-guide lint violations per specification, the number of breaking changes per period (target zero within a version), the time to deprecate and remove versions, the consumer contract test pass rate, the error rate by error code, and adoption and time-to-first-successful-call. Caveat: breaking-change counts depend on the definition of breaking in the organization.
- Data design: normal form violations with documented exceptions, unused or duplicate indexes, the migration failure and rollback rate, query latency percentiles on critical paths, and schema compatibility check results in CI. Caveat: a violation is only a defect when no documented exception explains it.
- Resilience and operability signals agreed at design time: the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation), SLIs and SLO attainment, and retry and circuit-breaker trip rates. Caveat: these measure the outcome of the design in operation, not the design itself.
- Usability metrics: task success rate, time on task, error rate, subjective satisfaction, and optional path-following and backtracking (NN/g); the System Usability Scale with an average of about 68 (MeasuringU). Caveats: quantitative studies need about twenty users per design and are expensive; SUS does not diagnose problems.
- Usability findings: the number and severity of problems found per test round, and the share fixed before the next round; five users per round for qualitative studies. Caveat: the count depends on the tasks and the participants, so compare only rounds of the same study.
- Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 A and AA issues found by audits (by level and criterion), the share fixed before release, and assistive technology test coverage. Caveat: automated tools find only a part of the issues.
- Security design: threat model coverage (data flows and trust boundaries modelled, threats with a decided response), and OWASP API Top 10 checks passed in review. Caveat: coverage shows that the team considered a threat, not that the mitigation works.
- Design review effectiveness: defects found in design review versus defects found later that trace to design (escaped design defects), and rework caused by late design changes. Caveat: the attribution of a late defect to design is a judgement, and a low count can also mean that nobody traced the defects.
- Adoption of the design system: the share of screens built from system components, and the number of one-off components. Caveat: high reuse is not the same as good UX.

### Failure modes

- Temporal decomposition: modules split by the order in which things happen instead of by the knowledge they hide, so the same knowledge leaks into several modules (Ousterhout; Parnas flowchart decomposition). One change then touches many modules.
- Shallow modules and classitis: many tiny classes and pass-through methods that add interface without hiding anything. This raises the cognitive load.
- Big design up front without feedback, or no design at all: either months of speculative documents that rot, or code-and-fix that accumulates entropy. Both ignore that design needs iteration and refactoring.
- Presumptive features and over-engineering: features built for imagined future needs (YAGNI), and patterns applied because they are known, not because the problem matches. This adds cost to build, carry and repair.
- Design docs that skip alternatives, non-goals and cross-cutting concerns, or that nobody updates after implementation. They mislead maintainers.
- Lost rationale: decisions without recorded context, so successors either blindly keep or blindly reverse them (Nygard).
- An API designed from the database schema or internal functions: verbs in URLs, leaked storage details, inconsistent naming, no pagination, unbounded lists, no idempotency for writes, errors as free text or HTTP 200 with an error body. Clients must learn internals, and they cannot retry or cache safely.
- Breaking changes shipped as minor updates, or a new major version for every change; versions never deprecated, so old versions become a permanent cost (Stripe, Fielding).
- Pagination or required fields added to an existing method later. Both are breaking changes (AIP-158, AIP-180).
- Reused protobuf tag numbers, changed field types, added required fields, or changed defaults. These cause silent data corruption or version skew.
- Destructive schema changes without transition phases, shared development databases, migrations done by hand, and storage and API messages coupled so storage cannot change. These cause downtime, data loss and frozen storage.
- Over-normalisation or under-normalisation without measurement; every column indexed or no column indexed; indexes never reviewed. Performance and integrity suffer.
- Anaemic or cargo-cult DDD: DDD vocabulary on a CRUD system, aggregates that span the whole database, one unified enterprise model that nobody can agree on, no ubiquitous language in the code. This is ceremony without benefit.
- Error handling that conflates bugs with recoverable errors, swallows exceptions, or exposes stack traces and internals to clients. Bugs hide, and internals leak.
- Reliability deferred to later: no timeouts, unbounded retries without circuit breakers, no bulkheads, shared fate between tenants (SRE NALSD; Azure patterns). Partial failures become total failures.
- Concurrency by accident: shared mutable state without a consistency model, long transactions that wait on user input, non-idempotent consumers that duplicate effects on redelivery. Data becomes corrupt under load.
- Security and privacy as a checklist at the end: no threat model, authorisation designed per endpoint instead of per object and property, no resource limits (OWASP API Top 10). These gaps are the main causes of API breaches.
- Untestable design: domain logic entangled with UI, database and transport, so tests need the full stack (Cockburn); observability left to operations after launch. Tests become slow and brittle, and failures are hard to diagnose.
- UX failure modes: a design for everyone and no one (no personas grounded in research), personas invented without data, journey maps that stop at discovery, no usability tests or one large late test, designers attached to high-fidelity prototypes, content written last, accessibility checked only by automated tools, one-off components outside the design system, and navigation designed before information architecture. Users get a product that does not fit their tasks.
- Design reviews as rubber stamps, or as gates that block for weeks; reviewers without the right expertise (security, accessibility, data) for the sections they approve. Problems pass, or work stalls.
- UML or diagrams treated as deliverables instead of communication; notations produced that nobody reads (SWEBOK: choose specifications by audience and usage). The effort is wasted.

### Tailoring by project size

Some practices are essential at every scale. Decide module boundaries by information hiding, and keep interfaces small and explicit. Write down the goals, the non-goals, the chosen design and the rejected alternatives for any non-obvious change, even as a one-page file or an ADR in the repository. Define every external contract (API, event, schema) before clients depend on it, and change it only compatibly. Model data at least conceptually and logically before you write DDL, and run schema changes as versioned migrations.

Handle errors deliberately with a consistent error format. Look at the design through the eyes of a user before you build: a sketch, a prototype, one test with a real user. Design in keyboard access, contrast and clear content from the start. Think about how the software will be tested, observed and operated.

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| Solo developer on a small repository | ADRs or a short DESIGN.md instead of long docs; a single OpenAPI or proto file plus a changelog as the API governance; normalise to 3NF, add indexes only for known queries, keep migrations in the repository; apply YAGNI hard and prefer deep modules over many small ones; for UX, sketch flows, test with two to five people from the target group, use an existing design system or component library, run an automated accessibility check plus keyboard-only use; threat-model in five minutes by a list of data flows and who may call what | Formal review boards, GoF pattern catalogues and design metrics can be skipped |
| Small product team | A lightweight design doc or RFC template for changes that cross module or team boundaries, with named reviewers and a short review meeting; a published API style guide (for example Zalando or Microsoft) instead of a self-written one; consumer contract tests and spec linting in CI; one person who owns the data model and the migration practice; research and a five-user usability test every iteration, and a small design system with reusable components; threat modeling for new features with external exposure; SLIs and golden-signal dashboards defined in the design; accessibility target WCAG 2.2 AA with manual checks | DDD context maps when the domain is complex; quantitative usability benchmarks; design-metric dashboards |
| Large or regulated organization | A formal design definition process with traceability from requirements to design to tests (ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207/15288). A design baseline under configuration management, with recorded design reviews and audits. An API stewardship or review board that enforces the style guide, the breaking-change rules and the deprecation periods. An organization-wide versioning policy (major version in path, date versions, or versionless evolution) and an API inventory. Enterprise data standards, data classification, retention and privacy reviews in the data design. Security and privacy sections and a threat model in every design doc, reviewed by specialists. A governed design system and accessibility audits with assistive-technology tests and a conformance statement (WCAG 2.2 AA is mandatory for the UK public sector and many regulated markets). Dedicated UX research, content design and accessibility roles. Design rationale kept for certification and regulatory evidence | Heavy UML models and document-based design where the team is co-located and the code is the design; formal methods, except for high-assurance components |

### Sources

- [Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK) v4.0 – Chapter 3 Software Design and Chapter 2 Software Architecture](https://ieeecs-media.computer.org/media/education/swebok/swebok-v4.pdf) – Official IEEE CS PDF (v4.0, released October 2024). Source for the definition of software design, the three stages (architectural, high-level, detailed), the design principles (abstraction, separation of concerns, modularisation, encapsulation, coupling, cohesion, uniformity, completeness, verifiability), the key issues (concurrency, events, persistence, distribution, errors, integration, security, variability), notations, methods (including user-centred design and DDD), design reviews, measures and V&V.
- [SEBoK – System Detailed Design Definition](https://sebokwiki.org/wiki/System_Detailed_Design_Definition) – Summary of the ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 design definition process: purpose, activities (initialise, establish design characteristics, assess alternatives, manage the design), inputs and outputs, relation to architecture, pitfalls.
- [IEEE SA – IEEE/ISO/IEC 12207-2017 Software life cycle processes](https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/12207/5672/) – Scope of the standard and its status (published 2017, superseded by 12207-2026). Places design definition and software detailed design in the process framework.
- [Parnas, On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules (1972)](https://wstomv.win.tue.nl/edu/2ip30/references/criteria_for_modularization.pdf) – Primary source for information hiding, the KWIC example and the benefits of decomposition by likely change.
- [Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design – book page](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/book.php) – Official page (editions, themes, disagreement with Clean Code). The book text itself was the source for complexity, deep modules, information leakage, temporal decomposition, define errors out of existence, comments and red flags.
- [Code Complete (2nd ed.) – reader notes on chapters 5–7](https://github.com/mgp/book-notes/blob/master/code-complete.markdown) – Secondary notes on McConnell's design challenges (wicked problem), desirable characteristics, heuristics and practices; web search summaries support them.
- [Dijkstra, EWD447 On the role of scientific thought (1974)](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~EWD/transcriptions/EWD04xx/EWD447.html) – Origin of "separation of concerns".

- [Robert C. Martin – Solid Relevance (2020)](https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2020/10/18/Solid-Relevance.html) – SOLID definitions and the argument for their continued relevance.
