## 8. Implementation (construction)

### Purpose

Construction changes requirements and design into source code that works, has tests, and is easy to maintain. SWEBOK v4 defines software construction as "the detailed creation and maintenance of software through coding, verification, unit testing, integration testing and debugging". The phase answers one question: how do we write code that is correct now and cheap to change later? Construction produces the largest number of configuration items in a project. Most defects, security weaknesses, and technical debt therefore enter the product in this phase.

SWEBOK names five fundamentals that guide the work: minimize complexity, anticipate and embrace change, construct for verification, reuse assets, and apply standards. The daily mechanics of the phase are version control, code review, dependency management, the automated build, and developer tests.

### Other names

- Software construction (SWEBOK v4 Knowledge Area 4, Code Complete)
- Implementation
- Coding
- Coding and unit testing
- Development
- Programming
- Build phase (informal)
- Construction (McConnell, Construx)

### Position in the life cycle

Construction follows requirements engineering (see section 5), architecture (see section 6), and detailed design (see section 7). It feeds testing (see section 9), integration and build (see section 10), and release and deployment (see section 11). SWEBOK v4 states that "what is considered construction depends on the life cycle model used".

In waterfall and V-model projects (see section 2), code work starts after detailed design. It ends with unit-tested modules that go to integration and system test. In iterative and agile projects, design, code, tests, and refactoring overlap inside each iteration. SWEBOK notes that "much design work is performed during construction". In DevOps and continuous delivery, each small change passes through an automated build, test, and deployment pipeline. Construction, integration, and delivery then form one continuous flow with fast feedback from production (see section 12).

Construction is therefore a continuous process for the life of the product, not a one-time phase. Maintenance and evolution (see section 13) are mostly construction again. Dependency updates, refactoring, and debt repayment continue as long as the code lives.

### Inputs

- A prioritized work item (a user story, an issue, or a bug report) with acceptance criteria and a definition of done.
- Requirements and design inputs: architecture decisions (ADRs), interface and API contracts, the data model, and the UX design (see sections 5, 6 and 7).
- Security requirements and the threat model for the component, and the applicable secure coding standard (OWASP, CERT) (see section 16).
- Coding standards and a style guide for each language, with linter and formatter configuration.
- A repository under version control with a branch policy, branch protection, and a CODEOWNERS or owners file.
- A defined developer environment (devcontainer, Dockerfile, Makefile, scripts) and a README with build, run, and test commands.
- An automated build and a CI pipeline that runs tests and static analysis on every push (see section 10).
- A dependency policy: allowed sources, license rules, update cadence, and vulnerability scans.
- A test strategy and test frameworks for unit and integration tests (see section 9).
- Access to the existing code base, its documentation, and the people who know it.
- For AI-assisted work: repository instruction files, the allowed tools, and the verification commands that the agent must run.

### Activities

- **Set up a reproducible developer environment** – Define the toolchain, the runtime versions, and the services in files that live in the repository: a devcontainer.json, a Dockerfile, a Makefile, or a normalized script set such as script/bootstrap, script/setup, script/test, and script/server. Document the run, test, and build commands in the README. The goal is that a new developer or an AI agent can clone, build, and run the tests with one command on the first day. Output: environment definition files, an EditorConfig file, a pre-commit configuration, and a verified "getting started" section.
- **Adopt, document, and automate coding standards** – Select a style guide for each language (for example the Google style guides) and record the project-specific rules in the repository. Enforce the format with an automatic formatter and the rules with linters, so that reviews do not discuss whitespace. Google reports that static analysis tools enforce about 90 percent of its style rules and that formatters end format debates. Output: a style guide, linter and formatter configuration, and presubmit or CI checks that block code that does not conform.
- **Plan the construction of each change** – Divide a feature into small slices that you can integrate independently (INVEST, vertical slices, tracer bullets) and decide the integration order. Select the construction approach: test-first or test-after, pair or solo, and feature flags for unfinished work. SWEBOK calls this construction planning and says that it defines the order of creation and integration. Output: a task list or an issue breakdown with small steps, and an integration plan.
- **Perform detailed design during construction** – Refine algorithms, data structures, module interfaces, and APIs at the code level. SWEBOK notes that "much design work is performed during construction". Use pseudocode, short design notes, or an ADR for decisions with a lasting effect. Design for minimal complexity, information hiding, and loose coupling, as the Code Complete class and routine checklists describe. Output: interfaces, skeletons, and ADRs for significant decisions.
- **Write readable, self-documenting code** – Select names that state the intent, keep each routine focused on one task, prefer clear code to clever code, and keep the layout consistent. Software Engineering at Google states: "We'd rather the code be tedious to type than difficult to read". Write comments that explain why, not what, and remove comments that repeat the code. Output: source code that a reviewer can understand without the author present.
- **Program defensively and handle errors deliberately** – Validate inputs at trust boundaries, use assertions for conditions that must never occur, and use error handling for conditions that can occur (Code Complete). Define a project-wide exception policy, create barricades so that bad data does not spread, avoid empty catch blocks, include context in error messages, and crash early when the state is corrupt. Log events through a shared handler, never log secrets or personal data, and return generic errors to users while you log the details on the server (OWASP). Output: consistent error-handling and log code, and a written policy.
- **Apply secure coding practices** – Follow a secure coding checklist (the OWASP Top 10 Proactive Controls, the OWASP Developer Guide checklist, the SEI CERT rules for C, C++, and Java) and know the CWE Top 25 and the OWASP Top 10 risk classes. Use allowlist input validation on the server, parameterized queries, output encoding, vetted cryptographic libraries, secure defaults, and least privilege. Prefer memory-safe languages where practical, and never push secrets to a repository (OpenSSF). Output: code that passes SAST and secret scans, with the security-relevant decisions recorded.
- **Write developer tests and debug** – Write automated tests together with the code: test first (red, green, refactor) or test after. The change is not done until tests exist and pass. SWEBOK states that construction testing "aims to reduce the gap between when faults are inserted into the code and when those faults are detected". Debug with a hypothesis, a failing test that reproduces the defect, and a fix at the root cause. Output: self-testing code and regression tests for fixed bugs.
- **Refactor continuously in small steps** – Improve the internal structure without a change to the observable behavior, one small refactoring at a time, with tests green before and after. Use code smells as triggers, do preparatory refactoring before a feature, and apply the boy-scout rule. Keep refactoring commits separate from feature commits, so that reviewers can check them quickly. Output: cleaner code and separate refactoring changes that are easy to review.
- **Manage dependencies** – Evaluate a package before you add it: maintenance activity, security practices, license, typosquatting risk, adoption, and your exit cost (OpenSSF). Declare all dependencies explicitly, isolate them, commit lockfiles for applications, and pin CI actions and container images by digest. Update regularly with an automated tool, scan for known vulnerabilities (OSV-Scanner, Dependabot), and publish an SBOM for releases. Output: a manifest, a lockfile, an update policy, and scan results.
- **Build with an automated, reproducible build** – One command builds the product from a clean checkout. The build tests itself and is fast (Fowler's ten-minute target). Make the build hermetic: declare every input, pin or vendor the tools, do not rely on host state, and aim for bit-for-bit reproducible artifacts with signed provenance (SLSA build levels). Output: build scripts or build-system configuration, and reproducible artifacts.
- **Use version control with a healthy mainline** – Keep everything in version control: code, tests, configuration, scripts, and AI prompts (DORA). Work in small commits on the trunk or on short-lived branches, integrate at least daily, and hide unfinished work behind feature flags or branch-by-abstraction. Write commit messages with an imperative subject line and a body that explains what and why. Use Conventional Commits when you want automated changelogs and version bumps. Protect the main branch with required reviews, status checks, and no force pushes. Output: a readable history and a deployable mainline.
- **Review code before it merges** – A person other than the author reads every change for design, functionality, complexity, tests, names, comments, style, and documentation (Google review guide). Authors write small, self-contained changes with clear descriptions. Reviewers respond within one business day and approve when the change improves code health, even if it is not perfect. Use severity labels (Nit, Optional, FYI), be courteous, and move unresolved disputes to a tech lead. Output: approved, merged changes with a review record.
- **Pair or mob program when the benefits exceed the costs** – Two developers (a driver and a navigator) or the whole team (a mob with a rotating driver) build a change together. The benefits are real-time review, spread of knowledge, onboarding, and less work in progress. The costs are fatigue and power dynamics. Google treats pair-programmed code as reviewed when the partners are qualified. Output: shared understanding and reviewed code.
- **Run static analysis and measure construction quality** – Run linters, SAST, type checkers, and complexity and duplication analyzers in the editor, in pre-commit hooks, and in CI. Show the findings at code review on the changed lines and keep the false-positive rates low (Google keeps effective false positives under 5 percent). Track the cyclomatic or cognitive complexity of each function and require a written reason to exceed the limit (NIST 500-235). Output: analysis reports, quality gates, and trend data.
- **Write and maintain in-code and repository documentation** – Keep a README (what the project does, why, how to start, where to get help, who maintains it), a CONTRIBUTING guide, docstrings on public modules and functions, ADRs for significant decisions, and a changelog. Treat documentation like code: version it, review it, and give it owners (Software Engineering at Google). Output: documentation that stays current with the code.
- **Construct for reuse and with reuse** – When code is necessary in more than one place, encapsulate it in a well-structured library with a stable, documented API and semantic versions, instead of a clone (SWEBOK). When you reuse, select, evaluate, integrate, and report the reused asset. InnerSource practices help large organizations share internal libraries across teams. Output: internal libraries, shared components, and API contracts.
- **Handle technical debt during construction** – Classify debt as prudent or reckless, and as deliberate or inadvertent (Fowler). Record deliberate debt in the tracker or in the code, and pay it down where change is frequent. Leave code better than you found it, but do not let a refactoring grow beyond the task. Output: debt items with owners, and small cleanup commits.
- **Use AI coding assistants with verification** – Give the assistant repository context (instruction files, style rules, commands), ask for small scoped changes, and require tests, a build, or a screenshot as proof of success. Review and understand generated code as you would review a human contribution. GitHub's guidance is "Understand suggested code before you implement it". Keep small batches and strong version control as the safety net (DORA). Output: AI-assisted changes that pass the same review and CI gates as any other change.
- **Integrate continuously and keep the build green** – Push to the mainline at least daily, let every push start the automated build and the tests, and fix or revert a broken build immediately. Incremental integration gives early feedback and keeps merges small (SWEBOK, Fowler). Output: a mainline that always builds and passes its tests.

### Outputs

- Source code merged to the mainline, with automated tests that pass in CI.
- A reviewed change record: a pull request or CL with a description, review comments, and an approval.
- A commit history with imperative, explanatory messages (Conventional Commits where used) that can drive changelogs.
- Build artifacts from an automated, reproducible build, with provenance where required.
- Updated documentation: README, CONTRIBUTING, docstrings, ADRs, and a changelog entry.
- An updated dependency manifest and lockfile; a clean vulnerability scan or triaged findings; an SBOM for releases.
- Static analysis and security scans with no new high-severity findings on the changed code.
- Feature flags registered and tracked for removal; technical debt items recorded with owners.
- Exit criteria (the definition of done): tests added and green, review approved, CI green, docs updated, no secrets committed, and the change deployable from the mainline.

### Roles

- Developer (author): designs at the code level, writes code and tests, keeps changes small, writes the change description, and addresses review comments.
- Reviewer: reads every line; checks design, functionality, complexity, tests, names, comments, style, and documentation; responds within one business day.
- Code owner or maintainer: approves changes in owned directories, and guards consistency and API stability.
- Tech lead: sets coding standards, resolves review disputes, and decides on debt payoff and exceptions.
- Pair partner or mob members (driver, navigator): real-time review and knowledge transfer.
- Security champion or AppSec engineer: reviews security-sensitive changes, and maintains the secure coding checklist and the SAST rules.
- Build or platform engineer: owns the build system, the developer environment, and the pre-commit and CI configuration.
- Test engineer: collaborates on testability, integration tests, and test data during construction.
- Technical writer (large organizations): reviews and structures documentation that crosses team boundaries.
- Product owner: clarifies acceptance criteria and accepts the result.
- AI coding assistant (a tool, not accountable): generates code and tests under human direction and review.

### Practices with consensus

- **Use an automatic formatter and linters, and enforce them in pre-commit hooks or CI, not in human review** – Machines apply rules consistently and free reviewers for design and correctness. Google says "the robots are better on average than the humans by a significant amount". Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 8 (Style Guides and Rules); Google Style Guides; pre-commit; EditorConfig; OpenSSF Concise Guide for Developing More Secure Software.
- **Optimize code for the reader: intention-revealing names, small focused routines, consistent style, simple code instead of clever code** – Code is read far more often than it is written. Reduced complexity is the first SWEBOK fundamental. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 ch. 4 (1.1 Minimizing Complexity, 3.3 Coding); Code Complete 2 checklists (Naming Variables, High-Quality Routines, Self-Documenting Code); Clean Code; Software Engineering at Google ch. 8; Google review guide (What to look for).
- **Comments explain intent and why; they do not repeat the code; rewrite difficult code instead of a comment on it** – Comments that repeat code go stale and add noise. What the code cannot say is what the comment must say. Evidence: Google review guide (What to look for); Code Complete 2 Good Commenting Technique checklist; Clean Code summary; Software Engineering at Google ch. 10.
- **Keep changes small and self-contained; split large work into stacked or vertical slices** – Small changes get a faster and more thorough review, introduce fewer bugs, and roll back more easily. Google: "100 lines is usually a reasonable size for a CL, and 1000 lines is usually too large". SmartBear: review no more than 200 to 400 lines at a time. Evidence: Google review guide (Small CLs); Software Engineering at Google ch. 9; SmartBear Best Practices for Peer Code Review; DORA Working in small batches.
- **Integrate to the mainline at least daily; avoid long-lived development branches** – Small merges are easier than big ones. DORA found that high performers have three or fewer active branches and merge to the trunk at least daily. Evidence: DORA Trunk-based development; Fowler Branching Patterns and Continuous Integration; Software Engineering at Google ch. 16; trunkbaseddevelopment.com.
- **A person other than the author reviews every change before it merges (pair programming with a qualified partner counts)** – Review catches defects and design problems early, spreads knowledge, and keeps the code base consistent. It also reduces the risk that one compromised contributor injects malicious code. Evidence: Google code review guide; Software Engineering at Google ch. 9; OpenSSF Concise Guide ("Review before accepting changes"); OpenSSF Scorecard Code-Review and Branch-Protection checks; Bacchelli and Bird (Microsoft Research).
- **Reviewers respond within one business day and approve when the change definitely improves code health, even if it is not perfect** – Slow reviews block the team and cause most complaints. "Technical facts and data overrule opinions and personal preferences". Evidence: Google review guide (Speed, Standard); Software Engineering at Google ch. 9 (24 working hours).
- **Write a clear change description: an imperative subject line, a blank line, and a body that explains what and why** – The description is the permanent record that future readers and tools (blame, revert, bisect) depend on. Evidence: Google review guide (CL descriptions); Chris Beams "How to Write a Git Commit Message"; Conventional Commits.
- **Deliver self-testing code: every change comes with automated unit or integration tests, written first or after** – Construction testing shortens the time between fault injection and detection. Tests make refactoring and CI safe. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 ch. 4 (3.4 Construction Testing, 4.16 Test-First Programming); Fowler SelfTestingCode and TestDrivenDevelopment; Code Complete 2 Major Construction Practices checklist; OpenSSF Concise Guide.
- **Refactor continuously in small, behavior-preserving steps with tests green; keep refactorings in separate commits** – Small steps rarely break things and let a system improve over time. A mix of refactoring and features hides both. Evidence: Fowler Refactoring (2nd ed.) and OpportunisticRefactoring; refactoring.com; Code Complete 2 Refactoring Safely checklist; Google review guide (Small CLs); Pragmatic Programmer tip "Refactor Early, Refactor Often".
- **Use assertions for conditions that must never occur and error handling for conditions that can occur; no empty catch blocks; a standard exception policy** – A separation of impossible and expected conditions keeps both failure detection and recovery explicit and consistent. Evidence: Code Complete 2 ch. 8 and Defensive Programming checklist; SWEBOK v4 ch. 4 (4.4, 4.5); Pragmatic Programmer tips "Crash Early" and "Use Assertions to Prevent the Impossible".
- **Validate input on the server with allowlists, encode output, return generic error messages to users, log details on the server, and never log secrets or personal data** – Attackers bypass denylists and client-side checks, detailed errors help attackers, and logged secrets leak. Evidence: OWASP Input Validation, Error Handling, and Logging Cheat Sheets; OWASP Developer Guide checklist; Code Complete 2 Defensive Programming security items.
- **Follow a recognized secure coding standard and know the common weakness lists** – Most vulnerabilities belong to well-known classes. Checklists and CERT rules make them avoidable and detectable by tools. Evidence: OWASP Secure Coding Practices QRG (now in the Developer Guide); OWASP Top 10 Proactive Controls; CWE Top 25; SEI CERT Coding Standards; SWEBOK v4 ch. 4 (3.6 Construction Quality).
- **Never commit secrets; use secret scans and push protection** – Committed credentials become targets and spread through clones and forks. Evidence: OpenSSF Concise Guide; GitHub secret scanning documentation.
- **Declare and isolate dependencies explicitly; commit lockfiles for applications so that every environment installs the same tree** – Implicit system packages and floating versions make builds non-reproducible and debugging inconsistent. Evidence: The Twelve-Factor App (Dependencies); npm package-lock.json docs; Cargo FAQ; Python Packaging "install_requires vs requirements files"; SWEBOK v4 ch. 4 (2.4 Managing Dependencies).
- **Evaluate a dependency before you adopt it, keep dependencies updated with an automated tool, and scan for known vulnerabilities** – Every dependency enlarges the attack surface and the supply chain. Out-of-date dependencies expose known flaws. Evidence: OpenSSF Concise Guide for Evaluating Open Source Software; OpenSSF Scorecard (Dependency-Update-Tool, Vulnerabilities, Pinned-Dependencies); Software Engineering at Google ch. 21; DORA Code maintainability; Dependabot; OSV-Scanner.
- **Automate the build; one command from a clean checkout; keep it fast; make it hermetic and reproducible** – A manual or host-dependent build is slow, error-prone, and impossible to verify. Reproducible builds let others verify the artifacts. Evidence: Fowler Continuous Integration; Software Engineering at Google ch. 18; Bazel hermeticity; reproducible-builds.org; SLSA build levels; scripts-to-rule-them-all; GNU Make manual.
- **Integrate static analysis into the developer workflow (editor, presubmit, code review) and keep false positives low** – Developers act on findings only when the findings are timely and actionable. Google keeps effective false positives below about 5 percent. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 20; OpenSSF Concise Guide; OpenSSF Scorecard SAST check.
- **Limit the complexity of each function and treat thresholds as signals that need a written justification to exceed** – Modules that are too complex are more error-prone, harder to test, and harder to change. The number of tests needed equals the cyclomatic complexity. Evidence: NIST SP 500-235 (limit of 10, exceptions with a written explanation); SonarSource Cognitive Complexity; SWEBOK v4 ch. 4 (1.1).
- **Keep a README with what, why, how to start, where to get help, and who maintains; add CONTRIBUTING; document public APIs with docstrings; record significant decisions as ADRs** – Documentation is read many more times than it is written. Decisions without a recorded rationale are blindly kept or blindly changed. Evidence: GitHub docs on READMEs and CONTRIBUTING; PEP 257; adr.github.io; Nygard "Documenting Architecture Decisions"; Software Engineering at Google ch. 10.
- **Protect the main branch: required review, required status checks, no force pushes** – Branch protection enforces the review and CI gates regardless of who pushes. Evidence: GitHub protected branches docs; OpenSSF Scorecard Branch-Protection; OpenSSF Concise Guide.
- **Manage technical debt deliberately: prefer prudent debt, record it, pay it down in high-churn code, and leave code better than you found it** – Cruft raises the cost of every change. The interest is highest where change is frequent. Evidence: Fowler TechnicalDebt and TechnicalDebtQuadrant; Clean Code boy-scout rule; Pragmatic Programmer "Don't Live with Broken Windows".
- **Review, understand, and verify AI-generated code exactly like human-written code; keep changes small and in version control** – AI output is often "almost right". DORA finds that AI amplifies existing practices and hurts stability without small batches and strong version control. Evidence: GitHub Copilot best practices; DORA 2024 and 2025 reports and AI Capabilities Model; Stack Overflow 2025 survey; METR 2025 study; SWEBOK v4 ch. 4 (5.1); Claude Code best practices.

### Contested points

- **Trunk-based development versus feature branches and git-flow** – DORA, Fowler, Google, and trunkbaseddevelopment.com favor trunk-based development with daily integration and short-lived branches. The git-flow author (Driessen, 2020 note) says that git-flow still fits "software that is explicitly versioned" or software with multiple supported versions, but teams that do continuous delivery should use a simpler flow such as GitHub flow. Fowler adds that teams with unstable builds may need release branches and feature branches first, and should grow toward a release-ready mainline. The choice depends on the release model, the number of supported versions, test automation, and team discipline.
- **How much pre-merge code review, and whether pair programming replaces it** – Google requires pre-commit review of every change but accepts pair-programmed code as reviewed. Fowler's pair programming article argues that asynchronous review is a bottleneck that conflicts with continuous integration. DORA lists heavy or asynchronous review as a pitfall for trunk-based development. trunkbaseddevelopment.com notes that very small teams may commit straight to the trunk. Regulated organizations and the OpenSSF Scorecard expect enforced review of every change. The answer depends on team size, trust, regulation, and CI strength.
- **Number of approvals and who may approve** – Google reports that most reviews have exactly one reviewer who combines the correctness, ownership, and readability roles. Many organizations require two approvals or a code-owner approval on protected branches (GitHub supports both). More approvals add safety but slow merges. The right number depends on risk and regulation.
- **What code review is for** – Defect detection is the stated motivation, but Bacchelli and Bird found that reviews are "less about defects than expected" and deliver knowledge transfer, team awareness, and alternative solutions. SmartBear's study reports measurable defect yields when size and rate are controlled. Teams should state their review goals explicitly and measure accordingly.
- **Pinned versions versus version ranges, and the value of semantic versioning** – Libraries should declare ranges (Python packaging, SemVer), while applications pin through lockfiles (npm, Cargo, Twelve-Factor). The OpenSSF Scorecard wants hash pins for CI actions and container images. Software Engineering at Google argues that SemVer "overconstrains" and "overpromises" (Hyrum's Law) and prefers live-at-head with downstream tests or minimum version selection. Cargo says that a committed Cargo.lock "depends on your package's needs". The choice depends on whether you ship a library or an application, and on how much testing backs the upgrades.
- **How many comments code should have** – Clean Code says "Don't comment bad code – rewrite it" and prefers code that explains itself. Code Complete and Software Engineering at Google expect file, class, and function comments as reference documentation. All agree that comments explain why and must stay current. They differ on how much documentation belongs in the code and how much belongs outside it.
- **TDD as a mandatory discipline versus self-testing code by any route** – Kent Beck and XP practitioners treat the red-green-refactor cycle as the default. Fowler states that TDD is one way to get self-testing code, and that tests written after also count, "although you can't consider your work to be done until you have the tests". SWEBOK describes both orders as construction testing. The choice depends on the design problem, the team, and the testability of the code.
- **Function size and complexity thresholds** – Clean Code says that functions should be small and "smaller than that". Code Complete asks whether the routine length is "determined naturally by its function and logic, rather than by an artificial coding standard". NIST 500-235 supports a cyclomatic limit of 10 with evidence, notes that limits up to 15 are used successfully, and exempts single multiway decisions with a written explanation. Thresholds are useful signals, not laws.
- **Strictness and size of style guides** – Google argues that rules must "pull their weight", that "a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds", and grants waivers. Other teams adopt a full external style guide unchanged to avoid debate. Small teams often rely on the formatter only. More rules help large codebases and tools; they cost cognitive load in small ones.
- **Squash merges and linear history versus merge commits** – GitHub offers "require linear history" (squash or rebase). Conventional Commits notes that in a squash-based workflow maintainers can clean up the messages at merge. Others keep the full merge history for traceability. No authoritative source mandates one option. It depends on whether the team values the history of each commit or one commit per reviewed change.
- **Code ownership model** – Fowler prefers collective ownership and warns that strong ownership creates bottlenecks; weak ownership is a compromise. Google uses OWNERS files and required owner approval. GitHub's CODEOWNERS supports both models. The choice depends on team size, codebase size, and trust.
- **Productivity and risk of AI-assisted coding** – DORA 2024 found that AI adoption raised individual productivity but reduced delivery throughput and stability. DORA 2025 found a positive effect on throughput and a continued negative effect on stability, with 90 percent of respondents using AI and 30 percent reporting little or no trust in generated code. METR's 2025 RCT found that experienced open-source developers took 19 percent longer with AI while they believed that they were 20 percent faster. Stack Overflow 2025 reports that 46 percent distrust accuracy and 66 percent cite "almost right" output as the top frustration. The effect depends on the task, experience, codebase familiarity, and verification practices.
- **Monorepo and the one-version rule versus multiple repositories** – Software Engineering at Google argues that removal of the choice of dependency version and commitment to a single trunk scales best, while it states that a monorepo "is not necessarily" the answer for everyone. Many organizations use multiple repositories with package versions. DORA's code maintainability capability asks for the functionality (search, reuse, one place to change), not for a specific repository layout.
- **How much defensive programming to keep in production** – Code Complete warns that too much defensive code makes programs "fat and slow" and adds defects. The architecture must decide between correctness (return no result rather than a wrong one) and robustness (keep running). Safety-critical and financial systems lean to correctness; consumer software often leans to robustness.
- **Feature flags versus branches to hide unfinished work** – Fowler and trunk-based development use release toggles so that incomplete work merges daily. The feature toggles article warns of toggle debt and combinatorial tests, and says that toggles are "inventory which comes with a carrying cost". Feature branches avoid that cost at the price of delayed integration. The right mix depends on the release cadence and toggle hygiene.

### Metrics

- Change size: lines and files changed per change (Google: about 100 lines is reasonable, 1000 is too large; SmartBear: 200 to 400 lines per review). Caveat: generated or mechanical changes are exceptions.
- Review latency: time to the first response and time to approval (Google: one business day maximum; SmartBear: review at most 60 minutes at a time). Caveat: speed must not become a rubber stamp.
- Inspection rate: lines reviewed per hour (SmartBear: under 500 LOC per hour keeps defect detection effective). Caveat: a high rate on a large change is a signal of a shallow review, not of a fast reviewer.
- Active branch count and age (DORA: three or fewer active branches; trunk merges at least daily). Caveat: count only branches with open work, and count release branches separately.
- Integration frequency: commits or merges to the trunk per developer per day; the share of work items finished within one week (DORA). Caveat: frequent pushes that break the build are not integration.
- Build time and build health: the commit build under ten minutes (Fowler), broken-build frequency, and time to fix or revert. Caveat: a build that is fast because it skips tests is not healthy.
- Test coverage of changed lines and the test pass rate. Caveat: coverage measures execution, not correctness; do not set coverage as a target in itself.
- Static analysis findings on new code, and the effective false-positive rate (Google keeps it under about 5 percent). Caveat: a count of findings rewards noisy tools.
- Cyclomatic or cognitive complexity per function, with the count of justified exceptions (NIST 500-235: limit 10; 15 used with stronger processes). Caveat: do not game the metric with split switch statements or averages.
- Code duplication percentage and cross-team change lead time (DORA code maintainability). Caveat: some duplication costs less than a shared library that nobody maintains.
- Dependency freshness: versions behind the latest, the share of pinned or locked dependencies, the time from vulnerability disclosure to a patched dependency, and the count of known vulnerable dependencies. Caveat: the newest version is not always the safest; the time to patch is the most important number.
- Secrets detected per month by secret scans (target zero; push protection blocks). Caveat: zero detections can mean zero leaks, or a scanner that does not know your secret formats.
- Defect escape: bugs found after merge per change, and the rework rate (changes reverted or reopened). Caveat: attribution to construction is imprecise.
- Review outcome metrics: defect density found in review, and the share of reviews with substantive comments. Caveat: SmartBear warns to use defect data for learning, not for individual performance.
- Toggle inventory: the number and age of feature flags that await removal. Caveat: permanent operational toggles belong in a separate count.
- Technical debt items recorded and closed, and the share of changes that touch high-churn files. Caveat: debt counts are subjective.
- AI-assisted change metrics: the share of AI-generated changes that pass CI on the first run, review comments per AI-generated change, and stability metrics (change failure rate) tracked together with adoption (DORA). Caveat: humans edit generated code, so attribution of a change to AI is often incomplete.

### Failure modes

- Long-lived branches and big-bang merges: conflicts grow, integration becomes painful, and refactoring stops (Fowler, Google).
- Large pull requests: reviewers skim, defects pass, and rollbacks become complicated. Google allows a reviewer to reject a change only because it is too large.
- Slow or stalled reviews: team velocity drops, developers batch more work, and frustration rises. Most complaints about review are about speed.
- Rubber-stamp approvals and reviews that check only style: defects and design problems pass. Style belongs to the formatter.
- Format debates by hand instead of a formatter and a linter: review time goes to whitespace, not to design and correctness.
- Skipped tests, or a skipped refactor step in TDD: "the most common way to screw up TDD is neglecting the third step" (Fowler), and the code degrades with each cycle.
- Clever code and poor names: the next reader, including the author, cannot follow it. Complexity is the enemy of verification.
- Comments that repeat code or go stale, and commented-out code left in the repository: readers stop trusting the comments and must read everything twice.
- Empty catch blocks, swallowed errors, and generic exception catches: they hide the root causes.
- Error messages that leak stack traces, server versions, or SQL to users, and logs that contain passwords, tokens, or personal data: they help attackers and break privacy rules.
- Denylist input validation or client-side-only validation, and string concatenation into queries and commands: attackers bypass the checks and inject code.
- Secrets committed to the repository, and long-lived credentials in CI: they become targets and spread through clones and forks.
- Unreviewed dependency adoption, abandoned or typosquatted packages, and dependency sprawl, with no lockfile: every environment differs, and the supply chain is open to attack.
- Unpinned CI actions and container base images, and no automated updates: known vulnerabilities stay for months.
- Non-hermetic builds that depend on host tools and state ("works on my machine"), manual build steps, and slow builds: they discourage integration and make results impossible to verify.
- Undocumented setup: the README lacks run and test commands, so onboarding takes days.
- Environment branches and configuration forks per environment: Fowler names this an anti-pattern, because the code in production is then not the code on the mainline.
- Toggle debt: release flags never removed and untested flag combinations add complexity and hidden failure paths.
- Reckless technical debt taken under deadline pressure: it slows the very features it was meant to speed up.
- Over-defensive code everywhere: fat, slow, and itself defective (Code Complete).
- Strong code ownership that blocks simple cross-module changes: it leads to duplication (Fowler).
- Style guides with rules that do not pull their weight, and exceptions never granted or always granted: the rules lose authority or cost more than they return.
- Static analysis ignored because of high false-positive rates, or because findings arrive outside the workflow: real findings get lost in the noise.
- Gamed metrics: functions split to satisfy complexity limits, tests written for coverage numbers, lines counted as productivity. The numbers improve while the code does not.
- Code freezes and integration phases instead of continuous integration (DORA): integration risk accumulates, and feedback arrives late.
- The AI "trust-then-verify gap": merged generated code that nobody understands, large AI-generated changes without tests, and prompts and agent files outside version control. Defects enter without review, and the changes cannot be reproduced.
- Cloned code instead of an extracted shared library, or the opposite, premature abstraction into an internal library that nobody maintains: fixes must be applied many times, or one unmaintained library blocks every user.
- Documentation and ADRs written once and never updated: readers stop trusting them.

### Tailoring by project size

Essential at every scale:

- everything in version control
- small commits with clear messages
- a README that states how to build, run, and test
- a one-command automated build
- automated tests with each change
- a formatter and a linter wired into pre-commit or CI
- no secrets in the repository
- a lockfile and regular dependency updates with vulnerability scans
- input validation and safe error handling at trust boundaries
- the habit to leave code better than you found it

These cost little and protect every project. They are also what an AI agent needs to verify its own work.

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| Solo developer on a small repository | Commit straight to main, or use very short-lived branches. Self-review the diff before you push, or let an AI reviewer in a fresh context read it, and run the tests. Keep a short README and a small number of ADRs for decisions that you will forget. Use Dependabot or Renovate and secret scans, which are free on public repositories. Pin CI actions and base images anyway. A formatter plus the default linter of the language is enough. | GitHub flow, only when you want a pull request as a checkpoint. A changelog or Conventional Commits if you publish releases. Skip CODEOWNERS, formal approval rules, SBOMs, and style guide governance. |
| Small product team (roughly 3 to 15 developers) | Trunk-based development with short-lived branches and pull requests. One reviewer per change, with reviews answered within a business day. Branch protection with required status checks. A written style guide that references an external guide and lists only the project deltas. CODEOWNERS for critical paths. A devcontainer or scripts so that everyone has the same environment. A definition of done that includes tests, docs, and no new static analysis findings. Feature flags for unfinished work, with a removal rule. An agreed exception and log policy. A dependency policy (allowed licenses, update cadence, who merges update PRs). ADRs in the repository. Pair or mob programming for onboarding and risky changes. A shared AI usage policy that requires the same review and CI gates for generated code. | SAST beyond the linter, signed commits, an SBOM, and reproducible builds. |
| Large or regulated organization | Everything above plus enforced policy: required reviews from code owners, often two approvals for sensitive paths, signed commits or verified provenance, required status checks that include SAST, secret scans, license and vulnerability scans, and audit trails that link commits to work items. Organization-wide style guides with arbiters and a waiver process. A curated internal dependency registry with approved versions (the one-version rule where feasible) and SBOMs for every release. Hermetic, reproducible builds with SLSA-level provenance. Static analysis integrated into the review tool with low false-positive rates. Internal libraries shared through InnerSource with trusted committers. Documented secure coding standards (CERT, OWASP) and security review for high-risk changes. An explicit AI policy that states the allowed tools, the data handling rules, and that humans remain accountable for every merged line. Regulated domains (safety, finance, health) add traceability from requirements to code to tests, coding standard conformance evidence (for example CERT or MISRA-type subsets), and justified exceptions for complexity limits. | Mob programming for all work, a full monorepo, and a live-at-head dependency policy. These need strong CI and tools to pay off. |

### Sources

- [SWEBOK Guide v4.0, Chapter 4 Software Construction (IEEE Computer Society, PDF)](https://ieeecs-media.computer.org/media/education/swebok/swebok-v4.pdf) – Primary standard-like reference; chapter 4 gives the definition, the fundamentals, construction management including dependencies, practical considerations, construction technologies, and tools including AI-assisted IDEs.
- [IEEE Computer Society – Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK) page](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering) – Confirms the v4.0 release (October 2024) and the 18 knowledge areas, including Software Construction.
- [Code Complete, 2nd Ed. Checklists (McConnell, compiled PDF)](https://www.matthewjmiller.net/files/cc2e_checklists.pdf) – Checklists on major construction practices, design in construction, class quality, routines, defensive programming, names, pair programming, inspections, safe refactoring, configuration management, integration, layout, comments, and self-documenting code.
- [Code Complete 2, Chapter 8 Defensive Programming (online chapter text)](https://flylib.com/books/en/2.823.1.69/1/) – Assertions versus error handling, barricades, correctness versus robustness, and how much defensive code to keep.
- [Clean Code (Robert C. Martin) – publisher page with table of contents](https://www.informit.com/store/clean-code-a-handbook-of-agile-software-craftsmanship-9780132350884) – Book premise and chapter list (names, functions, comments, format, error handling, unit tests, smells).
- [Summary of 'Clean Code' by Robert C. Martin (gist)](https://gist.github.com/wojteklu/73c6914cc446146b8b533c0988cf8d29) – Condensed rules: names, functions, comments, the boy-scout rule, smells; a secondary summary of the book.
- [Software Engineering at Google, Ch. 8 Style Guides and Rules](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch08.html) – Why rules, rules must pull their weight, optimize for the reader, consistency, and enforcement with formatters and static analysis.
- [Software Engineering at Google, Ch. 9 Code Review](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch09.html) – Review flow, three approval types, benefits, small changes (about 200 lines), one reviewer, and 24 working hours.
- [Software Engineering at Google, Ch. 16 Version Control and Branch Management](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch16.html) – Dev branches considered misguided, trunk-based development, the one-version rule, and monorepo caveats.
- [Software Engineering at Google, Ch. 21 Dependency Management](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch21.html) – Diamond dependencies, questions before an import, SemVer limits, live at head, and minimum version selection.
- [Software Engineering at Google, Ch. 18 Build Systems and Build Philosophy](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch18.html) – Task-based versus artifact-based builds, hermeticity, reproducibility, fine-grained modules, and explicit external dependencies.
- [Software Engineering at Google, Ch. 20 Static Analysis](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch20.html) – Integrate analysis into the workflow, developer happiness, effective false positives under 5 percent, and Tricorder.
- [Software Engineering at Google, Ch. 10 Documentation](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch10.html) – Documentation is like code, reference comments, design docs, landing pages, and freshness.
- [Google Engineering Practices – Code Review Developer Guide](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/) – What code review covers; pair programming counts as review.
- [Google – The Standard of Code Review](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html) – Approve when the change improves code health; facts overrule opinions; escalation.
- [Google – Speed of Code Reviews](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/speed.html) – One business day maximum response; LGTM with comments; large changes.
- [Google – Small CLs](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html) – 100 lines reasonable, 1000 too large; split strategies; separate refactorings.
- [Google – What to look for in a code review](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html) – Design, functionality, complexity, tests, names, comments, style, documentation, every line.
- [Google – Writing good CL descriptions](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/cl-descriptions.html) – Imperative first line; the body explains the problem and the approach.
- [Google – How to handle reviewer comments](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/handling-comments.html) – Author guidance: do not take it personally, fix the code, think collaboratively.
- [Google – How to write code review comments](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/comments.html) – Courtesy, explain why, severity labels (Nit, Optional, FYI).
- [Martin Fowler – Patterns for Managing Source Code Branches](https://martinfowler.com/articles/branching-patterns.html) – Mainline, healthy branch, integration frequency, release-ready mainline, git-flow versus GitHub flow versus TBD, and the environment branch anti-pattern.
