## 9. Testing, verification and validation

### Purpose

Testing exists to find defects and to evaluate the quality of software work products. With this evidence the stakeholders can make an informed release decision. Testing answers two questions. Verification asks whether the product conforms to its specified requirements. Validation asks whether the product satisfies the user needs and its intended use in its operational environment (IEEE 1012-2016). Testing cannot prove the absence of defects; it can only show their presence (ISTQB principle 1, Dijkstra). The real output of testing is therefore evidence and reduced risk, not certainty.

Quality control is the product-oriented, corrective part of quality management. Quality assurance is the process-oriented, preventive part (see section 15). Testing is the main form of quality control (ISTQB CTFL v4.0.1, 1.2.2). Testing also guards against regression and gives engineers the confidence to change code: "Automated testing enables software change at scale" (Software Engineering at Google). In regulated domains testing also produces the objective evidence that a product is fit for its intended use (FDA General Principles of Software Validation).

### Other names

- Software testing
- Verification and validation (V&V)
- Independent verification and validation (IV&V)
- Quality control (QC) – product-oriented and corrective; distinct from quality assurance (QA), which is process-oriented and preventive (ISTQB)
- Test and evaluation (T&E)
- Test engineering and test automation
- Static testing (reviews, inspections, static analysis) and dynamic testing
- Software Testing knowledge area (SWEBOK v4, Chapter 5)
- Test levels or test stages (waterfall; the right leg of the V-model)
- Continuous testing (DevOps; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1 clause 4.4.8)
- Checking versus testing (the context-driven school: Bach and Bolton)
- Shift-left testing and shift-right testing (testing in production)

### Position in the life cycle

Testing is not one phase. SWEBOK v4 calls it "a pervasive and holistic activity involving all the steps of any process development life cycle". Before testing comes the test basis: requirements and acceptance criteria (see section 5), architecture (see section 6), detailed design (see section 7), code (see section 8) and user documentation. Static testing (reviews, inspections, static analysis) starts as soon as the first drafts of these work products exist. Dynamic testing starts when executable units exist.

After testing, the results go to four consumers. The build and CI pipeline uses them as gates (see section 10). Release management uses them as exit criteria, in the test completion report and for the release decision (see section 11). Operations uses canaries, synthetic monitoring, chaos experiments and incident data (see section 12). Maintenance uses confirmation and regression testing of every change (see section 13).

In waterfall and in the V-model, each development level has a corresponding test level. Test analysis and test design for a level start during the matching development phase. The exit criteria of one level form part of the entry criteria of the next level (ISTQB 2.2). The table shows the mapping.

| Test level | Development level that it checks | Related section |
|---|---|---|
| Unit (component) testing | Detailed design | section 7 |
| Integration testing | Architecture | section 6 |
| System testing | System requirements | section 5 |
| Acceptance testing | User needs | sections 3 and 5 |

In iterative and agile life cycles every iteration performs static and dynamic testing at all levels. The team automates regression testing because it delivers increments often. The team writes tests before code (TDD, ATDD, BDD). The whole team owns quality, and the Definition of Done plays the role of the exit criteria (ISTQB 5.1.3; Scrum Guide).

In DevOps and continuous delivery, testing is continuous inside the deployment pipeline. Every change is a release candidate. The pipeline orders its stages by speed, so that the fast tests run first. Developers get feedback in under ten minutes (DORA). A subset of the tests keeps running in production as synthetic monitoring and probers (Fowler, Google). Google's SRE book treats tests that block bad code before release as tests with "zero MTTR".

The ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2 process model reflects this view. It has an ongoing organizational test process (policy, practices), per-project test management processes (planning, monitoring and control, completion) and dynamic test processes (design and implementation, environment and data, execution, incident reporting). A team can instantiate these processes for any life cycle model, including agile and DevOps. So testing is a continuous process with visible peaks (a release, a test level, an audit), not a one-time phase.

### Inputs

- Test basis – requirements and user stories with acceptance criteria, architecture and design documents, interface and API specifications, source code, user documentation and models. According to ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 the test basis can also be "an undocumented understanding of the required behavior".
- Quality requirements and risks – the product risk register (likelihood x impact); the ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristics to cover (functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility, safety); regulatory, contractual and legal obligations (see section 16).
- Organizational context – the test policy and the organizational test practices (29119-3), coding and review standards, CI/CD pipeline conventions, the Definition of Ready and the Definition of Done.
- Test items under configuration management – identified builds, packages, containers, infrastructure and configuration with version identifiers (see section 15).
- Test environments and test data – environment requirements, hermetic or production-like environments, seeded and masked data sets, service virtualizations, and readiness reports (29119-2 process 8.3; DORA test data management).
- Test oracles – specifications, executable models, previous versions (the regression oracle), pseudo-oracles and metamorphic relations, invariants and implicit oracles (crashes, exceptions), and human judgement (Barr et al. 2015).
- Entry criteria – for example: the smoke tests pass, the environment and the data are ready, testable requirements are available, and resources are available (ISTQB 5.1.3). For a review, the work product meets the inspection entry criteria (Fagan).
- Tooling – test frameworks, test doubles and mocking libraries, coverage and mutation tools, static analyzers, load and security tools, a defect tracker, and test management or CI dashboards.
- Historical data – the defect history and taxonomies for error guessing, flakiness statistics, and production telemetry and incidents for shift-right testing and risk analysis.

### Activities

- **Test planning and test strategy (risk-based)** – Define the test objectives, the scope, the approach, the test levels and types, the techniques and coverage targets, the entry and exit criteria, the environments, the data, the tools, the roles, the estimates and the schedule. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1 and 29119-2 make risk-based testing the recommended basis of every test strategy. The output is a test plan. The 29119-3 template has these parts: context, assumptions, stakeholders, communication, risk register, test strategy, activities and estimates, staffing, schedule. In a small team the plan can be one page or a section of the README.
- **Product risk analysis and test prioritization** – Identify the product risks, for example missing or wrong functions, wrong calculations, poor response time and security vulnerabilities. Assess the likelihood and the impact of each risk to get a risk level. Use the result to decide the scope, the depth, the techniques, the coverage and the execution order. Prioritize tests by risk, by coverage or by requirement priority (ISTQB 5.1.5, 5.2). Testing is "the primary approach to risk treatment in software development" (29119-1). The output is a prioritized risk register, and the test plan and the test suites trace back to it.
- **Static testing by review and inspection** – Examine requirements, designs, code, tests and other work products without execution. The forms are the informal review, the walkthrough, the technical review and the inspection (ISTQB ch. 3; ISO/IEC 20246). The Fagan inspection gives the formal template: planning, overview, preparation, an inspection meeting with a moderator, a reader, a recorder and the author, rework, and follow-up. Fagan's original data found 82 percent of all errors with design and code inspections (SEI 1993). Modern code review applies the same idea continuously. At Google, reviewers examine essentially every change before commit, authors keep changes to about 200 lines, and the review is also the first test of whether a change is understandable. Output: review records, defect lists, approved work products, and defects found before they cause failures.
- **Static analysis** – Run tools that analyze code without execution: linters, type checkers, formatters, complexity scanners and security scanners. Run them in the editor, in pre-commit hooks, in CI and in code review. Google's Tricorder shows what works at scale: analyze only the files that a change touches, keep the effective false-positive rate low (about 5 percent), show the results at review time, and offer fixes. ISTQB lists the typical findings: undefined variables, unreachable code, deviations from standards, and buffer overflows. Output: findings that the team treats like defects, and a quality gate that blocks known bad patterns.
- **Test analysis and test design with systematic techniques** – Analyze the test basis to identify test conditions, build a test model, identify coverage items, and derive test cases with expected results (29119-2 processes TD1 to TD3; 29119-4). Black-box techniques: equivalence partitioning; boundary value analysis (2-value and 3-value); decision tables and cause-effect graphing; state transition testing (all states, valid transitions, all transitions); combinatorial and pairwise testing (NIST: most faults involve one or two parameters, and nearly all involve six or fewer); scenario and use-case testing; syntax, random and metamorphic testing. White-box techniques: statement, branch and decision, condition, MC/DC and data-flow testing. Experience-based techniques: error guessing and fault attacks, checklist-based testing, and exploratory testing. Output: a small but sufficient test set with measurable coverage.
- **Test implementation and test automation engineering** – Turn the designed tests into executable, maintainable automated tests and test suites. Wire them into the local workflow and into the CI pipeline. Follow the maintainability rules from Software Engineering at Google: test behaviors through public APIs, test state and not interactions, put no logic in tests, write clear failure messages, and prefer DAMP over DRY. Use arrange-act-assert. Treat test code as product code (Microsoft, DORA). Choose frameworks for each level: xUnit-style unit frameworks, API and contract tools such as Pact, and browser tools such as Playwright with user-facing locators and isolated tests. Output: version-controlled test code, fixtures, test doubles, and an execution schedule ordered by speed.
- **Test environment and test data management** – Provide environments and data that make tests repeatable, isolated, and as faithful as the risk requires. Google describes the trade-off between hermetic single-process or single-machine SUTs and shared staging or production (high fidelity, high risk). Hermetic servers use fakes and in-memory stores. DORA's test data management capability asks for data that is adequate, available on demand, minimal, isolated for each test, and never a raw copy of production with sensitive data. 29119-2 defines a test environment and data management process with readiness reports. Output: reproducible environments (containers, local databases, service virtualization), seeded data sets, and documented environment and data requirements.
- **Unit and component testing, including TDD** – Developers test individual units in isolation or with real in-process collaborators. They use a unit test framework, and each test runs in milliseconds. Google's small tests run in one process and one thread, with no I/O and no network, which makes them fast and deterministic. Microsoft targets an average of under 60 ms per L0 test.
  - Test-driven development is an optional discipline. Beck's Canon TDD: write a test list, write one test, make it pass, refactor, repeat. Fowler: red-green-refactor. TDD drives the interface design and guarantees self-testing code. Industrial case studies reported 40-90 percent lower pre-release defect density with 15-35 percent more initial development time (Nagappan et al. 2008).
  - Output: the largest and fastest layer of the regression suite, and a design that is testable.
- **Integration testing and contract testing** – Verify the interactions between components and with external systems. Fowler distinguishes narrow integration tests from broad integration tests. A narrow integration test exercises the code that talks to a dependency, against a local instance or a test double. A broad integration test runs many live services. He recommends narrow integration tests plus contract tests.
  - Consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) let the team test each side in isolation against a shared contract. Fowler's contract tests check that the test doubles still match the real external service. ISTQB separates component integration testing from system integration testing. SWEBOK lists the top-down, bottom-up, sandwich and big-bang integration strategies.
  - Output: tests that catch interface and configuration defects early, without a deployment of the whole system.
- **System testing and end-to-end testing** – Test the complete, deployed system against its specification in a representative environment. Cover end-to-end tasks and non-functional characteristics (ISTQB 2.2.1). End-to-end tests through the UI give the most realistic signal, but they are slow and "notoriously flaky" (Vocke). Keep them to a minimum of high-value user journeys, give each test its own data in isolation, and prefer lower-level tests for the same behavior. Smoke tests or build-verification tests are a small subset that shows that the build is testable (SWEBOK 3.3.3; k6). Output: confidence that the assembled system works for its main scenarios, plus the smoke suite that gates the later stages.
- **Acceptance testing and ATDD/BDD** – Validate that the system satisfies the user and business needs and is ready to deploy. The forms are user acceptance testing, operational acceptance testing, contractual and regulatory acceptance testing, and alpha and beta testing (ISTQB 2.2.1; SWEBOK 2.1.4, 2.2.4). In ATDD and BDD the team (customer, developer, tester) writes the acceptance criteria as concrete examples before implementation, often in the Given/When/Then form (Dan North). The team automates the examples and keeps them as living documentation (Cucumber: discovery, formulation, automation; Fowler: Specification By Example). Output: executable acceptance tests traced to requirements, and an accepted, usable increment that meets the Definition of Done.
- **Non-functional testing across the ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics** – Plan and run the test types that the product risks demand.
  - Performance testing uses smoke, average-load, stress, soak, spike and breakpoint tests (k6), plus load, volume, scalability and elasticity testing (SWEBOK).
  - Security testing and penetration testing follow a framework such as the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (see section 16).
  - Usability testing observes real users who perform tasks (NN/g: five users find most problems in qualitative studies). Accessibility evaluation combines tools with human judgement and with users with disabilities (W3C WAI: "No tool alone can determine if a site meets accessibility standards").
  - Compatibility and portability testing covers browsers, devices and platforms. Localization and internationalization testing includes functional, visual and linguistic checks and in-context review (Microsoft). Installability, configuration, recovery and failover testing, and reliability testing with operational profiles, complete the list.
  - Output: evidence for each quality characteristic, and the non-functional defects found early enough to fix.
- **Exploratory and experience-based testing** – Testers learn, design and execute tests at the same time. A charter and a time-box guide each session, and the testers debrief afterwards (session-based test management; ISTQB 4.4.2). Bach: "in the presence of complexity, uncertainty, and change, exploration is essential". Fowler would "consider it a red flag if a team isn't doing exploratory testing at all". Google uses exploratory testing to find unanticipated behaviors, and then automates regression tests for what it finds. Output: defects that scripted tests cannot anticipate, new test ideas, and session notes.
- **Test execution, logging, confirmation and regression testing** – Run the test procedures according to the execution schedule: on every commit in CI, on demand locally, and on a timer for the slower suites. Compare the actual results with the expected results, log the results, and raise incidents (29119-2 processes 8.4 and 8.5). After each fix, run confirmation testing (a retest) and then regression testing guided by impact analysis. Regression suites grow and run often, so they are the prime candidate for automation (ISTQB 2.2.3). FDA: after any change, the team must re-establish the validation status with appropriate regression testing. Output: test execution logs, pass or fail results for each build, and a green or red signal that the team trusts.
- **Defect (incident) management and triage** – Record every anomaly with a unique id, a title, the date, the author, the test object and the environment, the context, reproducible steps, the expected and actual results, the severity, the priority, the status and references (ISTQB 5.5; 29119-3 incident report). Triage regularly to decide whether the work is wanted, its priority and timeline, and its owner (Chromium: P0 emergency to P3 not time-sensitive; "most issues have a half-life"). Classify the defects (IEEE 1044-style attributes, orthogonal defect classification) and run root-cause analysis, so that the team prevents the same defect class next time. Output: a trustworthy defect backlog, and input for process improvement.
- **Test monitoring, control, reporting and completion** – Gather metrics (progress, coverage, defects, risks, cost), compare them with the plan, and apply control directives such as a new priority order for the tests or more resources (ISTQB 5.3). Publish test status reports during testing, and a test completion report at milestones. The completion report contains a summary, deviations, an evaluation against the exit criteria, residual risks, test measures, reusable assets and lessons learned (29119-3). SWEBOK warns that thoroughness measures "are not sufficient in themselves" to decide when to stop. The decision weighs the cost of the remaining failures against the cost of more testing. Output: the information behind the release decision, and archived testware.
- **Test suite health – flaky tests, coverage and mutation analysis** – Keep the suite trustworthy. Quarantine non-deterministic tests at once and fix them quickly. Fowler suggests a cap such as eight tests or one week. Google reported in 2016 that about 1.5 percent of runs were flaky and that almost 16 percent of tests showed flakiness at some point. In a comment on its 2017 post, the author adds that one team found a real production bug in about one of six newly flaky tests.
  - Use code coverage to find untested code, not as a target (Fowler; Google thresholds of 60, 75 and 90 percent as acceptable, commendable and exemplary). Use mutation testing (PIT, Stryker; Google runs it on changed lines during code review) to check that the tests actually detect faults. Delete or rewrite change-detector tests and huge snapshots.
  - Output: a suite that fails only for real defects, and a known quality of the tests themselves.
- **Property-based testing and fuzzing** – Describe the input domain and a property that must hold for all inputs. The tool generates many inputs and shrinks each failing case to a minimal example (Hypothesis; MacIver defines property-based testing as fuzzing with a test harness that reasons about the expected behavior). Fuzzing feeds generated or mutated inputs to the program to find crashes and security bugs. OSS-Fuzz reported over 10,000 vulnerabilities and 36,000 bugs in about 1,000 projects. Both techniques address the oracle problem with implicit oracles (a crash, an exception) or with invariants. Output: edge-case defects that example-based tests miss, especially in parsers, serializers and algorithms.
- **Shift-right quality control – testing in production** – Extend testing into production, because pre-production cannot reproduce the real environment, traffic and diversity (Microsoft shift-right; Wilsenach "QA in Production"). Techniques: progressive tier or canary deployments with feature flags; synthetic monitoring that runs a subset of the automated tests against the live system and alerts on failure (Fowler); probers and canary analysis; A/B and diff testing; configuration tests; load tests; fault injection and chaos engineering with a steady-state hypothesis and a minimized blast radius (Principles of Chaos Engineering); disaster-recovery and failover drills (see section 12). Output: detection of failures that testing could not anticipate, validated resilience, and data that feeds back into risk analysis and regression tests.
- **Verification and validation evidence, traceability and independence for high-integrity contexts** – Where safety, security or regulation demand it, tailor V&V to an integrity level (IEEE 1012). Keep bidirectional traceability from requirements to tests, results and defects (29119-3 test traceability matrix; ISTQB 1.4.4). Apply the structural coverage criteria appropriate to the risk (FDA: branch coverage is a minimum for most products but insufficient for high integrity; 29119-4 MC/DC). Keep the independence of review (FDA principle 4.9). Retain the test documentation under configuration management as objective evidence. FDA's Computer Software Assurance guidance adds a risk-based choice between scripted and unscripted assurance activities. Output: an audit-ready evidence package and a defensible validation claim.

### Outputs

- A test plan with the test strategy, the risk register, the entry and exit criteria, estimates and a schedule; at organization level, a test policy and organizational test practices (29119-3).
- Test models, test design and test case specifications, test procedures and automated test scripts, test suites and an execution schedule; test data and test environment requirements and readiness reports.
- Review and inspection records, static analysis findings, and approved work products.
- Test execution logs, actual results and test results for each build, coverage measurements, mutation scores and flakiness statistics.
- Incident or defect reports with severity, priority and status; a triaged defect backlog; root-cause analysis results and change requests.
- Test status (progress) reports, and a test completion report with deviations, residual risk, lessons learned and archived reusable testware.
- A traceability matrix that links requirements, risks, tests, results and defects.
- Executable acceptance tests as living documentation (BDD, ATDD), and contract files for service boundaries.
- Exit criteria met. Typical criteria: the team executed the planned tests, reached the required coverage, automated the regression tests, and completed the static testing. No open defects remain above an agreed severity. In agile the Definition of Done has this role. ISTQB notes that an exhausted time or budget can also be a valid exit criterion if the stakeholders accept the residual risk.
- A release decision supported by evidence, and for regulated products the validation evidence package.
- Production-side assets: synthetic monitors, probers, canary analysis and chaos experiments that continue to run after release.

### Roles

- Developer or software engineer – writes and maintains the unit, integration and contract tests, practices TDD where the team chose it, fixes failing and flaky tests, and reviews code and tests. DORA and Google find that developers must own the automated tests.
- Tester, test analyst, QA engineer or SDET – does test analysis and test design with techniques, exploratory testing, automation frameworks, non-functional tests and defect reports; pairs with developers (DORA).
- Test management role (a test manager, a test lead, or the team itself in agile) – planning, monitoring and control, completion, risk management and reporting (ISTQB 1.4.5).
- Product owner, business analyst or customer – acceptance criteria and examples (ATDD, BDD), user acceptance testing, the Definition of Done, and the priority of defects.
- Review roles – author, moderator or facilitator, reader, scribe or recorder, reviewers, review leader and manager (ISTQB 3.2.3; Fagan). The author cannot moderate an inspection.
- Release or CI/CD engineer – pipeline gates, test stages ordered by speed, and environment provisioning.
- Operations or SRE – production tests, canary analysis, synthetic monitoring, fault injection and chaos experiments, and incident data fed back to the team.
- Specialists – performance engineer, security tester or penetration tester, accessibility specialist, UX researcher for usability tests, localization reviewers who are native speakers, and test environment and test data engineers.
- Independent V&V team, internal quality audit or external assessor – for high-integrity or regulated systems (IEEE 1012; FDA independence of review).
- Users – alpha and beta testers, crowdtesters, people with disabilities in accessibility evaluation, and participants in usability tests.

### Practices with consensus

- **Start testing early and keep it continuous (shift left)** – Review requirements and designs, write tests with or before the code, and run static analysis and unit tests on every change. Defects found late cost more to fix, and in many cases the cost grows exponentially. Early static testing also finds defects that dynamic testing cannot reach. Evidence: ISTQB CTFL v4.0.1 principle 3 and 2.1.5; Software Engineering at Google ch. 11; Microsoft "Shift testing left with unit tests"; FDA General Principles of Software Validation (defect prevention, time and effort); GOV.UK Service Manual.
- **Accept that exhaustive testing is impossible and that testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence; select tests by risk and by systematic techniques** – The input space is effectively infinite, so testing is always a sample. Risk-based selection focuses the effort where a failure would hurt most. Evidence: ISTQB principles 1 and 2; SWEBOK v4 ch. 5 (1.2.8, "finite", "selected"); ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1 introduction and 29119-2 (risk-based testing); FDA GPSV 5.2.5.
- **Distinguish verification from validation and do both** – Test against the specifications and against the user needs in the operational environment. A product can meet every written requirement and still fail its users (ISTQB "absence-of-defects fallacy"). Evidence: IEEE 1012-2016; FDA GPSV 3.1.2; ISTQB 1.1 and principle 7; SWEBOK v4 ch. 5 introduction.
- **Developers write, run and maintain the automated tests for their code; test code gets the same care and review as production code** – Ownership by the authors gives fast feedback, a testable design and suites that stay green. A separation of developers from tests leads to broken pipelines and test rot. Evidence: DORA "Test automation"; continuousdelivery.com "Test automation"; Microsoft shift-left ("Treat test code as product code"); Software Engineering at Google ch. 11 and 12; Fowler "UnitTest".
- **Make most automated tests small, fast, hermetic and deterministic; keep broad end-to-end tests few and focused on the critical journeys** – Small tests localize failures and run in seconds. Broad tests are slow, flaky and hard to diagnose. The exact ratio is debated, but the direction is not. Evidence: Google test sizes and ch. 11 (about 80/15/5); Google Testing Blog "Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests" (70/20/10); Vocke "Practical Test Pyramid"; DORA; Microsoft shift-left; Kent C. Dodds (few E2E tests even in the trophy).
- **Give developers test feedback in minutes** – Keep the local and CI suites under about ten minutes, order the pipeline stages by speed, and run slower suites later or on a timer. Slow feedback means that the team runs tests less often, finds defects later, and lets flaky failures pile up. Evidence: DORA "Test automation" (under ten minutes); Vocke (stage the pipeline by speed); Fowler "UnitTest" (compile suite and commit suite); Microsoft (L0 under 60 ms average, none over 2 s); Google hermetic servers.
- **Treat non-deterministic (flaky) tests as urgent defects** – Quarantine them so that the suite stays trustworthy, then fix the root cause fast. A test that fails at random gives no information, and a tolerated red build spreads to the whole suite. Evidence: Fowler "Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests"; Google Testing Blog 2016, 2017 and 2020 posts on flaky tests; DORA ("Test failures should indicate a real defect"); continuousdelivery.com ("20 tests that run quickly and are trusted" over 2,000 flaky tests); Microsoft shift-left.
- **Test observable behavior through public interfaces; verify state, not interactions; write tests that survive refactoring** – Tests coupled to the implementation break on every change, give false alarms, and block refactoring without more defects found. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 12 (unchanging tests, test via public APIs, state not interactions); Google "Change-Detector Tests Considered Harmful"; Vocke; Dodds; Playwright best practices (test user-visible behavior).
- **Prefer real implementations, then fakes; use stubs and mocks sparingly and only for slow, unreliable or external collaborators; verify test doubles with contract tests** – Over-mocking produces unclear, brittle tests that pass while the integration is broken, and doubles drift from the real service. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 13; Fowler "Mocks Aren't Stubs" and "ContractTest"; Pact documentation; Vocke; Fowler "IntegrationTest" (narrow integration tests plus contract tests).
- **Design tests with systematic techniques and measure the coverage of the coverage items** – The techniques: equivalence partitioning, boundary values, decision tables, state transition, combinatorial and pairwise testing, structural coverage, and error guessing. Techniques give a small, sufficient test set and an objective statement of what was covered. Ad hoc selection misses classes of faults. Evidence: ISTQB ch. 4; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-4 (techniques and coverage measurement); SWEBOK v4 ch. 5 section 3; FDA GPSV 5.2.5; NIST ACTS (pairwise effectiveness).
- **Use code coverage as a diagnostic to find untested code, never as a target or a proxy for quality; complement it with mutation testing and a review of test quality** – Coverage measures execution, not detection. Targets produce low-value tests, and 100 percent coverage is a warning sign of tests written to satisfy the metric. Evidence: Fowler "TestCoverage"; Google "Code Coverage Best Practices"; PIT and Stryker (mutation testing); Google "State of Mutation Testing at Google"; ISTQB 4.3 (statement coverage does not test all logic); FDA GPSV (statement coverage insufficient).
- **Review or inspect every significant work product in small chunks, with prepared reviewers, checklists and measurable exit criteria; keep the review results out of performance appraisals** – This applies to requirements, design, code and tests. Inspections find a large share of the defects before testing, at low cost. Small changes and preparation keep the defect-finding rate high. Evidence: Fagan 1976 via SEI "Materials for Teaching Software Inspections" (82 percent of errors; a rate drop from 50 to 15 defects/KLOC when the pace tripled); Software Engineering at Google ch. 9 (about 200 lines per change); ISTQB ch. 3; FDA GPSV (independence of review).
- **Combine automated checks with skilled human exploratory testing; do not treat automation as sufficient** – Scripts verify only what is in the script. Many production defects are surprises that need human judgement to find. Evidence: Fowler "ExploratoryTesting"; Bach "Exploratory Testing"; Bach and Bolton "Testing and Checking Refined"; Software Engineering at Google ch. 11 and 14; continuousdelivery.com; ISTQB 4.4.2; GOV.UK Service Manual.
- **Write acceptance criteria as concrete examples before implementation, with the business, development and testing perspectives together, and automate them as executable specifications** – Examples expose ambiguity early, create a shared language, and become regression tests and living documentation. Evidence: ISTQB 4.5 (user stories, acceptance criteria, ATDD); Cucumber "BDD" (discovery, formulation, automation); Dan North "Introducing BDD"; Agile Alliance "ATDD"; Fowler "SpecificationByExample"; SWEBOK v4 2.1.4.
- **Plan non-functional testing from the product risks and the ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics, and start it early** – This covers performance, security, usability, accessibility, compatibility, reliability and recovery. Late discovery of non-functional defects threatens the whole project. These qualities need specific methods, environments and sometimes real users. Evidence: ISTQB 2.2.2; ISO/IEC 25010:2023 scope (identification of testing objectives); 29119-4 Annex A; SWEBOK 2.2.7; GOV.UK Service Manual; W3C WAI; OWASP WSTG; NN/g; k6 test types.
- **After every change run confirmation testing for the fix and regression testing guided by impact analysis; automate the regression suite** – Small local changes can have large global effects. Unchanged but vulnerable parts need a new verification. Evidence: ISTQB 2.2.3; FDA GPSV 4.7; SWEBOK 2.2.5; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2 definitions of regression testing and retesting; Google SRE "Testing for Reliability".
- **Record defects so that the team can reproduce and prioritize them, triage them regularly, and feed the root causes back into prevention** – Without reproduction steps and triage the backlog decays, and the same defect classes recur. Evidence: ISTQB 5.5; 29119-3 incident report; Chromium triage best practices; IEEE 1044 (classification for causal analysis); SWEBOK 5.2.5.
- **Define entry and exit criteria (Definition of Ready, Definition of Done) for each level, report completion with the residual risk, and tailor the amount of test documentation to the context** – Explicit criteria make "done" transparent. Heavy documentation without a purpose slows teams, but auditability is needed where regulation or contracts demand it. Evidence: ISTQB 5.1.3 and 5.3; Scrum Guide (Definition of Done); 29119-2 and 29119-3 tailored conformance; Fagan entry and exit criteria; SWEBOK 5.1.8.
- **Manage test environments and data deliberately** – Keep them isolated for each test, reproducible, and production-like where fidelity matters, with minimal and masked data available on demand. Shared mutable environments and production data copies cause flaky tests, slow setup and privacy exposure. Evidence: DORA "Test data management"; Google "Hermetic Servers" and ch. 14 SUT types; 29119-2 environment and data management process; Playwright best practices (test isolation); Vocke (local database, local filesystem).
- **Continue quality control after release with monitoring, canaries, synthetic monitoring and controlled fault injection** – This is a complement to pre-release testing, not a replacement. Production has a breadth and a workload that no staging environment reproduces. Configuration changes are a top cause of outages. Evidence: Fowler "SyntheticMonitoring" and "QA in Production"; Microsoft "Shift right to test in production"; Google SRE ch. 17; Principles of Chaos Engineering; Software Engineering at Google ch. 14.

### Contested points

- **Shape of the automated test portfolio: pyramid, testing trophy or honeycomb** – The pyramid (Cohn; Fowler; Vocke; Google with about 80/15/5 or 70/20/10; DORA; Microsoft) puts most of the effort in unit tests. The trophy (Kent C. Dodds: "Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.") and the honeycomb (Spotify, for microservices) put most of the effort in integration tests. They argue that many unit tests make code hard to change. Fowler (2021) shows that much of the disagreement is definitional: "unit test" means a solitary test with mocks for one camp and a sociable test for the other. He quotes Searls: an argument about percentages "is a distraction". Fowler's own pyramid caveat: if the high-level tests are fast, reliable and cheap to change, fewer low-level tests are needed. The choice depends on the architecture (monolith or services), the cost and flakiness of broad tests in the stack, and the definition of the layers.
- **How much to mock: solitary versus sociable unit tests, mockist versus classical TDD** – Mockists isolate every collaborator and verify interactions. Classicists use real objects and verify state (Fowler "Mocks Aren't Stubs"). Google prefers real implementations, then fakes, and calls interaction testing a last resort. Dodds says that mocking removes confidence in the integration. Spotify avoids "implementation detail tests". Mockists gain precise failure localization and design pressure toward role interfaces. The choice depends on the team habits, the language, and whether the collaborators are slow, non-deterministic or external.
- **Test-driven development: how strong is the evidence, and should it be mandated?** – Beck defines Canon TDD precisely, but he says that other workflows that work are fine ("who cares?"). Industrial case studies at Microsoft and IBM found 40-90 percent lower pre-release defect density at 15-35 percent more initial time (Nagappan et al. 2008). Other studies and practitioners dispute how much of the effect comes from test-first and how much from testing as such. Fowler warns that a skipped refactor step is the most common failure. ISTQB and SWEBOK present TDD as one test-first approach, not as a requirement. The choice depends on the kind of code (algorithmic logic benefits most), the team skill and the design goals.
- **Coverage targets and thresholds** – Google publishes 60, 75 and 90 percent as acceptable, commendable and exemplary, and focuses on the incremental coverage of new code. Fowler expects the upper 80s or 90s from thoughtful testing, but he is suspicious of 100 percent. Dodds sees diminishing returns beyond about 70 percent. Safety and regulatory contexts mandate structural criteria such as branch or MC/DC coverage (29119-4; FDA notes that branch coverage is insufficient for high integrity; ISTQB requires all-transitions coverage for mission-critical and safety-critical state models). All agree that coverage is a floor, not a goal. The choice depends on the risk and on whether a standard prescribes a criterion.
- **Value and legitimacy of testing standards and certifications (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119, ISTQB)** – The 29119 series claims to define an internationally agreed set of standards for any testing in any life cycle, with tailored conformance for agile teams. The context-driven community (Association for Software Testing, International Society for Software Testing, the "Stop 29119" petition of 2014) objected to a lack of real consensus, a heavy documentation focus, the exclusion of context-driven approaches, and the risk that the standards become conditions of trade. SWEBOK v4 and ISTQB build on 29119. The choice depends on whether a contract or a regulator requires conformance, and on how much tailoring the team performs.
- **Can tools "test"? Automated testing versus checking** – Bach and Bolton define testing as evaluative exploration and checking as the mechanistic verification of propositions. In their view tools can only support testing, so "automated testing" is a misnomer. Google, DORA and Continuous Delivery treat automated testing as the central enabler of change at scale, and they also require human exploratory testing. The disagreement is partly vocabulary. Both camps agree that human judgement and automated checks are both necessary.
- **End-to-end and UI test automation: minimize or modernize?** – Google's "Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests" and Microsoft ("discourage the use of UI tests") argue that E2E tests are slow, flaky and hard to diagnose. Dodds argues that tests that resemble real use give the most confidence, and that modern tools (Playwright: web-first assertions, role-based locators, isolation, tracing) reduce flakiness. Fowler: the pyramid assumes that broad tests are expensive; when that assumption fails, the shape can change. The choice depends on the tooling maturity and on the cost of a wrong release.
- **Snapshot tests and other change-detector tests** – Jest documents snapshots as a valid assertion for any serializable output if the team keeps them small, deterministic and reviewed. Google's "Change-Detector Tests Considered Harmful" and Searls (via Dodds) argue that such tests fail on every change, encode no intent, and get blind updates. Dodds' compromise: snapshots for error messages, compiler output and styles, with custom serializers and a small scope.
- **How far to test in production, and how aggressively to run chaos experiments** – The Principles of Chaos Engineering "strongly prefer" experiments on production traffic with a minimized blast radius. Microsoft advises a limit of chaos to canary environments with little customer impact. Wilsenach ties the balance to the risk tolerance: medical devices need extensive pre-release testing, and social platforms can discover more in production. He requires a testing culture, continuous delivery and telemetry first. The choice depends on the consequences of a failure, the rollback speed and the observability.
- **Independent test teams versus whole-team ownership of testing** – ISTQB lists levels of independence, with benefits (different biases, challenged assumptions) and drawbacks (isolation, developers who lose responsibility, bottlenecks). FDA and IEEE 1012 require independence of review or IV&V for high integrity levels. DORA, Google and Microsoft push the ownership to the code author, with testers who pair and specialize. The choice depends on criticality and regulation. Most projects use several levels of independence at different test levels.
- **Mutation testing: gold standard or too expensive?** – PIT and Stryker present the mutation score as the best measure of test effectiveness. SWEBOK treats it as a recognized criterion. The costs are run time, equivalent mutants and unproductive mutants. Google made it workable only by mutation of changed, covered, non-arid lines during code review. The choice depends on the codebase size, the CI budget, and how much the team trusts coverage alone.
- **How much test documentation and planning is right** – 29119-3 offers templates for the policy, strategy, plan, status and completion reports, specifications and incident reports, and it explicitly allows electronic records and tailoring. Agile guidance favours lightweight artifacts. Regulated contexts need audit trails. ISTQB: the level of detail depends on the SDLC, the criticality and the need for an audit trail. The contested point is the default, not the extremes.

### Metrics

- Structural coverage (statement, branch or decision, condition, MC/DC, data-flow) – useful to find untested code, and required in some safety standards. Caveat: it measures execution and not detection, it cannot reveal missing functionality, and it becomes harmful as a target (Fowler; Google; ISTQB 4.3.3; FDA).
- Specification coverage – the equivalence partitions, boundary values, decision rules, states and transitions, and pairwise combinations covered (29119-4; ISTQB 4.2). Caveat: it depends on the quality of the test model.
- Requirements and risk coverage through traceability – the percentage of requirements or risks with passing tests, and the residual risk level (ISTQB 1.4.4, 5.3.1). Caveat: the measure is only as good as the traceability links and the tests behind them.
- Mutation score – killed mutants divided by generated mutants (SWEBOK 4.2.2; PIT; Stryker). Caveat: equivalent and unproductive mutants, and run time.
- Test execution metrics – tests planned, implemented, executed, passed, failed and blocked; execution time. Caveat: counts say nothing about value.
- Feedback time – the suite runtime locally and in CI (DORA: under ten minutes), the time from commit to first signal, and the time to fix a broken build (Microsoft example: about 30 minutes from pull request to merge with 60,000 unit tests). Caveat: speed alone says nothing about what the suite covers.
- Flakiness – the percentage of flaky runs and flaky tests, the size of the quarantine, and the age of quarantined tests (Google 2016: about 1.5 percent of runs, 16 percent of tests; Fowler: cap the quarantine). Caveat: automatic re-runs can hide flakiness from the count, and a newly flaky test can point to a real production bug (about one in six for one Google team, per a comment on the 2017 post).
- Defect metrics – defects found and fixed by severity and priority, defect density, the defect detection percentage for each phase, escaped defects to production, defect age, and defect clustering. Caveat: easy to game, and sensitive to the reporting culture.
- Review and inspection metrics – preparation time, the inspection rate (lines per hour), defects per KLOC found (SEI: defects per KLOC fell from 50 to 15 when the pace rose from 150 to 450 lines per hour), and review turnaround. Caveat: a faster rate lowers the find rate, so read the rate and the yield together.
- DORA outcomes and related shift-left measures – deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore (SWEBOK 4.1.1 lists these for test planning); DORA process measures: the share of tests authored by developers, bugs found in each phase, time spent on test failures. Caveat: the outcomes belong to the whole delivery system, not to testing alone.
- Reliability measures – failures in operation, MTBF, MTTR, reliability growth models, availability; SRE: tests that block bad code have "zero MTTR". Caveat: these measures arrive after release, so they confirm rather than prevent.
- Performance measures – response time percentiles, throughput, error rate and resource use under average, stress, soak, spike and breakpoint loads (k6). Caveat: the results hold only for the environment and the workload model that produced them.
- Usability and accessibility measures – task success rate, time on task, error counts (NN/g); WCAG conformance according to WCAG-EM. Caveat: tools alone cannot determine conformance (W3C).
- Exit-criteria satisfaction and test completion evaluation – planned tests executed, open high-severity defects, coverage reached, residual risk accepted (ISTQB 5.1.3; 29119-3 completion report). Caveat: thoroughness measures "are not sufficient in themselves" (SWEBOK 5.1.8).
- General caveats – no single metric is adequate; "tests wear out" (ISTQB principle 5); any metric used as a target invites gaming; compare trends, not absolutes.

### Failure modes

- Inverted pyramid (known as the "ice cream cone") or hourglass – many slow UI or end-to-end tests and few unit or integration tests. It hurts because the builds become slow, the tests become brittle, and diagnosis becomes hard (Fowler; Vocke; Google).
- Tolerated flaky tests – teams start to ignore red builds. The whole suite loses its value, and real defects hide behind the noise (Fowler; Google; DORA).
- Coverage as a target – engineers treat 80 percent as a ceiling, write tests that execute code without an assertion on behavior, and test trivial getters; the team chases 100 percent coverage for its own sake. It hurts because the metric rises while the detection power does not (Fowler; Google).
- Tests coupled to the implementation – over-mocking, interaction verification, change-detector tests and huge snapshots that get blind updates. Refactoring breaks the tests, and the tests stop catching defects (Google ch. 12 and 13; Dodds; Jest).
- Test code smells – obscure tests, conditional logic in tests, assertion roulette, test code duplication, erratic tests, slow tests, test logic in production, and hard-to-test code (Meszaros xUnit Test Patterns; Google "no logic in tests"). They hurt because the tests become hard to read, hard to trust and hard to maintain.
- Automation believed sufficient – no exploratory testing, no usability or accessibility evaluation with humans; the "absence-of-defects fallacy". The team ships a product that passes its checks and still fails its users (ISTQB; Fowler; W3C).
- Testing only at the end – no static testing of requirements and design, non-functional testing deferred until a full system exists, big-bang integration. Defects surface late and cost more (ISTQB; SWEBOK; Microsoft).
- Unclear test ownership – "without clear ownership, a test rots"; test code treated as second-class; testers as the only people who fix tests. The suite decays and the pipeline breaks (Google ch. 14; DORA; Microsoft).
- Shared mutable environments and data – tests depend on their order, on each other or on a shared database; production data copies with personal data; external dependencies in unit tests. The result is flaky tests, slow setup and privacy exposure (DORA; Microsoft; Google hermetic servers).
- Slow feedback – suites that take hours, so that developers skip them and batch changes; last-minute test runs create end-of-sprint surprises. It hurts because the team finds defects late and in large batches (Microsoft; DORA).
- Defect process decay – reports without reproduction steps or expected results, no regular triage, an old backlog ("most issues have a half-life"), severity and priority conflated. The backlog loses its value, and the same defects recur (ISTQB 5.5; Chromium).
- Review anti-patterns – inspections used for performance appraisal, a "feeding frenzy" on the author, too little preparation, inspection rates far above 150 lines per hour, reviews of huge changes. The defect-finding rate drops, and authors stop cooperating (SEI; Google ch. 9).
- Documentation for its own sake – full 29119-3 templates without tailoring, test plans that nobody reads, while the actual test design is thin. The effort goes to paper instead of to defects (context-driven critique; 29119 tailoring clauses).
- Faked green – deleted assertions, actual values copied into the expected values, failing tests skipped or deleted to pass the build (Beck "Canon TDD" common mistakes). The signal becomes a lie, and the team loses its safety net.
- Testability ignored in design – no seams and no dependency injection, so that unit tests become impossible and everything moves into slow end-to-end tests (Google ch. 13; Microsoft "Design products for testability").
- Tool-led automation – a tool bought without a strategy, unrealistic expectations, vendor lock-in, automation of what is better done manually, reliance on a tool instead of critical thinking (ISTQB 6.2). The investment produces little detection.
- Unsafe testing in production – synthetic traffic that pollutes analytics and business metrics; chaos experiments without a steady-state hypothesis, blast-radius control, telemetry or fast rollback (Fowler "SyntheticMonitoring"; Principles of Chaos; Microsoft). The test itself becomes the incident.
- Trusted test doubles without contract tests – stubs drift from the real service, and tests pass while the integration is broken (Fowler "ContractTest"; Pact).
- Metrics gaming – test counts or defect counts used as productivity measures, which distort behavior and reward volume over value (Fowler "TestCoverage"; SWEBOK on measures).

### Tailoring by project size

Essential at every scale: automated tests for the behaviors that matter, kept in version control and run on every change by CI; tests that are fast and deterministic, with flaky tests fixed or quarantined at once; a regression test for every fixed bug; some form of review before merge (a second person, or for a solo developer a self-review of the diff plus static analysis); a simple defect list; an explicit check before release; and at least a short manual exploratory pass through the critical paths. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 and FDA both state that the extent of testing follows the risk and the complexity, not the organization size.

| Project size | Essential | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| Solo developer on a small repository | The minimum viable test suite: unit tests for the core logic and for any tricky algorithm; one or two integration or smoke tests that exercise the main user journey end to end (not dozens); a regression test for each bug found; linters, a type checker, a formatter and a dependency or security scanner in CI; coverage enabled as a diagnostic only. A test strategy written as a paragraph in the README: what is tested at which level, how to run it, what must pass before a release. A self-review of the diff plus static analysis before merge, a simple defect list, and a short manual exploratory pass through the critical paths before each release. | TDD. Property-based tests, which pay off for parsers, serializers and algorithms. A single synthetic check or uptime monitor as the whole of testing in production for a deployed service. Not needed: a formal test plan, a test manager, templates, mutation testing, a dedicated test team, 29119 conformance. |
| Small team | Everything in the solo row, plus: a written test strategy that states the chosen shape (pyramid or trophy) and the rule that every behavior has an owner test; contract tests at service boundaries; containerized test environments and a test data discipline (isolated, seeded, masked); ATDD or BDD examples for the acceptance criteria; a Definition of Done that includes tests and review; a flaky-test policy (quarantine; fix within a week); a regular defect triage; exploratory charters before releases; performance smoke tests and an accessibility and security baseline; feature flags, canary releases and synthetic monitoring for anything customer-facing; test metrics as trends on a dashboard. Testers pair with developers and do not form a separate gate. | TDD as a team or personal discipline; property-based testing and fuzzing for parsers and protocols; mutation testing; chaos experiments; a dedicated tester or SDET role; 29119-style test plans and completion reports, unless a contract asks for them. |
| Large or regulated organization | Everything in the small-team row, plus: an organizational test policy and organizational test practices (29119-3); test plans and completion reports in a tailored 29119 form where audits or contracts require them; traceability matrices from requirements to tests, results and defects; defined entry and exit criteria for each level; independence of review or IV&V graded by integrity level (IEEE 1012); formal inspections with records for safety-critical or security-critical artifacts; the structural coverage criteria that the applicable standard requires (for example MC/DC); documented regression analysis after every change (FDA); environment and test data governance with masking; a central test infrastructure team (CI at scale, flakiness detection, mutation testing in code review, hermetic test environments); specialist groups for performance, security, accessibility and localization; chaos engineering with blast-radius controls; and release evidence packages. | Full 29119 conformance and heavy templates beyond what an audit, a contract or a regulator asks for; specific tools; a dedicated test team for areas where whole-team ownership with specialist support is enough; mutation testing outside the code review flow. |

Optional at every scale: specific tools, mutation testing, a dedicated test team, full 29119 conformance and heavy templates. Use them only where the risk, the contract or the regulator asks for them.

- [ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1:2022 Software testing – Part 1: General concepts (sample: foreword, introduction, scope, contents, terms)](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/81291/6694557ff8304df8841bb191a00ecc6f/ISO-IEC-IEEE-29119-1-2022.pdf) – Primary standard. Used for the concept list (V&V, test basis, test oracle, risk-based strategy, test practices, continuous testing, test environments and data, defects), the definitions (exploratory testing, error guessing, pairwise, compatibility, performance, portability), and the statement that 29119-2, 29119-3 and 29119-4 are normative with tailored conformance for agile.
- [ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2:2021 Software testing – Part 2: Test processes (sample)](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/79428/d2457e67b9db443b9504d2ef49a8724a/ISO-IEC-IEEE-29119-2-2021.pdf) – Primary standard. Multi-layer process model (organizational; test management: strategy and planning, monitoring and control, completion; dynamic: design and implementation, environment and data management, execution, incident reporting), definitions of regression testing, retesting, risk-based testing, test level and test type, and full versus tailored conformance.
- [ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3:2021 Software testing – Part 3: Test documentation (sample)](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/79429/27623aa24dba41a2876884c0ec57f5d7/ISO-IEC-IEEE-29119-3-2021.pdf) – Primary standard. List of documentation templates (test policy, organizational test practices, test plan contents, test status report, test completion report, test model and case specifications, data and environment requirements and readiness reports, execution log, incident report), definitions (test basis, test strategy, traceability matrix), and tailoring rules (electronic records allowed; any life cycle, including agile and DevOps).
