## 10. Integration, build and continuous integration

### Purpose

Integration combines separately built parts – modules, services, configuration and third-party dependencies – into a working whole. It then proves that the whole still works. The build turns the source at one commit into runnable, versioned artifacts in a repeatable way. Continuous integration (CI) makes both activities small and frequent. Each developer merges to the mainline at least daily. An automated, self-testing build verifies each merge within minutes.

The phase answers three questions. Does the system assemble? Does it still pass its tests? Can we trust the artifact that comes out? The phase exists because late and large integrations are unpredictable and expensive. Small integrations are cheap and keep the mainline releasable. In current practice the phase also produces the evidence that consumers use to trust a build: provenance, signatures and software bills of materials (SBOMs).

### Other names

- System integration – the Integration process of ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 and 12207
- Software integration or construction integration (SWEBOK v4 Construction KA, section 3.7)
- Integration testing (SWEBOK v4 Testing KA, section 2.1.2)
- Product integration (NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, 5.2)
- Continuous integration (CI); continuous build; presubmit and post-submit testing (Google)
- Trunk-based development – often used as a synonym for CI with daily mainline integration
- Software building and build automation (SWEBOK v4 SCM KA, section 6.1)
- Commit stage of the deployment pipeline (Humble and Farley, Continuous Delivery)
- The CI half of CI/CD; build engineering; release engineering (build side)
- Software supply-chain security of the build (SLSA Build track, NIST SSDF, CNCF Software Supply Chain Best Practices)

### Position in the life cycle

Upstream of this phase are architecture and detailed design (see sections 6 and 7), which fix the interfaces and the order of assembly, and implementation (see section 8), which delivers unit-tested components. Downstream are acceptance and system testing (see section 9), release management and deployment (see section 11), which consume the built artifacts. CI is the first stage of the deployment pipeline that feeds continuous delivery. The build also sits under configuration management (see section 15), and the supply-chain evidence from the build feeds security and compliance work (see section 16).

In waterfall and the V-model, integration is a separate phase on the right side of the V. Teams assemble components level by level from the bottom up (SEBoK, NASA). Integration testing follows unit testing and precedes system testing. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 and 12207 define an Integration process that "iteratively combines implemented system elements to form complete or partial system configurations" (15288 as quoted by SEBoK).

In iterative and agile methods, integration happens inside every iteration and, with CI, on every push. SWEBOK v4 states that CI "has been widely adopted in practice" and that construction, testing, delivery and deployment activities now mix.

In DevOps and continuous delivery, integration is a continuous, automated process and not a one-time event. A fast commit stage runs first, and slower pipeline stages follow. Google describes CI as "the continuous assembling and testing of our entire complex and rapidly evolving ecosystem". SWEBOK also places software building under configuration management (SCM KA 6.1). Supply-chain standards (SLSA, NIST SSDF, CNCF) attach their controls to the build step.

The phase is therefore two things. In plan-driven projects it is a one-time integration milestone. In CI-based projects it is a permanent background process.

### Inputs

- Source code, tests, build scripts, pipeline definitions, database schemas and migration scripts, configuration and infrastructure code – all kept in one version-controlled mainline (Fowler; DORA version-control capability; SWEBOK SCM KA).
- Unit-tested changes that build locally and, where the policy requires it, reviewed changes; SEBoK notes that each implemented element is verified before it enters integration.
- Architecture and interface definitions (interface control documents, API contracts) and an integration plan that fixes the order of assembly and the test means (SEBoK; NASA SE Handbook).
- Dependency manifests and lockfiles with pinned versions and hashes, plus an approved internal artifact repository or proxy for third-party packages (Software Engineering at Google ch. 18; Maven; CNCF).
- Automated test suites by level (unit, integration, acceptance) with stubs, drivers, mocks, test data and hermetic test environments (SWEBOK Construction KA; Google ch. 23).
- Environment definitions – container images, Dockerfiles, infrastructure as code – so that a reference build and test environment matches production (Fowler; CD patterns).
- A CI service and runners, least-privilege credentials or OIDC identities, and the branch-protection and required-check policy of the repository (GitHub, GitLab docs).
- Quality and security policy inputs: linter and static-analysis rules, SCA and license policy, secret-scanning rules, the target SLSA level and the SBOM format.
- Entry criteria for a change: it is small; it builds and passes tests locally or through pre-commit hooks; unfinished work is hidden behind keystone interfaces or feature flags; it is pushed to the mainline or to a branch that lives at most about one day.

### Activities

- **Define the integration strategy and plan** – Decide in what order the team assembles and verifies the parts, based on the architecture and the risks. Systems engineering sources (SEBoK, NASA) list global or big-bang integration, integration as parts arrive, incremental integration, subset or functional-chain integration, top-down, bottom-up and criterion-driven integration; most projects mix them. SWEBOK contrasts phased (big-bang) integration with incremental integration. It states that incremental integration gives easier error location, earlier delivery and better progress monitoring. In software the dominant strategy is continuous integration on every change. The output is an integration plan that names the aggregates, the order, the stubs, drivers and simulators, and the verification steps for each step.
- **Keep one version-controlled mainline that holds everything needed to build** – Put source, tests, build scripts, pipeline definitions, schemas, configuration and infrastructure code in one repository mainline. Then anyone can clone it on a minimal machine and build the product. Do not store build outputs in the repository; they are disposable. DORA now also lists AI prompts and agent configuration as things to version. This is the precondition for every other CI practice.
- **Automate the build as one command and choose the build tool deliberately** – Script the complete build – compile, package, schema setup, configuration – so that a single command produces the artifacts and no manual step exists. Task-based tools (Make, Ant, Maven, Gradle, Rake) run scripts with declared task dependencies. Artifact-based tools (Bazel, Buck, Pants) declare artifacts and inputs, which lets the tool parallelize, sandbox and cache safely. Software Engineering at Google argues that almost every new project benefits from an artifact-based tool from the start. Gradle shows that task-based tools can add build caches when inputs and outputs are declared correctly. The result is a deterministic build script under version control that developers and the CI service run identically.
- **Manage dependencies and the third-party supply of the build** – Declare every dependency explicitly. Pin versions rather than use ranges such as 1.+, verify hashes, prefer one version of each library across the codebase, and pull packages from an approved internal repository or proxy. Use automated update tools (Dependabot, Renovate) so that pinned versions do not freeze security fixes. Scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities and license problems before they enter the build. The output is a reproducible, auditable dependency set and a stream of small, tested update pull requests.
- **Make the build self-testing** – Run the automated test suite as part of the build and fail the build on any test failure. Put fast, reliable unit tests in the commit stage and slower integration and acceptance tests in later stages. Use stubs, drivers and mocks for incremental integration. Keep tests hermetic so that they do not depend on production back ends. Developers own the tests. The product is a green or red verdict that the team can trust.
- **Integrate small changes to the mainline at least daily** – Each developer pushes to the mainline every day, in changes of a few hours of work, on trunk or on branches that live about one day. Long-lived branches only defer integration and make it cost more. DORA found that high performers keep three or fewer active branches and have no code freezes or integration phases. Hide unfinished work with keystone interfaces, feature flags, branch by abstraction or dark launching. Then the team can integrate incomplete features without a release of them. The result is that integration becomes a non-event and merge conflicts stay small.
- **Run a build on every push in a reference environment – pipelines as code** – A CI service watches the mainline and every branch or pull request. It runs the pipeline on each push in a clean, hosted environment, so that differences between developer machines and production cannot hide problems. The team defines the pipeline as code in the repository (GitHub Actions workflow YAML, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile). The team reviews it like any other change and versions it with the branch it builds. The output is a status per commit and per pull request, and the same definition for every contributor.
- **Design the pipeline stages for fast feedback** – Split the build into a commit stage that finishes in about ten minutes and later stages that run slower tests and deploy to test environments. Fowler and DORA both treat ten minutes as the practical limit for the first stage. Order jobs so that the ones most likely to fail run first. Express job dependencies as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that independent jobs run in parallel. Skip jobs that the change cannot affect, and cancel superseded runs of the same branch. When a later stage finds a bug, add a fast test for it to the commit stage. The output is a pipeline whose feedback time stays short as the codebase grows.
- **Speed up builds with caching, incremental and remote execution** – Reuse work whose inputs did not change. Incremental builds skip unchanged targets. Build caches (local and remote) return stored outputs keyed on input hashes. Remote execution spreads actions across a worker pool. This only works when every input and output is declared (hermeticity); undeclared inputs cause incorrect cache hits. CI services add dependency caching (for example GitHub caches keyed on lockfile hashes, with size and retention limits). Monorepo tools add affected-target detection so that the build and the tests cover only the changed part of the graph. The result is lower build time and lower compute cost.
- **Protect the mainline with branch rules and a merge queue** – Configure protected branches: required status checks, required reviews or code owners, no force-push or deletion, optionally signed commits and linear history. On busy branches use a merge queue or merge train so that each change is tested against the exact combination that will land on the mainline. This prevents merge skew, where two pull requests pass separately but break together. The bors rule states it: the exact integration that ends up on the main branch was tested before anyone builds on it. The output is a mainline that stays green by construction rather than by luck.
- **Fix broken builds immediately and keep the build visible** – When the mainline build fails, the fix is the highest-priority task. The fastest remedy is usually to revert the offending change and debug elsewhere. Large organizations rotate a build cop and automate culprit finding and rollback. Broadcast status through dashboards, chat notifications and IDE integration, and show trends so that systemic problems become visible. The product is a mainline that everyone can pull and deploy from at any time.
- **Manage flaky tests** – Detect tests that pass and fail on the same code. Move them out of the critical path (quarantine), open a bug with a deadline, and fix or delete them. Remove the root causes – shared state, bare sleeps for asynchronous work, calls to remote services, clock and time dependence, resource leaks – and make tests hermetic. A retry is a mitigation, not a cure. Google reported in 2016 that 1.5% of test runs, almost 16% of tests and 84% of pass-to-fail transitions involve flakiness, and that its three-failures-in-a-row rule encourages people to ignore flakiness. The output is a test suite whose failures mean something.
- **Run static analysis, security scans and pre-commit hooks** – Run formatters, linters, type checkers and SAST in the pipeline and show findings in the code review, where developers already expect change. Keep the effective false-positive rate low, or developers ignore the tool. Add software composition analysis (SCA), secret scanning, infrastructure-as-code scanning and license checks as the policy requires. Surface results as pull-request annotations or SARIF alerts. Use pre-commit hooks (for example the pre-commit framework) for fast local checks. Run the same checks in CI, because client-side hooks are not versioned and can be bypassed with --no-verify. The output is earlier, cheaper detection of defects and policy violations.
- **Build once, version and store artifacts** – Produce each deployable artifact exactly once and promote that same binary, package or container image through every later environment; never rebuild per environment. Give every artifact a unique, immutable identifier – a semantic version for libraries, a build number or commit digest for services. Publish it to an artifact repository or registry (Maven-style repositories, package registries, OCI registries) with retention rules. Twelve-Factor adds that a release is build plus configuration and is append-only. The output is a traceable chain from commit to artifact to deployment.
- **Make builds hermetic and reproducible** – Isolate the build from the host: pin tool versions as inputs, vendor or hash-check external downloads, sandbox actions so that only declared inputs are visible, remove timestamps, locale and path differences, and record the build environment (for example a .buildinfo file or a container image). A reproducible build lets any party recreate bit-for-bit identical artifacts from the same source, environment and instructions. This enables verification by a rebuild, better caching and detection of compromised build systems. CNCF ranks verifiable reproducibility as a high-assurance control; SLSA relies on provenance rather than reproducibility. The output is a build whose result does not depend on who or what machine ran it.
- **Generate build provenance, sign artifacts and harden the build platform** – Have the build platform – not the build steps – emit signed provenance that records the builder, the source commit, the build definition and the resolved dependencies, as an in-toto attestation in SLSA provenance format. Sign artifacts and attestations, for example with Sigstore keyless signing (cosign, Fulcio certificates bound to an OIDC identity, Rekor transparency log) or hosted equivalents such as GitHub artifact attestations. Raise the SLSA Build level step by step: L1 provenance exists; L2 hosted builds with signed provenance; L3 isolated builds where signing secrets are not reachable from user-defined steps. Use ephemeral single-use workers, minimal network, least-privilege tokens, pinned actions and no secrets in caches or logs. Verification at consumption is what gives the security benefit. The output is artifacts whose origin a consumer can check.
- **Generate and distribute an SBOM** – Produce a software bill of materials at build time, when the build knows the exact dependency set, rather than only by a scan afterwards; CNCF notes that build-time SBOMs are more accurate. Use SPDX or CycloneDX. Include the NTIA minimum elements (supplier, component name, version, unique identifiers, dependency relationships, SBOM author, timestamp), state known unknowns, refresh the SBOM for every new build, and attach it as a signed attestation. Pair it with VEX statements where needed to say whether a known vulnerability affects the product. The output is a machine-readable inventory that consumers and vulnerability tools can use.
- **Test in a clone of production and make builds easy to obtain** – Run later pipeline stages against environments that match production in operating system, middleware versions, configuration and network topology, created from versioned scripts. Deploy to every environment with the same automated process and smoke-test each deployment. Publish the latest good build where testers, stakeholders and devices can fetch it; for mobile apps that means automated deployment to test devices. The output is confidence that what passed the pipeline will behave the same in production.
- **Secure and standardize the CI system itself** – Treat the pipeline as production infrastructure: least-privilege tokens, secrets injected at run time and masked, OIDC instead of long-lived cloud credentials, third-party actions pinned to commit SHAs, care with workflows that run on untrusted pull requests, self-hosted runners isolated and never shared with public repositories, audit logs kept. Large organizations template pipelines so that every project gets the same stages and gates and no one can bypass them. They allow pipeline changes only through pipeline-as-code. The output is a build system that attackers cannot use as a path into production.
- **Measure, control cost and improve the pipeline continuously** – Track pipeline duration, success rate, time to repair the build, queue time, flakiness, cache hit rate and minutes consumed. Hosted CI bills per minute with large multipliers for macOS and Windows, so cancel superseded runs, right-size runners, slim images and skip unaffected jobs. GitLab's guidance is to make small changes, watch the effect and iterate; Fowler's is to monitor build time and act before it creeps up. Review which required checks still earn their place. The output is a pipeline that stays fast, cheap enough and trusted.

The integration strategies that the sources name compare as follows.

| Strategy | Description | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Global or big-bang (phased) | Assemble all parts at once and test the whole. Acceptable only for simple systems with few interactions. | SEBoK; SWEBOK Construction and Testing KAs; Wikipedia |
| With the stream (as parts arrive) | Integrate each part when it arrives, in the order of delivery. | SEBoK |
| Incremental | Add one part or a small group at a time and verify after each addition. Faults are localized to the last part added. | SEBoK; SWEBOK |
| Subsets or functional chains | Integrate the parts that together deliver one function or chain, then combine the chains. | SEBoK |
| Top-down | Start with the top-level components and use stubs for the lower levels. | SEBoK; SWEBOK Testing KA; Wikipedia |
| Bottom-up | Start with the lowest-level components and use drivers for the upper levels; the NASA assembly sequence. | SEBoK; NASA; SWEBOK Testing KA; Wikipedia |
| Sandwich | Combine top-down and bottom-up and meet in the middle. | SWEBOK Testing KA; Wikipedia |
| Criterion-driven | Integrate first the parts that best satisfy a selected criterion, for example the highest risk or the most critical function. | SEBoK |
| Continuous integration | Integrate every change to the mainline and verify it with an automated build; the dominant software strategy. | Fowler; DORA; SWEBOK |

The SLSA Build track levels that the provenance activity names compare as follows.

| SLSA Build level | Requirement | Example |
|---|---|---|
| L0 | No requirements and no guarantees. | A local, unscripted build. |
| L1 | Provenance exists and describes how the artifact was built. | A scripted build that publishes provenance. |
| L2 | A hosted build platform runs the build and signs the provenance. | GitHub-hosted builds with artifact attestations (the default). |
| L3 | The build runs isolated; signing secrets are not reachable from user-defined steps. | GitHub reusable workflows; ephemeral single-use workers with minimal network. |

### Outputs

- A green mainline – the latest commit that the CI build verified (Google's "green head") – releasable at any time.
- Versioned, immutable build artifacts (binaries, packages, container images), built once and stored in an artifact repository or registry with unique identifiers and retention rules.
- Test reports, coverage data, static-analysis and security findings attached to the commit or pull request; build logs retained as records (SWEBOK treats build outputs as quality and compliance records).
- Signed build provenance attestations (SLSA provenance in in-toto format) and artifact signatures, plus a signed SBOM per release artifact, stored so that consumers can verify them.
- A release candidate – artifact plus its configuration – promoted to later pipeline stages and deployed to test environments; the latest executables available to testers and stakeholders.
- Integration records: integration and test reports, defect and change requests, revert and culprit decisions, and the quarantined-test list with owners and deadlines.
- Pipeline dashboards, notifications and trend data visible to the whole team.
- Exit criteria for a change: all required checks passed on the exact merged result; the build is green on the mainline; the artifact is traceable to the commit and, where policy requires, signed with provenance and SBOM; no policy-blocking findings remain; any broken build was fixed or reverted.

### Roles

- Developers – integrate small changes to the mainline daily, write and maintain the tests, run pre-commit checks, and fix or revert what they break; DORA states that developers are responsible for a green build.
- Build cop or build monitor (rotating) – watches the mainline, triages failures, reverts or assigns culprits, and keeps the suite green regardless of who broke it (Google).
- Build, release or platform engineers (DevOps, developer-experience or "software factory" team) – own the build tooling, pipeline templates, runners, caches, artifact repositories and signing infrastructure; standardize pipelines across projects.
- Architect or tech lead – fixes interfaces and the integration order, decides the integration strategy, and owns the branching and dependency policy.
- Test engineers and QA – design integration and acceptance tests, provide production-like test environments, and work alongside developers rather than in a separate phase (DORA).
- Security engineers and AppSec – define scanning rules, the SLSA target, and the signing and SBOM policy; review pipeline permissions and third-party actions.
- Reviewers and code owners – approve changes where branch protection requires review; SLSA Source Level 4 and the CNCF four-eyes principle require two trusted persons for protected branches.
- System integration engineer or integration team (hardware-software and large systems) – executes the integration plan, manages interfaces, and records integration results (SEBoK, NASA).
- Compliance, audit and release management – consume build records, provenance and SBOMs as evidence; set retention and archiving rules (NIST SSDF PS.3).
- Open-source maintainers – configure CI for pull requests from irregular contributors, branch protection and release signing (OpenSSF Scorecard checks).

### Practices with consensus

- **Keep everything needed to build in one version-controlled mainline, and keep build outputs out of it** – Anyone can clone and build on a clean machine; environments and releases become reproducible and traceable; comprehensive version control predicts continuous delivery. Evidence: Fowler, Continuous Integration (2024); DORA version control capability; SWEBOK v4 SCM KA 6.1; CNCF Software Supply Chain Best Practices; OpenSSF Scorecard (Binary-Artifacts check).
- **Automate the whole build as one command, scripted in version control, with no manual steps** – Computers do repetitive tasks reliably; a scripted build is the same on every machine and is the prerequisite for CI, caching and provenance. Evidence: Fowler 2024; DORA continuous integration capability; continuousdelivery.com principles; SWEBOK v4 SCM KA 6.1; CNCF ("automated through a pipeline defined as code").
- **Make the build self-testing and fail it on any test failure** – Without tests a green build proves nothing; fast automated tests are what let teams integrate daily and release on demand. Evidence: Fowler 2024 ("Instituting Continuous Integration without self-testing code won't work"); DORA CI and test automation capabilities; continuousdelivery.com CI page; SWEBOK v4 Construction KA.
- **Integrate to the mainline at least daily in small batches; keep branches short-lived; no code freezes or integration phases** – Integration effort grows faster than batch size; frequent small merges surface conflicts while they are cheap; DORA links trunk-based development to higher performance. Evidence: Fowler 2024; DORA trunk-based development capability; trunkbaseddevelopment.com; continuousdelivery.com; Software Engineering at Google ch. 16.
- **Trigger a build on every push, on a hosted reference environment, and run fast reliable checks before merge (presubmit)** – Catches environment differences and integration errors within minutes; hosted builds are also the base requirement of SLSA Build L1–L3. Evidence: Fowler 2024; DORA CI capability; Software Engineering at Google ch. 23; SLSA v1.1 requirements ("Hosted").
- **Fix a broken mainline immediately, usually by a revert; nothing has higher priority** – A red mainline blocks everyone and hides new breakages; a revert restores a known-good state fastest. Evidence: Fowler 2024 (quoting Beck); DORA CI and trunk-based development pages; Software Engineering at Google ch. 23 (rollbacks, build cops).
- **Keep the commit stage at about ten minutes and stage the pipeline: fast feedback first, deeper and slower checks later** – Slow builds push developers to batch changes and to stop waiting for results; staged pipelines keep feedback fast without loss of depth. Evidence: Fowler 2024 and the DeploymentPipeline bliki; DORA CI pitfalls (tests over 10 minutes); Humble CD patterns; GitLab pipeline efficiency docs; Google ch. 23 (presubmit wait about 11 minutes).
- **Build artifacts once, give each a unique immutable identifier, store them in an artifact repository and promote the same artifact through every environment** – What is deployed is what was tested; rollback and audit become trivial; configuration is injected per environment instead of rebuilt. Evidence: continuousdelivery.com patterns; Twelve-Factor build-release-run; GOV.UK Service Manual; DORA CI ("numbered, repeatable packages"); Maven repositories guide; SWEBOK v4 SCM KA 6.2.
- **Test in environments that clone production, created from versioned scripts, and deploy to every environment with the same automated process** – Environment drift hides defects until production; identical deployment paths get exercised many times before the production run. Evidence: Fowler 2024; continuousdelivery.com patterns; GOV.UK Service Manual; DORA version control capability.
- **Make build status visible to everyone, through dashboards and chat notifications, and track trends** – Visibility drives the behavior of a fast fix and shows systemic problems early. Evidence: Fowler 2024; DORA CI capability.
- **Pin and verify dependencies, build tools and CI actions; avoid floating version ranges; use one version of each library; automate update pull requests** – Unpinned inputs make builds irreproducible and open a supply-chain attack path; automated updates keep pinned versions from freezing security fixes. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 18; Bazel hermeticity; OpenSSF Concise Guide and Scorecard (Pinned-Dependencies, Dependency-Update-Tool); CNCF (lock and verify external requirements); GitHub Actions security hardening (pin to SHA); Dependabot docs.
- **Treat flaky tests as defects: quarantine them out of the critical path, fix or delete them quickly, and remove the root causes** – Ignored failures spread to the whole suite; tests must be reliable for a green build to mean releasable. Evidence: Fowler, Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests; Google Testing Blog 2016 and 2017; Software Engineering at Google ch. 23; DORA test automation capability.
- **Protect the mainline with branch protection or rulesets and required checks; on busy branches test the exact merged result with a merge queue or merge train** – Prevents unreviewed or untested changes and force-pushes; merge queues remove merge skew, where changes pass alone but fail together. Evidence: GitHub protected branches and merge queue docs; GitLab merge trains docs; bors "Not Rocket Science Rule"; OpenSSF Concise Guide and Scorecard (Branch-Protection); SLSA Source track; CNCF (use branch protection rules).
- **Run static analysis and security scans (SAST, SCA, secret scanning, IaC scanning) in the pipeline and surface results in code review with a low false-positive rate** – Finds defects and vulnerabilities before merge at low cost; developers act on results only when the signal is good. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 20; OWASP DevSecOps Guideline; OpenSSF Concise Guide; NIST SSDF PW.7; GitHub code scanning docs; SWEBOK v4 SCM KA 6.1.
- **Have the build platform emit signed provenance, sign release artifacts, generate an SBOM at build time, and verify these at consumption** – Lets consumers check that an artifact came from the expected source and build process; meets SLSA, SSDF and procurement (EO 14028) expectations. Evidence: SLSA v1.0–v1.2 specification; Sigstore docs; in-toto attestation framework; NTIA minimum elements, CISA and NIST SBOM pages; CNCF paper; NIST SSDF PS.2 and PS.3; OpenSSF Concise Guide; GitHub artifact attestations.
- **Define pipelines as code in the repository, review them like code, and standardize them across projects** – One source of truth, an audit trail and per-branch configuration; templates stop projects from bypassing gates. Evidence: Jenkins Pipeline as Code; GitHub Actions and GitLab CI docs; CNCF ("only allow pipeline modifications through pipeline as code"; "standardize pipelines across projects"); NIST SSDF PO.3 (toolchains as code).
- **Harden the CI system: least-privilege tokens, secrets never in logs or caches, OIDC for cloud access, ephemeral isolated build workers, audited changes** – The build system produces what runs in production and is a prime target; isolation and minimal credentials limit the blast radius. Evidence: GitHub Actions security hardening and caching docs; CNCF (single-use build workers, minimal network, segregated duties); SLSA Build L3 isolation; NIST SSDF PW.6 (dedicated, highly controlled build environment).
- **Prefer incremental integration over big-bang integration and plan the order of assembly from the architecture** – Faults are localized to the last part added; progress is visible; big bang is only acceptable for simple systems with few interactions. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 Construction KA 3.7 and Testing KA 2.1.2; SEBoK System Integration; NASA SE Handbook 5.2.
- **Caching and incremental builds require every input and output to be declared (hermeticity); otherwise cache hits are wrong** – Correct caching is what makes fast builds trustworthy; undeclared inputs cause stale outputs and "works after clean" confusion. Evidence: Gradle build cache docs; Bazel hermeticity; Software Engineering at Google ch. 18; GitHub Actions caching docs.

### Contested points

- **Review before merge (pull requests) versus direct commits to trunk** – Fowler states that pre-integration review "usually adds significant friction" and prefers pair programming or post-integration review. DORA lists heavy and asynchronous code review as a pitfall for trunk-based development. OpenSSF Scorecard, the CNCF paper (four-eyes principle) and SLSA Source Level 4 require two-party review before changes reach protected branches, and GitHub and GitLab build their workflows around it. The trunk-based development site reconciles the positions with branches that live less than a day and exist only for review and CI. The choice depends on regulation, trust in contributors (open source), team co-location and how fast reviews actually happen.
- **Monorepo versus polyrepo** – Google (Software Engineering at Google ch. 16, the CACM paper) argues that a monorepo makes the One Version rule, atomic changes and large-scale refactoring easy; monorepo.tools lists consistency and atomic cross-project changes. The same sources admit high tooling investment, Git performance limits, coarse access control and the need for remote caching and affected-target detection. Polyrepos give isolation, independent release cadence and granular permissions at the cost of cross-repo coordination and duplicated tooling. Google suggests a "virtual monorepo" as a middle path. The right answer depends on scale, team structure, compliance boundaries and available build tooling.
- **How much to run before merge, and whether any failure should block** – Fowler's commit stage runs unit tests with mocked services and defers slow tests. Google runs only fast reliable tests presubmit and accepts that about 5% of failures slip to post-submit, where rollback and build cops handle them. A sidebar in Software Engineering at Google argues that 100% green, like 100% uptime, is too expensive and that a block on well-understood failures can be wrong. Merge-queue proponents (bors, GitHub, GitLab) insist that the exact merged result must pass before it lands. Teams must choose between feedback speed, mainline purity and compute cost.
- **Semantic versioning versus "live at head" and minimum version selection** – semver.org defines MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH as the way to express compatibility and avoid dependency hell. Software Engineering at Google ch. 21 calls SemVer "a lossy-compression shorthand estimate" that overconstrains and overpromises because of Hyrum's Law; it prefers minimum version selection and argues that testing and CI provide actual evidence of compatibility. Most public ecosystems still run on SemVer; the critique matters mainly inside large organizations that can test every consumer.
- **Automatic retries of flaky tests** – Google uses automatic reruns and a "fails only if it fails three times in a row" flag, but reports that this encourages developers to ignore flakiness and delays real failure detection; one Google team found that a newly flaky test pointed to a real production bug one time in six. Fowler and DORA want quarantine with quick fixes and reliable tests, not tolerance. Retries are widely used in practice as a bridge; the disagreement is about how much tolerance is acceptable and for how long.
- **Build tool choice: task-based versus artifact-based systems** – Software Engineering at Google recommends an artifact-based tool such as Bazel for almost every new project because of correctness, sandboxing and caching. Many teams find Bazel's learning curve and ecosystem friction too high and stay with Maven, Gradle, npm or Cargo; Gradle's build cache shows that task-based tools can get far with declared inputs. The decision depends on codebase size, number of languages, need for remote execution and available expertise.
- **How far to push reproducible builds** – reproducible-builds.org and CNCF present bit-for-bit reproducibility as a strong security and quality control; CNCF rates it a high-assurance recommendation and notes it is "not a trivial task". SLSA deliberately relies on signed provenance from a trusted builder instead of a requirement for reproducibility. Many teams settle for hermetic builds plus provenance and leave full reproducibility to distributions and high-assurance products.
- **Pinning dependencies versus staying current** – Google ch. 18, Bazel, OpenSSF and CNCF insist on pinned versions and hashes for determinism and security. OpenSSF and CNCF also insist that dependencies stay up to date and recommend Dependabot or Renovate; Dependabot adds a default cooldown before it proposes non-security updates. The consensus is "pin plus automated updates", but the update cadence, grouping and auto-merge policy remain judgement calls.
- **Release branches** – trunkbaseddevelopment.com allows just-in-time release branches that the team deletes after the release. Software Engineering at Google calls release branches "generally benign" but notes that DORA's high performers have "practically nonexistent" release branches and fix forward from trunk. Teams that ship versioned products to customers usually keep them; teams that deploy from trunk many times a day do not.
- **Strict "branch must be up to date" checks versus merge queues** – GitHub's strict required-status-check mode guarantees that the tested tree equals the merged tree, but it forces every open pull request to rebase and rebuild after each merge. Merge queues and GitLab merge trains automate this at the cost of extra configuration (merge_group events, merged-results pipelines) and compute. Small teams with few merges per day rarely need a queue; busy repositories usually do.
- **Hosted versus self-hosted runners and cost control** – Hosted runners are free for public repositories and billed per minute otherwise, with macOS at about ten times the Linux rate. Self-hosted runners cut cost and give control over hardware, but GitHub says they "should almost never be used for public repositories" because pull requests can compromise them, and CNCF wants single-use isolated workers. The trade-off is cost and control against isolation and operational burden.
- **Weight of client-side pre-commit hooks** – The pre-commit framework and many teams run formatters and linters locally before each commit and again in CI. Others keep local hooks minimal because git hooks are not versioned, can be bypassed with --no-verify and slow down commits; they rely on server-side CI as the only gate. Both sides agree that CI must re-run the checks; they differ on how much to put in the developer's commit path.
- **Does classical CI apply to part-time open-source and solo work?** – Fowler writes that open-source projects with one or two maintainers and irregular contributors lack the full-time commitment that CI needs, and that feature branches and pull requests fit better there; DORA's capabilities target product teams. In practice solo and open-source repositories still gain most of the value from an automated self-testing build on every push and pull request, even when "daily integration by every member" does not apply.
- **What the words "continuous integration" mean** – Fowler and trunkbaseddevelopment.com state that a CI server on long-lived feature branches is not CI. continuousdelivery.com reports that fewer than 20% of teams that claim CI commit to trunk daily, trigger tests on each commit and fix builds within ten minutes. Much of industry uses "CI" for any automated build service. Readers of a reference should know which meaning a source uses.

### Metrics

- Commit-stage and full pipeline duration – target about ten minutes for the commit stage (Fowler, DORA); Google reports an average presubmit wait of about 11 minutes. Caveat: a cut in tests to hit the target defeats the purpose; measure p50 and p95, not only the mean.
- Mainline build success rate and time to repair a broken build – continuousdelivery.com uses "fixed within ten minutes" as a CI criterion; DORA measures build repair speed. Caveat: Software Engineering at Google warns that a 100% green target is as expensive as 100% uptime.
- Integration frequency – merges to trunk per developer per day, number of active branches (DORA target: three or fewer), branch age, pull-request cycle time and review approval time. Caveat: a count of commits rewards trivial commits; look at batch size and branch age together.
- Test flakiness – share of test runs with flaky results (Google: about 1.5%), share of tests that ever flake (about 16%), share of pass-to-fail transitions that are flaky (84%), size of the quarantine list and mean time to clean up (MTTCU). Caveat: retry counts hide real defects; a drop in flakiness because tests were deleted is not an improvement.
- Queue wait time, runner utilization and CI minutes or cost per month – hosted runners bill per minute (GitHub: about USD 0.006 per Linux minute, roughly ten times that for macOS); superseded-run cancellation, caching and path filters reduce it. Caveat: cost cuts that make developers run CI less often increase batch size.
- Cache hit rate and share of incremental or remote-cached actions – shows how much work the build reuses. Caveat: a high hit rate with undeclared inputs means wrong builds, so track "works after clean" incidents too.
- Where defects are found – unit tests should catch most (DORA test pyramid), then acceptance tests, then manual tests or production. Caveat: coverage percentages are easy to game; prefer mutation or escape-rate indicators.
- Supply-chain posture – OpenSSF Scorecard score, SLSA Build level reached, share of release artifacts with signed provenance and SBOM, number of known-vulnerable dependencies and their age, time to merge dependency updates. Caveat: a score measures the presence of controls, not their quality.
- Traceability – can every running version be traced to a commit and a pipeline run (GOV.UK; DORA: percentage of code, configuration and scripts under version control). Caveat: a link in a dashboard is not an audit unless the artifact is immutable and signed.
- Revert and rollback rate – how often mainline changes are reverted or post-submit failures are rolled back; Google uses it as a health signal for presubmit selection. Caveat: a very low revert rate can mean that people are afraid to revert.
- DORA four keys as outcome indicators – lead time for changes, deployment frequency, change failure rate, failed deployment recovery time – which CI influences but does not own. Caveat: outcome metrics lag and depend on release and operations practices too (see sections 11 and 12).
- Pipeline analytics – per-job duration and failure rate, critical path length in the job DAG (GitLab). Caveat: optimize the critical path, not the sum of all job times.

### Failure modes

- Long-lived branches and late big-bang integration – cause integration phases, merge hell and unpredictable delays; the cost grows faster than the size of the change (Fowler; SWEBOK).
- A CI server that runs on feature branches only, called "CI" – changes stay semi-integrated; conflicts and design divergence surface late (Fowler; continuousdelivery.com).
- Tolerance of a red mainline – people stop trusting the build, breakages pile up and the release date slips; the fix is revert first, debug later.
- Slow builds – once the commit stage exceeds roughly ten minutes, developers batch changes and stop waiting; flaky infrastructure and external services in the commit stage are common causes.
- Flaky tests left in the critical path – alert fatigue; 84% of pass-to-fail transitions at Google involve flaky tests; real failures get dismissed as noise.
- Builds that depend on the host – "works on my machine", snowflake build servers, floating version ranges and unpinned tools produce results that change from day to day and cannot be cached or audited (Google ch. 18; Bazel; CNCF).
- A rebuild per environment or mutated releases – what runs in production was never tested; this violates build-once and append-only releases (CD patterns; Twelve-Factor).
- Manual steps hidden in the build or deployment – undocumented clicks and tribal knowledge block reproducibility and on-call recovery.
- Incorrect cache hits – undeclared inputs or outputs make incremental and cached builds return stale results, which erodes trust and leads to routine "clean" builds (Gradle; Google ch. 18).
- Merge skew – two changes pass alone and break together when no merge queue or strict up-to-date check exists (GitLab; bors).
- Secrets and credentials exposed through CI – plaintext secrets in workflow files, secrets in caches readable by any fork, over-privileged tokens, script injection from untrusted pull-request input, pull_request_target misuse, shared self-hosted runners on public repositories; each gives an attacker a path into the build and from there into production (GitHub hardening).
- Unpinned third-party actions and dependencies – a compromised tag or package becomes a backdoor in every build (GitHub hardening; OpenSSF; CNCF).
- Provenance or SBOM produced but never verified or consumed – attestations alone give no security benefit (GitHub attestations docs); SBOMs generated only by post-hoc scans miss toolchain effects (CNCF).
- Pipelines that anyone can edit or bypass – unreviewed pipeline changes, administrators who modify running pipelines, projects that opt out of templates; the gates then guarantee nothing (CNCF).
- Static analysis with high false-positive rates or results shown outside the review flow – developers ignore the tool (Google ch. 20).
- Required checks and approvals that accumulate without review – slow merges, batching and "approve to unblock" behavior; DORA names heavy asynchronous review as a trunk-based-development pitfall.
- Multiple versions of the same dependency and transitive version drift – diamond dependency conflicts that are unsafe to change (Google ch. 16 and 18).
- A monorepo without monorepo tooling – every change rebuilds and retests everything and pipelines take hours; or a polyrepo without a shared-library strategy – a bug fix in a common library needs many sequenced pull requests (monorepo.tools; Google ch. 16).
- Cost optimization by running CI less often or skipping tests – larger batches, later feedback, more production failures; DORA's 2024 report stresses that small batches and robust testing remain essential even with AI assistance.

### Tailoring by project size

Essential at every scale: one version-controlled mainline that contains everything needed to build; a scripted one-command build; a self-testing build that runs on every push and pull request in a clean hosted environment; an immediate fix or revert of a broken mainline; pinned dependencies, tools and CI actions with least-privilege credentials; artifacts built once and traceable to a commit. What changes with scale is how many gates, how much supply-chain evidence and how much infrastructure the pipeline carries.

**Solo developer on a small repository.** Essential: use the hosted CI of the forge with a minimal pipeline as code. For GitHub Actions: trigger on push and pull_request; set permissions to contents: read; use concurrency with cancel-in-progress; steps: checkout, set up the language runtime with dependency caching (for example actions/setup-python with cache: pip), install, run the formatter or linter (for example ruff check), run the tests (for example pytest), optionally a small version matrix. Pin actions to a commit SHA and enable Dependabot for both packages and actions. Commit to main directly or through very short-lived branches. Keep the pipeline under ten minutes; with free minutes on public repositories cost is rarely an issue; on private ones watch macOS minutes. Optional: a light branch protection rule that requires the check (cheap); pre-commit hooks for format and lint if they stay fast; tagged releases with semantic versioning for anything that others depend on. Skip merge queues, SLSA L3, hermetic build systems and SBOM distribution unless the repository publishes packages or images – then add release signing or GitHub artifact attestations and an exported SBOM, which cost little. A minimal example:

```yaml
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<sha>
      - uses: actions/setup-python@<sha>
        with: { python-version: '3.12', cache: 'pip' }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: ruff check .
      - run: pytest
```

**Small product team.** Essential: work through short-lived branches with pull requests, required checks and review or code owners; protect main against force-push. Split the pipeline into a commit stage under ten minutes (unit tests, lint, SAST, secret scanning, SCA) and a later stage with integration and acceptance tests against containerized production-like environments, deployed with the same scripts used for production. Build each artifact once, publish it to a package or container registry with an immutable version, and promote it. Rotate a build-cop duty, post status to chat, and keep a quarantine list with deadlines for flaky tests. Use a hosted CI platform that signs provenance (SLSA Build L2 by default on GitHub; L3 with reusable workflows), generate an SBOM at build time and sign release artifacts with Sigstore or the platform's attestations. Automate dependency updates and pin everything. Measure duration, success rate, repair time and flakiness; fix creep before it becomes batching. Optional: a merge queue or merge trains, only once merges collide often; monorepo tooling with remote caching if the team keeps several deployables in one repository; hermetic build systems such as Bazel only if the codebase is multi-language and large.

**Large or regulated organization.** Essential: standardize pipelines as reviewed templates that projects cannot bypass, and allow pipeline changes only through pipeline-as-code; segregate duties so that no single person can both change the pipeline and attest a release (SLSA Source L4, CNCF four-eyes). Run builds on ephemeral, isolated, single-use workers with minimal network, secrets unreachable from build steps (SLSA Build L3), and retained audit logs. Archive each release with its provenance, SBOM and integrity data for forensics (NIST SSDF PS.3) and require verification of signatures and provenance before deployment. Make builds hermetic. Vendor or proxy all third-party material through an internal repository and scan it for vulnerabilities and licenses; distribute SBOM and VEX to customers and regulators. Keep the systems-engineering view where hardware or many suppliers are involved: a written integration plan with ordered aggregates, interface management and recorded integration results. Governance adds required reviews, evidence retention and traceability from requirement to commit to artifact, but the ten-minute commit stage, daily integration and revert-first discipline still apply – regulation is a reason for more automated evidence, not for slower integration. Optional, by assurance level and scale: verifiably reproducible builds for high-assurance products; investment in build infrastructure – an artifact-based build system or monorepo tooling with remote caching and execution, test-impact selection, automated culprit finding and rollback, merge queues or merge trains, flakiness tooling with automatic quarantine, and cost reporting per team.
