## 11. Release and deployment

### Purpose

In this phase, a verified build becomes a running service or a product in the hands of users. The phase also covers how the team decides when and how that happens. It answers four questions. What version do we ship? How does the version get from the repository to each environment and to the users? Who authorizes the release, and how do we recover when the release fails?

SWEBOK v4 defines a release as "distributing software and related artifacts outside the development activity, including internal releases and distribution to customers". It defines release management as "the identification, packaging and delivery of the elements of a product". The deployment pipeline, version schemes, changelogs, deployment strategies, change control, migrations, rollback and distribution channels are tools for one goal. That goal is to make releases low-risk, repeatable and routine. Humble and Farley state the goal as the ability to get "changes of all types ... into production, or into the hands of users, safely and quickly in a sustainable way".

### Other names

- Transition process (ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 technical process)
- Product Transition process (NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, section 5.5)
- Software Release Management and Delivery (SWEBOK v4, Software Configuration Management knowledge area, topic 6)
- Release engineering (Google SRE)
- Release and deployment management (ITIL v3); change enablement, release management and deployment management practices (ITIL 4)
- Continuous delivery (CD) and continuous deployment
- Deployment pipeline or delivery pipeline
- Safe deployment practices (SDP), progressive exposure, rollout, launch
- Shipping, go-live, cutover, installation and acceptance
- Software delivery performance (DORA)

### Position in the life cycle

Before this phase, integration, build and continuous integration produce a tested, versioned artifact (see section 10). After this phase, operations, observability and incident management run the released version (see section 12). Maintenance produces the next release (see section 13). Deprecation and retirement end the life of the release (see section 14).

In ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 the Transition process is one of 14 technical processes. It follows the Integration and Verification processes. It precedes Validation in the operational environment, Operation and Maintenance. The IEEE page notes that 12207-2017 is now superseded by a 2026 revision that is aligned with the 15288 process model. SWEBOK v4 places release management inside Software Configuration Management, next to the topics on the software build and the configuration audit. Section 15 covers the supporting processes.

In a waterfall or V-model project, release is a late phase that occurs mostly one time (see section 2 for the models). It contains installation, site preparation, the acceptance test, training and cutover, followed by periodic maintenance releases. NASA's Product Transition process shows this form: prepare, check the site readiness, package, deliver, install, confirm by acceptance test, and capture the records.

In Scrum and other iterative methods, every Sprint produces a usable Increment. The Scrum Guide says "An Increment may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint". It also says "The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value".

In DevOps and continuous delivery, release is a continuous process, not a phase. Each change flows through a deployment pipeline. Deployment (the move of a build to an environment) is decoupled from release (the step that makes a feature visible). The release decision becomes a business choice, made with feature flags or a push-button deploy.

ITIL 4 makes the same split. Deployment management moves components to live environments. Release management makes features available for use. Change enablement authorizes and schedules the changes.

### Inputs

- A build that passed continuous integration. The build is made once and stored as an immutable artifact with a unique identifier (commit hash, build number or version tag).
- The release scope and plan: the list of changes, the target version and the target date or train. Each item has met the Definition of Done.
- Everything needed to recreate each environment from version control: infrastructure code, deployment scripts, application and environment configuration, and dependency manifests.
- Database migration scripts, written for the expand and contract pattern, with a known record of the migrations that each environment has applied.
- A draft changelog or draft release notes, with deprecations and upgrade or installation instructions.
- A change record or change model when the organization requires one (standard, normal or emergency change), plus the approvals captured in the platform.
- Monitors, alerts and health checks that can tell a healthy rollout from a failed one, with agreed canary metrics.
- A tested rollback or roll-forward plan, with the previous release still available for redeploy.
- A launch or go-live checklist when the release is large or new: capacity, dependencies, failure modes, rollout plan and support readiness.
- Signing keys, publication credentials (preferably short-lived OIDC trusted publishing), store accounts, and the export-compliance and legal items for app stores.
- Facts about the target platform: supported versions in the field, upgrade paths (for example N-2), version skew limits and compatibility promises.

### Activities

The phase contains the activities below. Two tables after the list compare the deployment strategies and the release cadence examples.

- **Release plan and cadence** – Decide what goes into a release, when releases occur and who decides. SWEBOK v4 names "determining when to issue a release" as a core release-management concern. The severity of the problems fixed and the fault density of prior releases drive that decision. The options range from on-demand release of each change (continuous delivery) to fixed-cadence release trains. Chromium ships a milestone every four weeks, Rust every six weeks, Python every year and Django every eight months. SAFe plans by Planning Interval. The output is a release policy: cadence, train or on-demand, support and LTS windows, freeze rules and the release owner.
- **Version scheme and version identification** – Give every release an unambiguous identifier and a scheme that tells users what to expect. Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR changes for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward compatible functionality or deprecations, and PATCH for backward compatible fixes. A 0.y.z version means that anything can change. Pre-release tags (1.0.0-alpha) and build metadata (+sha) have defined precedence rules. CalVer (Ubuntu 24.04, pip YY.MINOR) suits projects with a "large or constantly-changing scope" or time-driven releases. A published version is never used again. npm states that a name and version combination "can never be used again, even if it is removed". The twelve-factor method calls the release history "an append-only ledger".
- **Release branch and tag** – Mark the exact source state that is released. Trunk-based development recommends a late, "just-in-time" release branch. The team makes bug fixes on trunk first and cherry-picks them to the release branch, never the reverse. Many teams can instead release from an annotated tag on trunk and create the branch later, only when a patch release is needed. Chromium branches each milestone from the daily canary build and accepts only merge requests after that point. Git annotated tags (`git tag -a`) carry the tagger, the date and a message, and can be signed. Push the tags explicitly. The output is a tag or a release branch that maps one version to one commit.
- **Build, package and attestation of the release artifact** – Build the binary or package once and promote that same artifact through every environment. The Google SRE book requires hermetic builds that are "insensitive to the libraries and other software installed on the build machine". The package step selects the correct variants of the product items for the intended platform. It produces installers, containers, wheels and archives, with checksums, a signature, a software bill of materials (SBOM) and build provenance. SWEBOK v4 names the SBOM "an important CM output" and names a digital signature as the integrity mechanism. SLSA Build L1–L3 grades how trustworthy the provenance is. Sigstore and `npm --provenance` give keyless signatures and public links to the build origin. Tools such as GoReleaser automate this step when a tag is pushed.
- **Changelog and release notes** – Record what changed, for humans. Keep a Changelog defines a changelog as "a curated, chronologically ordered list of notable changes for each version". The format groups the entries as Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security. The file has an Unreleased section, ISO 8601 dates and a [YANKED] mark for withdrawn releases. Keep a Changelog calls raw commit diffs and ignored deprecations bad practice. SWEBOK v4 says that release notes "describe new capabilities, known problems and platform requirements" and that the package contains installation or upgrade instructions. GitHub can generate release notes from merged pull requests with a `release.yml` template. Conventional Commits and semantic-release derive notes and version bumps from commit messages. The output is a CHANGELOG entry, a release-notes page and, for regulated products, a version description document (VDD).
- **Environment provision and promotion** – Define a sequence of environments (developer, test, staging or pre-production, production). Move the same artifact through them in order. The stages of the deployment pipeline give "increasing confidence, usually at the cost of extra time"; the early stages fail fast. Twelve-factor dev/prod parity keeps environments "as similar as possible". DORA's deployment automation capability asks for the same deployment process and the same packages for every environment. The state of any environment must be recreatable from version control. Infrastructure as code plus immutable or phoenix servers replace in-place changes with rebuilt images. This removes configuration drift and snowflake servers. GitHub Actions environments add protection rules: required reviewers, wait timers, branch or tag restrictions and environment-scoped secrets.
- **Configuration management for each release** – Keep configuration out of the artifact and under version control. Twelve-factor stores config in the environment and defines a release as build plus config, with a unique release ID that cannot be mutated. The SRE workbook treats configuration as a human-computer interface. It warns that a single configuration change can alter the behavior drastically. It requires gradual rollout, rollback and automatic rollback for configuration changes, and argues for fewer options. Humble and Farley's configuration management foundation requires that a team can "determine quickly and precisely the versions of every dependency used to create that environment". Feature-flag configuration is also configuration: prefer static, source-controlled flags, and use a central store only when dynamic changes are needed.
- **Pre-release verification and go-live criteria** – Check that the release candidate and the environment are ready before exposure. The checks include smoke tests after deployment, which confirm that the dependencies are reachable and the application runs. They also include acceptance tests, security and compliance scans and, for large launches, a launch checklist. Google's launch checklist covers architecture and dependencies, integration, capacity, failure modes, client behavior, processes and automation, the development process, external dependencies and rollout plans. The SRE Production Readiness Review verifies that a service meets "accepted standards of production setup and operational readiness". Google disciplined the checklist with one rule: every question must be substantiated by a previous launch disaster. The output is a go or no-go decision against written criteria.
- **Change authorization and release approval** – Decide who may authorize the change and record that decision. ITIL 4 change enablement exists to "maximize the number of successful service and product changes by properly assessing risks, authorizing changes to proceed, and managing the change schedule". It separates standard changes (pre-authorized, low risk, often automated), normal changes (assessed and authorized) and emergency changes. It states that not every change needs a change advisory board (CAB); the change authority can be a peer-review mechanism or an automated pipeline. DORA found "no evidence ... that a more formal, external review process was associated with lower change fail rates". DORA recommends peer review captured in the development platform, automated checks, and a CAB that coordinates rather than gates. In a small repository the approval is a reviewed pull request and a protected environment.
- **Deployment with a selected strategy** – Move the release into production with a strategy that matches the risk. Recreate or big bang stops the old version and then starts the new one; it causes downtime but "ensures no version mixing". Rolling update replaces instances gradually; Kubernetes controls it with maxSurge and maxUnavailable, readiness probes and a progress deadline. Blue-green runs two production environments and switches the router. It gives near-instant rollback but needs both versions to share one database schema. Canary releases deploy to a subset and ramp the traffic while the team watches the metrics. Dark launches call new code paths in production and do not show the results. Shadow traffic mirrors real requests to the new version as "fire and forget" copies. Feature flags separate deployment from release. A/B tests measure business outcomes, not regressions. Every strategy except big bang requires that two versions can run at the same time.
- **Database and data migrations** – Change schemas and data so that both the old and the new application version work during the rollout. Fowler's Parallel Change (expand, migrate, contract) is the base pattern. Evolutionary Database Design adds two rules. Every database change is a migration script under version control, with a changelog table. Destructive changes get a transition phase, for example a view that keeps the old name. GitLab's zero-downtime rules show the cost. A column drop takes three releases (ignore the column in code, drop it, remove the ignore). Indexes are added concurrently. Column renames use triggers to keep the data in sync. DORA found that teams strong at continuous delivery "store their database changes as scripts in version control and manage these changes in the same way they manage production application changes". Twelve-factor runs migrations as one-off admin processes against the same release.
- **Progressive exposure, canary evaluation and bake time** – Expose the change to more users only while the health signals stay good. The SRE workbook defines the canary process as "a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation". It lists three needs: a way to deploy to a subset, an evaluation method, and integration into the release pipeline. Choose few metrics that indicate user-facing problems and that are attributable to the change. Size the canary population and duration for statistical confidence. Do not run overlapping canaries. Azure's safe deployment practices add deployment rings with bake times "measured in hours and days rather than minutes". They add a health model that halts the rollout on any user-facing alert. App stores offer the same mechanism. Google Play has staged rollout percentages that the developer increases manually. The App Store has a phased release over seven days (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 percent). The developer can pause it for up to 30 days.
- **Feature flag life cycle** – Use flags to ship incomplete code dark, to ramp features, to switch operational behavior and to run experiments. Then remove them. Hodgson's taxonomy distinguishes release, experiment, ops and permissioning toggles by longevity and dynamism. Release toggles should live days to weeks. Decision points should be decoupled from logic, configuration should be source-controlled, and each flag needs an owner, a description and an expiry date. Teams should treat flags "as inventory" and keep the inventory low; the Knight Capital loss is the standard warning. Flags also multiply the test states, so test the combinations that will exist in production. The output is a flag registry and a cleanup task for each flag.
- **Rollback, roll-forward, hotfix and emergency release** – Prepare the recovery path before the change. Rollback redeploys the previous immutable release (twelve-factor), switches the router back (blue-green) or reroutes the users to the old version (canary). Kubernetes keeps a revision history for `kubectl rollout undo`. Roll-forward fixes the problem in a new release when rollback is impossible, for example after a contract-phase schema change. Azure's guidance lists rollback, roll-forward and redeploy of the last known good version, and warns that rollback of stateful changes is complex. Emergency releases follow a defined faster path with reduced bake time and accelerated approvals, but they still run the gates "as an out-of-band exercise". ITIL's emergency change and SWEBOK's "emergency path ... with change process performed afterward" say the same. Mobile apps cannot be rolled back on the device, so they need server-side kill switches and forced-update paths.
- **Publication and distribution to users and registries** – Deliver the artifact through the channel that the product uses. For services, the pipeline deploys to production. For libraries, publish to a package registry. `npm publish` supports dist-tags and `--provenance`. PyPI trusted publishing uses short-lived OIDC tokens instead of long-lived API tokens. Go modules need a `/v2` path suffix for major versions 2 and higher. For CLIs and desktop apps, use GitHub Releases with binaries and checksums, Homebrew taps and installers. Sign the code, notarize on macOS (sign, submit, staple), and supply an auto-update feed such as the Electron autoUpdater. For mobile apps, pass the store review and use the test tracks and the staged rollout. Google Play offers internal (up to 100 testers), closed, open and production tracks. For on-premises products, supply installers, upgrade guides and supported upgrade paths; Kubernetes supports three minor releases and a defined upgrade order. Supply LTS lines where needed; Node.js gives 30 months and Django LTS three years. GitHub protected repositories make published release tags and assets immutable.
- **Transition to operations and customers** – Hand the released version to the people who run and support it. For a service this means runbooks, alerts and on-call ownership; at Google, the SRE team accepts the service through a PRR or an early engagement. For a customer-installed product, the NASA transition process describes site readiness surveys, packages, delivery and installation. It continues with functional and acceptance tests, training, manuals and the capture of transition records. ITIL 4 puts the matching duties in deployment management and release management. It asks for a change schedule that the service desk and the users can see. The output: the service is operable by its operators and usable by its users, with documented installation, operation and support.
- **Release communication and records** – Tell the affected people what changed and keep the evidence. Publish the release notes, update the documentation and the status pages, announce the release to users and internal teams, and notify customers of deprecations. PEP 101 ends every Python release with announcements and updates to the release PEP. GOV.UK requires auditable deployments: "know which version of your service is running in each environment at all times" and trace changes back to commits. Regulated organizations keep the change record, approvals, test evidence, SBOM, provenance and deployment log as a compliance trail. SWEBOK v4 notes that release management may track distribution to customers, so that they can be notified of newly reported problems.
- **Post-release verification and release closure** – Confirm that the release is healthy and complete the records. Watch the health model through the bake time and run post-deployment smoke tests. Confirm the change record as successful or failed; this feeds the change failure rate. Remove completed feature flags, delete finished release branches, move fixed issues to done, and record lessons from any incident in a blameless postmortem. DORA counts a deployment that needs a hotfix, rollback or patch as a failed change. DORA counts the unplanned deployment that fixes a user-facing bug as rework. The output is a closed release with metrics, cleanup done and the next release unblocked.
- **Deprecation policy and support life cycle** – Retire features and versions on a published schedule. SemVer requires a deprecation to appear in the documentation and in a minor release before the removal in a major release. Keep a Changelog has a Deprecated section. The Kubernetes policy gives concrete rules. GA APIs are not removed within a major version. Beta APIs get at least nine months or three releases. Deprecated CLI elements must emit warnings. The Kubernetes API server returns a Warning header and a metric for deprecated calls. RFC 9745 (Deprecation header) and RFC 8594 (Sunset header) let HTTP APIs announce dates in-band. Django removes a deprecated feature only after two feature releases. Microsoft's Modern Lifecycle Policy gives 30 days notice for required actions and 12 months notice before the end of support. The output is a written deprecation policy, a support matrix and deprecation notices in releases.
- **Measurement and improvement of the release process** – Treat the release process as a product. Track DORA's five software delivery metrics: deployment frequency, change lead time, change failure rate, failed deployment recovery time and rework rate. Also track the share of changes that need manual approval and the wait time for approval. Count the manual steps in a deployment and the time that code waits in the pipeline. Model the current delivery process as a pipeline and look for bottlenecks and automation opportunities. Review the launch checklists yearly and remove stale items. Hold blameless postmortems for failed releases. Humble and Farley warn against treatment of continuous delivery as an end state. DORA warns against metrics used as targets and against rankings between teams.

The deployment strategies compare as follows.

| Strategy | Mechanism | Strength | Cost or condition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Recreate (big bang) | Stop the old version, then start the new one | No mixed versions; simple | Downtime; rollback is all-or-nothing; the only option when versions cannot coexist |
| Rolling update | Replace instances gradually (Kubernetes maxSurge, maxUnavailable, readiness probes, progress deadline) | Cheap; built into orchestrators; revision history for undo | Less control; all users see the change gradually; two versions coexist |
| Blue-green | Run two production environments and switch the router | Near-instant switch and rollback | Double infrastructure; one shared database schema; missed transactions at cutover |
| Canary release | Deploy to a subset, ramp the traffic, watch the metrics | Real-load evidence; exposure limited to a cohort | Needs metrics, a traffic split and version coexistence; does not work on client-side binaries |
| Dark launch | Call new code paths in production and hide the results | Tests new code under real load without user impact | Needs a flag or a request route to hide the results |
| Shadow traffic | Mirror real requests to the new version as "fire and forget" copies (Istio mirroring) | No user impact; real request mix | Extra capacity; the mirrored responses are discarded |
| Feature flags | Deploy the code dark, release by a flag switch | Separates deployment from release; kill switch | Flag inventory and test combinations |
| A/B test | Split users between variants and compare business outcomes | Measures business results | Not a regression test; needs analysis |

The release cadence and support examples from the record compare as follows.

| Project or policy | Cadence | Support and deprecation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chromium | Milestone every four weeks, branched from the daily canary build; weekly stable refresh; canary, dev, beta and stable channels | Extended stable line; merge requests only after the branch point |
| Rust | Six-week release train; nightly, beta and stable channels; unstable features behind feature flags on nightly | "Stability without stagnation" |
| Python | Annual release (PEP 602) with 17-month development phases; PEP 101 release checklist | Five years of support per release |
| Django | Feature release every eight months; patch releases in between | LTS for three years; a deprecated feature is removed after two feature releases |
| Node.js | Current, Active LTS and Maintenance phases | 30 months of support per LTS line |
| Kubernetes | Three minor releases supported at one time; patch cadence per line | Version skew policy and defined upgrade order; GA APIs kept within a major version, beta APIs nine months or three releases |
| SAFe Agile Release Train | Cadence and synchronization through Planning Intervals; Release Train Engineer | n/a |
| Microsoft Modern Lifecycle Policy | Continuous servicing | 30 days notice for a required action; 12 months notice before the end of support |

### Outputs

- The new version runs in production, or the new package, app or installer version is available to users. It is traceable to one commit and one immutable artifact.
- A tag or release branch, a version number that follows the declared scheme, and a GitHub or GitLab release object where applicable.
- Artifacts in a registry with checksums, signatures, SBOM and build provenance; pre-release, latest and LTS channels set.
- An updated CHANGELOG and published release notes, with deprecations, known problems, platform requirements and installation or upgrade instructions.
- A deployment record: who deployed what, where and when, with approvals and test evidence. The change record is closed as successful, failed or rolled back.
- Environments updated from version-controlled definitions and configuration; the previous release kept available as the rollback point.
- Health confirmed after the bake time: canary metrics within thresholds, smoke tests green, no user-facing alerts; or a rollback or roll-forward completed.
- Database migrations applied and recorded, with expand phases live and contract phases scheduled.
- Operations handover complete: runbooks, alerts, on-call ownership, customer support briefed, and training delivered for customer-installed systems.
- Announcements sent, documentation and status page updated, deprecation notices issued.
- Metrics recorded (deployment frequency, lead time, failure, recovery, rework), feature flags cleaned up or scheduled for removal, lessons captured.
- Exit criterion: the release is in use, observable, recoverable and recorded; for a cadence-driven product, the next train is open.

### Roles

- **Developer** – makes the change deployable, writes the migration scripts and the release-notes lines, and guards unfinished work with flags. The developer reviews the changes of peers; the peer review is the approval in DORA's model. The developer owns the change through production ("you build it, you run it").
- **Release engineer or release manager** – defines and automates the steps from source to deployment (Google SRE). The role owns the pipeline and the packages, runs the release checklist and coordinates the experts. PEP 101 names a Release Manager plus Windows and macOS experts. In SAFe this role is the Release Train Engineer.
- **Site reliability engineer or operations** – runs the canary evaluation, the health models, rollback, capacity and incident response. The role performs production readiness reviews and may co-own the release process.
- **Platform or DevOps team** – provides the deployment pipeline, the environments, infrastructure as code, the flag service and observability as a self-service product.
- **Product owner or product manager** – decides what to release and when to make a feature visible. The role owns the release scope, the deprecation communication and the customer-facing notes.
- **Change authority (ITIL 4)** – a delegated person, team, peer-review mechanism or automated rule that authorizes normal and emergency changes. The change advisory board, where it exists, coordinates and improves the process; it is not a gate for every change.
- **Quality and test engineers** – maintain the automated gates, the acceptance and smoke tests, and the test evidence attached to the release.
- **Database administrators** – review schema changes and advise on online migrations and performance. DORA notes that collaboration between developers and DBAs is a delivery performance factor.
- **Security and compliance** – signatures, provenance, SBOM, vulnerability checks, the audit trail and regulatory evidence; export compliance for app stores.
- **Technical writer and support** – release notes, upgrade guides, documentation, customer notifications and support readiness.
- **Launch coordination engineer (Google) or launch manager** – audits large launches against the checklist and mediates between teams.
- **External gatekeepers** – app store reviewers, the change windows of enterprise customers, and package registry policies.

### Practices with consensus

- **Release small changes often and keep the software deployable at all times** – Small batches reduce the number of changes between versions. They make faults easier to find and revert, and they give the users and the team faster feedback. Heavyweight, infrequent releases raise the risk; they do not lower it. Evidence: Google SRE Book: Release Engineering ("Frequent releases result in fewer changes between versions"); Martin Fowler: ContinuousDelivery; DORA: Working in small batches; DORA: Continuous delivery; GOV.UK Service Manual: Deploying software regularly; Azure Well-Architected Framework: safe deployment practices; Software Engineering at Google, ch. 24 ("faster is safer").
- **Build once, then promote the same immutable artifact through every environment with the same automated process** – A rebuild per environment or a manual deployment means that the tested item is not the shipped item. One artifact plus one script per environment gives repeatability and an audit trail. Evidence: Martin Fowler: DeploymentPipeline; continuousdelivery.com: Patterns; DORA: Deployment automation; The Twelve-Factor App: Build, release, run; Google SRE Book: Release Engineering (hermetic builds); SWEBOK Guide v4.0 (software building).
- **Keep everything needed to recreate an environment in version control: infrastructure, deployment scripts, configuration, dependencies and migrations** – Environments become reproducible and auditable, drift disappears, and disaster recovery and compliance become mechanical. Evidence: continuousdelivery.com: Configuration management; Martin Fowler: InfrastructureAsCode; Martin Fowler: ImmutableServer; DORA: Deployment automation; AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar: Deploy using immutable infrastructure; GOV.UK Service Manual.
- **Separate configuration from the build and give each release a unique, immutable identity** – The same artifact must run in every environment. Config in the environment and an append-only release ledger make rollback a redeploy of a known release. Evidence: The Twelve-Factor App (Config); The Twelve-Factor App: Build, release, run; Google SRE Workbook: Configuration Design and Best Practices; Martin Fowler: Feature Toggles (source-controlled toggle configuration).
- **Use a declared version scheme and never reuse or mutate a published version** – Users, package managers and dependency resolvers rely on the contract: SemVer for libraries and APIs, CalVer for time-driven products. Registries enforce immutability for the same reason. Evidence: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0; Calendar Versioning (CalVer); Go modules: Module version numbering; npm Docs: npm publish; GitHub CLI manual: gh release create (immutability note); Pro Git: Git Basics – Tagging.
- **Keep a curated, human-readable changelog and release notes that state deprecations and upgrade steps** – Users cannot act on commit dumps. SWEBOK, Keep a Changelog and SemVer all require a deprecation notice before removal. Evidence: Keep a Changelog 1.1.0; SWEBOK Guide v4.0 (release notes and VDD); Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (deprecation guidance); GitHub Docs: Automatically generated release notes.
- **Decouple deployment from release with feature flags, dark launches and progressive exposure** – Code can reach production continuously while the business decides when users see a feature. Unfinished work ships dark. The risk is limited to a cohort. Evidence: Martin Fowler: Feature Toggles; Martin Fowler: DarkLaunching; Martin Fowler: CanaryRelease; continuousdelivery.com: Patterns; Google SRE Book: Reliable Product Launches at Scale (feature flag frameworks); Software Engineering at Google, ch. 24; ITSM Professor: ITIL 4 release management versus deployment management.
- **Roll out gradually, watch a small set of user-facing metrics, and stop or roll back automatically on bad signals** – Production load and data differ from any staging environment. A time-limited canary with a defined evaluation catches regressions before they reach everyone. Evidence: Google SRE Workbook: Canarying Releases; Google SRE Book: Reliable Product Launches at Scale; Azure Well-Architected Framework: safe deployment practices; AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar: Deploy using immutable infrastructure (automated rollback); Martin Fowler: CanaryRelease; Google Play Console Help: staged rollouts; App Store Connect Help: phased release.
- **Make database changes backward compatible and run them as versioned migrations (expand, migrate, contract)** – Blue-green, canary and rolling deployments require two application versions to share one schema. Irreversible schema changes make rollback impossible. Evidence: Martin Fowler: ParallelChange; Martin Fowler and Pramod Sadalage: Evolutionary Database Design; GitLab Docs: Avoiding downtime in migrations; DORA: Database change management; Martin Fowler: BlueGreenDeployment.
- **Have a rehearsed recovery path, rollback to the previous release or a fast roll-forward, before every production change** – Failures will occur. Recovery time, not the absence of failure, distinguishes good delivery. Rollback is cheap only when releases are immutable and schemas are compatible. Evidence: The Twelve-Factor App: Build, release, run; Kubernetes Docs: Deployments (rollout undo); Azure Well-Architected Framework: safe deployment practices (rollback, roll-forward, redeploy); Martin Fowler: BlueGreenDeployment; Martin Fowler: CanaryRelease; DORA: the four keys (failed deployment recovery time).
- **Authorize changes through peer review and automated checks recorded in the delivery platform, and reserve heavyweight external approval for genuinely high-risk changes** – DORA found that external approval boards slow delivery without a lower change failure rate. ITIL 4 itself moved to standard (pre-authorized) changes and a decentralized change authority. Captured peer review satisfies segregation of duties. Evidence: DORA: Streamlining change approval; Accelerate; ITIL 4 change enablement (AWS Well-Architected and itsm.tools summaries); GitHub Docs: Using environments for deployment (protection rules).
- **Deploy during business hours with zero-downtime techniques** – If a deployment needs a maintenance window or night work, the process is not yet safe. Zero-downtime patterns make deploys routine and keep the responders available. Evidence: DORA: Continuous delivery ("nobody has to work outside of regular business hours"); GOV.UK Service Manual: Deploying software regularly (zero-downtime deployments); continuousdelivery.com: Patterns (blue-green).
- **Sign artifacts, publish provenance and use short-lived publication credentials** – A release is also a supply-chain event. Signatures and provenance let consumers verify the origin. Short-lived tokens limit the damage from a leaked credential. Evidence: SLSA v1.0: Build track levels; Sigstore: Overview; PyPI Docs: Trusted Publishers; npm Docs: npm publish (--provenance); SWEBOK Guide v4.0 (digital signature, SBOM); Apple Developer: Notarizing macOS software before distribution.
- **Use a written go-live or launch checklist for large or new launches, and keep it short and evidence-based** – Checklists stop repeated launch mistakes. Unbounded checklists become bureaucracy, so each item needs a concrete past failure behind it. Evidence: Google SRE Book: Reliable Product Launches at Scale; Google SRE Book: The Evolving SRE Engagement Model (Production Readiness Review); PEP 101 (release checklist); NASA Systems Engineering Handbook 5.5 Product Transition.
- **Publish a deprecation and support policy and honor it in every release** – Users plan their upgrades around the policy. Abrupt removals break integrations and erode trust. Evidence: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0; Kubernetes Deprecation Policy; Django's release process; Microsoft Modern Lifecycle Policy; RFC 9745 and RFC 8594; Keep a Changelog 1.1.0.
- **Measure delivery with DORA's metrics to learn, not to rank teams** – Throughput and stability move together in high performers. The metrics show where the pipeline hurts, but they become manipulated when used as targets or as comparisons between teams. Evidence: DORA: the four keys guide; Accelerate; DORA 2023 and 2024 reports.

### Contested points

- **Continuous deployment versus continuous delivery** – In continuous deployment, every green change goes to production automatically. In continuous delivery, a human chooses when. Fowler, Humble and DORA define continuous delivery as the ability to deploy on demand and treat automatic deployment as an optional extra step. Continuous deployment suits web services with strong automated tests and observability. It does not fit app-store apps, on-premises products, or safety-critical or contract-driven releases where a human or an external gate is required. The choice depends on the product type, the size of the possible damage, regulation and test confidence.
- **Change advisory boards and external approvals versus peer review inside the pipeline** – ITIL 4 keeps a change authority and a CAB for normal and emergency changes. It also accepts pre-authorized standard changes and a decentralized authority. DORA's research found no stability benefit from external approvals. DORA recommends peer review plus automation, with the CAB as coordinator. Regulated organizations still need segregation of duties and audit evidence. The contest is about how that evidence is produced, not about whether it exists.
- **Fixed-cadence release trains versus on-demand release** – Chromium, Rust, Python and Django use calendar trains. SAFe builds a whole operating model on cadence. Software Engineering at Google argues that trains enforce trade-offs ("no binary is perfect", "meet your release deadline"). Continuous delivery advocates prefer to release each change when it is ready. Trains fit products with many teams, platform partners, distributors or store reviews. On-demand release fits single services with independent deploys. Many organizations do both: they develop on a cadence and release on demand.
- **SemVer versus CalVer, and who picks the number** – SemVer is the default for libraries and APIs; Go enforces it with `/v2` paths. CalVer fits operating systems and large, time-driven products. Stripe uses date-named API versions, pins each account to a version, and says "Versioning is always a compromise". semantic-release and Conventional Commits remove human judgment from the version bump. Critics note that commit metadata does not prove compatibility. SemVer's own FAQ pushes projects to 1.0.0 once they are in production, yet many projects stay at 0.x.
- **Rollback versus roll-forward as the default recovery** – Rollback is fastest when releases are immutable and data-compatible (twelve-factor, blue-green, Kubernetes undo). Some teams prefer roll-forward (a hotfix) because rollback of schemas, queues and caches is unreliable, and because a rolled-back fix still has to ship. Azure lists both, plus the redeploy of the last known good version. The answer depends on whether the release included contract-phase data changes, and on how fast the pipeline can ship a fix.
- **How many environments, and how much to trust staging** – Twelve-factor and DORA ask for production-like environments and the same process everywhere. Fowler's canary and dark launch articles argue that production itself is the only faithful test environment. Progressive exposure can then reduce the dependence on staging. Staging is expensive to keep identical; too many environments slow the promotion. Small teams often use ephemeral preview environments plus canaries instead of a permanent staging stack.
- **Blue-green versus canary versus rolling** – Blue-green gives an instant switch and rollback but doubles the infrastructure and has the "missed transactions" problem during cutover. Canary gives real-load evidence but needs metrics, traffic splits and version coexistence. Rolling is cheap and built into orchestrators, but it exposes all users gradually with less control. Recreate or big bang is still correct when versions cannot coexist, or for very small systems. The choice depends on statefulness, traffic volume, tools and the tolerance for mixed versions.
- **Feature flags: a practice that enables, or a generator of debt** – Flags enable trunk-based development, dark launches and kill switches; Google and DORA treat them as core. Hodgson and the Knight Capital case show the cost: combinatorial test states, stale flags and accidental reuse. Teams disagree on whether to use a vendor flag service or static configuration, and on how strict the expiry should be.
- **Release branches versus releases from trunk tags** – trunkbaseddevelopment.com prefers late, short-lived release branches with fixes cherry-picked from trunk. It calls a release from a trunk tag a "decent optimization". Products that must support several versions (Chromium extended stable, Django LTS, Kubernetes three minor lines) need long-lived release branches and backport policies. Teams that deploy one service continuously need neither.
- **Curated changelog versus generated release notes** – Keep a Changelog rejects commit-log dumps and wants human-curated entries. GitHub generates notes from pull requests, and semantic-release generates them from commit messages. Generated notes scale and are consistent; curated notes serve users better. Many projects generate a draft and then edit it.
- **Deprecation periods** – There is no common number. SemVer requires only a minor release that contains the deprecation. Kubernetes gives GA APIs the whole major version, and beta APIs nine months or three releases. Django removes after two feature releases. Microsoft promises 12 months before the end of support. The correct period depends on how fast the users can upgrade (clients of a web service versus on-premises enterprise installations).
- **Mobile staged rollout controls** – Apple automates a seven-day percentage ramp that the developer can pause. Google Play requires the developer to raise the percentage manually, and the developer can halt the rollout. Neither lets the developer roll back the binary on the devices. Teams therefore argue between server-side kill switches, forced-update minimum versions and slower ramps.
- **Weight of throughput against stability in the DORA clusters** – In 2024 the medium cluster had a lower change failure rate than the high cluster. DORA still ranked the faster, less stable group as higher. Some practitioners read this as proof that the metrics can diverge and that cluster labels should not drive decisions. DORA still states that elite performers achieve both.
- **Emergency releases: bypass the gates or compress them** – ITIL has an emergency change type with expedited authority. SWEBOK shows an emergency path with the change process completed afterwards. Azure says that the gates should still run "as quickly as possible as an out-of-band exercise". Organizations differ on how much evidence can be collected after the fact.

### Metrics

- **Deployment frequency** – how often the team deploys code to production or releases it to end users (DORA throughput). Caveat: count the deployments of one application, not an aggregate across teams. A monorepo or a library has a different natural rate than a service.
- **Lead time for changes** – the time from commit to code that runs in production (DORA throughput). Caveat: define the start (first commit or merge) and keep it stable. Long waits for approval show up here.
- **Change failure rate** – the share of deployments that cause a failure that needs a hotfix, rollback or patch (DORA stability). Caveat: the value depends on an honest definition of failure and on a record of the rollbacks. Survey-based values differ from system-derived values.
- **Failed deployment recovery time** (formerly time to restore) – the time to recover from a failed deployment (DORA stability). Caveat: DORA narrowed this metric from all incidents to deployment-caused incidents in 2023. Measure consistently from detection or from the deploy.
- **Rework rate** – the share of deployments that were unplanned and made to fix a user-facing bug (DORA 2024, the fifth metric). Caveat: the metric is survey-defined and correlates with the change failure rate.
- **DORA 2024 cluster thresholds**, as summarized by secondary sources – elite: deploy on demand, lead time under one day, change failure rate about 5 percent, recovery under one hour. High: daily to weekly deploys, one to seven days lead time, about 10 percent, recovery under one day. Between 2023 and 2024 the high cluster shrank from 31 percent to 22 percent of respondents. The low cluster grew from 17 percent to 25 percent. Caveat: DORA warns against the use of the levels as targets or rankings (Goodhart's law).
- **Change approval metrics (DORA)** – the percentage of changes that require manual approval, the time spent in wait for approval, and whether the teams understand the approval process. Caveat: a low approval count only helps when automated checks and peer review replace the manual gate.
- **Deployment automation metrics (DORA)** – the number of manual steps per deployment, the percentage of the pipeline that is automated, and the time that code waits between stages. Caveat: a deliberate manual release decision is a wait, not a defect; count it separately from manual work.
- **Release process health** – deployment duration, pipeline duration, the number of rollbacks and hotfixes, and out-of-hours deployments (target zero per DORA and GOV.UK). Also release train adherence (milestones shipped on the date) and the size of the change set per release. Caveat: these are process indicators; read them together with the DORA outcome metrics.
- **Progressive exposure metrics** – canary error rate, latency and saturation versus the control; the time spent in each ring; the percentage of rollouts halted automatically. Caveat: each additional canary metric adds less value (SRE workbook).
- **Feature flag inventory** – the number of active flags, the age of release flags, and the flags past their expiry (Hodgson). Caveat: the inventory is only complete when every flag is registered with an owner and an expiry date.
- **Distribution and adoption** – the percentage of users or installations on the latest and on supported versions (app stores, on-premises, libraries), and the upgrade success rate. Also the time for a security fix to reach users and the number of supported release lines. Caveat: stores, registries and telemetry each cover only part of the user base.
- **Supply-chain posture** – the share of releases with signatures, SBOM and SLSA-level provenance; the use of trusted publishing instead of long-lived tokens. Caveat: a signature proves the origin, not the absence of vulnerabilities.
- **Lagging outcome signals** – incidents attributable to releases, customer-reported regressions, and the support load after a release. Caveat: the attribution is often unclear.

### Failure modes

- **Big-bang releases after long freezes** – the risk accumulates, the diagnosis is hard, and rollback is all-or-nothing (SRE, DORA, GOV.UK, Azure SDP).
- **Small changes regrouped into a large batch before release or test** – this defeats small-batch work (DORA small batches pitfall).
- **Manual, undocumented deployments and hand-edited servers** – they create snowflake servers, configuration drift and unreproducible environments (Fowler Immutable Server and Infrastructure as Code; DORA deployment automation).
- **A different deployment process or a rebuilt artifact per environment** – the tested item is not the shipped item (Fowler Deployment Pipeline; DORA).
- **Staging that does not resemble production** – problems appear only in production (twelve-factor dev/prod parity).
- **Secrets and environment-specific configuration baked into artifacts, or configuration changes pushed to all instances at once without rollback** – one bad value reaches every instance and cannot be undone quickly (twelve-factor; SRE workbook configuration).
- **Heavyweight external approval boards as the main safety control** – slower, larger releases with no measured stability gain; the approvals become a formality (DORA streamlining change approval).
- **Schema changes that are not backward compatible or are coupled to the application deploy** – rollback becomes impossible and zero-downtime deploys fail (GitLab migrations; Fowler Parallel Change; DORA database change management).
- **No rehearsed rollback or roll-forward path** – the team discovers during an incident that rollback of stateful components is impossible (Azure SDP; twelve-factor).
- **Canaries without defined metrics, too short, with too many metrics, or several at the same time** – the evaluation says nothing (SRE workbook canary guidance).
- **Feature flag debt** – stale flags, accidental reuse of flag names and untested flag combinations; the Knight Capital loss is the canonical example (Hodgson).
- **Bugs fixed directly on a release branch with trunk forgotten, or long-lived release branches that drift** – the fix is lost from the next release, or the branches diverge (trunkbaseddevelopment.com).
- **Version and tag errors** – a reused version number, lightweight or unpushed tags, a bump with no changelog, 0.x in production, or a republish after a yank. Users and tools lose the version contract (SemVer, Keep a Changelog, npm, Git).
- **Release notes that are commit dumps, omit deprecations or use ambiguous dates** – users cannot act on them (Keep a Changelog).
- **Removal of features or APIs without the published deprecation period, or with no warnings emitted** – integrations break without notice (Kubernetes policy, SemVer, RFC 9745).
- **Unsigned artifacts, long-lived publish tokens in CI, no provenance** – a compromised token becomes a supply-chain incident (PyPI trusted publishers, SLSA, Sigstore).
- **Out-of-hours deployments and maintenance windows treated as normal** – a sign that the process is not safe, and the responders are tired (DORA continuous delivery; GOV.UK).
- **Launch checklists that grow without evidence or are never pruned** – the teams skip them (SRE Reliable Product Launches).
- **Mobile releases without a server-side kill switch or a minimum-version path, and backend changes that break old clients still in the field** – the binary cannot be recalled from the devices (Fowler Canary Release on client-side software; App Store and Play staged rollout limits).
- **Emergency changes that bypass all gates and never complete the record, or emergency paths so slow that teams avoid them** – either the evidence is lost or the path goes unused (ITIL emergency change; Azure emergency SDP protocols).
- **DORA levels used as targets or as team rankings** – this produces manipulation of the numbers instead of improvement (DORA four keys guide).
- **Continuous delivery treated as a tool purchase or an end state** – the process does not improve further (continuousdelivery.com implementing).

### Tailoring by project size

Some items are essential at every scale:

- Everything needed to build and deploy is in version control.
- The artifact is built once and deployed by a script, not by hand.
- Each release has a unique version and a tag.
- Configuration and secrets live outside the artifact.
- The team always knows which version runs where.
- The team can return to the previous release.
- A changelog or release notes exist.
- Small changes ship often.

Other items are optional and scaled by risk: the number of environments, canary and flag tools, formal approvals, launch checklists, the depth of signatures and provenance, LTS lines and deprecation windows. The table shows how the phase scales.

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solo developer on a small repository | Select SemVer (or CalVer for a time-driven tool) and state it in the README. Create annotated tags and push them. Let CI build, test and publish on a tag (GoReleaser, `npm publish --provenance`, PyPI trusted publishing), so that no long-lived token sits on a laptop. Use GitHub Releases with generated notes plus a short hand-written summary, and a CHANGELOG with an Unreleased section. Keep one deploy command or workflow for the service, with config in environment variables. Back up before migrations and write migrations as expand-first scripts. Roll back by a redeploy of the previous release or a revert of the commit. For desktop or CLI apps, sign the code and, on macOS, notarize. For mobile apps, use the store test tracks and the staged rollout, and build a remote kill switch early. | A permanent staging environment (skip it unless the product needs it; use preview deployments and a quick production smoke test instead). CABs and release trains (skip them). Feature flags only when a change is too big for one pull request. |
| Small team | Add a deployment pipeline with stages (CI, test or staging, production) and protected environments whose required reviewer is the peer reviewer, so that approval and segregation of duties are in the platform. Use rolling or blue-green deploys from the hosting platform and a simple canary (internal users first) with two or three agreed health metrics. Adopt expand and contract migrations as a team rule. Keep a flag registry with owners and expiry dates. Write release notes per version and deprecation notices with a fixed window. Track the DORA metrics lightly from the pipeline and discuss them in retrospectives. Deploy in business hours. Agree a release owner rotation and a written rollback procedure. For libraries, publish semantic versions with a support statement. For mobile apps, keep a release train aligned to the store review times. | A permanent staging stack instead of preview environments; a vendor flag service instead of static configuration; a launch checklist for a new service; SBOM publication and SLSA L3 provenance; LTS lines; formal change records beyond the reviewed pull request. |
| Large or regulated organization | Formalize ITIL-style change enablement: pipeline-driven deployments registered as pre-authorized standard changes, normal changes for risky work, and an emergency model with post-hoc review. Keep an audit trail from commit to production (who, what, when, approvals, tests, SBOM, provenance, signatures at SLSA L3). Let the CAB coordinate schedules and improve the process; it must not be a gate on each deploy. Run progressive exposure with rings, bake times and automated rollback across regions. Require production readiness or launch reviews for new services and prune the checklist yearly. Run release trains or a release calendar across many teams with a release manager or RTE, extended or LTS lines for enterprise customers, published support matrices, version skew and upgrade-path rules, and contractual deprecation periods. Separate release management (features made available) from deployment management (builds moved), as ITIL 4 does. Fund a platform team so that all of this is self-service. Measure the approval wait time and the manual steps so that the controls do not silently slow delivery. | The number of rings and regions in the rollout; a launch coordination role for the largest launches; the length of extended support lines beyond the standard window; on-demand release for single services that do not depend on the train; a vendor flag service or an in-house one. |

### Sources

- [Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/) – Primary specification for MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, pre-release and build metadata, 0.y.z, deprecation and the 1.0.0 guidance.
- [Keep a Changelog 1.1.0](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/) – Changelog principles, change types, the Unreleased section, bad practices and yanked releases.
- [Calendar Versioning (CalVer)](https://calver.org/) – CalVer scheme components, when to use it, and example projects.
- [Conventional Commits 1.0.0](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) – Commit message convention mapped to SemVer bumps and generated changelogs.
- [semantic-release (GitHub README)](https://github.com/semantic-release/semantic-release) – Automated version determination, notes, tags and publish; the philosophy of removal of human version decisions.
- [Go modules: Module version numbering](https://go.dev/doc/modules/version-numbers) – SemVer semantics in Go, the meaning of v0 and v1, and the /v2 module path rule.
- [Stripe: APIs as infrastructure – future-proofing Stripe with versioning](https://stripe.com/blog/api-versioning) – Date-based API versions, per-account pins, version change modules and trade-offs.
- [Martin Fowler: Feature Toggles (Pete Hodgson)](https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html) – Toggle categories, longevity, implementation, configuration, the toggle inventory and the Knight Capital warning.
- [Martin Fowler: BlueGreenDeployment](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BlueGreenDeployment.html) – Mechanism, rollback, database handling and the missed-transactions caveat.
- [Martin Fowler: CanaryRelease](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CanaryRelease.html) – Mechanism, benefits, rollback, multiple versions, the difference from A/B tests and the client-side caveat.
- [Martin Fowler: DarkLaunching](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/DarkLaunching.html) – Dark launches, shadow execution of new code, and the relation to flags and canaries.
- [Martin Fowler: ContinuousDelivery](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ContinuousDelivery.html) – Definition, the four conditions, and continuous delivery versus continuous deployment.
- [Martin Fowler: DeploymentPipeline](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/DeploymentPipeline.html) – Pipeline stages, build once, fast feedback first, and manual authorization stages.
- [Martin Fowler: ParallelChange](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ParallelChange.html) – The expand, migrate, contract pattern for interfaces and schemas.
- [Martin Fowler and Pramod Sadalage: Evolutionary Database Design](https://martinfowler.com/articles/evodb.html) – Migrations under version control, the transition phase, frequent releases and parallel change for databases.
- [Martin Fowler: ImmutableServer](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ImmutableServer.html) – Immutable and phoenix servers, configuration drift and snowflake servers.
- [Martin Fowler: InfrastructureAsCode](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/InfrastructureAsCode.html) – Definition, practices (definition files, version everything, continuous tests, small changes) and benefits.

- [Google SRE Book: The Evolving SRE Engagement Model](https://sre.google/sre-book/evolving-sre-engagement-model/) – Production Readiness Review purpose, checks and phases; early engagement.

- [Google SRE Workbook: Configuration Design and Best Practices](https://sre.google/workbook/configuration-design/) – Configuration as an interface, the risks of config changes, gradual rollout and rollback of config, and fewer options.
