- [IEEE SA: IEEE/ISO/IEC 12207-2017](https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/12207/5672/) – Abstract and scope of 12207:2017; the note that a 2026 revision supersedes it.
- [Wikipedia: ISO/IEC 12207](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO/IEC_12207) – A map of the 12207:2017 process groups and the 14 technical processes including Transition; the 2026 alignment with 15288.
- [arc42 quality model: ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207](https://quality.arc42.org/standards/iso12207) – A summary of the process groups; used as a secondary map only.
- [NASA Systems Engineering Handbook 5.5 Product Transition](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/5-5-product-transition/) – The transition process purpose, inputs, activities (readiness, site, packages, delivery, installation, acceptance) and outputs; integration versus end-user delivery.
- [SWEBOK Guide v4.0 (IEEE Computer Society PDF)](https://ieeecs-media.computer.org/media/education/swebok/swebok-v4.pdf) – Software Configuration Management KA topic 6, Software Release Management and Delivery (software build, release management, VDD, release notes, SBOM, digital signature, CD pipeline); the definitions of continuous delivery and continuous deployment in the Operations and Maintenance KAs. Read from the PDF with pdftotext.
- [RFC 9745: The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9745.html) – Deprecation header semantics and the relation to the Sunset header (RFC 8594).
- [Microsoft Lifecycle: Modern Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/lifecycle/policies/modern) – Continuous servicing, 30 days notice for a required action, and 12 months notice before the end of support.
- [Release It! Second Edition (Pragmatic Bookshelf page)](https://pragprog.com/titles/mnee2/release-it-second-edition/) – Book overview: production-first design, stability patterns, zero-downtime deployments and continuous delivery.

## 12. Operations, observability and incident management

### Purpose

Operations keeps a released system in service for its users, at the agreed level of service, for the whole production life of the system. SWEBOK v4 defines software engineering operations as the activities and tasks that deploy, operate and support a software system and keep its integrity and stability.

The phase answers five questions. Is the service healthy now? How do we know before the users tell us? What do we do when the service is not healthy? How do we recover data and capacity after a disaster? How do we learn from a failure so that the next failure is smaller?

Each part of the phase answers one of these questions. Observability and monitoring supply the evidence. Alerts and on-call duty supply the response. Incident management and blameless postmortems supply the learning loop. SLOs with error budgets supply the decision rule that balances reliability against the speed of change.

### Other names

- Operation process (a technical process in ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207)
- Software Engineering Operations knowledge area (SWEBOK v4, chapter 6)
- Service Operation (the ITIL v3 life cycle stage) – ITIL 4 replaced it with practices such as incident management, problem management, monitoring and event management, and service level management
- IT service management (ITSM) or IT operations
- Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) or production engineering
- Production operations, the run phase, or Day-2 operations
- Operate and Evolve (AWS Well-Architected Operational Excellence)
- Application support or production support
- The "Ops" side of DevOps – "you build it, you run it"
- Service management and service delivery

### Position in the life cycle

Before this phase, release management and deployment (see section 11) deliver a system that runs. Architecture (see section 6), detailed design (see section 7) and testing (see section 9) decide how operable that system is. After this phase, maintenance and evolution (see section 13) change the system, and retirement (see section 14) ends it. In ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 the Operation process is a technical process. It follows transition and validation, runs in parallel with the Maintenance process, and ends with Disposal. SWEBOK summarizes the process in four activities: prepare for operation (define an operation strategy), perform operation (operate and monitor), manage the results of operation (record and address anomalies), and support the customer.

In a waterfall or V-model project, operations appears as a separate "operation and maintenance" phase after acceptance. A formal handover from the project team to an operations group is common. In iterative and agile delivery, operations starts at the first production release and continues for every increment. Each increment adds operational load, and each retrospective can pull in lessons from production. In DevOps, continuous delivery and SRE, operations is continuous and shared. The team that builds a service also runs it, or it shares the pager with SRE. SLOs and error budgets feed back into planning (see section 4), and production telemetry drives the next change.

The plan for operations starts before the first release: a production readiness review, a capacity plan, runbooks and backups. The process ends only at decommissioning. Operations is a continuous process, not a one-time phase.

### Inputs

- A deployed and released system with its deployment artifacts, its configuration and a tested rollback path (from release management, see section 11).
- Non-functional requirements and agreed service levels: availability, latency, durability, correctness, recovery objectives (RTO and RPO), and any SLA contract with consequences (see section 5).
- SLI and SLO definitions with an error budget policy, or the decision and the data to create them (SRE book and SRE workbook).
- Architecture documentation: request flow diagrams, dependencies, single points of failure, expected failure modes and overload behavior (Google launch checklist).
- Instrumentation in the code: metrics, structured logs, traces and events, plus monitoring and alert configuration, ideally as code.
- The results of a production readiness or operational readiness review (PRR, ORR or launch checklist) and any open risks.
- An operations plan or concept of operations: roles, on-call rota, escalation paths, support hours, response time targets, supplier and cloud contracts (the SWEBOK operations plan).
- Runbooks and playbooks for each alert and for deploy, rollback, restore and failover.
- Capacity forecasts, load test results and scaling limits (quotas and autoscaler bounds).
- Backup and disaster recovery plans with recovery objectives and a test schedule (NIST SP 800-34).
- Access, credentials, secrets and change management rules for production.
- Incident history and postmortems from earlier releases or from similar systems.
- Entry criteria: an owner is reachable; the main user journey is monitored from outside and from inside; an alert reaches a human; the rollback and the restore were exercised at least once.

### Activities

- **Operations planning and service-level definition** – Write the operations plan or CONOPS before the release: scope, roles, support hours, suppliers, budgets, and the way users report problems. Define SLIs from the user's point of view (availability, latency, freshness, durability). Set SLOs with the agreement of the stakeholders. Write an error budget policy that says what happens when the budget is used up. The activity produces the SLO document, the error budget policy and the operations plan that the later activities use.
- **Production readiness and launch review** – Before a launch or a handover, review the service against a checklist (Google PRR and launch checklist, AWS ORR). The review covers architecture and dependencies, instrumentation and monitoring, emergency response, capacity, change management and performance. The questions come from earlier incidents, so the review stops known causes of impact from a repeat. The activity produces a list of improvements, a go or no-go decision, and a training and onboarding plan.
- **Instrumentation and telemetry collection** – Emit logs, metrics, traces and events from the application and the infrastructure. Correlate them with request and trace identifiers, structured formats and consistent semantic conventions (OpenTelemetry). Write logs as event streams to standard output and let the platform route them (12-factor). The activity produces the telemetry data that monitoring, diagnosis and SLO measurement need. The OpenTelemetry Collector or a vendor agent ships the data to a backend.
- **Monitoring and alert design** – Decide which conditions page a human, which conditions create a ticket, and which conditions only appear on a dashboard. Page on symptoms that affect users, not on causes. Prefer SLO burn-rate alerts over static thresholds. Review each new alert for precision, recall, detection time and reset time. Combine black-box checks from outside with white-box metrics from inside. The activity produces alert rules, routing and escalation policies, and an alert review log.
- **Dashboards and service reports** – Build dashboards that each answer one question: SLO compliance and error budget burn, the four golden signals per service, and drill-down views for diagnosis. Produce periodic service reports: SLA attainment, incidents, capacity, security events, cost and user satisfaction (ITIL service level management, SWEBOK service reporting). The activity produces shared situational awareness and the input for operational reviews.
- **On-call operation and escalation** – Run a rota of primary and secondary responders with agreed response times, clear escalation paths, handoffs between shifts, and compensation for work out of hours. Keep the load sustainable: at most about two paging incidents per 12-hour shift and at least 50 percent engineering time. Keep minimum team sizes for 24x7 coverage. The activity produces a schedule, acknowledged and resolved pages, and pager-load data for review.
- **Incident detection, triage and response** – Declare an incident when a second team is necessary, when users see impact, or when the problem is not solved after one hour. Assign an incident commander, an operations lead and a communications lead. Keep a live incident document. Mitigate first: roll back, drain traffic, shed load or degrade before you look for the root cause. Classify the severity with pre-agreed response expectations, and pick the higher level when unsure. The activity produces a restored service, an incident record and a timeline.
- **Incident communication and status pages** – Communicate in concentric circles: responders, front-line support, managers, all staff, then customers. Use pre-written templates and a status page as the single source of truth. Send an update at least every hour, even when the update is "still investigating". Acknowledge early, state the known impact, promise the next update, and address questions about data loss or security. The activity produces stakeholder updates, a public status history and fewer support tickets.
- **Postmortems, problem management and action tracking** – After a significant incident, write a blameless postmortem. Include the impact with numbers, the timeline, the contributing causes and what went well. Add action items that are prioritized, owned, tracked and dated. Review the document with senior engineers, publish it broadly within days, and track the completion of the actions. ITIL problem management covers the same loop with problem records, known errors and workarounds. The activity produces the postmortem document, tracked fixes and organizational learning.
- **Runbooks, playbooks and operational documentation** – Keep a runbook for each alert and for each routine procedure (deploy, rollback, restore, failover, scale). Keep a playbook for major incident response, and a service overview with contacts and dependencies. Google reports about a 3x improvement in MTTR with playbooks, and DORA finds that documentation quality predicts reliability. Review the documents after each incident and each drill. The activity produces current operational documentation that any team member can execute in an emergency.
- **Toil measurement and automation** – Identify manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical work that scales with the service. Measure it in hours or tickets and cap it (Google targets less than 50 percent). Engineer toil out of the system, reject low-value requests, provide self-service interfaces, and automate responses with safeguards. The activity produces toil reports, automation and self-service tools, and free engineering time.
- **Capacity planning, provisioning and autoscaling** – Forecast organic growth and planned events. Add headroom for redundancy (for example N+2). Load-test to map raw resources to real service capacity, and provision ahead of the lead time. Configure autoscaling conservatively with minimum and maximum bounds, cool-down periods, kill switches and dependency checks, so that scaling does not overload the backends. The activity produces the capacity plan, load test results and the scaling configuration.
- **Performance and overload management** – Manage latency and throughput in production. Monitor tail latency. Set deadlines and propagate them. Limit retries with exponential backoff and jitter. Use per-customer quotas and request criticality. Shed load and degrade gracefully before resources run out. Break retry loops and cascade loops with timeouts, circuit breakers and bulkheads. The activity produces a service that serves its rated load under excess traffic, and a set of known emergency levers.
- **Change, release and configuration control in production** – Record, classify and risk-assess every production change. Roll out progressively with canaries and feature flags, watch for regressions, and roll back fast; about 70 percent of outages follow a change. Keep environments reproducible from one source of truth (infrastructure as code) and manage maintenance windows openly. The activity produces change records, safe rollouts and an audit trail.
- **Patching and vulnerability management in operations** – Treat patches as planned preventive maintenance. Know when a new vulnerability affects your assets, choose a risk response, execute a routine or emergency patch or a workaround, and verify the result. Group assets into maintenance groups with their own cadences, and handle assets that cannot be patched with compensating controls (NIST SP 800-40r4). The activity produces a patched estate, a vulnerability status and documented exceptions.
- **Backup, restore testing and data integrity validation** – Back up data, documents, software and configuration. Keep at least three copies on two media, with one copy offsite and one copy offline or immutable (3-2-1). Test restores regularly, because "no one really wants to make backups; what people really want are restores". Add soft deletion and out-of-band validators to detect corruption early. The activity produces restorable backups, evidence of restore tests and known recovery times.
- **Disaster recovery and business continuity** – Derive the RTO and the RPO from a business impact analysis. Choose a strategy that fits them (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, or multi-site active-active). Write the plan and exercise it with tabletop and functional tests, including failback. Manage configuration drift at the recovery site and prefer automation for the steps. The activity produces the DR plan, test reports and evidence that the objectives are met.
- **Resilience testing, drills and chaos engineering** – Run disaster role-play (Wheel of Misfortune), incident drills and company-wide recovery tests (DiRT). Run chaos experiments: define the steady state, form a hypothesis, inject a real-world fault with a limited blast radius and stop conditions, then verify and fix. Start in pre-production and move to production when it is safe. The activity produces verified recovery paths, trained responders and a backlog of resilience fixes.
- **Cost management (FinOps) and efficiency** – Make cost visible to the engineers who create it. Allocate spend to services, detect anomalies, forecast and budget, then optimize usage and rates in an inform–optimize–operate cycle. Treat utilization and efficiency as operations concerns, because provisioning and performance drive cost. The activity produces cost reports, unit economics and optimization actions.
- **Operations support, service desk and supplier management** – Provide a single point of contact for users. Handle service requests and incidents with agreed priorities. Manage the suppliers and cloud providers whose SLAs the service depends on (ITIL service desk and service request management; SWEBOK supplier management). The activity produces tickets, support records and supplier performance reviews.
- **Operational reviews and continuous improvement** – Hold regular production meetings. Review SLO compliance and the error budget, the pager load, open postmortem actions, capacity, cost and risk, and adjust SLOs, alerts and priorities. Manage operational risk continuously and agree the risk tolerance with the product owners. The activity produces prioritized reliability work for the backlog and updated targets.
- **Ownership and handover model management** – Decide and revisit who runs the service. The options are: the team that builds it ("you build it, you run it"); a shared model with SRE after a PRR; or a platform team that provides operations as a service. Avoid silo handovers. Allow SRE to hand the pager back when the operational load is too high. The activity produces an explicit ownership agreement, onboarding and offboarding steps, and shared tools.

### Outputs

- A service that runs and meets its SLOs, with SLO compliance and error budget reports per window.
- Telemetry data, dashboards, alert rules and monitoring configuration kept as code.
- On-call schedules, escalation policies, pager-load data and acknowledged incident records.
- Incident records with timelines, severity, impact numbers, status page history and stakeholder communications.
- Postmortem documents with prioritized, owned and tracked action items; problem records, known errors and workarounds.
- Current runbooks, playbooks, service overviews and contact lists.
- Capacity plans, load test results, autoscaling and quota configuration, and cost reports.
- Backup sets with evidence of restore tests; a DR plan with test reports that show the achieved RTO and RPO.
- Patch and vulnerability status, change records and an audit trail.
- Minutes of operational reviews, toil measurements and a prioritized reliability backlog that feeds back into planning and maintenance (see sections 4 and 13).
- Exit criteria per increment or review: the service is within its SLO, no SEV1 or SEV2 incident is open, postmortem actions are tracked, the rollback and the restore were exercised, and the on-call load is sustainable.
- Exit criteria for a handover to SRE or operations: the production readiness review passed, training and onboarding are done, and access and change rights are transferred.
- The operations process itself ends only when the service is retired; its records feed the decommissioning plan (see section 14).

### Roles

- Service owner or product manager: sets reliability targets with the users in mind, agrees the SLOs, and decides how to spend the error budget.
- Software engineers (developers): instrument the code, fix production bugs, share on-call duty, and complete postmortem action items; in "you build it, you run it" they own operations.
- SRE or operations engineers: design monitoring and alerts, automate toil, plan capacity, run the emergency response, perform production readiness reviews, and may hand the pager back when the load is too high.
- On-call engineer (primary and secondary): acknowledges pages within the agreed time, triages, mitigates and escalates.
- Incident commander: holds the incident state, delegates and decides. Operations lead: the only person or group that changes the system. Communications lead: updates the stakeholders. A scribe and a deputy support the commander (Google IMAG, PagerDuty).
- Subject matter experts or resolvers, customer liaison and internal liaison (PagerDuty roles).
- Postmortem owner and reviewers or approvers: drive the document and validate the causes and the actions (PagerDuty, Atlassian).
- Platform engineering team: provides self-service deployment, monitoring and infrastructure as a service (SWEBOK operations engineer role, DevOps Topologies).
- Service desk and support staff: first-line contact, ticket triage and service requests (ITIL).
- Problem manager, change manager and service level manager in ITIL-style organizations.
- Security and vulnerability management: prioritize patches and handle security incidents (see section 16).
- FinOps practitioner and finance: cost allocation, forecasts and optimization.
- Business continuity or DR coordinator, compliance and audit in regulated settings.
- Leadership: funds reliability work, enforces the error budget policy, models blameless behavior and gives time for drills.
- Suppliers and cloud providers: deliver managed services under the SLAs that the service depends on.

### Practices with consensus

- **Define SLIs from the user's point of view, set SLOs below 100 percent, and use the error budget to balance reliability work against feature work** – 100 percent is the wrong target. Users cannot tell extra nines apart, and an error budget gives an objective rule for when to slow the rate of change. Evidence: Google SRE book (Embracing Risk; Service Level Objectives); SRE Workbook (Implementing SLOs; Example Error Budget Policy); OpenTelemetry observability primer; DORA monitoring and observability.
- **Page on user-visible symptoms; make each page urgent, actionable and novel; send the rest as tickets or dashboard signals** – A page to a human is expensive, and cause-based or noisy alerts teach responders to ignore pages. Evidence: Google SRE book (Monitoring Distributed Systems); Prometheus alerting practices (Ewaschuk's philosophy); DORA monitoring and observability; GOV.UK monitoring guidance.
- **Measure the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) or RED/USE, and look at percentiles and histograms, not averages** – Averages hide tail latency, and the four signals cover most user-facing failures at a low cost. Evidence: Google SRE book (Monitoring Distributed Systems; Service Level Objectives); Grafana dashboard best practices.
- **Combine black-box (external, synthetic) monitoring with white-box (internal) metrics, logs and traces** – External checks still work when the infrastructure is down, and internal signals explain why. Evidence: Google SRE book (Monitoring Distributed Systems); DORA monitoring and observability; GOV.UK monitoring the status of your service.
- **Instrument applications with correlated, structured telemetry, use an open standard such as OpenTelemetry, and write logs as event streams to stdout** – Correlated traces, metrics and logs let teams debug novel problems without new code, and open standards avoid lock-in. Evidence: OpenTelemetry docs (what is OpenTelemetry; signals; primer); Honeycomb observability articles; 12-factor logs; SWEBOK v4 monitoring and telemetry.
- **Use an incident command structure with one commander, an operations lead, a communications lead, a live incident document and explicit handoffs** – Unmanaged incidents suffer from freelance changes, poor communication and tunnel vision. A structure agreed in advance reduces the chaos. Evidence: Google SRE book (Managing Incidents); SRE Workbook (Incident Response); PagerDuty incident response roles; Atlassian incident handbook.
- **Mitigate first and find the root cause later: roll back, drain, shed load or degrade, then investigate** – Users want the errors to stop, not an explanation. Generic mitigations shorten the impact. Evidence: SRE Workbook (Incident Response); Google SRE book (Effective Troubleshooting); Atlassian incident values ("restore service quickly").
- **Classify incidents with a small severity scale that has pre-agreed response expectations, and choose the higher level when unsure** – Severity decides who is paged and when. A debate about it during an incident wastes time. Evidence: PagerDuty severity levels; Atlassian severity levels.
- **Communicate early and on a fixed cadence during incidents, with a status page as the source of truth and pre-written templates** – Silence is read as inaction. Regular updates cut the support load and protect trust. Evidence: Atlassian incident communication; SRE Workbook (Incident Response); GOV.UK uptime and availability guidance.
- **Write blameless postmortems for significant incidents, publish them widely within days, and track prioritized, owned, dated action items** – Blame hides information. A postmortem without follow-up is the same as no postmortem. Evidence: Google SRE book (Postmortem Culture); SRE Workbook (Postmortem Culture); PagerDuty postmortem process; Atlassian postmortems; How Complex Systems Fail; AWS ORR (Correction of Errors).
- **Keep on-call duty sustainable: a bounded pager load, minimum team sizes for 24x7, compensation, clear escalation and psychological safety to escalate** – Overload causes burnout and bad decisions under stress. Underload causes skill decay. Evidence: Google SRE book (Being On-Call); SRE Workbook (On-Call); PagerDuty being on-call.
- **Maintain runbooks and operational documentation, and review them after incidents and drills** – Playbooks give about 3x better MTTR at Google, and documentation quality predicts reliability in DORA research. Evidence: Google SRE book (Introduction; Being On-Call; Accelerating SREs to On-Call); PagerDuty what is a runbook; DORA documentation quality; GOV.UK operations manual advice.
- **Measure toil and cap it; automate repetitive operations and provide self-service** – Toil scales with the service and crowds out engineering. Automation and uniformity let the number of humans grow slower than the number of machines. Evidence: Google SRE book (Eliminating Toil); SRE Workbook (Eliminating Toil); AWS Operational Excellence design principles; SWEBOK v4 automating operations.
- **Plan capacity from forecasts plus load tests, keep headroom, and configure autoscaling, load balancing and load shedding as one system with bounds and kill switches** – Launches can exceed the estimates many times over, and uncoordinated scaling and shedding create feedback loops. Evidence: Google SRE book (Introduction; Reliable Product Launches; Addressing Cascading Failures); SRE Workbook (Managing Load); SWEBOK v4 capacity management.
- **Protect against overload with timeouts, deadlines, retry budgets with exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads and graceful degradation** – Every integration point fails at some time. Without these patterns one slow dependency cascades into a full outage. Evidence: Google SRE book (Handling Overload; Addressing Cascading Failures); Release It! (publisher page and chapter summary); Martin Fowler CircuitBreaker.
- **Back up data with the 3-2-1 rule and an offline or immutable copy, and test restores regularly** – Ransomware reaches connected backups, and nobody knows that an untested backup is restorable. Evidence: Google SRE book (Data Integrity); NCSC offline backups and ransomware-resistant backups; NIST SP 800-34; AWS REL13-BP03; SWEBOK v4 backup and DR.
- **Set the RTO and the RPO from the business impact, pick a matching DR strategy, and exercise failover and failback on a schedule** – The only recovery path that works is the one you test. Stricter objectives cost more, so match them to the need. Evidence: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1; AWS Reliability pillar DR pages; Google Cloud DR planning guide; SWEBOK v4.
- **Review production readiness before a launch and periodically, with a checklist derived from past incidents** – Readiness reviews catch missing monitoring, capacity and response plans before the users find them. Evidence: Google SRE book (Evolving SRE Engagement Model; Reliable Product Launches); AWS Operational Readiness Reviews; GOV.UK Service Standard point 14.
- **Treat patches as routine preventive maintenance with a risk-based plan and defined emergency paths** – Unpatched known vulnerabilities are a leading cause of compromise, and ad-hoc patches cause outages. Evidence: NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4; SWEBOK v4 security controls in operations.
- **Practice failure: drills, game days and chaos experiments with a hypothesis, a limited blast radius and stop conditions** – Responders and systems behave differently under a real failure. Practice builds muscle memory and finds unknown weaknesses. Evidence: Principles of Chaos Engineering; AWS REL12-BP04; Google SRE book (Emergency Response; Accelerating SREs to On-Call); SRE Workbook (Incident Response).
- **Make cloud cost visible to the engineers who incur it, and manage it continuously (inform, optimize, operate)** – Variable cloud cost is an operations outcome. Unowned resources and low utilization waste money silently. Evidence: FinOps Foundation framework and principles; Google SRE book (Introduction: efficiency and performance); SRE Workbook (Eliminating Toil: cost engineering).
- **Give the team that builds the service operational responsibility, or use a shared-ownership model; do not throw software over a wall** – Operational feedback improves design and quality. Silos misalign incentives. Evidence: AWS blog on the Vogels interview ("you build it, you run it"); DevOps Topologies; SRE Workbook (How SRE Relates to DevOps); Google SRE book (Introduction); SWEBOK v4 introduction.

### Contested points

- **Who runs production: the builders, a dedicated SRE or operations team, or a platform team.** Amazon's "you build it, you run it" gives full ownership to the team that builds the service. Google's SRE model hands over after a production readiness review and can hand the pager back; Google also notes that many services should stay with the developers. DevOps Topologies says that there is no single right topology, only bad ones for a given organization. DORA 2024 finds that platform engineering raises productivity but can reduce stability and throughput if it is done without developer independence. The choice depends on scale, the number of services, maturity, regulation and staff.
- **Monitoring versus observability, and the "three pillars".** OpenTelemetry and most vendors present traces, metrics and logs as the signals of observability. Charity Majors and Honeycomb argue that these are only data types. Pre-aggregated metrics destroy the detail needed to explore unknown unknowns, and observability needs wide structured events with high cardinality. DORA treats monitoring (known conditions) and observability (diagnosis of unknown conditions) as complementary. The practical split depends on system complexity and budget; simple systems get far with metrics and logs.
- **MTTR and time-based incident metrics.** DORA keeps failed deployment recovery time as a key metric. Google's "Incident Metrics in SRE" and the VOID report show that incident durations are skewed and have a high variance. Means therefore hide improvement and invite manipulation. These sources recommend SLO-based measures, incident counts, the cost of coordination and per-incident analysis. AWS distinguishes the RTO (a target for a single event) from the MTTR (a mean over many events). Use durations for learning, not as targets.
- **Root cause versus contributing factors.** Atlassian's template uses five whys and a root cause. Google's postmortems list the root cause or causes but focus on systemic fixes. Cook's "How Complex Systems Fail" and the VOID report argue that a single root cause is a social construct. A catastrophe needs several small failures. The trend goes towards contributing factors and systemic action items; a strict single-cause form fits simple systems only.
- **How hard the error budget policy should bite.** The SRE workbook example freezes all releases except P0 and security fixes when the budget is used up. It allows feature work to continue when the cause was external or misclassified. The same example says that a halt regardless of cause satisfies customers more. Small organizations often cannot freeze releases or hand back the pager, and use conditional prioritization instead. The right level depends on the business tolerance and on who can enforce it.
- **Alert design: pure symptom alerts versus leading indicators and simple thresholds.** Google recommends multiwindow, multi-burn-rate SLO alerts and warns against cause-based alerts. DORA's proactive failure notification recommends alerts on leading indicators, for example at about 20 percent before a threshold, which is cause-based. Prometheus guidance allows capacity alerts as tickets. Low-traffic services break the burn-rate mathematics and need synthetic traffic, aggregation or relaxed SLOs. Teams choose by the traffic level and the cost of a miss.
- **Severity scales and who declares incidents.** PagerDuty uses five levels, with SEV-1 and SEV-2 as major incidents. Atlassian uses three levels and notes that severity (impact) differs from priority (urgency). Google declares an incident when a second team is necessary, when customers are affected, or when one hour has passed. Scales should be tailored to the team size and the traffic; a larger scale adds precision but also debate.
- **Chaos engineering and tests in production.** Principles of Chaos says that experiments must run in production, because behavior differs elsewhere. AWS guidance recommends a start in pre-production, canary deployments, stop conditions and synthetic traffic, and no experiments on a workload known to be broken. Google's Chubby planned outages and DiRT are production exercises. Regulated organizations often forbid fault injection in production; blast-radius control decides.
- **Automatic versus manual failover and recovery.** AWS warns that automatic failover based on health checks can cause unnecessary outages and data loss, so manual initiation of automated steps is common. SWEBOK states that automated failover daemons cut recovery time drastically. The choice depends on the RTO, the data consistency needs and the confidence in the health signals.
- **How much to invest in dashboards.** Grafana recommends curated, hierarchical, version-controlled dashboards with a strategy. DORA lists "dashboard perfection" as a pitfall, because dashboards go stale, and Majors argues that predefined dashboards cannot answer new questions. Consensus exists on a small set of SLO and golden-signal dashboards; beyond that, opinions differ.
- **ITIL and ITSM formality versus SRE and DevOps lightness.** ITIL 4 defines 34 practices and a service value chain, and it explicitly aligns with Agile and DevOps. The practice guides were revised in 2023 to take the view of the service consumer. SWEBOK notes that many organizations still run conventional IT operations processes, while SWEBOK itself focuses on DevOps, IaC and SRE. Regulated or outsourced environments need ITSM formality; small product teams usually need only the basics of incident, problem and change management.
- **On-call staff minimums and compensation.** Google's SRE book requires at least 8 engineers for single-site 24x7 coverage (later 9 in the workbook), or 6 per site for multi-site coverage. It also requires paid compensation. Many startups run on-call duty with two or three people, sometimes unpaid. The sources agree that the load must be bounded; they disagree on what minimum staff level is acceptable when the business cannot fund it.
- **Postmortem triggers and timing.** PagerDuty requires a postmortem meeting within 3 calendar days for SEV-1 and within 5 business days for SEV-2. Atlassian requires postmortems only for SEV-1 and SEV-2. Google lists triggers such as user-visible downtime, data loss, on-call intervention and monitoring failure, and publishes within days. Lightweight reviews for minor incidents are debated; over-formal processes stop people from writing them.

### Metrics

- SLO compliance per rolling window, and the error budget that remains and its burn rate – the primary indicators of operational health. Caveat: SLIs must be measured close to the user, or they mislead.
- Availability as a success ratio, latency at p50, p95 and p99, error rate, saturation and throughput (the golden signals); freshness, correctness and coverage for pipelines; durability for storage. Caveat: averages hide the tails.
- Alert quality: precision, recall, detection time and reset time per alert; pages per shift; the share of alerts that were actionable; acknowledgement times and silenced alerts (DORA). Caveat: count incidents, not alerts, because one incident can fire many alerts.
- Incident counts by severity, and the time to detect, mitigate and restore per incident. Caveat: duration distributions are skewed and have a high variance, so MTTR means are poor for trend decisions and targets (Google Incident Metrics in SRE; VOID report). Use distributions, counts and per-incident analysis.
- DORA software delivery metrics that touch operations: failed deployment recovery time, change failure rate and deployment rework rate. Caveat: apply them per service, not in aggregate, and do not use them as competitive targets.
- Toil as a percentage of engineering time (target less than 50 percent), and on-call health: incidents per shift (target at most 2 per 12 hours), the 21-day trailing pager load, and pages out of hours. Caveat: self-reported toil needs consistent units.
- Postmortem action item completion rate and age, and the recurrence of the same incident class. Caveat: a closed ticket is not the same as a reduced risk.
- Capacity headroom and utilization, forecast accuracy, load test results versus demand; cost per unit of work, budget variance and anomalies (FinOps unit economics). Caveat: these measures only help when someone owns them and reviews them on a cadence.
- Achieved RTO and RPO in DR tests versus the targets, time since the last restore test, backup success rate and restore test pass rate. Caveat: untested recovery paths give no evidence.
- Patch latency for critical vulnerabilities and the size of the vulnerability backlog. Caveat: counts ignore exposure and exploitability.
- Service reports in ITSM terms: SLA attainment, ticket volumes, service request lead time and customer satisfaction. Caveat: SLA credits do not compensate users for real downtime (GOV.UK).
- Survey measures of dashboard and alert usability and of documentation quality (DORA). Caveat: perception data lags changes in practice.
- Goodhart's law applies to all of the above: a metric that becomes a target gets gamed (severity inflation or deflation, closed tickets, silenced alerts).

### Failure modes

- Cause-based or noisy alerts, pages that need no action, and email alerts that need human interpretation – responders skim or ignore pages, and real incidents are missed (alert fatigue).
- No SLOs, SLOs without consequences ("dormant SLOs"), or a 100 percent target – there is no objective basis to trade reliability against change, and every outage becomes an argument.
- An SLO that is over-achieved for a long time – dependents build on the real behavior and break when the service returns to its promised level (Google's Chubby example).
- Unmanaged incidents: no commander, freelance changes, poor communication, late declaration, and a search for the root cause while users still see errors – the impact lasts longer and the response adds damage.
- Blameful postmortems, vague or unowned action items, delayed publication and a limited audience – people hide information, and the same failure returns.
- Operational overload: more than 50 percent toil or more than two pages per shift – burnout, attrition and worse decisions. Operational underload – skills decay until a crisis exposes the gap.
- Untested backups and DR plans, a single backup copy, or backups connected to production – ransomware or a bad deployment destroys both the data and the recovery.
- Uncoordinated autoscaling, load balancing and load shedding, unbounded retries, missing deadlines and synchronized clients – retry storms, thundering herds and cascading failures.
- Monitoring of the infrastructure only and not of the user journeys, and reliance on averages – tail latency and partial outages go unnoticed.
- Dashboard sprawl, or over-curated "perfect" dashboards that nobody maintains – stale views that mislead during incidents.
- A hand-over between silos (known as "throw over the wall"), "Dev don't need Ops", a DevOps team silo, or "fake SRE" (renamed sysadmins) – incentives stay misaligned, and operability does not improve.
- Outdated runbooks and tribal knowledge – the one person who knows becomes a single point of failure.
- Unsafe change practice: big-bang rollouts, no canary, no tested rollback, emergency changes that bypass review – most outages follow changes.
- Patches treated as optional or applied only in emergencies – known vulnerabilities stay exploitable, and emergency patches cause outages.
- Chaos experiments without a hypothesis, blast radius limits or stop conditions, or on systems already known to be broken – outages without learning.
- A copy of a large organization's process on a tiny team, or no process at all – very small entities need adapted practice (SWEBOK on ISO/IEC 29110).
- Cost ignored until the invoice arrives – unowned resources, idle capacity and no unit economics.
- Gamed metrics: MTTR targets, severity manipulation, silenced alerts to hit the numbers – the measures stop describing reality.

### Tailoring by project size

Some practices are essential at every scale. Know when the service is broken before the users tell you. Have a rehearsed way to restore the service (rollback) and the data (restore). Write down how to operate the system. Learn from failures without blame. Keep the cost in view. Keep the response load humane. Other practices are optional at every scale: specific tools, a formal ITIL process, chaos engineering, 24x7 paging when the users do not need it, and SLA contracts. The table gives the additions per scale.

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| Solo developer on a small repository | One external uptime check on the main user journey that notifies you. Error tracking that groups exceptions and alerts on new or regressed issues. Structured logs to stdout, kept for a few weeks. Automated backups with one offsite or offline copy, and a restore test every quarter and after each schema change. A one-page runbook (deploy, rollback, restore, location of secrets, provider contacts). One simple SLO, such as 99.5 percent successful requests over 30 days, and one alert on sustained errors. Dependency updates and patches on a cadence. A cost budget alert. A short note after any outage with one fix. | A pager at night, unless the users need it. Tracing, dashboards, drills and formal roles. A formal ITIL process, chaos engineering and SLA contracts. |
| Small product team | Everything from the solo row, plus: a shared on-call rotation with escalation, sustainable hours and compensation. An incident channel and a lightweight incident commander role. A three-level severity scale. A status page with templates. A postmortem template for SEV1 and SEV2 with tracked actions. SLOs per user journey with burn-rate alerts. One dashboard per service. A runbook per alert. A production readiness checklist and a load test before big launches. A DR plan with an RTO and an RPO, and one failover test per year. A patch cadence. A monthly cost review. Toil tracking. | Specific tools beyond OpenTelemetry plus a managed backend, which is usually enough. A formal ITIL process. Chaos engineering. 24x7 paging when the users do not need it. SLA contracts. |
| Large or regulated organization | Everything from the small team row, plus: a formal operations plan and ITSM practices (incident, problem, change enablement, service desk, service level management, service continuity), and SLAs with customers. Dedicated SRE or platform teams with PRR or ORR programs and explicit engagement and handback rules. Multi-site on-call at the minimum staff levels. Trained incident commanders, communications leads and liaisons, including regulatory notification paths. Central observability standards and retention rules. DR tests per NIST SP 800-34 style plans, with tabletop and functional exercises, and evidence kept for audit. Vulnerability management with patch SLAs and documented exceptions. A FinOps function. A chaos engineering and game day program with blast-radius controls. Documentation standards. Metric governance, so that SLOs and not MTTR targets drive decisions. | The specific tool set and the exact ITIL scope. The choice between an SRE model and a platform model. Fault injection in production where regulation forbids it (run the program in pre-production). 24x7 paging for services whose users do not need it. |
