## 13. Maintenance and evolution

### Purpose

Maintenance and evolution keep delivered software useful, correct, secure and changeable until it is retired. ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 states the purpose of the maintenance process: sustain the capability of the system to provide a service, monitor it, record incidents, take corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive actions, and confirm the restored capability. The phase answers one question: how does a team change a system that people already depend on, without a break in service, at an acceptable cost? Lehman's laws explain why the work never ends. The team must continually adapt a used E-type system, and its complexity and perceived quality decay unless work counters them.

The phase consumes the majority of the life cycle cost – Glass gives 40 to 80 percent – so it is the main economic lever of a software product. It also covers the slow work of technical debt paydown, the replacement of dependencies and platforms, the deprecation of features, and the modernization of legacy systems.

### Other names

- Software maintenance
- Software evolution
- Maintenance process (ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017, 6.4.13; elaborated in ISO/IEC/IEEE 14764:2022)
- Software sustainment (the ISO/IEC/IEEE 14764 term for support, maintenance and operation performed together)
- Software Maintenance knowledge area (SWEBOK v4, chapter 7)
- Live phase (GOV.UK Service Manual)
- Operations and maintenance (O&M); post-delivery support
- Sustaining engineering; application management (ISO/IEC 16350)
- Programming integrated over time (Software Engineering at Google)
- Legacy modernization; legacy displacement; reengineering; brownfield development
- Continuous improvement of a live service

### Position in the life cycle

Before this phase, development, integration, testing, acceptance and deployment deliver a baseline (see sections 8 to 11). A transition hands the baseline to the maintainers, together with tests, documentation and environments. After this phase, disposal or retirement ends the work. That happens when users no longer need the service, or when it is not cost-effective to keep it running (ISO 14764 clause 7; GOV.UK; see section 14).

In a waterfall or V-model, maintenance is the last and the longest phase. It starts after acceptance or a warranty period. It usually lasts years, while development lasts months (SWEBOK). In iterative and agile work, the same team develops and maintains. Every sprint mixes features, defects and debt, and maintenance becomes continued development (SWEBOK 2.2.5; Scrum Guide). In DevOps and continuous delivery, maintenance merges with operations (see section 12). CI, continuous testing and deployment automate the change loop, and SLIs, SLOs and SLAs frame the service (SWEBOK 4.4; Google SRE).

In ISO/IEC/IEEE 14764, the operation process triggers maintenance through a problem report or a modification request. Maintenance then invokes the technical processes – design, implementation, integration, transition – to make the change. Large enhancements become a new development project. ISO 14764 also defines pre-delivery maintenance activities: planning, supportability and logistics. The topic therefore starts before the release. Maintenance is a continuous process, not a one-time phase. Google frames it as "programming integrated over time".

### Inputs

- A delivered and accepted software baseline under configuration management, with source, build, tests, data and environments (SEE/STE) – ISO 14764 1.3; SWEBOK 3.2.3.
- A maintenance strategy and plan: scope, maintenance organization, processes, resources, cost estimate, records and reports, and the way users submit MRs and PRs – ISO 14764 clauses 6.1 and 9; SWEBOK 3.2.2.
- Agreements and service levels: support hours, severity definitions, response and resolution targets, supplier contracts and licenses – ISO 14764 8.3; SWEBOK 3.2; Atlassian SLA guide; Red Hat severity policy.
- A transition from development: knowledge, documentation, tests, known defects and open risks, with early maintainer involvement during development – SWEBOK 1.2, 3.2; ISO 14764 8.7.
- Incoming modification requests (MR, also called change requests) and problem reports (PR) from users, operators, monitoring, security bulletins and incidents – ISO 14764 3.1.8, 3.1.11.
- Operational signals: monitoring, incident records, support tickets, user satisfaction, web analytics – GOV.UK Service Manual; SWEBOK 1.2.
- A dependency inventory (manifests, lock files, a dependency graph or an SBOM), vulnerability feeds and end-of-life dates for runtimes, frameworks and operating systems – OWASP A06; endoflife.date; Scorecard.
- A single ordered backlog that already contains features, defects, architecture work and known technical debt – Scrum Guide; Kruchten et al. "four colours".
- A published versioning, deprecation and support policy (for example semver or an LTS schedule) – semver.org; Node.js, Python and Django release policies.
- Assigned ownership: maintainers, a triage owner, code owners, documentation owners – Mozilla triage policy; Software Engineering at Google ch. 10, 15.

### Activities

ISO/IEC/IEEE 14764 classifies each change by maintenance category. The categories fall into two groups: corrections and enhancements. The table below gives the categories that the activities refer to.

| Category | Group | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Corrective | Correction | A reactive modification that corrects a discovered problem. |
| Preventive | Correction | A modification that detects and corrects latent faults before they become failures. |
| Emergency | Correction | An unscheduled temporary change that keeps the system operational until the proper corrective fix (ISO 14764 3.1.5). |
| Adaptive | Enhancement | A modification that keeps the product usable in a changed or changing environment, for example a new platform or runtime. |
| Additive | Enhancement | A modification that adds new functionality for users. |
| Perfective | Enhancement | A modification that improves performance, maintainability or information for users (ISO 14764 3.1.9). |

The activities of the phase are:

- **Prepare for maintenance: strategy, plan and agreements** – Define the maintenance strategy, scope, organization, processes, tools, resources and cost estimate before delivery (ISO 14764 6.1 and clause 9; SWEBOK 3.2.2). Agree service levels, support hours and supplier terms with users or customers. Plan from the decision to build, because the maintenance phase lasts until retirement. Output: a maintenance plan, agreements and a resourced maintenance organization.
- **Transition from development to maintenance** – Move the product, tests, documentation, environments and knowledge to the maintainers in a controlled and coordinated sequence (SWEBOK 3.2; ISO 14764 term "transition"). Involve maintainers early in development to reduce the later cost (SWEBOK 1.2; ISO 14764 8.7). Output: an accepted baseline under configuration control and a team that can support it immediately.
- **Intake, recording and triage of problem reports and modification requests** – Receive PRs and MRs through a help desk or an issue tracker and record them (ISO 14764 3.1.8, 3.1.11). Confirm the reproduction, find duplicates, ask for missing information, and reject support requests politely. Classify each item as a correction or an enhancement and by category (corrective, preventive, adaptive, additive, perfective, emergency). Set severity (impact) and priority (when to fix) as separate fields. Route the item to an owner within a fixed time. Mozilla scans new bugs daily for security issues and triages them fully within one week. Kubernetes uses needs-triage and priority labels with 30-day and 90-day follow-ups. Output: a triaged, labelled and ordered queue.
- **Impact analysis and feasibility review** – For each MR or PR, identify the affected components, systems and interfaces. Estimate effort, cost, risk and test needs, and propose options (ISO 14764 6.2; SWEBOK 2.1.3). Decide to accept, reject, defer, give a temporary workaround, or reroute work above the agreed size to a development project. Track workarounds until their removal. Output: a documented decision, estimate and plan per request.
- **Program comprehension and reverse engineering** – Read code, tests and history, and build models of structure and behavior before any change. This is the most difficult maintenance task (Glass fact 44; SWEBOK 2.1.1). Use code browsers, static and dynamic analyzers, slicers, cross-referencers, dependency analyzers and visualization (SWEBOK 4.1, 4.3, 5). Reverse engineering creates higher-level representations without a change to the system. Redocumentation and design recovery are its subareas. Restructuring keeps the behavior while it changes the form (Chikofsky and Cross 1990). Output: understanding, notes, diagrams and corrected documentation.
- **Implement the modification** – Make the change with the normal development processes, tailored for maintenance, under configuration control (ISO 14764 6.2.4, 6.2.8; SWEBOK 3.2). For emergency maintenance, apply an unscheduled temporary change that keeps the system operational, and schedule the proper corrective fix (ISO 14764 3.1.5). For code without tests, follow Feathers: get the code under test first (cover and modify), write characterization tests that pin the current behavior, find seams and break dependencies, and then change. Output: the code change, tests and documentation updates.
- **Regression testing and verification of the change** – Re-run the selective set of tests that shows the modification caused no unintended effects (SWEBOK 2.1.2 definition of regression testing). Keep an automated suite so that CI validates every change, including infrastructure changes. Google's "Beyoncé rule" states: if CI did not catch it, the infrastructure change is not at fault. Output: test evidence for review and release.
- **Review, approve, plan and deliver maintenance releases** – Review and record each change. Approve it through the configuration control board or code review, and decide the release content with users (ISO 14764 6.2.5 to 6.2.10; SWEBOK 3.2.2, 3.2.3). Assess the release risk and prepare a back-out plan. Version releases with a declared scheme; in semver, patch is for fixes, minor for compatible additions and major for breaking changes. Write a changelog for humans (Keep a Changelog). Output: a released version, release notes and an updated baseline.
- **Backlog management and refinement** – Keep one ordered backlog as the single source of work. Make invisible work visible next to features: defects, architecture and technical debt (Scrum Guide; Kruchten et al. "four colours in a backlog"). Refine continuously: split, clarify, estimate, order, add acceptance criteria, and delete duplicates and stale items (Scrum Guide; Atlassian). Output: a ready, ordered backlog that planning can pull from at any time.
- **Technical debt identification, measurement and paydown** – Identify debt through code review, complexity metrics, developer feedback and recurrent pain (Atlassian; SWEBOK 2.3.1). Record each item with cause, consequence, impact and effort in a register or in the backlog (GOV.UK). Measure with tools (remediation effort, debt ratio, maintainability rating – SonarQube), but remember that tools see only a part of the landscape (Kruchten et al.). Pay down debt where change is frequent, because the interest is highest there, and use preparatory refactoring before features (Fowler). Output: a visible debt inventory, explicit decisions and less friction.
- **Refactoring, opportunistic and planned** – Make small behavior-preserving changes and keep the tests green after each step (refactoring.com). Practise the boy-scout rule, comprehension refactoring and preparatory refactoring as part of daily work. Avoid rabbit holes, and refactor unfamiliar code only with tests (Fowler, Opportunistic Refactoring). For larger restructurings, keep the system releasable with Branch by Abstraction and Parallel Change (expand, migrate, contract) instead of long-lived branches. Output: an improved internal structure with unchanged observable behavior.
- **Large-scale changes across a codebase** – Treat changes that cannot land as one atomic commit as a process: propose and authorize, generate the change with tooling, shard by ownership, test and review each shard, submit, and block backsliding with static analysis (Software Engineering at Google ch. 22). Infrastructure or platform owners run the migration, not each team separately. Output: a migrated codebase and removed old patterns.
- **Dependency, security and platform update management** – Keep an inventory of all components and versions (OWASP A06). Automate update pull requests with Dependabot or Renovate. Separate security updates from routine version updates. Group and schedule updates to limit noise. Automerge only low-risk updates, and only with tests (Renovate). Monitor CVE and NVD feeds, remove unused dependencies, use official sources, pin build dependencies, and track the end-of-life dates of runtimes, frameworks and operating systems (endoflife.date; Scorecard). Upgrade regularly, because deferred upgrades get harder and larger (Software Engineering at Google ch. 1, 21). Output: a current, supported dependency set with an audit trail.
- **Deprecation and removal** – Mark obsolete APIs, features and systems. Give actionable and relevant warnings. Set an owner, a deadline and milestones. Provide migration tooling, and then delete (Software Engineering at Google ch. 15). Choose advisory deprecation for small systems and compulsory deprecation with staffing for critical ones. Announce a deprecation in a minor release and remove the item in a major one (semver). Frameworks such as Django keep a shim for two feature releases. Output: less code to maintain and users on the replacement.
- **Legacy modernization, reengineering and migration** – Decide between in-place evolution, incremental displacement and a rewrite. Make the decision after the team understands the outcomes, decomposes the system by seams and plans incremental delivery (Fowler et al., Patterns of Legacy Displacement). Prefer the strangler fig: a facade routes calls, new components replace old ones piece by piece, the old system is retired, and the transitional architecture is removed (Fowler; Microsoft). Reengineering combines reverse engineering with forward engineering or restructuring (Chikofsky and Cross). Avoid feature-parity big-bang rewrites (Spolsky). Output: a modernized system and retired legacy parts.
- **Documentation maintenance** – Treat documents like code: source control, owners, reviews, and changes together with the code. Add freshness dates, and delete or mark obsolete documents (Software Engineering at Google ch. 10). Keep README, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY, SUPPORT and issue templates current (GitHub). Update user and operator documentation as part of each change; ISO 14764 3.1.9 counts "improvements of information for users" as perfective maintenance. Output: current, owned documentation and a changelog.
- **Knowledge transfer and bus-factor management** – Find single points of failure and "haunted graveyards". Write down tribal knowledge, mentor, review code, rotate duties, and reward teaching (Software Engineering at Google ch. 3). Measure the contributor absence factor – the smallest set of people who make 50 percent of the contributions (CHAOSS). Most open-source projects score 2 or less (Wikipedia, Avelino et al.). For open-source projects, recruit co-maintainers, document the governance and plan the succession (opensource.guide). Output: shared ownership and resilience to departures.
- **User support, help desk and SLA management** – Run a help desk or support tiers – self-service, first-line, second-line, product engineers, vendor (Wikipedia, Technical support) – that triggers the assessment, prioritization and costing of MRs (SWEBOK 3.2). Define severity levels by business impact (Red Hat), response and resolution targets, remedies and escalation (Atlassian). Keep SLAs (contracts with consequences) apart from SLOs (internal targets) (Google SRE). Feed support data back into the backlog (GOV.UK). Output: resolved tickets, SLA reports and improvement items.
- **Maintenance measurement and service monitoring** – Collect effort by maintenance category, the number of MRs per period, effort per MR, size, complexity, maintainability sub-characteristics and customer satisfaction, and trend them by category (SWEBOK 2.4; ISO 14764 8.5). Monitor service health indicators such as performance, support tickets and analytics (GOV.UK). Output: data for planning, estimation and process improvement.
- **Protect capacity and manage interrupts** – Decide how much of the team stays on the live service, and keep continuous improvement funded (GOV.UK). Polarize time: rotate ticket and interrupt duty so that the others keep their focus, and review classes of interrupts for root causes (Google SRE). Output: predictable capacity for both planned work and maintenance.
- **Open-source and solo-repository upkeep** – Document the scope and the response expectations. Use issue and PR templates and labels such as "good first issue". Learn to say no. Automate CI, releases and dependency updates (opensource.guide; GitHub). Publish a security policy, pass Scorecard checks (Maintained, Dependency-Update-Tool, Vulnerabilities), decide a stale-issue policy and a release cadence, seek funding or sponsorship, set time limits and take breaks (opensource.guide; actions/stale; Tidelift). Output: a healthy, maintained repository.
- **Retirement handoff (disposal)** – When users no longer need the service, or when it is not cost-effective, invoke the disposal process: strategy, notification, migration, archiving (ISO 14764 clause 7; GOV.UK). Output: the decision and plan that end this phase; the details belong to section 14.

### Outputs

- Released maintenance versions: corrections, adaptations, enhancements and emergency patches. Each version is numbered, documented in release notes or a changelog, and recorded in configuration management.
- Closed or decided MR and PR records with classification, impact analysis, approval, test evidence and links to the change (ISO 14764 6.2).
- Updated tests (including characterization and regression tests), documentation, runbooks and operator information.
- An ordered backlog and a technical debt register with explicit decisions (pay down, accept, monitor).
- Current dependency manifests and lock files, an updated inventory or SBOM, and records of security patches and upgrades.
- Deprecation notices, migration guides, and the removal of obsolete code and systems.
- Modernized or migrated components and retired legacy parts.
- Maintenance measurements: effort by category, MR counts, SLA reports, maintainability metrics, customer satisfaction.
- Knowledge artefacts: ownership files, onboarding documents, recorded decisions, governance documents.
- Exit criteria per change: reviewed, tested, approved, released, recorded, and the workaround removed.
- Exit criterion for the phase: a retirement decision when users no longer need the service or when the cost is not justified. The decision hands over to the disposal process.

### Roles

- Maintainer or maintenance organization – performs analysis, design, code, test and documentation for changes; owns the maintenance plan (ISO 14764; SWEBOK).
- Operator and help desk – run the system, record incidents, raise problem reports and modification requests, and give first-line support (ISO 14764 5.2; SWEBOK 3.2).
- Users, customers and acquirers – report problems, request modifications, and agree the release content and the service levels.
- Triage owner – makes sure that new bugs are assessed on time, sets severity and priority, and routes bugs (Mozilla triage policy); in Kubernetes, SIG triagers.
- Product owner or product manager – orders the backlog and balances features, defects and debt (Scrum Guide; Atlassian).
- Developers and engineers – implement changes, refactor, review, and keep tests green; in agile teams the same people develop and maintain (SWEBOK 2.2.5).
- Configuration control board and release manager – approve changes, decide the release content, and keep baselines (SWEBOK 3.2.3).
- Testers and QA – plan regression tests and verify fixes (Bugzilla VERIFIED state).
- Security and SRE or operations – vulnerability monitoring, patch SLOs, on-call and ticket rotations, SLOs (OWASP; Google SRE).
- Infrastructure or platform teams – run large-scale changes and compulsory deprecations for their dependents (Software Engineering at Google ch. 15, 22).
- Deprecation process owner and documentation owners – drive removals and keep documents fresh (Software Engineering at Google ch. 10, 15).
- Open-source maintainers, committers, contributors and sponsors – triage, review, release, govern and fund the project (opensource.guide).
- Suppliers and outsourcers – contracted maintenance under SLAs (SWEBOK 2.2.4).

### Practices with consensus

- **Plan and budget for maintenance from the start, because it dominates the life cycle cost** – Maintenance typically consumes 40 to 80 percent of the software cost. The maintenance phase lasts until retirement, while development lasts months. Early planning, maintainability requirements and early maintainer involvement lower the total cost. Evidence: Glass, Facts and Fallacies (fact 41); ISO/IEC/IEEE 14764:2022 introduction and clause 9; SWEBOK v4 7.1.2 and 7.3.2.2; Wikipedia, Software maintenance.
- **Classify every change by maintenance category and measure effort by category** – The corrective, preventive, adaptive, additive, perfective and emergency categories show where the money goes. They stop the misconception that bug fixing is most of the cost, and the data supports estimation. Evidence: ISO/IEC/IEEE 14764:2022 3.1; SWEBOK v4 7.1.6, 7.2.3 and 7.2.4; Lientz, Swanson and Tompkins 1978 via Schach et al. 2003.
- **Most maintenance effort is enhancement and adaptation, not bug fixing** – Surveys report over 80 percent (SWEBOK) or roughly 60 percent (Glass) of maintenance as enhancement. Maintenance is therefore continued development, and organizations should staff and value it as such. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 7.1.4; Glass facts 42 and 43; Lehman laws I and VI.
- **Triage continuously with separate severity and priority, defined levels and a fixed cadence** – Severity describes the impact; priority describes the schedule. A mix of the two conflates scope with urgency. Time-boxed triage keeps the queue honest and surfaces security issues early. Evidence: Mozilla triage policy, severity and priority guides; Kubernetes issue triage guidelines; GitLab issue triage tutorial; Red Hat severity definitions; ISO/IEC/IEEE 14764 impact analysis tasks via SWEBOK 7.2.1.3.
- **Keep an automated regression suite and put code under test before a change** – Regression testing is selective retesting that shows the change caused no unintended effects. Code without tests is legacy code; characterization tests pin the current behavior, so that changes become verifiable. Thorough tests make arbitrary changes safe. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 7.2.1.2; Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code (preface, ch. 13); Software Engineering at Google ch. 1 and 22; Renovate automerge guidance.
- **Refactor continuously in small, behavior-preserving steps as part of normal work** – Cruft slows every later change. Gradual improvement in frequently changed areas pays the highest return and keeps the system releasable. Evidence: refactoring.com; Fowler, TechnicalDebt and OpportunisticRefactoring; SWEBOK v4 7.4.2; Cunningham 1992.
- **Make technical debt explicit, record it, and decide on it deliberately** – Invisible debt cripples velocity. A list of debt items in the backlog or in a register, with impact and effort, lets teams prioritize paydown against features and shows the cost of inaction. Evidence: Kruchten, Nord and Ozkaya 2012; Fowler, TechnicalDebtQuadrant; GOV.UK, Classifying and measuring tech debt; Atlassian technical debt guide; SWEBOK v4 7.2.3.1.
- **Keep dependencies current with automation, an inventory and vulnerability monitoring** – Outdated components are a top-10 web risk. Automated update PRs, CVE monitoring, the removal of unused dependencies and regular small upgrades beat rare large ones, which grow harder with every deferred release. Evidence: OWASP Top 10 A06:2021; GitHub Dependabot docs; Renovate docs; OpenSSF Scorecard checks; Software Engineering at Google ch. 1 and 21.
- **Track end-of-life dates and follow published support policies for runtimes and frameworks** – Unsupported platforms stop receiving security fixes. A known calendar lets teams schedule adaptive maintenance instead of a reaction. Evidence: endoflife.date; Node.js release schedule; Python devguide versions; Django release process; Ubuntu release cycle; OWASP A06.
- **Prefer incremental replacement over big-bang rewrites for legacy systems** – Cut-over rewrites delay value, lose embedded bug fixes and fail on feature parity. Strangler-fig displacement spreads risk and investment over time and delivers early. Evidence: Fowler, StranglerFigApplication and Patterns of Legacy Displacement; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Strangler Fig; Spolsky 2000; Software Engineering at Google ch. 15.
- **Deprecate with notice, owners, warnings, a migration path and a removal date, then actually remove** – Code is a liability; two systems that do one job cost more than one. Hyrum's law means that every observable behavior has dependents, so removal needs discovery tooling, actionable warnings and backsliding prevention. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 15 and 22; hyrumslaw.com; semver.org; Django deprecation policy; Keep a Changelog.
- **Treat documentation like code: owned, reviewed, versioned and pruned** – Documents without owners go stale. Freshness dates, reviews in the normal workflow and the deletion of obsolete pages keep documentation trustworthy for maintainers. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 10; opensource.guide best practices; GitHub community health files; Keep a Changelog.
- **Spread knowledge and reduce single points of failure** – A bus factor of one stalls a project. Documentation, mentoring, code review, rotation and co-maintainers make the system changeable by more than one person. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 3; Wikipedia, Bus factor (Avelino et al. 2016); CHAOSS contributor absence factor; opensource.guide leadership and governance.
- **Run large or cross-cutting changes with tooling, sharding, testing and backsliding prevention, not long-lived branches** – Changes that cannot be atomic need automation and ownership-based shards. Branch by abstraction and parallel change keep the trunk releasable throughout. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google ch. 22; Fowler, BranchByAbstraction and ParallelChange.
- **Define support levels with the SLA separate from the SLO, and route severe issues fast** – An SLA is a contract with consequences; an SLO is an internal target. Severity by business impact plus response and resolution targets sets expectations and focuses the work. Evidence: Google SRE book, Service Level Objectives; Atlassian SLA guide; Red Hat severity policy; SWEBOK v4 7.3.2.
- **Protect the capacity and the well-being of maintainers** – Interrupt work destroys flow. Dedicated ticket rotations and a written scope let maintainers say no. Unpaid, solo maintainers burn out and quit, which is a security and continuity risk. Evidence: Google SRE book, Dealing with Interrupts; opensource.guide best practices; Tidelift 2024 maintainer survey; Ford Foundation, Roads and Bridges.

### Contested points

- **How maintenance effort is really distributed across categories** – The 1978 survey by Lientz, Swanson and Tompkins reported 17.4 percent corrective, 18.2 percent adaptive and 60.3 percent perfective work. SWEBOK and Glass repeat the "mostly enhancement" message. Schach et al. (2003) measured the change logs of three products. They found corrective maintenance more than twice the survey value, and three times the value in the combined data. The answer depends on the product type, the maturity and the way categories are recorded. Any single percentage is indicative only.
- **Should the development team also maintain, or should a separate maintenance organization do it** – SWEBOK lists the pros and cons of both. A single product team responds faster and keeps maintainability in focus, but failures disrupt new development and knowledge concentrates in few people. A separate function needs a handoff, and people dislike maintenance-only roles. Agile and product-management practice favours one team. Outsourced, regulated or legacy portfolios often use a separate maintainer. SWEBOK says: decide case by case, and keep the documentation regardless.
- **Rewrite versus incremental modernization** – Spolsky calls a from-scratch rewrite the single worst strategic mistake. Fowler, Thoughtworks and Microsoft recommend incremental displacement. Google observes that in-place evolution usually costs less once the turndown is counted. Microsoft lists the cases where the strangler fig does not fit: calls cannot be intercepted, there is no access to the legacy source, the system is small, or fast decommissioning is required. Wikipedia also notes rewrites when the source is unavailable or when a license forbids reuse. The choice depends on size, risk, access and the required speed.
- **What counts as technical debt and how to measure it** – Cunningham meant code that no longer matches the current understanding, and he insists that the metaphor never justifies poor code. Fowler's quadrant separates prudent from reckless and deliberate from inadvertent debt. Kruchten, Nord and Ozkaya limit debt to the invisible results of past decisions and exclude defects and missing features. They warn against an equation of debt with what static analyzers detect. SonarQube-style remediation effort and debt ratio give comparable numbers but miss architectural and technological debt. Teams must decide how broad the term is and combine tool metrics with human judgement.
- **How to fund debt paydown: fixed budget, opportunistic refactoring, or register-driven prioritization** – Fowler argues that opportunistic refactoring should be continuous and should not need a special backlog allocation, with zero tolerance for cruft in high-churn areas. Atlassian recommends that teams address debt inside sprints with a strict definition of done. GOV.UK used a central register with impact and effort ratings and a support team that prioritized platform stability, then support burden, then debt. Kruchten et al. want debt tasks in the common backlog. Fixed percentages are common in industry, but no authoritative source in this record prescribes one. The right mix depends on the debt level, the churn and the organizational trust.
- **Dependency update cadence: live at head and automerge versus cooldowns and pinning** – Google's internal model is "live at head" with CI as the evidence, and Google argues that semantic versioning is lossy shorthand. Dependabot applies a default three-day cooldown for version updates. Renovate recommends automerge only for low-risk updates (lock file maintenance, dev dependencies, non-major) and only with tests. OpenSSF Scorecard rewards the pinning of build dependencies by hash. OWASP warns that monthly or quarterly patching under change control leaves exposure. The choice depends on test strength, supply-chain risk appetite and release cadence.
- **Advisory versus compulsory deprecation** – Google finds that advisory deprecations work only when the replacement is compelling ("hope is not a strategy" – the migration needs a plan, not hope), and that compulsory deprecations need staffing, otherwise they become unfunded mandates. Open-source ecosystems mostly use advisory deprecation with semver signals and long notice (Django: two feature releases; Node.js: 30 months of LTS). The choice depends on whether one organization can fund and enforce the migration.
- **Automatic closure of stale issues and pull requests** – Kubernetes marks issues stale after 90 days and closes them unless they are frozen. actions/stale defaults to 60 days plus 7. opensource.guide stresses explicit, documented "no" decisions and templates rather than guilt-driven silence, and maintainer capacity is finite (60 percent unpaid per Tidelift). Automatic closure trades contributor goodwill for a manageable queue. The right setting depends on the volume, the response capacity and the exemption rules.
- **Long-term-support lines versus short support windows** – Ubuntu offers 5 years of standard support and up to 15 years with paid extensions. Django and Node.js designate LTS releases. Python supports each version for 5 years. Go supports only the two newest major releases. Longer support eases consumers and regulated deployments, but it multiplies backports and keeps old code alive. Short windows force regular upgrades. The choice depends on the audience, the deployment cycle and the maintainer capacity.
- **How much of the maintenance effort is program comprehension** – Glass states that understanding the existing product takes roughly 30 percent of the maintenance time and is the hardest task. SWEBOK v4 says "a significant portion" without a number. Tooling, documentation quality and team continuity change the share, so estimates vary widely.
- **Tiered support versus product-team-owned support** – Classical tiered models (self-service, L1 to L3, vendor) resolve most cases cheaply at the lower tiers (Wikipedia, Technical support). GOV.UK keeps the service team accountable for support data and improvement in the live phase, and Google SRE assigns ticket duty rotations inside the team. The choice depends on ticket volume, criticality and whether support knowledge should flow back into the product.

### Metrics

- Effort and cost by maintenance category (corrective, preventive, adaptive, additive, perfective, emergency), trended per period – SWEBOK 7.2.4. Caveat: survey data understates corrective work compared with measured change logs (Schach et al.).
- Number of MRs and PRs per period, effort per request, queue size and age, time to triage, and time from report to fix by severity – SWEBOK; Mozilla; Kubernetes. Caveat: zero-bug targets distort behavior; Mozilla aims to prevent backlog degradation rather than zero.
- SLA and SLO attainment: response and resolution time by severity, uptime – Atlassian; Google SRE. Caveat: an SLA without consequences is really an SLO.
- Regression and reopen indicators: escaped regressions per release, reopened bugs, VERIFIED versus RESOLVED counts – Bugzilla life cycle. Caveat: the numbers depend on consistent use of the workflow.
- Technical debt measures: remediation effort, technical debt ratio (debt divided by the cost to develop), maintainability rating A to E, cognitive complexity – SonarQube. Caveat: tools detect only code-level debt, not architectural or technological debt (Kruchten et al.).
- Maintainability sub-characteristics: modularity, reusability, analysability, modifiability, testability, supportability – SWEBOK 7.2.4 (ISO/IEC 25010 model). Caveat: they need baselines and context.
- Dependency health: the count of outdated and vulnerable dependencies, the age of the oldest unmerged update PR, and Scorecard scores for Maintained (at least one commit per week over 90 days), Dependency-Update-Tool, Vulnerabilities and Pinned-Dependencies – OpenSSF Scorecard. Caveat: activity is a proxy, not proof of quality.
- End-of-life exposure: the number of components past or within N months of the end of support – endoflife.date; Node.js, Python and Ubuntu schedules. Caveat: support dates differ between vendors, and paid extensions move them.
- Bus factor or contributor absence factor: the minimum number of contributors who produce 50 percent of the contributions – CHAOSS. Caveat: commit counts ignore review and knowledge work.
- Debt register health: items open, items resolved, high-impact items, age – GOV.UK practice. Caveat: the register shows only the debt that people recorded.
- Documentation freshness: the share of documents past their review date, and documents without an owner – Software Engineering at Google ch. 10. Caveat: a recent review date does not prove that the content is correct.
- Lehman-style evolution trends: size growth per release, complexity growth, effort per release – Lehman 1996. Caveat: the laws are statistical observations on E-type systems, not targets.
- Customer or user satisfaction with maintenance and support – SWEBOK 7.3.2.1. Caveat: satisfaction is subjective and lags behind the causes.
- Maintainer sustainability signals for open source: the number of active maintainers, the share that is paid, the response time to issues, and the time since the last release – Tidelift 2024; opensource.guide. Caveat: surveys are self-reported, and project-level counts do not show how much time each maintainer has.

### Failure modes

- Maintenance treated as low-status work and understaffed – maintainers leave, knowledge is lost, and the largest cost phase gets the least attention (Glass fact 43; SWEBOK staffing).
- Reaction only to incidents – technical debt and security exposure build up until a change becomes expensive (GOV.UK Service Manual; Lehman laws II and VII).
- "Haunted graveyards" – Google's term for business-critical code that nobody dares to change, because it has no tests and nobody understands it (Software Engineering at Google ch. 3, 22).
- Big-bang rewrites and feature-parity traps – years without shippable code, lost embedded bug fixes, and competitors gain time (Spolsky; Fowler et al.).
- Deferred upgrades – each skipped release makes the next upgrade larger and more painful, and end-of-life platforms stop getting security fixes (Software Engineering at Google ch. 1, 21; OWASP A06).
- Deprecation without owners, staffing or removal dates – unfunded mandates, repeated backsliding, and two systems maintained forever (Software Engineering at Google ch. 15).
- Warning and alert fatigue – too many non-actionable deprecation or dependency warnings, so engineers ignore all of them (Software Engineering at Google ch. 15; Renovate on notification noise).
- Use of the debt metaphor as an excuse for sloppy code, or the belief that agile iteration makes a team immune to debt – the metaphor loses its value and the debt grows unseen (Cunningham; Kruchten et al.).
- Debt measured only by what static analysis finds – architectural and technological debt stay invisible (Kruchten et al.).
- Severity conflated with priority, no triage cadence, needinfo requests left open, or a backlog that nobody prunes – the queue loses its meaning and urgent items hide among stale ones (Mozilla; Kubernetes; Scrum Guide).
- Code changed without tests – "edit and pray" instead of "cover and modify" (Feathers's terms for a change without and with a test safety net), or regression tests skipped because full retesting is expensive, so defects escape (Feathers; SWEBOK 7.2.1.2).
- Long-lived branches for large changes – merge conflicts and integration pain; branch by abstraction or sharded large-scale changes avoid them (Fowler; Google ch. 22).
- Dependency updates automerged without tests, or everything pinned and never upgraded – either broken builds or growing exposure (Renovate; Scorecard).
- Users broken by a change to observable behavior that the contract never promised – Hyrum's law (hyrumslaw.com; Google ch. 21).
- Documentation without owners or freshness checks – stale documents mislead maintainers (Google ch. 10).
- Bus factor of one and maintainer burnout – 60 percent of open-source maintainers are unpaid, and 61 percent of the unpaid ones work solo; the xz backdoor showed how a lone maintainer becomes an attack surface (Tidelift; OpenSSF; Wikipedia, Bus factor).
- Enhancements grouped with corrections in reports – management concludes that bug fixing costs more than it does (SWEBOK 7.1.4).
- Handoff friction between developers and a separate maintenance team, or developers pulled off new work by production failures – both slow delivery and maintenance (SWEBOK 7.2.2.5).
- No disposal decision – services kept alive with few users and rising cost (GOV.UK; ISO 14764 clause 7).

### Tailoring by project size

Some practices are essential at every scale: a record of every change request and bug; a classification habit (fix, adaptation, enhancement, prevention, emergency); automated tests that CI runs before a change lands; a published version and a changelog per release; automated dependency updates and vulnerability alerts; awareness of the end-of-life dates for the runtime, the framework and the OS; small continuous refactoring; documentation updated together with the code; and at least one other person, or a written record, that can take over. The table below shows what each scale adds and what stays optional.

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| Solo developer on a small repository | Keep it light. Use the issue tracker as the backlog and as the debt register; labels are enough. Enable Dependabot or Renovate with grouping and a cooldown, and add a security policy file. Triage in a fixed weekly slot; close what you will not do and say why. Use semver and Keep a Changelog. Write the README, CONTRIBUTING and SUPPORT expectations so that you can say no. Pick a stale policy consciously. Set time limits, plan succession or archiving, and consider sponsorship. | SLAs; formal impact analysis; LTS branches; stale bots; governance documents. |
| Small product team | Add one ordered backlog that shows features, defects, architecture work and debt side by side; weekly refinement; a named triage owner with written severity and priority levels; agreed support hours and response targets, with SLOs before SLAs; an interrupt or ticket rotation; a lightweight debt register with impact and effort; automerge only for low-risk dependency updates with tests; a deprecation policy for your APIs; documentation owners and freshness checks; pairing and code review that keep the bus factor above one; effort by category measured from the tracker. | A formal ISO 14764 maintenance plan; LTS releases; large-scale-change tooling; tiered support. |
| Large or regulated organization | Make the process explicit and auditable: a maintenance strategy and plan per ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 and 14764; MR and PR records with impact analysis; CCB approvals; traceability to tests and releases; SLAs with users and suppliers; measurement by category; a disposal process. Add a component inventory or SBOM with CVE monitoring and patch SLOs; a published LTS and security support policy; a deprecation program with owners, milestones, discovery and migration tooling; static checks that block backsliding; an authorized large-scale-change process run by platform teams. Invest in knowledge programs (mentoring, readability, rotation) and in dedicated maintenance or support capacity, so that product teams keep their delivery capacity. Keep records as evidence for regulators and for the eventual retirement. | Most elements above are mandatory at this scale; optional choices are the support model (tiered versus product-team-owned), the length of the LTS windows, and the degree of automerge for dependency updates. |
