## 14. Retirement and disposal

### Purpose

Retirement ends the operational life of a software system, a service, an API, a component or a package in a controlled way. It answers four questions. Is the system still worth the cost to run it? Who depends on it? What happens to its data and its users? How does the organization remove it without risk, cost or legal exposure that remains behind? ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 gives the Disposal process three purposes. End the existence of a system or a system element for a specified use. Handle replaced or retired elements and waste products. Attend to critical disposal needs that agreement, policy, environment, law, safety or security set. Software Engineering at Google adds the economic reason: code is a liability, not an asset, and an obsolete system costs money and attention until someone removes it.

A good retirement keeps what must be kept: records, evidence, knowledge and a pointer to the successor. It destroys what must not persist: personal data, secrets, dangling DNS records, unused accounts and billing. It also makes the removal an explicit, owned and verified project. It does not rely on the hope that usage will fade by itself.

### Other names

- Disposal process – ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, technical process 6.4.14.
- Retirement stage – the ISO/IEC/IEEE 24748-1 life cycle stage; SWEBOK v4 uses the same name.
- System disposal – NIST SP 800-37 RMF Task M-7.
- Component disposal – NIST SP 800-53 control SR-12.
- Phase F: Closeout – NASA Systems Engineering Handbook.
- Service retirement, retired services – ITIL service portfolio.
- Application retirement, "Retire" – one of the AWS 7 Rs migration strategies.
- Decommissioning, teardown, turndown (Google), turn-off, shutdown.
- End of life (EOL), end of support (EOS), end of sale, sunsetting, sunset policy.
- Deprecation – of APIs, libraries, packages, features and flags; yanking or retraction – of package versions.
- Archiving – of repositories, of projects on PyPI, of records; mothballing – preservation for a possible return to service.
- Legacy displacement, legacy decommissioning – martinfowler.com.

### Position in the life cycle

Retirement follows operation (see section 12) and maintenance (see section 13). It is the last technical process in ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, where its name is Disposal. It is also the last stage, "retirement", in the ISO/IEC/IEEE 24748-1 stage model that SWEBOK v4 quotes. SWEBOK v4 says that the maintenance phase "usually lasts until the software is retired by the disposal process". SWEBOK v4 also lists "Retire the software" as one of the reasons for maintenance work.

In sequential models – waterfall, the V-model and NASA Phase F – retirement is the closing phase. It is usually paired with the transition of a replacement. NIST SP 800-160 v1r1 notes that an organization commissions a new system and decommissions the old one with the Transition and Disposal processes at the same time. In the NIST Risk Management Framework, retirement is Task M-7 in the Monitor step. NIST SP 800-53 SR-12 notes that disposal activities occur throughout the SDLC, not only at the end.

In iterative and agile work, retirement is mostly a continuous process. Teams deprecate and remove features, endpoints, flags, API versions, library versions, environments and cloud resources release by release. Rules such as Semantic Versioning, PEP 387 or the Kubernetes deprecation policy set the cadence. In DevOps and continuous delivery, teams automate decommissioning with infrastructure as code, with lifecycle and retention policies, and with automatic decommissioning of resources (AWS Well-Architected COST04).

So retirement is both a one-time phase for a whole system and a recurring process for its parts. The retirement of one system often feeds the concept phase of its successor (see section 3). NIST SP 800-37 describes an SDLC that ends in a disposal, and that disposal can start another system initiation.

### Inputs

- A documented retirement decision and its trigger. Triggers in the sources include: a negative cost-benefit or lock-in analysis (SWEBOK v4 economics, "retirement decisions"); low business value with low quality (the legacy assessment in Sommerville); zombie or idle workloads (AWS: CPU and memory under 5 percent, or no inbound connection for 90 days); a replacement that is ready; a vendor end of life; a policy or contract change; a security risk that cannot be fixed; a user need that no longer exists (GOV.UK).
- Portfolio and inventory records: the CMDB or asset register entry, the system component inventory, the security and privacy plans, risk assessment results (the NIST SP 800-37 Task M-7 inputs) and infrastructure-as-code definitions.
- A dependency and consumer map: upstream and downstream systems, API clients, data feeds, scheduled jobs, integrations, third-party services, and the owner of each (AWS "capture dependencies"; Google discovery tooling).
- A data inventory with classification, the retention schedule or records policy, the legal hold status and the applicable law (GDPR Articles 5 and 17, the HIPAA six-year documentation rule, sector rules).
- Contracts, licenses, SLAs, processor agreements (the return-or-delete clause in GDPR Article 28(3)(g)) and vendor notice obligations.
- A list of users and stakeholders with their channels. The list includes assisted-digital and offline users, and API consumers who need long lead times (GOV.UK).
- Evidence that the replacement meets its acceptance criteria, if a replacement exists – for example functional parity and performance benchmarks met for 30 days (Azure CAF).
- Formal approval to proceed: workload and business owner sign-off (Azure CAF), a change request through change management (AWS), or the decision of an authorizing official in regulated settings (NIST RMF).
- Funds and staff for the deprecation and migration work. Google warns that compulsory deprecations without staff fail.
- Entry criteria: the decision is recorded, an owner is named, the plan is approved, the data disposition is decided, notice is given or scheduled, and a rollback path is defined.

### Activities

- **Assess and decide end of life** – Review the system against cost, value, quality, risk and strategy. Decide whether to keep, re-engineer, replace or scrap it. SWEBOK v4 frames a retirement decision as an exit from an activity altogether, planned or spontaneous, and influenced by lock-in and exit costs. Google warns that old is not the same as obsolete, and that in-place evolution is often cheaper than replacement plus turndown. The output is a recorded decision with rationale, scope and a target date.
- **Appoint an owner and write the retirement plan** – Name an accountable owner and a team. Then write a disposal strategy and plan: scope, schedule, milestones, resources, communication, data disposition, rollback and success criteria. Google states that without explicit owners a deprecation is unlikely to progress. NIST SP 800-37 Task M-7 expects a disposal strategy as an output, and NIST SP 800-160 task DS-1 defines its security aspects. Change management approves the plan (see section 15).
- **Discover dependencies and consumers** – Find every caller, integration, data feed, scheduled job, downstream report and operational tool that touches the system. Use code search, build graphs, logs, network monitoring, CMDB data and, where necessary, short intentional outages to reveal hidden users (Google). AWS recommends that the team records owner, billing, hosting and replication details. AWS also warns that assets labelled "no longer required" are often still consumed elsewhere. The output is a dependency register with named contacts.
- **Announce the deprecation and give notice** – Tell users, stakeholders, API consumers, support channels and the service portfolio what changes, when it changes, what they must do, and what happens to their data (GOV.UK). Use a fixed date and the users' own channels, including posters or contact centres for assisted-digital users. Notice periods in the sources range from 30 days for a required action to 12 months for the end of a service (Microsoft, Google Cloud terms), and a minimum five-year support period under the EU Cyber Resilience Act. The output is a dated notice record.
- **Emit deprecation signals in code, APIs and registries** – Mark the element as deprecated where users will see it: compiler or runtime warnings (PEP 387, JEP 277 forRemoval), HTTP Deprecation and Sunset headers with links to migration documents (RFC 9745, RFC 8594), API warnings and metrics (Kubernetes), package registry deprecation messages (npm deprecate), Go module "Deprecated:" comments, and PyPI archival notices. Release the deprecation in a minor version before you remove the element in a major version (SemVer). Warnings must be actionable and relevant, so that they do not cause alert fatigue (Google).
- **Migrate users and data and cut over to the replacement** – Move users, data and integrations to the successor, if one exists. Give export or portability support (GDPR Article 20), and do the transfer under the data-protection policy with the users informed (GOV.UK). Prefer an incremental cutover: parallel operation (SEBoK), a transitional architecture, event interception, canary release and progressive routing (martinfowler.com legacy displacement; see section 11). Keep the rollback path until the success criteria hold (Azure CAF). Remove the transitional scaffolding when it has served its purpose. The output is a cutover report.
- **Freeze, restrict and shut down in a controlled way** – Stop new sign-ups or writes, and make the system read-only. Then apply restrictive controls for a period to confirm that nothing still needs the system, but keep the ability to revert (AWS COST04-BP02 "prevent access"). Then decouple the application from upstream and downstream services, shut it down, and remove schedules and cron jobs so that it cannot relaunch (AWS). Preserve the settings and document the uninstall so that the team can repeat or reverse it.
- **Archive records, documentation and knowledge** – Select what must be kept under the retention schedule, the law or a legal hold. Archive it in a usable, access-controlled, immutable form with documented retrieval procedures, and test those procedures before shutdown (Azure CAF, National Archives digital continuity). Archive architecture, runbooks, decisions and data with deprecation notices and timestamps. NIST SP 800-160 task DS-3.3 and NASA Phase F require an archive of technical information to permit audits and to build a knowledge base. Share the findings with the successor team (GOV.UK).
- **Delete personal data and sanitise storage** – Erase data that is no longer necessary (GDPR Articles 5(1)(e) and 17), including copies in backups, or put it beyond use (ICO). Make processors delete or return data at the end of the contract (Article 28(3)(g)). Sanitise media with a method that matches the sensitivity: clear, purge or destroy. Cryptographic erase is often the only purge option for cloud and virtual storage (NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, NCSC). Verify the result and record a certificate of sanitization or other deletion evidence (NIST SP 800-88 Appendix C, ISO 27002 8.10). Keep the records that the law requires before you sanitise.
- **Tear down infrastructure and remove code** – Destroy compute, storage, databases including DR and backup instances, load balancers, auto scaling groups, images, snapshots, elastic IPs and environments. Prefer the infrastructure-as-code tooling that created them (AWS COST04-BP02). Record the metadata and take final backups first if policy requires them, and check minimum-storage-duration fees. Delete the retired code paths and add backsliding prevention so that nobody reintroduces them (Google). The output is an empty resource inventory for the system.
- **Clean up DNS, certificates, domains and redirects** – Remove DNS records that point at decommissioned resources; a dangling record invites a subdomain takeover (OWASP WSTG, GOV.UK "retire a repo"). Revoke public and private certificates, or let them expire, and reclaim IP addresses (AWS). Keep a secure redirect from the old address to the successor or to a retirement page for a defined period. GOV.UK gives two cases: a service that was live for less than 6 months keeps TLS and redirects until one year after it went live. A service that was live for longer keeps them for one year after retirement, or until the current certificate expires, whichever comes first. Decide the fate of the domain and guard it against re-registration.
- **Revoke access, secrets, accounts and integrations** – Remove user and service accounts, API keys, tokens, OAuth apps, webhooks, deploy keys, SSO entries and third-party SaaS connections. Disconnect the system from monitoring, alerting, patching, backup, configuration, release, security, antivirus and encryption tooling so that nothing continues to touch it (AWS "disconnect operational tools"). NIST SP 800-37 adds a review of control inheritance relationships. The output is a completed access and integration checklist.
- **Terminate licenses, contracts and subscriptions and reclaim cost** – Identify the licenses tied to the system. Then cancel, transfer or reassign them, update the license register and the CMDB, and notify the vendors so that costs are recovered (AWS, Azure CAF). Cancel SaaS subscriptions, support contracts and paid plans. Confirm that billing drops to zero, and watch for residual charges such as archived repositories on legacy billing plans (GitHub). Record the realised savings.
- **Update inventories, catalogues and documentation** – Update the CMDB, the asset register, the service catalogue (retired services with historical information, ITIL), the system component inventory, and the security and privacy plans (NIST SP 800-37 Task M-7 outputs). Replace architecture diagrams, on-call rotas, runbooks, escalation paths and monitoring dashboards. Mark legacy documents as deprecated with redirects to the current ones (Azure CAF). This prevents wasted incident time on assets that no longer exist.
- **Retire repositories and packages** – Add a retirement notice and a successor pointer to the README, close issues and pull requests, cancel workflows, and then archive the repository rather than delete it (GitHub, GOV.UK). A deletion removes team permissions and private forks permanently, and only some repositories can be restored within 90 days (GitHub). Deprecate package versions with a message rather than unpublish them, because an unpublish breaks dependants (npm). Yank or retract only broken or vulnerable versions (PyPI, cargo, Go). Accept that some registries are immutable (Maven Central). Remove Pages sites and their DNS. Transfer the repository if another owner takes over; redirects follow the transfer.
- **Offer open-sourcing or hand-over** – Where the code or the knowledge still has value, open-source it, or hand it to a successor, a community fork or another organization. GOV.UK suggests that the team shares knowledge and open-sources elements when the private or voluntary sector takes over. opensource.guide advises maintainers to ask someone to take over and to link to an active fork. Before publication, review the code for secrets, licensing and ownership (GOV.UK open-source guidance). Mark the project status clearly if it will be unmaintained.
- **Monitor after retirement and close the grace period** – Watch for traffic to old endpoints, load balancers and redirects during a defined period (AWS, Kubernetes, GOV.UK redirect rules). Watch also for deprecated-API metrics, failed integrations, support contacts and audit alerts. Keep a rollback or restore path until the grace period ends (Azure CAF). Monitor periodically for dangling DNS (OWASP). Then perform the final deletion of retained snapshots that are no longer needed.
- **Verify, evidence, learn and close** – Confirm that no detrimental security factors remain, that the environment is in the agreed secure state, and that archives and baselines are in place (NIST SP 800-160 DS-3). Collect evidence: approvals, notices, deletion and sanitization certificates, inventory updates and cost records. Hold a lessons-learned review and file the final report (NASA Phase F). Assign named owners for residual obligations such as retention expiry and redirect sunset. Then obtain sign-off.
- **Dispose of hardware and meet environmental rules** – For systems with physical elements, sanitise or destroy media before release, reuse or recycling (NIST SP 800-53 MP-6, SP 800-88). Prevent components from re-entry into the supply chain (SR-12, SP 800-160 DS-1.7). Obey environmental and hazardous-material law (SEBoK). Decide between disposal and mothballing with periodic inspections if a return to service is possible.

### Outputs

- An approved retirement decision and a disposal strategy or plan, with owner, scope, dates and rollback (the NIST SP 800-37 Task M-7 output "disposal strategy").
- A dependency and consumer register with sign-off from each dependent owner.
- Dated deprecation notices, sunset dates and a communication log; runtime and registry deprecation markers in place.
- A migration and cutover report, data export and transfer evidence, and the acceptance record of the successor.
- Archived records, documentation and knowledge with retention metadata, access controls and tested retrieval procedures.
- Deletion and sanitization evidence: certificates of sanitization, processor deletion confirmations and erasure logs (NIST SP 800-88 Appendix C; ISO 27002 8.10).
- Infrastructure teardown confirmation: an empty resource inventory; DNS and certificates cleaned; accounts, secrets and integrations removed; monitoring and backup jobs stopped.
- License and contract termination confirmations, and a record of cost savings.
- An updated CMDB, asset register, service catalogue (retired), component inventory, security and privacy plans, diagrams and runbooks.
- An archived repository with a README notice and a successor pointer; deprecated package versions; a transfer or an open-source release if chosen.
- Post-retirement monitoring results, and the end date for redirects and residual obligations.
- A lessons-learned record and a final closure report with sign-off.
- Exit criteria: no active consumers; data disposition complete and evidenced; all resources, accounts, secrets, DNS and billing removed; required records archived; the monitoring period passed without incident; remaining obligations assigned to named owners.

### Roles

- Product, service or workload owner – makes or sponsors the decision, approves the plan, and signs off completion (Azure CAF; in the NIST RMF the system owner holds primary responsibility for Task M-7).
- Engineering team or maintainers – perform the technical removal, emit deprecation signals, migrate code and tear down infrastructure. Google recommends a dedicated deprecation team that does the migration work for consumers.
- Operations, SRE, DevOps, platform and network teams – controlled shutdown, IaC destroy, DNS, certificates, load balancers, monitoring removal and post-retirement monitoring.
- Security professionals and the system security officer – disposal security strategy, access revocation, sanitization and dangling-resource checks (NIST SP 800-160; the security.gov.uk activity described in the GOV.UK context).
- Privacy officer or DPO, and legal or compliance staff – erasure, retention, legal hold, processor obligations and regulatory notices.
- Records management officer or archivist – advises on retention so that sanitization does not destroy records that must be kept (NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2).
- Change manager or change advisory board, and authorizing official – approvals, audit trail and risk acceptance.
- Finance, FinOps, procurement, license and asset managers – contract termination, license reclamation, billing checks, CMDB and asset register updates.
- Communications and support staff, contact centres – user notices, assisted-digital channels and post-retirement queries (GOV.UK).
- Users, API consumers, downstream teams, and third-party suppliers or processors – migrate, confirm that no dependency remains, and delete or return data.
- Successor team, community or receiving organization – receives knowledge, data, code or a transferred repository.

### Practices with consensus

- **Treat removal as an owned, planned and staffed project with a written plan and explicit milestones** – Deprecation work is invisible until it is finished, and it competes badly with visible maintenance. Without an owner and staff it stalls, or it lands on consumers as an unfunded mandate. Evidence: Software Engineering at Google, Chapter 15; NIST SP 800-37 Task M-7 (disposal strategy); NIST SP 800-160 DS-1; AWS application retirement best practices; SWEBOK v4 (retirement plan and decisions).
- **Map dependencies and consumers before you switch anything off, and notify each owner** – Hidden consumers break when a system disappears: Hyrum's law, forgotten batch jobs and downstream reports. Documentation and subject-matter experts are often gone. Evidence: AWS "Capture dependencies" and "assessing applications to be retired"; Software Engineering at Google (discovery tooling, intentional outages); NIST SP 800-37 Task M-7 (notify users and application owners).
- **Give advance notice with a fixed date through the users' own channels, and give API consumers the longest lead time** – Users and integrators need time to change software and processes. Predictable notice is written into vendor terms and into law. Evidence: GOV.UK "Retiring your service"; Microsoft Modern Lifecycle Policy (30 days to act, 12 months before the end of support); Google Cloud terms 1.4(e) (12 months); Kubernetes deprecation policy; EU Cyber Resilience Act Article 13; RFC 9745 and RFC 8594.
- **Deprecate before you remove: ship at least one release with visible, actionable warnings and a migration path, then remove in a breaking release** – Warnings give consumers a chance to move without surprise. The warnings must be targeted, or consumers ignore them. Evidence: Semantic Versioning FAQ; PEP 387; JEP 277; Kubernetes deprecation policy (warnings, audit annotations, metrics); npm deprecation docs; Software Engineering at Google (actionable and relevant warnings).
- **In registries and code hosting, prefer deprecate, archive, yank or retract over unpublish or delete** – Published artefacts are build inputs for others. Removal breaks downstream builds without warning; deprecation keeps the artefacts installable with a signal. Evidence: npm deprecation docs and unpublish policy; PyPI archival and yanking docs; cargo yank; Go module retract and Deprecated comments; Maven Central immutability FAQ; GitHub archiving versus deleting; GOV.UK "Retire a repo".
- **Decide the disposition of every data set from the retention schedule: delete what is no longer necessary, keep what law or legal hold requires, and evidence both** – Storage limitation and the right to erasure forbid the retention of personal data without need. Audit, tax, health and legal rules require the retention of certain records for years. Evidence: GDPR Articles 5(1)(e), 17 and 28(3)(g); ICO storage limitation guidance; ISO 27002:2022 control 8.10 (as summarised by ISMS.online); 45 CFR 164.316 (HIPAA six years); NIST SP 800-37 Task M-7 (record retention); Azure CAF; NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (records management officer).
- **Sanitise storage with a method that matches the data sensitivity, verify the result and keep a record; use cryptographic erase for cloud and virtual storage** – Residual data on released media is a common leak path. Multi-pass overwrites are obsolete and ineffective on SSDs. Cloud customers cannot reach the physical media. Evidence: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (clear, purge, destroy, cryptographic erase, verification, certificate of sanitization); NCSC secure sanitisation guidance; NIST SP 800-53 MP-6 and SR-12.
- **Remove DNS records, certificates, accounts, secrets, integrations and operational tooling hooks as part of teardown, and keep secure redirects for a defined period** – Dangling DNS enables a subdomain takeover. Stale accounts and keys widen the attack surface. Forgotten tooling hooks generate noise and cost. Evidence: OWASP WSTG "Test for Subdomain Takeover"; GOV.UK "Retire a repo" and "Retiring your service"; AWS "Remove network assets" and "Disconnect operational tools"; AWS COST04-BP02.
- **Update the CMDB, inventories, service catalogue and documentation, and archive legacy documents with deprecation notices** – Stale records cause wasted incident time, false alerts and compliance gaps. The portfolio must show the service as retired. Evidence: NIST SP 800-37 Task M-7 (updated inventory and plans); AWS "Update asset information"; Azure CAF "Update documentation"; ITIL retired services catalogue (itsm.tools).
- **Reclaim licenses and stop billing, and automate resource decommissioning where possible** – Cost is a large part of the justification for retirement. Unused licenses, zombie resources and forgotten backups continue to charge. Evidence: AWS Well-Architected COST04 (BP02–BP05); AWS "Perform license management"; Azure CAF "Reclaim and optimize software licenses"; AWS 7 Rs "Retire".
- **Cut over to a replacement incrementally with parallel operation, explicit success criteria and a rollback path; remove transitional scaffolding afterwards** – A big-bang replacement of a system that works is the highest-risk option. The team must plan service continuity for consumers. Evidence: SEBoK "System Disposal and Retirement" (parallel operation); martinfowler.com "Patterns of Legacy Displacement"; Azure CAF (success criteria, grace period); NIST SP 800-160 (Transition and Disposal used concurrently).
- **Archive knowledge and lessons learned, and share them with the successor** – Retirement is the point where an organization loses institutional knowledge. Future systems and audits depend on what is kept. Evidence: NASA Phase F Closeout; NIST SP 800-160 DS-3.3; GOV.UK "Retiring your service"; opensource.guide (hand-over); National Archives digital continuity.

### Contested points

- **Length of the notice or deprecation period** – Vendor policies differ. Microsoft gives 30 days for a required action and 12 months before the end of a product with no successor, with up to three years for some Azure services. Google Cloud terms give 12 months unless a materially similar replacement exists, and the policy excludes pre-GA features. Kubernetes ties removal to releases: a beta API is removed 9 months or 3 releases after deprecation, and a GA CLI element 12 months or 2 releases after deprecation. Python's PEP 387 requires warnings for at least two minor versions and prefers five years. SemVer requires only one minor release. The EU Cyber Resilience Act fixes a minimum five-year support period for products with digital elements. The right length depends on the contract, the regulation, the size and kind of the user base (internal, external, API consumers, assisted-digital users), and whether a successor exists. Security emergencies can shorten the period (PEP 387, Google Cloud terms).
- **Advisory versus compulsory deprecation, and who does the migration work** – Google argues that advisory deprecations rarely finish ("hope is not a strategy"), and that compulsory deprecations must be staffed so that the team that deprecates also migrates the consumers. Many organizations instead set a deadline and leave the migration to the consumers. Centralised migration scales in a monorepo with large-scale-change tooling. In loosely coupled or external ecosystems, only deadlines plus tooling and documentation are feasible.
- **Delete immediately versus retain, and what "deletion" means for backups** – GDPR Article 17 and storage limitation point to prompt erasure. Article 17(3), legal holds and retention laws (for example the six years of HIPAA) require that some data is kept. The ICO accepts that backup copies are put "beyond use" where full deletion is impractical, while a strict reading wants deletion from backups too. Offline storage is still processing. The answer depends on the jurisdiction, the data category and the documented retention schedule of the organization.
- **Unpublish or yank a package version versus leave it available** – Registries disagree. Maven Central is immutable. npm allows an unpublish only within 72 hours, or for packages with no dependants and low downloads, and recommends deprecation. PyPI and cargo yank hide versions from new resolutions without deletion. Go retracts through a new version. OpenSSF lists an unpublish policy that prevents the replacement of versions and the reuse of deleted names as a package repository security capability. Security-driven removal of leaked credentials or malware is generally accepted, but cargo notes that a yank does not stop the spread through existing lockfiles. The choice depends on the harm from the artefact versus the harm from broken builds.
- **Open-source or hand over at retirement versus archive privately** – GOV.UK encourages teams to share code and knowledge with successors, including through open source. opensource.guide encourages maintainers to find new maintainers or to link to forks. Others prefer private archival, because unmaintained public code carries security and reputational risk, and publication requires a review for secrets, licenses and ownership (GOV.UK open-source guidance). PyPI archival and GitHub archiving exist to make "published but unmaintained" explicit.
- **How long to keep redirects, read-only access and monitoring after switch-off** – GOV.UK sets one year of redirects after retirement for a service that was live for more than 6 months (or until the current certificate expires, whichever comes first). AWS suggests a check for remaining traffic before the removal of load balancers. Azure recommends a grace period for rollback. Some teams keep redirects indefinitely to preserve links; others cut hard to reduce cost and attack surface. The choice depends on link value, cost, security exposure and contractual obligations.
- **Evolve in place, re-engineer, replace or scrap** – Google's chapter finds that in-place evolution is usually cheaper than replacement once the turndown cost is counted. Sommerville's legacy assessment recommends four responses: scrap low-value, low-quality systems; re-engineer high-value, low-quality systems; replace high-quality, low-value systems; and maintain the rest. martinfowler.com warns that feature-parity replacements are risky. The AWS 7 Rs include retire and retain as first-class strategies. The decision depends on business value, quality, dependencies, lock-in and the available budget.
- **Sanitization strength: logical methods versus physical destruction** – NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 says that purge (including cryptographic erase) should be preferred over clear, and that multi-pass overwrites add little, especially on SSDs. NCSC recommends physical destruction to 6 mm particles for highly sensitive data, and accepts a factory reset for encrypted devices. In cloud storage, cryptographic erase may be the only option, and customers must rely on provider assurance. Assurance needs and cost drive the choice.
- **Full disposal versus mothballing for a possible return to service** – SEBoK and NIST SP 800-160 DS-1 allow preservation with storage criteria and periodic inspections when the system may be needed again. Others argue that mothballed systems rot, continue to cost, and are never revived. The decision depends on regulatory or business continuity needs.
- **Automated decommissioning versus human approval gates** – AWS Well-Architected recommends automatic decommissioning of resources and enforced lifecycle policies. Azure CAF and change-management guidance require explicit owner approval and documented success criteria before removal. Automation suits ephemeral, tagged, low-risk resources. Approvals suit systems of record and regulated data.

### Metrics

- **Remaining consumers** of the deprecated system or API, measured from logs, build graphs or metrics such as the Kubernetes `apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis` gauge. Caveat: this counts only known callers, and yearly or rare jobs do not show up in short windows (AWS uses 90-day windows).
- **Traffic to retired endpoints, load balancers and redirects after cutoff**, and support or contact-centre queries about the retired service. Caveat: bots inflate the counts, and assisted-digital users may not appear in web metrics.
- **Migration completion**: the percentage of users, tenants, integrations or call sites moved to the successor; the time from the deprecation announcement to removal, compared with the planned date; the number of overdue deprecations. Caveat: a percentage hides the last few consumers, and those usually take the most effort.
- **Decommissioning completeness**: planned versus actually removed resources, accounts, DNS records, certificates, secrets and integrations; orphaned or unowned resources found by cost or inventory tooling (AWS COST04). Caveat: tooling finds only resources that are tagged or in the inventory.
- **Cost**: run-rate before and after, realised savings, licenses reclaimed, contracts terminated, and residual charges (for example archive early-deletion fees). Caveat: Google notes that maintenance and deprecation costs are diffuse and hard to measure.
- **Data disposition**: data sets archived versus deleted, erasure requests closed, certificates of sanitization issued versus the media count, and processor deletion confirmations received. Caveat: evidence exists only for known data copies.
- **Security hygiene after retirement**: dangling DNS records, stale accounts or keys, vulnerabilities still attributed to retired assets, and false alerts from stale monitoring. Caveat: a zero count shows only that the scans found nothing, not that nothing remains.
- **Process health**: approvals and change records present, the lessons-learned review held, and the inventory and CMDB updated within a target time. Caveat: these are leading indicators, not proof of a clean retirement.

### Failure modes

- **Advisory deprecation with no owner, deadline or staff** – usage never drops, and two systems run forever (Google: "hope is not a strategy"; compulsory deprecations without staff feel mean-spirited). It hurts because the organization pays for both systems and the migration never completes.
- **Switch-off without dependency discovery** – hidden consumers, annual batch jobs and downstream reports break, often weeks later. The institutional knowledge was lost with departed subject-matter experts (AWS). It hurts because nobody connects the failures with the retired system, so the diagnosis takes long.
- **DNS records, certificates, Pages sites or CNAMEs left behind** – dangling records get hijacked (OWASP, GOV.UK). It hurts because an attacker can serve content under the organization's name.
- **Forgotten accounts, tokens, webhooks, OAuth apps, SaaS integrations and operational tooling hooks** – the attack surface and the noise remain. It hurts because each stale credential is a way in, and each stale hook generates alerts and cost.
- **Zombie resources, DR copies, snapshots and backups** that continue to bill and keep personal data alive, and forgotten minimum-storage-duration fees. It hurts because cost and legal exposure continue after the declared retirement.
- **Data mistakes in both directions** – deletion of records needed for audit, tax, health or litigation, or retention of personal data past its purpose without a lawful basis. It hurts because both directions break the law or lose evidence.
- **Unpublish of a package or deletion of a repository** – downstream builds break, history and redirects are lost, and a reused name can hijack the old redirect (npm, GitHub). It hurts because other people's builds and links depend on the artefact.
- **CMDB, catalogue, runbooks and dashboards not updated** – incident responders chase assets that no longer exist, and alerts fire for retired systems. It hurts because it wastes incident time and erodes trust in the records.
- **Big-bang replacement driven by feature parity**, with no parallel operation or rollback (martinfowler.com, SEBoK). It hurts because it is the highest-risk cutover, and there is no way back when it fails.
- **No owner for residual obligations** – redirects, retention expiry, archived access and domain renewal – so they lapse or cost forever. It hurts because the retirement never closes.
- **Poor communication** – notice only on a web page that users no longer visit, no message to API consumers or assisted-digital users, and no statement about what happens to their data (GOV.UK). It hurts because users lose access or data without warning, and they lose trust.
- **Disposal treated as an external activity of someone else** with hidden costs and low priority, so that nobody designs or budgets for it (SEBoK). It hurts because the cost arrives anyway, later and larger.
- **Emotional attachment and political friction** that keep obsolete systems alive (Google). It hurts because cost and risk continue for reasons that are not technical.
- **Retirement without evidence** – no approvals, certificates or logs, so that audits and data-subject requests cannot be answered. It hurts because the organization cannot prove what it did.

### Tailoring by project size

Some steps are essential at every scale: make and record a clear decision with a date; tell users and dependants in their own channels before the switch-off; deprecate before you remove; decide for each data set whether to keep or delete it, and do it; remove DNS, secrets, accounts, integrations and billing; leave a pointer to the successor; keep a short record of what was done. Open-sourcing or hand-over is optional at every scale, but it needs a secrets and license review first. The table shows what each scale adds.

| Scale | Essential | Optional |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solo developer on a small repository | Write the retirement notice and the successor pointer in the README. Deprecate the package version with a message rather than unpublish it. Archive the repository instead of deletion. Cancel CI, hosting, domains and paid services. Revoke tokens and keys. Remove DNS and Pages. Export or delete any user data. Tag a final release. | A formal plan, certificates of sanitization and CMDB entries. Open-sourcing or hand-over after a secrets and license review. |
| Small team | Add a one-page retirement plan with an owner and dates. Do a dependency check (logs, code search, ask the integrators). Communicate with users with a notice period and a migration guide. Export and delete data against a simple retention note. Tear down through infrastructure as code. Work through a cleanup checklist (DNS, certificates, secrets, SaaS subscriptions, licenses, monitoring). Check the cost after shutdown. Keep a short monitoring and rollback window. Hold a retrospective. Approvals can be lightweight, but write them down. | Formal certificates of sanitization, a CMDB and a service catalogue entry. Open-sourcing or hand-over after a secrets and license review. |
| Large or regulated organization | Add a portfolio-level decision and formal approvals (change management, authorizing official). Write a disposal strategy per NIST RMF Task M-7 with security aspects per NIST SP 800-160. Do a records management and legal-hold review. Produce certificates of sanitization and deletion evidence (NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, ISO 27002 8.10). Retain compliance evidence for the required years. Obey contractual and regulatory notice periods and collect processor deletion confirmations. Staff a deprecation or migration team with discovery and backsliding-prevention tooling. Update the CMDB and the service catalogue. Monitor after retirement, keep audit trails and record lessons learned. For physical elements, dispose of hardware and obey environmental law. | Open-sourcing or hand-over after a secrets and license review. Mothballing with storage criteria and periodic inspections where a return to service is possible. |

### Sources

- [Software Engineering at Google, Chapter 15: Deprecation](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch15.html) – Free online chapter; used for why and how to deprecate, advisory versus compulsory deprecation, warnings, ownership, tooling and cost arguments.
- [GOV.UK Service Manual – Retiring your service](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/retiring-your-service) – Government guidance on user needs, communication (users, API users, assisted digital), data, redirects and domain rules after retirement.
- [GOV.UK Developer Docs – Retire a repo](https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/manual/retiring-a-repo.html) – Checklist for the retirement of a repository: README notice, close issues and PRs, remove Pages DNS, archive, update docs and references.
- [GOV.UK Service Manual – Making source code open and reusable](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/making-source-code-open-and-reusable) – Conditions to open code (secrets review, license, ownership, history); used for the open-source option.
- [NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization (PDF)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-88r2.pdf) – Primary text read via pdftotext: clear, purge and destroy, cryptographic erase for cloud storage, verification, certificate of sanitization, records management officer.
- [NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 publication page](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/88/r2/final) – Publication date September 2025 and scope.
- [NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1 publication page](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/88/r1/final) – Confirms that Rev. 1 was withdrawn on 26 September 2025 and superseded by Rev. 2.
- [NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework (PDF)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-37r2.pdf) – Task M-7 System Disposal: inputs, outputs, roles and discussion (media sanitization, inventory updates, record retention, notify users).
- [NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems (PDF)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1.pdf) – Appendix H.14 Disposal reprints the ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 Disposal process purpose and adds security outcomes and tasks DS-1 to DS-3; notes that Transition and Disposal run concurrently.
- [NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-12 Component Disposal (csf.tools mirror)](https://csf.tools/reference/nist-sp-800-53/r5/sr/sr-12/) – Control text and discussion: disposal throughout the SDLC, prevent components from entry into secondary markets.
- [NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 MP-6 Media Sanitization (csf.tools mirror)](https://csf.tools/reference/nist-sp-800-53/r5/mp/mp-6/) – Sanitize before disposal, release or reuse; enhancements on review, tracking and verification.

- [Wikipedia – ISO/IEC 15288](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO/IEC_15288) – Map of process groups, technical processes that end with Disposal, and editions (2008, 2015, 2023).
- [GDPR Article 17 – Right to erasure](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/) – Grounds for erasure, duty to inform other controllers, exceptions in paragraph 3.
- [GDPR Article 5 – Principles](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-5-gdpr/) – Storage limitation 5(1)(e) and accountability 5(2).
- [GDPR Article 20 – Right to data portability](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-20-gdpr/) – Structured, machine-readable export and direct transmission where feasible.
- [GDPR Article 28 – Processor](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-28-gdpr/) – Article 28(3)(g): the processor deletes or returns personal data after the end of services unless law requires storage.

- [ISMS.online – ISO 27002:2022 Control 8.10 Information Deletion](https://www.isms.online/iso-27002/control-8-10-information-deletion/) – Secondary summary of the control: deletion methods, evidence of deletion, vendors and cloud providers, related controls 7.14, 5.33 and 8.13.
- [45 CFR 164.316 – HIPAA policies, procedures and documentation (Cornell LII)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.316) – Six-year retention of required documentation from creation or last effective date; an example of compliance evidence retention.
- [NCSC – Secure sanitisation of storage media](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/secure-sanitisation-storage-media) – UK guidance: factory reset for encrypted devices, overwrite and verify, destruction to 6 mm, seek assurance from cloud providers after the end of the contract.
- [AWS Well-Architected – COST 4: How do you decommission resources?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/cost-04.html) – Lists best practices BP01 to BP05 for decommissioning.

- [AWS Well-Architected – COST04-BP05 Enforce data retention policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/cost_decomissioning_resources_data_retention.html) – Lifecycle policies and automated deletion to reduce decommissioning and storage cost.
- [AWS Prescriptive Guidance – Best practices for retiring applications before decommissioning infrastructure](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/migration-app-retirement-best-practices/best-practices.html) – Dependencies, stakeholder communication, controlled shutdown, change management, disconnect operational tools, asset information, licenses, network (IPs, DNS, certificates, load balancers), databases, storage scrubbing, backups, handover.

- [AWS Prescriptive Guidance – Best practices for assessing applications to be retired (introduction)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/migration-retiring-applications/introduction.html) – More than 10 percent of portfolios can be turned off; risk that assets labelled unused are consumed elsewhere; need for upstream dependency knowledge.

- [Microsoft Modern Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/lifecycle/policies/modern) – Minimum 30 days' notice for a required action, 12 months before the end of support with no successor, up to three years for some Azure services.
- [Google Cloud Platform Terms of Service](https://cloud.google.com/terms) – Section 1.4(e) Discontinuation of Services: at least 12 months' notice unless a materially similar replacement exists; exceptions for law, security and burden; not for pre-GA.
- [Google Cloud – Services subject to the Deprecation Policy](https://cloud.google.com/terms/deprecation) – Scope of the deprecation policy; pre-GA features excluded.
- [Kubernetes – Deprecation Policy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy/) – API and CLI deprecation rules, minimum support periods by stability level, warnings, audit annotations and the apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis metric.
- [RFC 8594 – The Sunset HTTP Header Field](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8594.html) – Advisory sunset timestamp and sunset link relation for resources that will become unavailable.

- [Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/) – FAQ: deprecate in a minor release with documentation, remove in a major release after at least one minor release with the deprecation.

- [JEP 277 – Enhanced Deprecation](https://openjdk.org/jeps/277) – @Deprecated since and forRemoval elements; forRemoval warns of removal in a future release.
- [npm Docs – Deprecating and undeprecating packages or package versions](https://docs.npmjs.com/deprecating-and-undeprecating-packages-or-package-versions) – Deprecation message on install, removal from search, strong recommendation to deprecate instead of unpublish.
- [npm Unpublish Policy](https://docs.npmjs.com/policies/unpublish) – 72-hour rule, conditions for older packages (no dependants, under 300 weekly downloads, single owner), recommendation to deprecate.
- [PyPI Blog – Project Archival](https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2025-01-30-archival/) – The archival marker blocks new uploads and shows a notice, but does not remove the project or block installs.
- [PyPI Docs – Yanking a release](https://docs.pypi.org/project-management/yanking/) – Installers ignore yanked releases unless pinned exactly; use sparingly and give a reason.
- [Cargo – cargo yank](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-yank.html) – Removes a version from new resolutions without deletion; existing lockfiles unaffected; exceptional use only.
- [Go Modules Reference – retract directive and module deprecation](https://go.dev/ref/mod#go-mod-file-retract) – Retract via a new higher version; retracted versions remain available; "Deprecated:" comment for modules.
- [Maven Central – Can I change a component?](https://central.sonatype.org/faq/can-i-change-a-component/) – Published components are immutable; publish a new version instead.
- [OpenSSF – Principles for Package Repository Security](https://repos.openssf.org/principles-for-package-repository-security) – Level 2 capability: an unpublish policy that prevents the replacement of versions and the reuse of deleted names.
- [GitHub Docs – Archiving repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/archiving-a-github-repository/archiving-repositories) – Read-only effects, unarchive, recommendation to close issues and update the README, legacy billing note.

- [Open Source Guides – Best Practices for Maintainers](https://opensource.guide/best-practices/) – Step away, ask someone to take over, link to active forks, communicate availability.
- [martinfowler.com – Patterns of Legacy Displacement](https://martinfowler.com/articles/patterns-legacy-displacement/) – Incremental replacement patterns, transitional architecture removed after use, feature-parity warning.
