- [NASA Systems Engineering Handbook – 3.9 Project Phase F: Closeout](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/3-9-project-phase-f-closeout/) – Implement decommissioning and disposal planning, archive technical information, document lessons learned.
- [The National Archives (UK) – Stage 4: Maintain digital continuity](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/information-management/manage-information/policy-process/digital-continuity/step-by-step-guidance/step-4/) – Keep information usable through change and when records systems are migrated or replaced.
- [Cyber Resilience Act, Article 13 (text mirror)](https://www.european-cyber-resilience-act.com/Cyber_Resilience_Act_Article_13.html) – Support period of at least five years, end date stated at purchase, end-of-support notification, security updates available for at least ten years; the EUR-Lex page returned empty content.
- [itsm.tools – The ITIL Service Portfolio Management Process Explained](https://itsm.tools/itil-service-portfolio-management-benefits-explained/) – Secondary ITIL source: service pipeline, catalogue and retired services catalogue; the portfolio tracks services to retirement and decommissioning. Official ITIL 4 practice guides were not accessible.
- [Sommerville, Software Engineering 10th ed. – Chapter 9 Software Evolution slides (SlideShare)](http://www.slideshare.net/software-engineering-book/ch9-evolution) – Legacy system assessment: scrap, continue to maintain, re-engineer or replace, based on business value and system quality.

## 15. Supporting and management processes

These processes do not build the product directly. They keep the project and the organization able to build, change, explain and account for the product over its whole life. ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 and 15288 group them into technical management, organizational project-enabling and agreement processes; older editions of 12207 said supporting life cycle processes. They run across all phases: technical management for the life of a project, project-enabling processes at organization level, and agreement processes at the acquirer–supplier boundary. In practice they appear as version control, change control, decision records, risk registers, metrics, retrospectives, audits, platforms, team design, supplier management, governance and ethics. Without them a project can ship once, but it cannot reliably ship again, explain itself or learn. Project planning, assessment and control are technical management processes too; section 4 describes them.

### Configuration management

**Purpose**

Software configuration management (SCM or CM) identifies the items that form the product, controls changes to them, records their status and audits them. The aim is that the team can rebuild and trace any release and that the shipped product matches its specification and documentation. ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 lists CM as a technical management process; SWEBOK v4 notes that it applies equally to iterative and incremental development. In a waterfall or V-model, CM gates the phase transitions: NASA sets functional, allocated, product and as-deployed baselines at design reviews, and configuration audits precede the product baseline. In agile and DevOps work the same functions are continuous. Version control holds everything, pull-request review is the change control, and pipelines enforce build and release control (see sections 10 and 11). The entry condition is a repository with an accountable owner and a CM approach agreed before the first baseline.

**Activities**

- CM planning: decide what SCM covers and who holds change authority. Decide which tools and software libraries the team uses, how it controls vendor and subcontracted software and interfaces, and which branching and merging strategy it follows. SWEBOK v4 lists the plan sections: introduction, SCM management, SCM activities, schedules, resources and plan maintenance. SQA reviews the plan. A small repository needs a short section in the README or CONTRIBUTING file; regulated work needs a formal plan in the style of IEEE 828.
- Configuration identification and baselines: select the configuration items (code, build scripts, tests, documentation, data, tools, infrastructure and pipeline definitions). Give each item a unique identifier and version. Group approved versions into baselines that change only through change control. NASA names four baselines; in git a tagged release on a protected branch is a baseline. Track the relationships between items, today often in a software bill of materials (SBOM). DORA adds AI prompts and agent configuration to the items that belong in version control.
- Change control: request and record every change to a controlled item, and evaluate its impact and cost. An authority proportionate to the baseline and the risk accepts, modifies, defers or rejects the change. SWEBOK v4 allows one person in small projects; large systems use a configuration control board (CCB) with an SCM representative, authority levels and an emergency path. Deviations and waivers are written authorizations to depart from a requirement. Pull requests with required review on a protected branch, linked to an issue, are the everyday form; the record of the decision is the product.
- Status accounting and audits: record and report what each item and baseline contains, which changes are implemented, which deviations and waivers apply and which verification evidence exists. This supplies evidence for security, legal and regulatory needs. A functional configuration audit checks that an item meets its specification; a physical configuration audit checks that the as-built product matches its documentation; in-process audits check baselines during development. Audit records can gate a release.
- Build and release management: reproduce any release from controlled sources, tools and build instructions; continuous integration does this on every commit. Identify, package and deliver the product with release notes, a version description, installation instructions and an SBOM; sign the artifacts where needed. The CM concern is traceability from a release back to its change requests.

**Outputs**

An SCM plan or CM section, a configuration item list and identification scheme, baselines and tags, and software libraries and artifact repositories. Change requests and decisions, CCB minutes or pull-request review records, and deviations and waivers. Status reports, functional and physical configuration audit reports, in-process audit findings, the SBOM, release notes and a version description. Per release, the baselines are audited and the contents are traceable; at project closure or retirement the records are archived or disposed of per the retention rules (see section 14).

**Practices with consensus**

- Keep every artifact needed to build, test, deploy and understand the system in version control. This includes code, dependencies, build and deployment scripts, infrastructure and environment definitions, database schema and reference data, tests, documentation, AI prompts and agent configuration. This gives reproducibility, traceability, disaster recovery and auditability, and DORA finds that it predicts continuous delivery. Evidence: DORA "Version control"; SWEBOK v4 SCM knowledge area; Pro Git; NASA SE Handbook 6.5.
- Control changes to baselines through a defined process whose approval authority is proportionate to risk – from one accountable person to a CCB with levels and an emergency path. Record every change and its decision. An unrecorded change cannot be audited or rolled back; a board heavier than the risk slows flow. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 SCM knowledge area; IEEE 828-2012; NASA SE Handbook 6.5; DORA capabilities catalog (streamlining change approval).
- Make builds and releases reproducible from controlled sources, tools and instructions; know what each release contains (SBOM, version description, release notes); audit baselines before release. Reproducibility serves recovery, maintenance and regulatory evidence; the audits confirm that the shipped product matches its specification and documentation. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 SCM knowledge area; NASA SE Handbook 6.5; DORA "Version control".

**Metrics**

SWEBOK v4 lists change requests per configuration item, average change cycle time, change traffic and breakage or rework, and baseline status. It adds build reproducibility, the number and severity of audit findings, and integrity indicators such as artifact hashes and signatures.

### Documentation and knowledge management

**Purpose**

ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 calls this information management and knowledge management; NASA calls it technical data management. The organization plans, creates, stores, controls, disseminates, archives and disposes of project information with defined ownership, access rules and retention. Knowledge management turns individual knowledge into shared capability. The aims are a bus factor above one, a short time to productive work, and a culture in which a person can ask questions and admit ignorance safely.

**Activities**

- Documentation as code: keep documentation in version control with plain-text markup, review, issue tracking and automated checks. Diátaxis sorts content by reader need into tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation. Typical artifacts are README, CONTRIBUTING, LICENSE and CODE_OF_CONDUCT files, design documents, ADRs, runbooks and playbooks, and a handbook; owners, freshness dates and review types (technical, audience, writing) keep them alive. Runbooks support operations (see section 12); PagerDuty distinguishes runbooks from playbooks, gives Limoncelli's seven runbook sections and stresses that they must stay current.
- Knowledge management: canonical sources, mentors, Q&A channels, tech talks, code review and a searchable handbook.
- Onboarding: a learning checklist, a buddy or mentor, golden-path tutorials, curated postmortems, disaster role-play and shadowing, as Google SRE and Spotify describe.

**Outputs**

The documentation set (README, CONTRIBUTING, LICENSE, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, design documents, ADR log, runbooks and playbooks, tutorials, how-to guides, reference, explanation, handbook) with ownership and freshness metadata. Retention and archival records. Knowledge assets such as an onboarding checklist and learning path, mentor assignments, a postmortem repository, tech talks and Q&A archives. When a person leaves, the knowledge is transferred and the access is removed.

**Practices with consensus**

- Treat documentation as code: store it with the code, give it an owner, review it, test it in CI, date it, and structure it by reader need. Unowned wiki pages rot and duplicate; documents inside the engineering workflow get reviewed and updated; DORA finds that quality documentation amplifies the benefit of every technical capability it studied. Evidence: Write the Docs "Docs as Code"; Software Engineering at Google chapter 10; DORA "Documentation quality"; Diátaxis.
- Onboard people with structure: a learning checklist, a mentor or buddy outside the reporting line, golden-path tutorials, curated postmortems, shadowing and a starter project. Trial by fire alienates capable people; structured paths shorten the time to confident contribution and spread knowledge. Evidence: Google SRE book "Accelerating SREs to On-Call and Beyond"; Spotify Golden Paths; Software Engineering at Google chapter 3.

**Metrics**

- DORA's eight-item measure of documentation clarity, findability and reliability.
- Document ownership coverage, freshness dates and the proportion of pages with a last-reviewed date.
- Golden-path tutorial completion during onboarding (Spotify: the first two weeks).
- Time to first merged change and first on-call shift, bus factor per component, and the proportion of knowledge in canonical sources (Software Engineering at Google, SRE book).

### Measurement

**Purpose**

ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 names a measurement process; the industry also speaks of developer productivity, developer experience (DevEx), engineering effectiveness and engineering enablement. The organization commits to measure, plans measures from stated information needs, collects and analyzes data inside the processes it measures, reports to stakeholders and evaluates the measurement process itself. The inputs are the goals, risks, problems and regulatory reports of the stakeholders. SWEBOK v4 warns to focus surveillance on insight, not on the measurements themselves.

**Activities**

- Derive measures top-down. Goal Question Metric (GQM) gives each metric a question and a goal with purpose, issue, object and viewpoint. Google's Goals–Signals–Metrics (GSM) does the same, with a triage step that drops any measure that would not change a decision.
- Measure delivery at service level with the DORA keys; combine perceptual survey data with system data as SPACE and DevEx prescribe.
- Report aggregates, never individual scores; use several metrics; remember that a measure used as a target stops being a good measure.

**Outputs**

A measurement plan, collected data, indicators and dashboards (for example the four keys per service and survey results), and measurement evaluation reports.

**Practices with consensus**

- Derive metrics from explicit goals and questions. Use a small balanced set that mixes system data with perceptual survey data, measure teams and systems rather than individuals, and never let a metric become the goal. Single activity metrics get gamed (Goodhart's law), individual metrics distort behavior, and surveys and logs disagree often enough that both are needed. GQM, GSM, SPACE and DORA say this independently. Evidence: Basili, Caldiera and Rombach on GQM; Software Engineering at Google chapter 7; the SPACE framework (InfoQ summary); DORA four keys guide; Beck and Orosz; Wikipedia on Goodhart's law.
- Use the DORA four (now five) keys – change lead time, deployment frequency, change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time and rework rate – as service-level outcome measures. Improve them together, because speed and stability are not a trade-off. The metrics are validated across years of research and are outcome-oriented; measurement per application avoids false comparisons between teams. Evidence: DORA four keys guide; CNCF Platforms White Paper (uses DORA to measure platform value); Beck and Orosz (recommend DORA as outcome metrics).

**Metrics**

- DORA five keys per application or service; do not compare teams or set the keys as targets.
- SPACE: satisfaction and well-being, performance, activity, communication and collaboration, efficiency and flow. Pick metrics from at least three dimensions, include at least one perceptual measure, and never use a single activity metric (lines of code, commits, PR counts).
- DevEx: feedback loop speed, cognitive load and flow state, captured by developer surveys combined with system data; triangulate survey and log data.
- Google GSM with the QUANTS categories (quality, attention, intellectual complexity, tempo, satisfaction); if no action would follow, do not measure; never use it for individual reviews.
- GQM-derived metrics, objective or subjective, each traced to a question and a goal.
- General caveats: vanity metrics look good but do not guide action (Ries). Goodhart's and Campbell's laws predict gaming when a measure becomes a target. Fowler notes that output and business value attribution remain hard, so all productivity metrics are proxies.

### Engineering foundations and empirical methods

**Purpose**

SWEBOK v4 collects the engineering methods that every phase uses in its Engineering Foundations knowledge area (chapter 18). The methods are the engineering decision process, measurement theory, statistics, empirical studies, modeling and simulation, standards and root cause analysis. Section 1 scopes the three foundations knowledge areas as background knowledge; this subsection describes the methods that the supporting processes apply directly. The Scrum Guide states the same idea for iterative work: "Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking", with transparency, inspection and adaptation.

**Activities**

- Apply the engineering decision process to each significant choice. Understand the real problem, define the criteria, identify the feasible solutions, evaluate them, select one, and monitor the result (SWEBOK ch. 18). Record the decision with its criteria and alternatives, as an ADR or a trade study (see Decision management above).
- Give each measure an operational definition and a scale type. Write the exact measurement method, with the unit and the precision. Classify the measure as nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio or absolute, and use only the statistics that the scale permits (SWEBOK ch. 18; Stevens). Use medians and counts for ordinal data; do not average maturity levels or severity ranks.
- Treat metrics as distributions. Use percentiles and histograms for latency and durations, because averages hide the tail (Google SRE). Standardize the indicator definitions, so that teams do not reason from first principles each time.
- Draw inferences with care. Name the population and the sample, prefer interval estimates to point estimates, and remember that correlation does not show causation (SWEBOK ch. 18). Do not trust a before/after comparison, because time is a large source of change (SRE Workbook).
- Run a designed experiment when you need a causal answer. State the hypothesis and the success signal first (ThoughtWorks). Use a control population that you measure at the same time, and size the sample and the duration (Kohavi; SRE Workbook; NIST/SEMATECH ch. 5). Record the result and the decision: continue, pivot or stop.
- Model, simulate and prototype with a stated purpose. Use Monte Carlo forecasts for delivery, simulations for capacity questions, and spikes for feasibility. Do not mistake a prototype for the product (SWEBOK ch. 18).
- Perform a blameless root cause analysis on incidents, defects and process problems. Select the problem by frequency and severity, and gather evidence before you conclude. Apply a structured technique: 5 whys, change analysis, an Ishikawa diagram, fault tree analysis or FMEA (SWEBOK ch. 18; ASQ; Lean Enterprise Institute). Separate proximate causes from root or contributing causes (Atlassian). Assume that people acted with good intent on the information they had (Google SRE).
- Turn root causes into verified actions. Give each action an owner, a priority and a due date, and track the closure (SRE Workbook; Atlassian: 4 or 8 week SLOs). Observe the effect; recurrence of the incident class is the test.
- Use evidence before you adopt a practice or a tool. Look for systematic reviews and controlled studies, appraise their quality, and adapt them to the context (Kitchenham; ACM SIGSOFT Empirical Standards; Wohlin).
- Identify the standards that apply to the product and the process, and treat them as design constraints (SWEBOK ch. 18).

**Outputs**

Decision records with criteria and alternatives. Experiment records with the hypothesis, the control, the result and the decision. Postmortem and RCA records with the timeline, the causes and owned actions. An evidence note for each adopted practice or tool. A list of applicable standards and conformance decisions.

**Practices with consensus**

- Run a blameless root cause analysis after each significant incident, write the record down, and verify that the corrective action works. Blame hides the information that prevents recurrence, and an action that nobody verifies may not prevent it. Evidence: Google SRE book chapter 15; SRE Workbook chapter 10; Atlassian incident postmortem handbook; SWEBOK v4 chapters 12 and 18.
- Go past the first why with a structured technique, and separate proximate causes from root or contributing causes. A fix of the obvious symptom leaves the cause in place. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 chapter 18; Atlassian postmortem handbook and Team Playbook; Lean Enterprise Institute 5 whys; ASQ root cause analysis.
- Compare against a control population, not against last week. Time is one of the largest sources of change in observed metrics. Evidence: SRE Workbook "Canarying Releases"; Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi, Tang and Xu); NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook chapter 5; ThoughtWorks hypothesis-driven development.
- Respect scale types and report distributions, not only averages. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 chapter 18; Wikipedia "Level of measurement" (Stevens); Google SRE book "Service Level Objectives" and "Monitoring Distributed Systems"; ISO/IEC/IEEE 15939; BIPM JCGM vocabulary.

**Contested points**

- One root cause versus contributing factors. Atlassian's template asks for the root cause, and Google writes "root cause(s)". Cook argues that complex systems fail through multiple contributing failures, and that hindsight bias distorts the analysis. A regulated CAPA record needs a documented cause; a complex socio-technical system needs contributing factors and systemic actions.
- A formal measurement and causal-analysis process (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15939; CMMI) versus lightweight team practice (DORA metrics, retrospectives, postmortems). SWEBOK presents both; the mix depends on size, contract and risk, as for process improvement above.

### Quality management and assurance

**Purpose**

Software quality management (SQM) sets the quality policy and objectives. Software quality assurance (SQA) gives evidence that the processes are appropriate and the products are of suitable quality. A quality management system (QMS) holds both. The quality requirements, the acceptance criteria and the system integrity level set how formal and how independent SQA and V&V must be. A contract or regulation can also impose CM audits, QA independence, records and reports. SQA is not testing (see section 9). In agile work a Definition of Done and pull-request review carry much of the quality control.

**Activities**

- QMS: management sets a quality policy and objectives and assigns responsibility and authority independent of project pressure. It plans the quality activities and their cost of quality (prevention, appraisal, internal and external failure), evaluates the QMS, and drives corrective and preventive actions with root cause analysis and a defect taxonomy. The reference models are ISO 9001:2015 (clauses 4–10, seven quality management principles, internal and certification audits; ISO/IEC/IEEE 90003 interprets it for software) and CMMI. SWEBOK v4 stresses that management support, training and resources are mandatory or the QMS is paper.
- SQA: write an SQA plan; perform process assurance (are the defined processes followed), product assurance (reviews, inspections, V&V planning), and reviews and audits. IEEE 730-2014 sets the requirements for initiating, planning, controlling and executing SQA. For critical systems the SQA function is organizationally independent, and third parties often perform the audits.

**Outputs**

A quality policy and QMS documents, an SQA plan, review and audit records, nonconformity and corrective action records, and cost-of-quality data.

**Practices with consensus**

- Separate quality assurance from testing: SQA plans and assures processes and products through reviews, audits and V&V oversight, with independence proportional to criticality; quality control (testing, inspections) measures the artifacts. To equate SQA with testing leaves process conformance and early work products unassessed; critical systems need an SQA function free from project pressure. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 Software Quality knowledge area (SQA definition, process and product assurance, reviews and audits); IEEE 730-2014 scope.

**Metrics**

The SWEBOK v4 Software Quality knowledge area lists defect density, error density, failure rate and mean time to failure. It adds the cost of quality split into conformance (prevention, appraisal) and nonconformance (internal and external failure), review coverage, audit nonconformities and corrective action closure time.

### Process improvement

**Purpose**

ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 calls the organizational part life cycle model management. SWEBOK v4 covers process definition, adaptation, assessment and improvement (SPI) in its software engineering process knowledge area; Pressman calls all these cross-cutting activities umbrella activities. SWEBOK v4 states that no ideal process exists: each project must select, adapt and apply processes, and ISO/IEC 29110 gives profiles for very small entities. Incident reports, defect data, retrospective findings and measurement results from earlier work feed the improvement. SWEBOK notes that adaptive projects emphasize formal plans less and monitoring and control more. Most supporting activities are continuous. A few are event-driven: a configuration audit before a release, onboarding when a person joins, supplier selection at acquisition, a maturity appraisal when a customer requires it.

**Activities**

- Life cycle model management and tailoring: the organization defines, maintains and improves its policies, life cycle models, processes and procedures. Each project selects a life cycle model (see section 2; ISO/IEC/IEEE 24748-3 guides the application of 12207), picks the processes it needs, adapts them to product size, criticality and stakeholders, and records the decisions and rationale. The output is a documented, right-sized process that the team follows and that measurement can check.
- Continuous improvement: run a retrospective each iteration (the Scrum Guide puts inspection and adaptation into every Sprint Retrospective) and a blameless postmortem after each significant incident. Choose a few improvements, act on them soon and check the result (PDCA, kaizen; "no kaizen without a standard"). Norm Kerth's Prime Directive sets the blameless frame.
- Process assessment: organizations may assess capability or maturity against CMMI (benchmark appraisals) or ISO/IEC 330xx (the successor of ISO/IEC 15504 SPICE); both presuppose documented standards. DORA treats learning culture and team experimentation as capabilities in its catalog.

**Outputs**

Retrospective action items and their status, postmortem action items, an improvement backlog, process assessment or appraisal results when performed, and the recorded tailoring decisions.

**Practices with consensus**

- Run a regular, blameless improvement loop: retrospectives each iteration, postmortems after incidents, a few actions at a time, then check results (PDCA, kaizen). Continuous small improvements compound; blame suppresses the information needed to improve; a retrospective without acted-on actions is theatre. Evidence: Scrum Guide (Sprint Retrospective); Google SRE book "Postmortem Culture"; Lean Enterprise Institute on kaizen and PDCA; SWEBOK v4 Process knowledge area 3.4; Retrospective Prime Directive.
- Tailor all supporting processes to the project: document which processes apply and why, and drop what does not add value. Standards themselves require tailoring; small entities have their own profiles; heavy process on a small repository produces paper, not quality. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 Process knowledge area 2.8 (life cycle adaptation, ISO/IEC 29110); Wikipedia and arc42 summaries of ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207; GOV.UK team setup by phase.

**Metrics**

CMMI maturity levels 1 Initial to 5 Optimizing (V2.0 2018, V3.0 2023, benchmark appraisals); ISO/IEC 330xx capability levels 0 Incomplete to 5. Caveat: level ratings measure process presence, not product outcomes, and small organizations rarely justify the cost.

### Risk management

**Purpose**

ISO 31000 defines risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives. The risk management process identifies, analyzes, treats and monitors risks and opportunities over the whole project, not only at the start. The risk sources are technical, cost, schedule, programmatic, security and safety risks, and opportunities. The quality and risk expectations are agreed before the first release.

**Activities**

Identify risks and opportunities; analyze likelihood and consequence; prioritize; plan treatment (avoid, reduce, transfer, accept, or pursue an opportunity); track status against trigger thresholds; revisit the list at intervals. A risk register holds the list and serves compliance needs. NASA adds risk-informed decision making and continuous risk management. The team can agree project abandonment conditions with the stakeholders in advance.

**Outputs**

A risk register with owners, exposure, treatment plans, triggers and review dates; abandonment conditions where agreed.

**Practices with consensus**

- Manage risk continuously with a living risk register: identify, analyze likelihood and consequence, prioritize, treat, monitor against triggers, and revisit at intervals. Risks change as the project learns; a register written once at kickoff is decoration; ISO 31000 and NASA both frame risk management as an ongoing loop integrated into decisions. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 Software Engineering Management knowledge area 2.5; NASA SE Handbook 6.4; ISO 31000 overview.

**Metrics**

Open risks by exposure (likelihood x consequence), risk trend or burndown, triggers exceeded, and time from identification to treatment (NASA, SWEBOK).

### Decision management

**Purpose**

The decision management process makes significant decisions with stated criteria, an explicit set of alternatives, an evaluation method and a recorded rationale. Later readers can then trust the decision report.

**Activities**

Evaluate the alternatives with a trade study, a decision matrix or a cost-benefit analysis. Capture architecture decision records (ADRs) in the repository with title, context, decision, status and consequences; superseded records stay and point to their replacement; templates include Nygard's format, MADR and Y-statements. NASA's decision analysis process is the heavyweight form of the same idea. The architect or technical lead makes and records the architecturally significant decisions (see section 6).

**Outputs**

Decision records and trade-study reports with criteria, alternatives, rationale and consequences.

**Practices with consensus**

- Record significant decisions with their context, alternatives, rationale and consequences, and keep superseded records. Newcomers otherwise either blindly accept or recklessly reverse decisions they do not understand; a written rationale supports audits and later trade-offs. Evidence: Nygard "Documenting Architecture Decisions"; adr.github.io; NASA SE Handbook 6.8 Decision Analysis; SWEBOK v4 Professional Practice (trade-off analysis).

### Infrastructure and platform

**Purpose**

The infrastructure management process provides environments, tools, CI/CD, observability, identity and secrets, artifact storage and data services to the projects. Platform engineering packages these as a self-service internal product with golden paths and templates. The purpose is to reduce the cognitive load of the stream-aligned teams, not to centralize control.

**Activities**

A platform team owns the internal developer platform as a product. It researches developer needs, starts with the thinnest viable platform, documents it, supplies golden paths and templates, and measures adoption, satisfaction and delivery outcomes. Spotify uses golden paths with Backstage and in onboarding. Bottcher warns against backlog coupling, where product teams wait in the ticket queue of a central team.

**Outputs**

Environments, pipelines, the internal developer platform, golden-path templates and tutorials, a platform roadmap and adoption metrics.

**Practices with consensus**

- Treat the internal platform as a product: self-service, compelling rather than mandated, thinnest viable platform first, golden paths with documentation, measured by adoption, satisfaction and delivery outcomes. Platforms reduce cognitive load and backlog coupling only when teams choose them; relabelled centralized infrastructure does not. Evidence: CNCF Platforms White Paper; Evan Bottcher on martinfowler.com; Spotify Golden Paths; Team Topologies key concepts; DORA 2024 report (with caveats).

**Metrics**

CNCF Platforms White Paper: active users and retention, request-to-fulfillment latency, net promoter score or satisfaction, and the DORA metrics of the platform users.

### People, roles and teams

**Purpose**

The human resource management process acquires, develops and retains people with the needed skills, defines roles and responsibilities, trains people and designs teams. Its inputs are the people, skills and hiring capacity at hand and the existing team structure and communication paths, which Conway's law links to the structure of the system. Roles must be assigned before the team grows past one person.

**Activities**

Team Topologies recommends small, stable, cross-functional stream-aligned teams with bounded cognitive load, supported by platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem teams in three interaction modes. The reverse Conway manoeuvre aligns teams with the intended architecture. GOV.UK requires multidisciplinary teams, changes the roles by phase, splits work to minimise dependencies and coordinates several teams with a standup of standups. Peopleware argues that the sociology of a team matters more than the technology, that flow needs quiet, and that management can kill a team (teamicide) or let it jell. Psychological safety, humility, respect and trust, and a generative culture belong to this process. So does a sustainable on-call load (Google: at least 50% engineering time, at most two incidents per 12-hour shift). The sources name these roles across the supporting processes:

- Product manager – owns the product vision and its fit with organizational priorities, prioritizes and accepts work, represents users and the business in portfolio and governance forums.
- Product Owner (Scrum) – one person, not a committee; owns the Product Goal and creates, orders and keeps transparent the Product Backlog.
- Service owner (GOV.UK) – holds overall responsibility for the service; decides in governance and assessments.
- Delivery manager, Scrum Master or project manager – establishes the working environment, removes impediments, runs planning, monitoring and control, facilitates retrospectives, coaches the organization in empirical process.
- Engineering manager – staffs and develops the team, designs team structure and cognitive load, sets on-call limits, sponsors measurement and improvement, protects stable priorities.
- Architect or technical lead – makes and records ADRs, runs trade studies, sets technical standards and interface control, advises on make-buy-reuse.
- Developer – keeps everything in version control, follows branching and review rules, writes and reviews documentation, records decisions, reports risks and quality honestly, follows the code of ethics.
- Tester or QA engineer – plans and performs quality control, contributes to the Definition of Done, reports the defect data that feeds improvement.
- SQA function – independent in critical systems; writes the SQA plan, performs process and product assurance, supports reviews and audits, tracks corrective actions.
- Configuration manager and CCB – own the SCM plan, identification scheme, baselines, change authority, status accounting and audits; one person or the tech lead in small projects.
- Release manager – decides when to release, packages and delivers, produces release notes and the SBOM, keeps release traceability.
- SRE, DevOps or web operations engineer – runs production, maintains runbooks and playbooks, keeps the on-call load sustainable, runs blameless postmortems.
- Platform engineer and platform product manager – build and run the internal developer platform as a product, maintain golden paths, documentation and templates, measure adoption and satisfaction.
- Enabling team or coaches – help stream-aligned teams acquire capabilities (testing, security, CM practices) for a limited time, then step back.
- UX designer, interaction and service designer, user researcher, content designer – provide user evidence and design; content designers and technical writers also own parts of the documentation set.
- Technical writer – designs the documentation architecture (Diátaxis), writes developer-facing docs, sets style and review practice, acts as documentation champion.
- Security lead – sets security requirements for processes, supplier and open-source intake and contractor access (see section 16).
- Performance analyst or data analyst – designs and interprets measurement, builds dashboards, guards against vanity metrics.
- Procurement, legal and OSPO – negotiate contracts, check licenses and IP, run open-source consumption and contribution policy, enforce export and privacy rules.
- Governing body, steering group or portfolio board – sets direction, decision rights and risk appetite, funds and stops initiatives, monitors outcomes, asks for evidence.
- Everyone – psychological safety, knowledge sharing, honest reporting and ethical conduct are shared duties, not a role.

**Outputs**

Organization design: team structure and interaction modes, role definitions, hiring and training plans, on-call rotas and load limits.

**Practices with consensus**

- Organize around small, stable, cross-functional teams with bounded cognitive load, and align team boundaries with the intended architecture (Conway's law, reverse Conway manoeuvre); avoid activity-oriented teams that force handoffs. Communication structure shapes system structure; stable teams build shared context; overloaded teams make poor decisions. Evidence: Team Topologies key concepts; Martin Fowler "Conway's Law"; Scrum Guide (typically 10 or fewer people, cross-functional, self-managing); GOV.UK "Running more than one service team".
- Build psychological safety and a generative (performance-oriented, information-sharing) culture: humility, respect, trust, blameless inquiry into failure, trained messengers, shared risk. A Westrum-style generative culture predicts software delivery and organizational performance; safety is the precondition for learning and knowledge sharing. Evidence: DORA capability "Generative organizational culture"; Software Engineering at Google chapters 2 and 3; Google SRE "Postmortem Culture".

**Metrics**

The Westrum culture composite from validated survey items (information flow, treatment of messengers, shared responsibility, response to failure, reception of novelty), used by DORA. Operational load and sustainability per Google SRE: at least 50% of SRE time on engineering, at most two incidents per 12-hour on-call shift, a team of at least eight for single-site 24/7 coverage.

### Portfolio, acquisition and supply

**Purpose**

Portfolio management is an organizational project-enabling process; acquisition and supply are the agreement processes of ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207; governance of IT (ISO/IEC 38500, COBIT) sits above both. The PMBOK covers the same ground in its procurement, risk, quality, resources and communications knowledge areas. Together they decide which products and projects exist and how they are funded, what the organization buys, builds or reuses, and who holds which decision rights. The inputs are the organizational strategy and policies, the applicable contracts and regulations, and the candidate suppliers, COTS, SaaS and open-source components with their licenses. The decision to build or buy comes before this topic (see section 3).

**Activities**

- Portfolio management: leadership selects, prioritizes, funds, sustains and stops projects or products so that the portfolio fits strategy, capacity and risk appetite. It runs pipeline management, resource and financial management, change control of the portfolio and risk management across initiatives; PMI and Axelos publish portfolio standards. Lean portfolio management adds strategy and investment funding, agile portfolio operations and lean governance with guardrails. DORA 2024 shows that unstable priorities damage productivity and raise burnout, even with transformational leadership and good documentation, so the output must be a stable, communicated set of priorities.
- Acquisition and supply: the acquirer decides make, buy or reuse; SWEBOK lists COTS, custom development by another party, open source, loaned software and SaaS as acquisition classes. Agreements define scope, deliverables, quality requirements, intellectual property, penalties and contract type (fixed price, time and materials, cost plus); the supplier plans, delivers and supports; the acquirer monitors compliance. Teams evaluate open-source components for authenticity, maintenance, security, license and fit (OpenSSF guide), and organizations may run an open source program office (OSPO) for consumption and contribution policy. GOV.UK advises: buy only the skills you need, plan knowledge transfer, own your data and code, use break clauses and avoid lock-in. It adds: count the total cost of ownership, keep supplier diversity, and be open with open source and open standards.
- Governance and compliance: a governing body evaluates, directs and monitors; management executes. Governance sets decision rights, accountabilities, controls and evidence requirements. COBIT 2019 offers 40 governance and management objectives with design factors for right-sizing; ISO/IEC 38500 defines governance of IT for the governing body. GOV.UK gives six principles for agile delivery: do not slow down delivery, decide when needed at the right level, do it with the right people, go see for yourself, do it only if it adds value, trust and verify. Compliance evidence usually comes from CM status accounting, audits, measurement records and decision records.

**Outputs**

Portfolio decisions (funded and stopped initiatives, priorities, guardrails, capacity allocation). Agreements and supplier records (make-buy decisions, contracts, supplier evaluations and monitoring, open-source approvals and license inventory, OSPO policies). Governance records (decision rights, policies, control evidence, compliance reports, audit trails).

**Practices with consensus**

- Evaluate third-party and open-source components before adoption (authenticity, maintenance, security posture, license, quality); with contractors or suppliers keep ownership of code, data and knowledge, transfer knowledge deliberately and avoid lock-in. Unfiltered dependency intake is a common attack surface; lost knowledge and lock-in turn a purchase into a liability. Evidence: OpenSSF Concise Guide for Evaluating Open Source Software; SWEBOK v4 Management knowledge area 3.2; GOV.UK "Working with contractors or third parties" and "Define your purchasing strategy"; TODO Group OSPO guide.
- Keep governance lightweight and evidence-based: decide at the right level when needed, do not slow delivery, go and see, do only what adds value, trust and verify. Scale formality with regulation and risk. Governance exists to make good decisions visible and accountable, not to add meetings; COBIT design factors and GOV.UK both say right-size it. Evidence: GOV.UK governance principles for agile service delivery; ISACA COBIT 2019 (design factors, governance versus management); ISO/IEC 38500 overview.

**Metrics**

Supplier and dependency health: OpenSSF Scorecard and Best Practices badge, known vulnerabilities via deps.dev, maintainer count and release cadence, license compliance. Contract metrics such as break clause intervals (GOV.UK: at most two years) and supplier performance reviews. Portfolio: alignment of funded work to strategy, work in progress at portfolio level, and stability of priorities (DORA 2024).

### Professional practice and ethics

**Purpose**

SWEBOK v4 chapter 14 and the ACM/IEEE-CS Software Engineering Code of Ethics and Professional Practice frame the conduct of practitioners. The inputs are the code of ethics and the legal obligations on intellectual property, NDAs, licensing, privacy, export control and liability.

**Activities**

Practitioners put the public interest first, report quality and risk honestly, keep confidentiality, give credit to others, do not certify unacceptable products and do not build dark patterns. They know the legal frame and provide the documentation that users need for safe use. They develop communication, teamwork, stakeholder and equity, diversity and inclusion skills, understand group dynamics, and keep learning. Violations include the concealment of inadequate work and the falsification of data.

**Outputs**

This process produces conduct more than artifacts. The visible traces are honest status and risk reports, correct attribution and license compliance in the supplier records and the documentation set, and user documentation for safe use.

**Practices with consensus**

- Adhere to a professional code of ethics and know the legal frame: public interest first, honest reporting, confidentiality, credit, privacy, IP and licensing, no deceptive patterns. Software affects public safety and welfare; professional societies enforce the codes, and the codes give guidance when imperatives conflict. Evidence: ACM/IEEE-CS Software Engineering Code of Ethics (computer.org); SWEBOK v4 Professional Practice knowledge area.

### Contested points

- Measurement – can developer productivity be measured, and at what level? McKinsey (2023) claims yes, with DORA, SPACE and new individual-level metrics such as contribution analysis and talent capability scores. Kent Beck and Gergely Orosz reply that four of the five new metrics measure effort or output, not outcome or impact, and that individual metrics get gamed (Goodhart's law, the Facebook survey example). Martin Fowler argues that productivity cannot be measured because software output itself resists measurement. Google measures only aggregate effects and forbids metrics in individual performance reviews; DORA says measure per application and do not compare teams. The choice depends on purpose: improvement of a system is feasible, a ranking of people is harmful.
- Measurement – DORA metrics or survey scores as targets or OKRs. DORA warns against the metrics as goals because of gaming. The SPACE paper gives the one-hour PR SLA example that caused interruptions and alert fatigue; Beck reports survey scores negotiated once they entered performance reviews. Some organizations still set four-keys targets per team. The practical test is Eric Ries's distinction between actionable and vanity metrics.
- Process improvement – maturity and capability models (CMMI, ISO/IEC 330xx) versus lightweight empirical improvement. Regulated and contracting organizations use CMMI benchmark appraisals and ISO/IEC 330xx assessments because customers require them and they structure improvement. Critics note that CMMI says what, not how, that small organizations rarely reach higher levels, and that appraisals can become audit-driven theatre. Agile practitioners rely on retrospectives, postmortems and DORA capabilities instead. SWEBOK presents both as valid framework-based methods; the mix depends on contractual requirements, size and risk.
- Documentation – how detailed runbooks and playbooks should be. The Google SRE Workbook records a live disagreement: some engineers want general, slow-changing playbook entries that assume a trained responder; others want step-by-step instructions to cut variability and recovery time. Detailed playbooks go stale at the rate production changes. The suggested compromise is a minimal agreed structure plus the conversion of recurring knowledge into automation and better monitoring; Limoncelli's seven-section runbook is the detailed end of the spectrum.
- Documentation – where documentation should live, and how much to write in agile. Google moved away from wikis because of obsolescence, duplicates and missing ownership; Write the Docs and DORA favour docs-as-code; GitHub still suggests wikis for extensive documentation beyond the README. SWEBOK notes that "working software over comprehensive documentation" is often misread: documents are still needed, though adaptive projects emphasize formal plans less. The answer depends on audience, change rate and who must edit.
- Infrastructure and platform – platform engineering as benefit or hidden cost. CNCF, Team Topologies, Bottcher and Spotify report reduced cognitive load and faster delivery from platforms built as products. DORA 2024 finds that platform engineering raises individual and organizational productivity, but it is associated with decreased change stability and throughput unless it is implemented with developer independence in mind. Bottcher warns that relabelled centralized infrastructure and mandates are not platforms. Whether to build one depends on team count, duplication and the ability to run it as a product.
- Configuration management – formal change control boards versus streamlined approval. NASA-style CCBs with change classes and waivers suit safety-critical, contract-driven work. DORA lists streamlined change approval as a capability and finds that heavyweight external approval slows delivery without better stability; SWEBOK allows a single accountable person in small projects. The deciding factors are integrity level, regulation and whether the approval can be automated into the pipeline.
- People – co-location and office layout versus remote, asynchronous, handbook-first work. GOV.UK prefers co-located teams and a standup of standups for multi-team coordination. Peopleware argues for quiet, interruption-free space and flow; SWEBOK notes that private offices raise individual productivity while shared spaces boost collaboration. GitLab's handbook-first, asynchronous model shows a fully remote alternative. The trade-off is between informal knowledge flow and focus, and depends on geography and documentation discipline.
- People – role definitions: product manager versus product owner, dedicated QA versus whole-team quality, the need for a technical writer. Scrum insists that the Product Owner is one person, not a committee. GOV.UK separates service owner and product manager and lists QA/tester and technical writer as optional roles present mainly in beta and live phases. Many teams fold testing into the Definition of Done and documentation into the developers' work; DORA recommends documentation champions or technical writers. Which roles are distinct depends on scale, criticality and funding.
- Quality – independence of quality assurance. SWEBOK and IEEE 730 call for an SQA function that is technically, managerially and financially independent in critical systems, and name independent V&V for the most critical. Most product teams embed quality work in the team and rely on peer review and CI. The integrity level and the regulatory regime decide how much independence is required.
- Portfolio, acquisition and supply – open-source contribution and consumption policy: strict gatekeeping versus default-open. TODO Group describes OSPOs with review boards, license compliance and approval processes; SWEBOK warns about unfiltered access to package repositories. GOV.UK's Technology Code of Practice says be open and use open source by default, and the GitHub Open Source Guides encourage contribution. Regulated industries and security posture push toward gating; speed and talent retention push toward openness.
- Risk management – how formal the register must be. The sources agree on the loop but not on the artifact. A solo developer can keep risks in an issue list, while NASA and compliance regimes expect a formal register with owners, exposure and triggers. Whether to agree abandonment conditions in advance is likewise a project-level choice.
- Decision management – how heavy a decision record should be. The spectrum runs from a one-page ADR (Nygard) through MADR and Y-statements to NASA's full decision analysis with trade studies and decision matrices. The sources agree that the team must record the rationale; they differ on method and formality, which depend on the cost of a wrong decision.
- Professional practice and ethics – how far individual responsibility reaches. The codes rank the public interest above employer and client, but they give principles, not procedures, for the case where honest reporting of risk conflicts with project pressure or confidentiality. Whether a licensing regime applies differs by jurisdiction and profession.

### Failure modes

- Measurement: individual activity metrics (lines of code, commits, PR counts) or survey scores tied to performance reviews. People optimize the number and the measure stops meaning anything (Goodhart's law, Beck and Orosz, Software Engineering at Google chapter 7).
- Measurement: vanity metrics and dashboards that nobody acts on. Each department builds its own private reality from the same numbers (Ries; Google's rule that measurement without a planned action is pointless).
- Measurement: setting DORA metrics or NPS as team targets and comparing teams, which DORA explicitly warns against.
- Configuration management: version control that holds only application code, while infrastructure, configuration, scripts and docs live elsewhere; late commits and long-lived branches that create merge conflicts (DORA).
- Configuration management: change control that is either absent (untraceable, unauditable changes) or far heavier than the risk (external approval boards that slow delivery without better stability).
- Configuration management: releases that cannot be rebuilt because tools, build instructions or dependencies were not under control; no SBOM or version description, so nobody knows what shipped.
- Documentation: unowned wikis and documentation graveyards with obsolete, duplicated, contradictory pages; documentation written once and never reviewed (Software Engineering at Google chapter 10).
- Documentation and knowledge: rumour-driven development and information islands; a bus factor of one; work hidden until it is perfect (Spotify; Software Engineering at Google chapters 2 and 3).
- Documentation and operations: playbooks that bloat until nobody reads them, or no playbooks at all; on-call overload from noisy alerts that leaves no engineering time (SRE book and workbook).
- Knowledge management: onboarding by trial by fire; no checklist, mentor or canonical starting point (SRE book).
- Decision management: decisions without recorded rationale, which leads to blind acceptance or reckless reversal by later teams (Nygard).
- Risk management: a risk register filled in at kickoff and never revisited; risks that are uncertainties nobody owns (SWEBOK, NASA).
- Quality: quality assurance equated with testing; process conformance and early work products never assessed; no SQA independence where integrity levels require it (SWEBOK, IEEE 730).
- Quality and process improvement: process theatre, where the organization maintains maturity appraisals, ISO certificates or SCM plans for the auditor while the actual work bypasses them. SWEBOK warns to focus surveillance on insight, not on the measurements themselves.
- Process improvement: retrospectives without tracked actions, or blame-oriented postmortems that teach people to hide failures (Scrum Guide, SRE postmortem culture, Westrum pathological culture).
- Process improvement: over-documentation of plans in adaptive projects while monitoring and control get too little investment, or the reverse in predictive projects (SWEBOK Management knowledge area 2.7).
- People: teams organized by activity (front end, back end, QA) that require handoffs, frequent reshuffling of teams, and unbounded cognitive load (Fowler on Conway's law, Team Topologies).
- Infrastructure and platform: platforms that are mandated, relabelled centralized infrastructure with ticket queues (backlog coupling), or platforms that reduce developer independence and stability (Bottcher, DORA 2024).
- Portfolio: unstable priorities from the portfolio level; DORA 2024 finds that this harms productivity and raises burnout even with strong leaders and good documentation.
- Acquisition and supply: vendor lock-in, automatic contract extensions, contractors who leave with the knowledge, no exit strategy, unclear ownership of code and data (GOV.UK).
- Acquisition and supply: unvetted dependencies such as typosquatted or abandoned packages, unclear licenses, hype-driven adoption; unfiltered access to package repositories as an attack surface (OpenSSF, SWEBOK).
- Professional practice and ethics: concealment of inadequate work, falsified data, certification of unacceptable products, dark patterns, ignored privacy and IP obligations (SWEBOK Professional Practice, ACM/IEEE-CS code).

### Tailoring by project size

Some practices are essential at every scale:

- Keep everything needed to rebuild and understand the system in version control.
- Have one entry point document (README) that says what the system is, why, how to start, where to get help and who maintains it.
- Record non-obvious decisions.
- Keep a short list of known risks.
- Know what you depend on and under which license.
- Have some feedback loop that turns failures into changes.
- Act ethically and lawfully.

Optional at every scale, unless a customer, regulator or contract demands it: formal certification, maturity levels, independent audits, and written plans for their own sake. The three scales below add to the essentials.

- Solo developer on a small repository. You are the change authority, the CCB and the SQA function, which SWEBOK explicitly allows. Use git with meaningful commits, tags as baselines and a protected main branch; let CI rebuild and test on every push so that releases are reproducible. Add LICENSE and README and, if the repository is public, CONTRIBUTING and CODE_OF_CONDUCT (GitHub Open Source Guides). Keep a docs folder with a few ADRs and one or two how-to guides; follow Diátaxis loosely instead of a documentation site. Keep a TODO or issues list that doubles as risk register and improvement backlog; write a one-paragraph postmortem when something breaks. Vet dependencies with the OpenSSF checklist before you add them. Measure only what changes a decision (for example test status, deploy frequency, time to restore). Skip CM plans, QMS documents, portfolio processes and appraisals. Follow the code of ethics and the law on IP, privacy and licenses.
- Small product team (roughly three to ten people, one or a few services). Agree a branching and merging strategy, and make pull-request review on a protected branch the change control. Link changes to issues and write release notes. Define roles: a single product owner or manager, a tech lead who owns the ADRs, and a person accountable for quality and the Definition of Done. Set up an on-call rotation with runbooks. Treat docs as code with owners and freshness dates; keep a lightweight handbook and an onboarding checklist with a buddy. Hold a retrospective each iteration and a blameless postmortem per significant incident, and track the actions. Review the risk register during planning. Measure the DORA keys per service plus a short periodic developer survey (SPACE or DevEx style), never per person. Keep governance light: decisions at the right level, trust and verify, no steering committee heavier than the team. Consume a managed platform or paved road instead of a platform of your own. Evaluate open-source and SaaS dependencies before adoption. With contractors, plan knowledge transfer and own the code and data.
- Large or regulated organization (many teams, contracts, safety or compliance requirements). Add a formal SCM plan per project or product line in the style of IEEE 828, and a CCB with authority levels and an emergency path. Add status accounting that produces compliance evidence, functional and physical configuration audits before product baselines, and SBOMs for every release. Run an independent SQA function per IEEE 730 with a QMS (ISO 9001 with the ISO/IEC/IEEE 90003 interpretation) where customers or regulators require it. Use CMMI or ISO/IEC 330xx assessments when contracts demand them, and keep them tied to real improvement. Manage the portfolio explicitly (strategy, funding, guardrails, stable priorities) and run governance per ISO/IEC 38500 or COBIT 2019, right-sized with design factors. Design teams with Team Topologies: stream-aligned teams with bounded cognitive load, a platform team that runs the internal developer platform as a product with golden paths, and enabling teams for capability gaps. Run a measurement program (commit, plan, perform, evaluate) that reports aggregates and avoids individual scores. Establish an OSPO or equivalent for open-source consumption and contribution policy, procurement with break clauses and exit strategies, contractor access control and knowledge transfer. Structure onboarding with checklists, mentors, curated postmortems and shadowing. Apply professional licensing, privacy, export and data-retention rules where they exist, and keep records for the product life or the regulated retention period.
