## 16. Security, privacy and compliance across the life cycle

Security, privacy and compliance form one cross-cutting concern that runs from concept (section 3) to retirement (section 14). The discipline exists because software fails in the hands of attackers, not only in the hands of users. It answers four questions for every project: what can go wrong, what the law and the customer require, what the team will do about it, and how the team proves it. SWEBOK v4 states the core belief: it is much better to design security into software than to patch it in later. NIST SSDF gives the same aim – fewer vulnerabilities in released software, less impact from the ones that remain, and no repeats. Privacy and compliance extend the question from "can an attacker break it?" to "does it respect people, licenses, accessibility and the regulator?", so the intended result is a system that is secure by design, secure by default, lawful to ship, and backed by evidence. The discipline has many names: secure SDLC (SSDLC), Security Development Lifecycle (SDL), Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF, NIST SP 800-218), DevSecOps or shift-left security, software assurance, application security (AppSec) and product security, software security (SWEBOK v4 Knowledge Area 13), security engineering and secure by design, privacy engineering (privacy by design, data protection by design and by default), governance, risk and compliance (GRC) for software, and software supply-chain security.

### Frameworks

Five frameworks define the field. **NIST SP 800-218, the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) v1.1** (February 2022), is a list of high-level outcomes in four practice groups: Prepare the Organization (PO.1 to PO.5), Protect the Software (PS.1 to PS.3), Produce Well-Secured Software (PW.1 to PW.9) and Respond to Vulnerabilities (RV.1 to RV.3). It does not prescribe an implementation and integrates into any SDLC. It maps each practice to BSIMM, SAMM, ISO/IEC 27034 and US Executive Order 14028. NIST also published SP 800-218A for generative AI, and an initial public draft of SSDF v1.2 on 17 December 2025. **The Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle (SDL)** is 20 years old and is now Microsoft's DevSecOps approach. Its ten practices cover standards and metrics, proven security features, threat modeling and design review, cryptography and identity standards, the supply chain and the engineering environment, security tests, monitoring and response, and training. Microsoft states that they apply to waterfall and to DevOps and CI/CD alike. **OWASP SAMM** (version 2.0) is a prescriptive maturity model: five business functions (Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification, Operations), fifteen practices, two streams per practice and three maturity levels. It offers assessments and roadmaps and explicitly refuses a one-size-fits-all approach. **BSIMM** is descriptive. BSIMM16 (January 2026) reports the 128 activities that 111 organizations actually do, in four domains and twelve practices, and tracks trends such as just-in-time training and SBOM growth. **ISO/IEC 27034** is the international standard for application security, with an organization-level normative framework and application security controls; SSDF maps to it. Related guides describe the same practices: SAFECode's Fundamental Practices (third edition, 2018), the SWEBOK v4 Software Security knowledge area, the NCSC eight principles for secure development and deployment, and the OpenSSF guides (Concise Guide, Best Practices Badge, Scorecard, Baseline).

The frameworks relate as layers. SSDF is the outcome list that regulators and customers reference. SDL and SAFECode are practice sets that say how. SAMM says what an organization should do and at which maturity, and BSIMM says what peers do. ISO/IEC 27034 gives the certifiable structure. The practical approach is to pick one as the internal language and map the others to it for customers and regulators (see the contested points below).

Every framework starts the program with three standing activities. First, establish the program, policy, roles and criteria (SSDF PO.1, PO.2, PO.4; SDL practice 1; SAMM Governance). This defines who owns security, the risk tolerance, a written application security policy, a security lead and champions, the security requirements and standards, and the severity criteria, remediation deadlines and checks that a release must pass. The result is a policy, a roles matrix and release criteria that every later activity references. Second, train and build awareness (SDL practice 10; SAMM Education & Guidance; OWASP Security Champions Guidebook; NCSC: keep your security knowledge sharp; PCI DSS 6.2 requires secure coding training). Give everyone who builds software security awareness training, give role- and technology-specific guidance, and embed a security champion in each team as the local contact and advocate. BSIMM16 reports a trend to just-in-time learning tied to real findings. Third, measure and improve. Define a few metrics that show whether the program works, set targets, and benchmark against SAMM maturity levels or BSIMM observations. Analyze the root causes of escaped vulnerabilities and incidents (SSDF RV.3; SAFECode SDL feedback), and update requirements, standards and training. SAMM Strategy & Metrics sums it up: to measure is to know.

### Security work by phase

The shape of the work follows the life cycle model (see section 2). In a waterfall or V-model project it appears as gates: security requirements in the requirements phase, a threat model and design review at design, secure coding and static analysis at construction, security tests and a penetration test before release, a release readiness check, and vulnerability response in maintenance. In iterative and agile work the same activities shrink to the size of a sprint. Abuse cases become acceptance criteria, the team updates the threat model per epic or significant change, and the definition of done includes passed security checks. In DevOps and continuous delivery the checks live in the pipeline – secret scanning, SAST, SCA, IaC scanning, DAST on a staging build, signed artifacts with provenance – and operations adds monitoring, incident response and continuous vulnerability management. The work starts in concept and feasibility (risk profile, regulatory scope) and ends only at decommissioning (data deletion, end of security support). The OWASP Threat Modeling Manifesto calls it a journey of understanding, NIST SP 800-61r3 treats incident response and lessons learned as continuous, and supply-chain and privacy obligations (EU CRA, GDPR) last for the whole support period.

The inputs come from the phases before each activity:

- the business context and risk appetite (SAMM Strategy & Metrics level 1: identify drivers related to risk tolerance);
- existing organizational policies, security requirements and coding standards (SSDF PO.1 expects requirements from internal and external sources);
- the regulatory and contractual scope – jurisdictions, personal data, payment data, health data, AI use, public-sector or product-safety status (GDPR, PCI DSS, HIPAA, EU CRA, EU AI Act, accessibility law, customer security questionnaires);
- the accessibility obligations and target conformance level (WCAG 2.2 AA, EN 301 549, Section 508, the ADA rule);
- the system model – architecture diagrams, data flow diagrams, trust boundaries, entry points and assets;
- the data inventory – what personal data the system collects, why, where it flows and how long it stays (GDPR Article 30 records, DPIAs and retention need it);
- dependency manifests and lock files, build and deployment pipeline definitions, and infrastructure as code;
- the identity and access model – who can push, merge, release, deploy and read secrets;
- threat intelligence and known-weakness lists – OWASP Top 10, CWE Top 25, CISA KEV, EPSS, past incidents and previous penetration-test findings;
- supplier and open-source component information – licenses, maintenance status and vendor SBOMs (OWASP Component Analysis recommends that you require them);
- existing vulnerability reports, security advisories and open scanner findings.

| Phase | Security work | Privacy work | Compliance work |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concept (section 3) | Identify risk drivers and risk tolerance; build the application risk profile (SAMM Threat Assessment); choose the target assurance level (ASVS level, OpenSSF Baseline level) | Find out whether the product processes personal data, and for which purposes; start the data inventory | Build the obligations register: GDPR, PCI DSS, HIPAA, EU CRA, EU AI Act, accessibility law, contracts and customer questionnaires |
| Planning (section 4) | Assign the security lead and champions; budget the threat model, tools, penetration test and remediation time; set severity criteria and remediation deadlines | Plan the DPIA when the processing is high risk; name the data protection contact | Decide which audits and attestations the product needs (SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS, CE marking, SSDF self-attestation); plan evidence collection |
| Requirements (section 5) | Write testable security requirements from ASVS; write and rate abuse cases per feature; turn countermeasures into acceptance criteria | Specify the lawful basis, data minimisation, retention and data subject rights (GDPR Articles 5 and 25) | Specify the WCAG target, the license policy and the regulatory requirements; trace each to features and tests |
| Architecture (section 6) | Threat model with data flow diagrams and trust boundaries (STRIDE, PASTA, attack trees); apply the design principles and zero trust; standardise cryptography, identity and logging; hold the design review | Privacy threat model (LINDDUN); pseudonymisation and encryption; data flows and storage locations | Document security decisions as audit evidence; design logging, documentation and human oversight for high-risk AI systems; settle data residency |
| Design (section 7) | Review component, API and data designs against the threat model; specify secure defaults, access control and error handling; update the threat model | Design consent, deletion, export and retention functions; keep personal data out of logs | Design the user interface against WCAG 2.2 AA; review the license of each planned component |
| Implementation (section 8) | Code to the standard (OWASP Top 10, CWE Top 25, Proactive Controls); prefer memory-safe languages; vet dependencies; keep secrets out of code; review every change before merge | Implement minimisation, pseudonymisation and retention rules as specified | Add SPDX license headers; keep the license inventory current; build accessible components |
| Testing (section 9) | SAST, DAST, IAST, fuzzing and abuse-case tests; penetration test with the OWASP WSTG before go-live and after major change; retest fixes | Test deletion, export, retention and access rights; verify that logs hold no personal data | Accessibility audit with automated, manual and assistive-technology tests; license scan; control tests for auditors |
| Integration and CI (section 10) | Secret scanning with push protection; SAST, SCA, IaC and container scans; hardened build flags; pinned actions and read-only tokens; isolated builds | Use synthetic test data, not real personal data | Collect evidence from the pipeline (review logs, scan results); enforce the license policy and the blocking thresholds |
| Release and deployment (section 11) | Check the release criteria; sign artifacts; generate provenance (SLSA) and an SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX); ship secure default configuration and hardening guidance; archive the release | Sign off the DPIA before processing starts; publish the privacy notice | Publish the SBOM, NOTICE files, accessibility statement and attestations (SSDF under EO 14028, CE marking under the CRA) |
| Operations (section 12) | Monitor; run incident response (NIST SP 800-61r3); manage and patch vulnerabilities by risk; keep the disclosure channel live | Notify breaches within 72 hours (GDPR Article 33); answer data subject requests; enforce retention | Run audits (SOC 2 Type 2, ISO/IEC 27001 surveillance, PCI DSS); report actively exploited vulnerabilities under the CRA; keep records current |
| Maintenance (section 13) | Update dependencies; publish advisories and CVEs; analyze root causes; update the threat model per significant change; retest after major change | Re-assess the DPIA and the records of processing on change | Keep evidence fresh; track license changes in dependencies; re-audit accessibility after UI change; meet support-period duties under the CRA |
| Retirement (section 14) | Announce the end of security support; revoke keys and credentials; publish final advisories; archive sources and releases | Delete or return personal data; confirm the deletion; end retention | Keep the records the law requires; meet license obligations for archived distributions; document disposal as evidence |

The outputs accumulate across the phases:

- Governance: the security policy, roles matrix and release criteria (SSDF PO.1, PO.2, PO.4); the application risk profile; the register of applicable laws, standards and contracts; training records and a list of security champions; a metrics dashboard with targets and the program change backlog.
- Design: security and privacy requirements and abuse cases, traceable to features and tests at a chosen ASVS level; the threat model (data flow diagrams with trust boundaries, threat list, mitigations, accepted risks, updated per significant change); a design review record with documented security decisions and the cryptography and identity standards.
- Build: the dependency inventory or SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX), the dependency policy and the automated update stream; reviewed code that conforms to the coding standard and merges through protected branches; a secrets inventory in a secrets manager, with secret scanning, push protection and MFA enforced; pipeline scan results (SAST, SCA, secrets, IaC, DAST, fuzzing) with triage decisions and a trend; a penetration test report, retest results and risk-acceptance decisions; signed release artifacts with build provenance at a stated SLSA level; archived releases; secure default configuration and hardening documentation.
- Operation: the vulnerability backlog with severities, remediation deadlines and root-cause actions; SECURITY.md, security.txt, the disclosure policy, security advisories and CVE records; the incident response plan, incident records, regulatory notifications and post-incident improvement actions.
- Privacy, licensing, accessibility and compliance: the data inventory, DPIAs, retention schedule, privacy controls and GDPR accountability records; the license inventory, NOTICE and attribution files, license policy and REUSE-compliant headers; accessibility audit results, fixes and an accessibility statement or conformance report; control mappings, an evidence repository, audit reports and attestations (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, SSDF self-attestation, CE marking).
- Exit criteria, per release and not per project: release criteria met; no open vulnerability above the agreed threshold (for example nothing medium-or-higher known for more than 60 days – OpenSSF Badge); DPIA signed off before processing starts; license and accessibility checks passed; disclosure channel live.

Many roles share the work. The product owner or business owner sets the risk tolerance, accepts residual risk and prioritises security work in the backlog. The security lead or application security engineer owns standards, threat modeling support, tool configuration, triage and penetration test coordination. A security champion – a developer in each team – promotes practices, does first-line triage and liaises with the security team (SAMM Education & Guidance level 1). Developers write secure code, fix findings, review each other's changes and maintain threat models. Architects apply the design principles, run design reviews and own cryptography and identity decisions. Testers and QA turn abuse cases into tests, run DAST and accessibility tests and verify fixes.

DevOps, platform and SRE engineers secure pipelines, secrets, signing, provenance, runtime monitoring and patching. The release manager enforces release criteria, SBOM and signing, and archives releases. The data protection officer or privacy engineer owns the data inventory, DPIAs, retention and breach notification. Legal and the open source program office (OSPO) own license policy, notices, CLAs or DCO and supplier contracts. The accessibility specialist runs WCAG audits and assistive technology tests and writes the accessibility statement. Compliance, GRC and internal audit do control mapping, evidence collection and audit liaison. The incident response team (CSIRT) and the product security incident response team (PSIRT) handle incidents, vulnerability intake and coordinated disclosure. External parties complete the picture: penetration testers, auditors (a CPA for SOC 2, a certification body for ISO 27001, a QSA for PCI DSS), security researchers and finders, coordinators (CERT/CC), CNAs and suppliers.

### Threat modeling

Threat modeling analyzes a representation of the system to find what can go wrong. The Threat Modeling Manifesto frames it as four questions: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good enough job. The common method draws data flow diagrams with trust boundaries, entry points and assets (OWASP Threat Modeling Process). It then lists threats per element with STRIDE – spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege (Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool) – and ranks them. For each threat the team chooses a response: mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept. Alternatives are PASTA (a seven-stage risk-centric process), attack trees, and LINDDUN for privacy threats; the OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet also names OCTAVE and VAST.

Teams model early, repeat it for each significant change, and keep the model alive instead of a one-time document. The Manifesto values a culture of finding and fixing design issues over checkbox compliance. It names four anti-patterns: the hero threat modeler, admiration for the problem, overfocus on details, and the search for a perfect representation. The outputs are a threat list, mitigations that become requirements and tests, and a record of accepted risk. Abuse cases complement the model at feature level. For each feature the team describes how an attacker could misuse it, rates it (the OWASP Abuse Case Cheat Sheet uses CVSS in a workshop format), and decides which countermeasures become acceptance criteria (see section 5).

### Secure design and coding

Security requirements come first. The team translates business objectives, threats and regulations into testable requirements (SSDF PO.1 and PW.1; SAMM Security Requirements, with a supplier security stream; SWEBOK 4.1). OWASP ASVS 5.0 (released 30 May 2025; seventeen chapters V1 to V17; Levels 1 to 3) is the requirement catalogue. Design applies the eight principles of Saltzer and Schroeder (1975): least privilege, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least common mechanism, economy of mechanism, and psychological acceptability. Modern guides add defense in depth (NIST glossary), secure defaults, and zero trust (NIST SP 800-207: no implicit trust based on network location). The team reviews the design against the requirements and the threat model before code exists (SSDF PW.2; SDL practice 3). It standardises cryptography, identity and access management, and logging (SDL practice 4; SAFECode design practices). The OWASP Secure Product Design Cheat Sheet and Google's Building Secure and Reliable Systems (design for least privilege, understandability, resilience and recovery) give the detail. The output is an approved design with documented security decisions (see sections 6 and 7).

Construction follows a coding standard that addresses the OWASP Top 10:2025, the CWE Top 25 and language-specific pitfalls. The 2025 CWE list leads with cross-site scripting, SQL injection, CSRF, missing authorization and out-of-bounds write. Developers apply the OWASP Top 10 Proactive Controls (2024, C1 to C10): access control, cryptography, input validation and exception handling, secure defaults, secure identities, logging and the others. They prefer memory-safe languages and frameworks that make the safe path the default. They reuse proven security features instead of custom cryptography, authentication or session handling (SDL practice 2; SSDF PW.4), and they handle errors and untrusted data safely (SSDF PW.5; SAFECode secure coding practices; Google chapter 12). Another person reviews every change before merge (SSDF PW.7; OpenSSF Scorecard Code-Review; SLSA Source Level 4). At release the software ships with secure settings by default, so that installation does not create a weak configuration (SSDF PW.9; Proactive Control C5). The team documents the security-relevant settings, disables unused features and provides hardening guidance (see section 8 for construction in general).

### Security testing and analysis

Automated tests run on every change: secret scanning, static application security testing (SAST), software composition analysis (SCA), infrastructure-as-code and container scans, dynamic testing (DAST) against a running build, interactive testing (IAST) where available, and fuzzing for parsers and memory-unsafe code (SSDF PW.7 and PW.8; OWASP DevSecOps Guideline; OpenSSF Best Practices Badge). OSS-Fuzz gives open-source projects continuous fuzzing. The compiler and build use hardening options (SSDF PW.6). The team defines which findings block a merge and who triages the rest. The output is scan results with triage decisions and a trend of open findings. SWEBOK v4 lists static analysis and dynamic tests as the core security tools; section 9 gives the general test process.

Manual work complements the tools. A qualified, authorised tester (NCSC CHECK or equivalent) tests the running system as an attacker, with the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide as the checklist, before go-live and after major change. NCSC treats a penetration test as a snapshot that validates the team's own process, not as the main way to find vulnerabilities. GOV.UK separates routine vulnerability scans from penetration tests and says who should test and when. Red teams extend this to people and operations. A vulnerability disclosure program comes first; a paid bug bounty comes only when triage and remediation are mature (OWASP Vulnerability Disclosure Cheat Sheet). The outputs are a findings report, a retest and risk-acceptance decisions.

### Supply chain security

Supply-chain failures are category A03 in the OWASP Top 10:2025, and the work has three parts. The first part is component management. Evaluate every dependency before adoption, and prefer well-maintained and well-secured components over custom code (SSDF PW.4; OpenSSF Concise Guide). Keep an inventory of components and their licenses; OWASP Component Analysis names the risks – known vulnerabilities, outdated, license, unmaintained. Set a policy on maximum component age, end-of-life components and allowed licenses. Use lock files, an automated update tool (Dependabot, Renovate) and SCA to find known vulnerabilities. The outputs are a dependency policy, an inventory or SBOM, and a stream of update pull requests.

The second part is secrets and engineering environments. Keep credentials out of source code and configuration. Store them in a secrets manager with least-privilege access, audit trails and rotation, and prefer short-lived credentials such as OIDC tokens (GitHub Actions OIDC, PyPI Trusted Publishers). Enable secret scanning with push protection, and rotate an exposed secret at once instead of removal from history only (OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet; GitHub docs). Harden developer endpoints and build and test environments, and require multi-factor authentication for everyone who can change code (SSDF PO.5; NCSC developers collection; OpenSSF Concise Guide; GitHub has required 2FA for contributors since 2023). The outputs are a secrets inventory and hardened environments.

The third part is build and release integrity. Protect code from unauthorised change and protect each release: branch protection, signed commits or two-party review, hosted builds that generate signed provenance, isolated build environments, and release artifacts signed with Sigstore (Cosign, Fulcio, Rekor, keyless signing) or similar (SSDF PS.1 to PS.3; SLSA Build Levels 1 to 3 and Source Levels 1 to 4; OpenSSF Scorecard Signed-Releases, Pinned-Dependencies and Token-Permissions). Pin third-party CI actions to commit SHAs, give workflow tokens read-only defaults, guard against script injection, and do not check out untrusted code in `pull_request_target` workflows (GitHub Actions hardening). Generate an SBOM in SPDX (ISO/IEC 5962:2021) or CycloneDX (ECMA-424, with VEX) for each release. SLSA v1.2 is the current version; it adds a Source track (version control, history and provenance, continuous technical controls, two-party review) to the Build track. The outputs are verifiable artifacts, provenance, SBOMs and a release archive (see sections 10 and 11).

### Vulnerability management and disclosure

Vulnerability management runs for the whole support period. The team finds and confirms vulnerabilities in its own code and its dependencies. It prioritises by severity and exploitability – CVSS v4.0 for severity, EPSS and CISA KEV for exploitation likelihood – and remediates within defined timelines. It analyzes root causes so that the class of bug does not return (SSDF RV.1 to RV.3). NIST SP 800-40r4 treats patching as preventive maintenance, and the OWASP Vulnerability Management Guide describes the detection, reporting and remediation cycle. The OpenSSF Badge sets a concrete bar: no medium-or-higher vulnerability publicly known for more than 60 days. The outputs are a tracked vulnerability backlog, fixes and root-cause actions (see section 13).

Coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) handles reports from outside. The project publishes how to report: SECURITY.md in the repository, a security.txt file at /.well-known/ per RFC 9116 with Contact and Expires fields, and private vulnerability reporting on GitHub. It acknowledges reports quickly (Badge: within 14 days), coordinates a fix and an embargo with the reporter, requests a CVE ID from a CNA such as GitHub, and publishes an advisory with affected and fixed versions and credit. The CERT Guide to CVD names six phases adapted from ISO/IEC 30111 – discovery, reporting, validation and prioritisation, remediation, public awareness, deployment – and four disclosure choices: no, private, limited and full disclosure. NVD enriches CVE records with CVSS, CWE and CPE data, and GitHub advisories feed the Advisory Database and Dependabot alerts. Under the EU CRA, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities to the authorities from 11 September 2026. The outputs are a disclosure policy, advisories and CVE records.

Incident response prepares before incidents: roles, contact lists, playbooks, logs that support investigation, and tested recovery. NIST SP 800-61r3 (April 2025) maps incident response to the CSF 2.0 functions Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, with lessons learned that feed Improvement. HIPAA 45 CFR 164.308 requires incident procedures and contingency plans. The team detects, contains, eradicates and recovers, then notifies. GDPR Article 33 requires notice to the supervisory authority within 72 hours after the controller becomes aware of a personal data breach, unless risk is unlikely. Blameless post-incident reviews (GOV.UK) feed changes back into requirements, tests and training. The outputs are incident records, notifications and improvement actions (see section 12).

### Privacy and data protection

Privacy engineering builds the GDPR Article 5 principles into the system: lawful, fair and transparent processing, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, and accountability. Article 25 requires data protection by design and by default, so that the system processes only the data necessary for each purpose. EDPB Guidelines 4/2019 (adopted October 2020) give design elements per principle. Article 35 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before high-risk processing: a systematic description, an assessment of necessity and proportionality, the risks, and the measures. Article 32 names pseudonymisation and encryption among the security measures. Retention schedules with automated deletion and privacy threat modeling with LINDDUN (seven privacy threat types; GO, PRO and MAESTRO variants; a complement to STRIDE) complete the toolset. NISTIR 8062 adds the engineering objectives predictability, manageability and disassociability, and the NIST Privacy Framework (version 1.0, 2020; 1.1 in development) gives a program structure. The outputs are a data inventory, DPIAs, retention rules, privacy controls and accountability records. The operational reason is simple: data you do not hold cannot leak.

### Licensing and open-source compliance

A repository without a license gives users no permission, because default copyright applies (choosealicense.com). The first step is therefore a license file (MIT, Apache-2.0, GPL-3.0 or another). The team records the license of every component with SPDX identifiers and expressions, for example Apache-2.0, GPL-3.0-or-later or MIT OR Apache-2.0; the SPDX License List (version 3.28.0) supports AND, OR and WITH. It checks compatibility before it combines code: the GNU GPL FAQ explains compatibility, Apache-2.0 is compatible with GPLv3 in one direction but not with GPLv2, and a combination must be distributable under the GPL version involved. It produces the notices and source offers that the licenses demand. REUSE file headers, a LICENSES directory and REUSE.toml make licensing machine-readable. A policy of allowed and denied licenses, reviewed by legal, governs new components (OWASP Component Analysis). Large organizations formalise this as an OpenChain program – ISO/IEC 5230 for license compliance and ISO/IEC 18974 for security assurance. The outputs are a license inventory, NOTICE files and compliant distributions.

### Accessibility obligations

Teams design and test user interfaces against WCAG 2.2 Level AA (October 2023; also ISO/IEC 40500:2025). Its four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. Automated checks find only part of the success criteria, so manual tests and tests with assistive technology complete the audit. The team publishes an accessibility statement where the law requires it. Four legal drivers apply. The European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882) applies to covered products and services from 28 June 2025, with transitional periods, a microenterprise exemption and a presumption of conformity through harmonised standards such as EN 301 549 (aligned with WCAG 2.1). The 2024 ADA Title II rule requires WCAG 2.1 AA for US state and local government web content and apps, with exceptions and deadlines now in April 2027 and April 2028. Section 508 (2018 refresh) requires WCAG 2.0 AA for US federal ICT. UK public sector bodies must meet WCAG 2.2 AA and publish an accessibility statement, with enforcement. The outputs are audit results, fixes and a conformance statement. Accessibility is a design input in section 7, not a pre-launch audit.

### Regulation and assurance overview

Compliance starts with classification. The team builds an application risk profile (SAMM Threat Assessment stream A) and an obligations register. Does the product process personal data, payment card data or health data? Does it operate in a high-risk AI use case? Is it a product with digital elements under the EU CRA? Is it public-facing and subject to accessibility law? The answers decide the target assurance level (ASVS Level 1, 2 or 3; OpenSSF Baseline Level 1, 2 or 3) and the audits and reports the product will need. The main regimes are these:

- SOC 2 – CPA examinations against five trust services criteria: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy.
- ISO/IEC 27001:2022 – a certifiable management system with 93 Annex A controls in organizational, people, physical and technological themes, certified in staged audits with surveillance.
- PCI DSS – Requirement 6 for secure development (6.2 requires training and review), with self-assessment questionnaires, QSAs, Reports on Compliance and ASV scans.
- HIPAA – administrative, physical and technical safeguards (45 CFR Part 164 Subpart C) with required and addressable specifications, risk analysis, training, incident procedures and contingency plans.
- The EU AI Act – risk tiers, obligations for high-risk systems (risk management, data governance, logging, documentation, human oversight, robustness and cybersecurity) and rules for general-purpose AI.
- The EU Cyber Resilience Act – manufacturer obligations for products with digital elements, in force since 10 December 2024, reporting duties from 11 September 2026, full application from 11 December 2027, and CE marking.
- US Executive Order 14028 – SSDF, SBOMs, critical software and self-attestation for suppliers to the federal government.
- GDPR and the accessibility laws above.

The team maps the controls it operates to these regimes. It collects evidence automatically from the pipeline – review logs, scan results, tickets, signed provenance – so that audits and attestations do not require manual reconstruction. The outputs are control mappings, an evidence repository, audit reports and attestations. NCSC and GOV.UK stress that security must be proportionate to risk. NIST CSF 2.0 (2024) gives the Govern-to-Recover structure that SP 800-61r3 reuses (see section 15 for the supporting processes that hold this evidence).

### Practices with consensus

- **Build security in across the whole life cycle instead of a test at the end** – design flaws are cheaper to fix before code exists; a late penetration test finds only what is left. Every framework orders its practices by life cycle stage for this reason. Evidence: SWEBOK v4 Software Security KA; NIST SP 800-218 SSDF; Microsoft SDL; SAFECode Fundamental Practices; NCSC developers collection; OWASP SAMM.
- **Threat model early and keep it current, with a simple shared method (four questions, DFD plus STRIDE or similar)** – it finds design-level issues that scanners cannot, and it produces mitigations that become requirements and tests. Evidence: Threat Modeling Manifesto; OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet and Threat Modeling Process; Microsoft SDL practice 3; NIST SSDF PW.1; OWASP SAMM Threat Assessment.
- **Apply least privilege, defense in depth, fail-safe and secure defaults, complete mediation and open design** – these principles limit the blast radius and make the safe path the default. They have held since 1975 and appear in every modern guide. Evidence: Saltzer and Schroeder 1975; NIST glossary (defense in depth); NIST SP 800-207 (zero trust); OWASP Secure Product Design Cheat Sheet; OWASP Proactive Controls C5; NIST SSDF PW.9; Google Building Secure and Reliable Systems.
- **Reuse proven security features, frameworks and libraries; do not write your own cryptography or authentication** – vetted components have been reviewed and attacked; custom security code usually has not. Evidence: Microsoft SDL practice 2; NIST SSDF PW.4; OWASP Proactive Controls C2, C6, C7; OpenSSF Concise Guide.
- **Keep dependencies current and monitored with an automated update tool plus software composition analysis** – known vulnerabilities in components are a top cause of breaches; supply-chain failures are A03 in the OWASP Top 10:2025. Evidence: OpenSSF Concise Guide; OpenSSF Scorecard Dependency-Update-Tool and Vulnerabilities checks; GitHub securing-your-repository docs; OWASP Component Analysis; OWASP Top 10:2025.
- **Never store secrets in repositories; use secret scanning with push protection, a secrets manager, least-privilege access, rotation and short-lived credentials** – leaked credentials are directly exploitable and travel with every clone; rotation, not history rewriting, is the fix. Evidence: OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet; GitHub secret scanning docs; OpenSSF Concise Guide; OpenSSF Baseline Level 1; PyPI Trusted Publishers; GitHub Actions hardening (OIDC).
- **Require multi-factor authentication for everyone who can change code or release** – account takeover of a maintainer compromises every downstream user. Evidence: OpenSSF Concise Guide (first recommendation); GitHub 2FA requirement for contributors (2023); OpenSSF Baseline Level 1; NIST SSDF PO.5.
- **Review every change before merge and protect the main branch** – a second person catches mistakes and malicious changes; protected branches prevent history rewrites and direct pushes. Evidence: OpenSSF Concise Guide; OpenSSF Scorecard Code-Review and Branch-Protection; SLSA Source Levels 2 to 4; OpenSSF Baseline; PCI DSS Requirement 6.2; NIST SSDF PW.7.
- **Automate security tests in CI with a combination of tools (secret scanning, SAST, SCA, and DAST or fuzzing where applicable)** – automation finds common weaknesses on every change at low marginal cost and gives auditable evidence; no single tool finds everything. Evidence: NIST SSDF PW.7 and PW.8; OWASP DevSecOps Guideline; OpenSSF Concise Guide; OpenSSF Best Practices Badge (static and dynamic analysis criteria); SWEBOK v4 (static analysis and dynamic testing); OSS-Fuzz.
- **Sign releases, generate build provenance and publish an SBOM** – consumers must be able to verify that an artifact came from the official source and know what is inside it; regulators now require it. Evidence: NIST SSDF PS.2; SLSA Build track; Sigstore; OpenSSF Scorecard Signed-Releases; OpenSSF Concise Guide; US EO 14028 (NIST); EU Cyber Resilience Act; OpenSSF Baseline Levels 2 and 3; SPDX; CycloneDX.
- **Publish a vulnerability disclosure policy and contact (SECURITY.md, security.txt, private reporting) and respond within a stated time** – researchers need a safe, findable channel; without one, reports go public or nowhere. Evidence: RFC 9116; GitHub security policy and private vulnerability reporting docs; OpenSSF Concise Guide; OpenSSF Best Practices Badge (respond within 14 days); OWASP Vulnerability Disclosure Cheat Sheet; NIST SSDF RV.1.3; CERT Guide to CVD.
- **Fix vulnerabilities through coordinated disclosure, publish advisories with fixed versions, and assign CVE IDs** – users can only protect themselves if they learn about the flaw and the fix together; advisories feed automated alerts. Evidence: CERT Guide to CVD; OWASP Vulnerability Disclosure Cheat Sheet; GitHub repository security advisories (GitHub as CNA); NVD CVE process; OpenSSF Concise Guide.
- **Prioritise vulnerabilities by risk, not by CVSS base score alone, and track time to remediate** – CVSS measures severity, not risk; exploitation likelihood (EPSS, KEV) and context decide urgency. Evidence: FIRST CVSS v4.0 specification (severity, not risk); FIRST EPSS; NIST SP 800-40r4; OWASP Vulnerability Management Guide; NIST SSDF RV.2.
- **Analyze root causes of vulnerabilities and incidents and feed changes back into requirements, tools and training** – one fix does not prevent the class; continuous improvement is how the vulnerability rate falls. Evidence: NIST SSDF RV.3; SAFECode (Secure Development Lifecycle Feedback); NIST SP 800-61r3 (lessons learned into Improvement); NCSC principle 8 (plan for security flaws).
- **Design for data protection by design and by default, minimise data, limit retention, and run a DPIA before high-risk processing** – these are legal obligations in the EU, and they reduce breach impact everywhere because data you do not hold cannot leak. Evidence: GDPR Articles 5, 25, 32, 35; EDPB Guidelines 4/2019; NISTIR 8062; LINDDUN.
- **Prepare and test incident response, including regulatory notification timelines** – incidents are frequent and long; preparation decides detection and containment time, and the law sets deadlines (GDPR 72 hours, CRA reporting from September 2026). Evidence: NIST SP 800-61r3; GDPR Article 33; EU Cyber Resilience Act; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.308; GOV.UK Service Manual (blameless postmortems).
- **Use WCAG 2.x Level AA as the accessibility target for user interfaces** – it is the common baseline that US, EU and UK law reference, and the W3C standard. Evidence: W3C WCAG overview; ADA Title II rule (WCAG 2.1 AA); Section 508 (WCAG 2.0 AA); GOV.UK (WCAG 2.2 AA); European Accessibility Act via harmonised standard EN 301 549.
- **Track component licenses with SPDX identifiers, check compatibility, and ship required notices** – license terms are legal obligations; incompatibility blocks distribution, and missing notices breach the license. Evidence: SPDX and SPDX License List; REUSE specification; OWASP Component Analysis; GNU GPL FAQ and Apache GPL compatibility page; choosealicense.com; OpenChain ISO/IEC 5230.
- **Train developers and appoint security champions** – people who do not know the pattern write most vulnerabilities; embedded champions scale scarce security staff. Evidence: Microsoft SDL practice 10; OWASP SAMM Education & Guidance; OWASP Security Champions Guidebook; NCSC principle 2; OpenSSF Best Practices Badge (secure-design knowledge criterion); PCI DSS 6.2.
- **Treat penetration tests as periodic validation of your own process, not as the primary way to find vulnerabilities** – a penetration test is a snapshot; gaps between tests leave unknown exposure, so continuous tests must come first. Evidence: NCSC penetration testing guidance; GOV.UK vulnerability and penetration testing; OWASP Vulnerability Disclosure Cheat Sheet (bug bounty only for mature programs).
- **Choose the assurance level by risk (ASVS level, SAMM target maturity, OpenSSF Baseline level) instead of everything everywhere** – frameworks explicitly refuse one-size-fits-all; proportionality keeps security sustainable. Evidence: OWASP ASVS 5.0 levels; OWASP SAMM about page; OpenSSF Baseline levels; NIST SSDF (integrates into any SDLC, does not prescribe implementation); GOV.UK (proportionate to risk).

### Contested points

- **Which threat modeling method, and how heavy** – STRIDE with data flow diagrams (Microsoft, OWASP) is simple and teachable. PASTA proponents (VerSprite) argue that checklist methods do not validate exploitability or tie threats to business impact, and propose a seven-stage risk-centric process. The Threat Modeling Manifesto sides with lightweight, continuous, team-owned modeling and warns against the hero threat modeler and the perfect representation. The choice depends on risk, team maturity and whether a business-level risk analysis is needed. Most teams start with STRIDE and add depth where risk justifies it.
- **Prescriptive versus descriptive maturity models, and framework proliferation** – OWASP SAMM is prescriptive (what you should do, three maturity levels). BSIMM is descriptive (what 111 firms actually do, 128 activities in BSIMM16). NIST SSDF is a high-level outcome list that maps to both, plus SDL, ISO/IEC 27034 and SAFECode. Organizations disagree on which to adopt as the backbone; the practical answer is to pick one as the internal language and map the others to it for customers and regulators.
- **Vulnerability prioritisation: CVSS, EPSS, KEV or internal risk** – FIRST itself says CVSS measures severity, not risk, and recommends CVSS together with EPSS and KEV. Many contracts, PCI DSS scans and SLAs are still written in CVSS terms, so teams must report in CVSS even when they prioritise by exploitation likelihood and exposure.
- **Disclosure deadlines and embargoes** – Google Project Zero uses a fixed 90 days, and CERT/CC historically used 45 days. The CERT Guide to CVD now says there is no single right answer, and that all embargoes are contingent on circumstances such as active exploitation or independent discovery. Full-disclosure advocates argue that users deserve immediate information; coordinated-disclosure advocates argue for fix first. A policy should be explicit and published, and it depends on fix complexity, the number of parties and vendor responsiveness.
- **Bug bounty versus vulnerability disclosure program** – OWASP recommends a bounty only for organizations with mature vulnerability management; critics point to triage noise and cost. The consensus is that every project needs a disclosure channel; bounties are optional and come later.
- **Pin dependencies versus update fast** – OpenSSF Scorecard and GitHub recommend pinning (lock files, actions pinned to commit SHAs) for reproducibility and tamper resistance; others warn that strict pinning delays security fixes. The working compromise is pinning plus an automated update bot; libraries often keep looser ranges than applications.
- **Block the pipeline on findings versus warn only** – OpenSSF Baseline Level 3 expects SAST and SCA findings to block changes; many teams find that a block on noisy tools causes alert fatigue and bypasses. The OWASP Vulnerability Management Guide warns that a working scanner is not the same as managed vulnerabilities. Teams tune thresholds per tool and per severity.
- **Memory-safe language mandates** – OpenSSF recommends memory-safe languages, and the CWE Top 25 2025 still lists out-of-bounds write, use after free and buffer overflow in the top 14. A rewrite of existing C and C++ is costly and slow, so positions range from new code only to incremental migration of attack-surface components.
- **Certifications and compliance as a proxy for security** – customers and regulators demand SOC 2 reports, ISO/IEC 27001 certificates and PCI DSS attestations. The Threat Modeling Manifesto values a culture of finding and fixing design issues over checkbox compliance, and NCSC and GOV.UK stress proportionate, risk-based security. Most practitioners treat certification as a floor and an evidence mechanism, not as the goal.
- **SBOM value today** – US EO 14028 and the EU CRA push SBOMs, and BSIMM16 reports growth driven by self-attestation requirements. Consumption tools and VEX (exploitability statements) are still maturing, so some producers see SBOMs as compliance output rather than as a security control. OWASP Component Analysis argues that the inventory itself is pivotal for risk identification.
- **Zero trust: architecture or slogan** – NIST SP 800-207 defines zero trust as an evolving set of paradigms with no implicit trust by network location; vendors use the term loosely. Teams should adopt the concrete tenets (authenticate and authorise every access, least privilege, assume breach) rather than the label.
- **Which WCAG version is the legal baseline** – WCAG 2.2 (2023) is the current W3C standard and the UK public-sector requirement. The US ADA Title II rule and EN 301 549 (used by the European Accessibility Act) still reference WCAG 2.1 AA, and Section 508 references WCAG 2.0 AA. Teams usually build to 2.2 AA and report against the version the jurisdiction names.
- **Regulatory timelines and scope are still moving** – the EU CRA applies fully from 11 December 2027, with reporting duties from 11 September 2026. The Commission's AI Act page (read August 2026) lists high-risk obligations from December 2027 and product-integrated systems from August 2028, later than the dates originally discussed. The ADA Title II deadlines were extended to April 2027 and April 2028. NIST SSDF v1.2 is in draft (initial public draft December 2025). Teams should check current dates rather than rely on secondary summaries.

### Metrics

A program needs a few metrics with targets, and each metric has a caveat.

- Open vulnerabilities by severity and age, and mean or median time to remediate. Caveat: the value depends on scanner coverage, and a team can game it when it closes or downgrades findings.
- Share of vulnerabilities fixed within the agreed deadline; the OpenSSF Badge bar is no medium-or-higher vulnerability publicly known for more than 60 days. Caveat: the severity is CVSS-based, not risk-based.
- Time to acknowledge and time to fix external vulnerability reports (the Badge expects acknowledgement within 14 days). Caveat: this measures the process, not product security.
- OpenSSF Scorecard score per check (0 to 10) and in aggregate. Caveat: it measures the presence of practices such as branch protection, pinned dependencies and signed releases, not the absence of vulnerabilities.
- SLSA Build and Source level reached per pipeline; percentage of releases signed and with provenance and SBOM. Caveat: a level is a floor, not a guarantee.
- ASVS requirement coverage at the chosen level (requirements verified versus total). Caveat: verification quality varies between self-assessment and independent test.
- SAMM maturity scores per practice (0 to 3) and BSIMM activity counts for benchmarks. Caveat: SAMM is self-assessed, BSIMM describes peers, and neither measures outcomes.
- Control coverage across repositories: percentage with MFA enforced, branch protection, secret scanning and push protection, SCA and SAST enabled, and a dependency update bot active. Caveat: enabled is not tuned.
- Dependency health: number of known-vulnerable or end-of-life components, median dependency age (OWASP suggests a three-year limit), percentage pinned. Caveat: counts differ across databases.
- Threat model coverage: percentage of epics or significant changes with an updated threat model; mitigations implemented versus identified. Caveat: a count of documents does not measure quality.
- Tests: SAST and DAST findings per release and the false-positive rate, fuzzing coverage and crash count, penetration test findings by severity and the retest closure rate. Caveat: tool-dependent and not comparable across products.
- Incident response: time to detect, time to contain, time to notify (GDPR 72 hours; CRA early warning, notification and final report deadlines), number of incidents, lessons-learned actions closed. Caveat: small samples and heavy tails.
- Privacy: DPIAs completed before processing started, records of processing kept current, retention rules enforced automatically, data subject request turnaround. Caveat: mostly qualitative.
- Licensing: percentage of components with an identified SPDX license; policy violations found before release. Caveat: detection depends on scanner accuracy for embedded or vendored code.
- Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA success criteria that pass in audits, open issues by level, accessibility statement up to date. Caveat: automated tools find only part of the criteria.
- Training and culture: training completion, champions per team, participation in reviews. Caveat: completion does not equal competence.
- Compliance: audit findings and control test failures per period, evidence freshness. Caveat: a clean audit proves control operation within scope, not security outcomes.

### Failure modes

- Security as a late gate: the first security activity is a penetration test days before launch, so design flaws surface when they are most expensive and the release slips or ships with accepted risk.
- Checkbox compliance without a culture of finding and fixing design issues (Threat Modeling Manifesto) – certificates exist, vulnerabilities remain.
- Threat modeling anti-patterns: the hero threat modeler, admiration for the problem, overfocus on details, and the search for a perfect representation, so models are never finished or never used.
- Generic security requirements ("the application must be secure") with no abuse cases, so nothing is testable and nothing is built.
- Tool sprawl and alert fatigue: many scanners, no triage ownership, thousands of unreviewed findings; a working scanner mistaken for vulnerability management (OWASP Vulnerability Management Guide).
- Secrets in repositories, long-lived tokens, and the belief that removal of a secret from history fixes the leak – GitHub and OWASP say rotate at once.
- Unpinned dependencies, CI actions referenced by mutable tags, write-by-default workflow tokens and `pull_request_target` checkouts of untrusted code, which open the build to supply-chain attack.
- Adoption of abandoned or end-of-life components with no update path, and third-party code treated with less scrutiny than in-house code (SAFECode).
- Custom cryptography, custom authentication or custom session handling instead of vetted frameworks.
- No disclosure channel, or an unresponsive one, so researchers publish without coordination or give up; advisories published without a fixed version, so users get an alert with nowhere to go (GitHub).
- Privacy as an afterthought: collect everything, keep it forever, run the DPIA after launch, no deletion capability.
- License contamination and missing notices: copyleft code combined with proprietary code without review, Apache-2.0 code under GPLv2, or a repository with no license at all.
- Accessibility retrofits: WCAG treated as a pre-launch audit instead of a design input, which leads to inaccessible components and legal exposure.
- Penetration test as the only assurance, on an annual cadence, which leaves months of unknown exposure (NCSC).
- No root-cause analysis: the same vulnerability class returns release after release (SSDF RV.3).
- Untested incident response: no contact list, no logs to investigate, notification deadlines discovered during the incident.
- Security team as a bottleneck with no champions, one-time training, and developers who do not know the common vulnerability patterns.
- Evidence reconstructed by hand before each audit instead of collected continuously from the pipeline.

### Tailoring by project size

Some practices are essential at every scale: multi-factor authentication for everyone who can push or release; no secrets in the repository; dependencies kept current with a lock file and an update bot; a LICENSE file; a way to report a vulnerability (SECURITY.md or private reporting); least privilege and secure defaults; a response to reported vulnerabilities that also fixes the root cause; and collection of only the personal data you need. The specific threat modeling method, IAST, fuzzing breadth, penetration test cadence, bounty and certification scope are optional and risk-scaled at every level.

**Solo developer on a small repository.** Essential: use the free platform features. Enable 2FA or passkeys, turn on secret scanning with push protection, Dependabot or Renovate, branch protection on the default branch, and CI with tests and one static analysis tool or linter. Pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs with read-only tokens, sign releases or use trusted publishing, add SECURITY.md with a contact and enable private vulnerability reporting, and add a LICENSE. Keep a short threat model in the docs if the project has users or handles data, and state the support policy for security fixes. Target OpenSSF Baseline Level 1, a passing OpenSSF Best Practices Badge and a rising Scorecard. Optional: SBOM and SLSA provenance (cheap on hosted CI), fuzzing for parsers, an ASVS Level 1 self-check, and WCAG basics for any UI.

**Small product team.** Essential: written security requirements at ASVS Level 2; a threat model per epic or significant change; mandatory code review; SAST plus SCA plus secret scanning that block on high severity; DAST against staging; a secrets manager with rotation; a penetration test before launch and after major changes; vulnerability deadlines by severity; an incident runbook with a contact list and the GDPR 72-hour rule; a data inventory with a retention schedule, and a DPIA when the team processes personal data at scale; a license allow-list with generated NOTICE files; a WCAG 2.2 AA audit and accessibility statement for public-facing products; one security champion; short role-based training; SBOM and signed releases per version; OpenSSF Baseline Level 2. Optional: start to collect audit evidence from the pipeline if customers will ask for SOC 2 or ISO 27001, and add a bug bounty after the disclosure process is mature.

**Large or regulated organization.** Essential: a formal program aligned to SSDF or SDL and measured with SAMM or BSIMM; published policies and standards; a security architecture review board and standardised, tooled threat modeling; ASVS Level 2 or 3 by risk; a PSIRT and a CSIRT, CNA status and a vulnerability disclosure program; SLSA Build Level 3 and Source Level 3 or 4, signing infrastructure, and SBOM with VEX; supplier security requirements in contracts; audit programs (SOC 2 Type 2, ISO/IEC 27001 certification with surveillance audits, PCI DSS Report on Compliance, HIPAA risk analysis); a data protection officer, DPIAs and records of processing; regulatory reporting under the CRA, GDPR and the AI Act for high-risk systems; an open source program office with OpenChain ISO/IEC 5230 conformance; an accessibility program against EN 301 549 or Section 508 with conformance reports; a training curriculum and a champions network; metrics dashboards with targets; OpenSSF Baseline Level 3 for open-source projects. Optional: a bug bounty and a red team once the disclosure program is mature, and the breadth of the certification scope.
